Low-cost LiDAR is sparse and noisy, causing perceptual aliasing and false correspondences; there is a need for initialization-free loop closure and global alignment that runs on resource-constrained edge platforms.

Method: 1) extract tree trunks as stable landmarks; 2) encode trunk topology with Delaunay triangulation for compact scene representation; 3) screen candidate submaps using edge-length and radius statistics; 4) perform edge-radius consistency verification and aggregate strong/weak vertex support to form weighted correspondences; 5) compute topology-derived reliability weights and feed into a decoupled robust pose estimator that estimates yaw, horizontal translation, and elevation translation under gravity alignment.

Result: Experiments on simulated and real forest datasets show DTIF achieves accurate registration with low computational overhead, achieving a favorable balance among robustness, efficiency, and deployability on resource-constrained edge platforms.

Conclusion: DTIF provides an effective, lightweight trunk-topology framework for reliable loop closure detection and global registration in GNSS-denied forest environments, balancing robustness, efficiency, and deployability.

Abstract: Accurate forest inventory and large-scale mapping are essential for ecosystem monitoring and sustainable forest management. Multiple low-cost edge platforms enable efficient large-area data acquisition, but merging independently constructed local maps in GNSS-denied understory environments still requires initialization-free loop closure detection and global registration. This task is challenging because low-cost LiDAR point clouds are sparse and noisy, while repetitive trunk layouts and the lack of distinctive geometric landmarks lead to severe perceptual aliasing and false correspondences. To address these issues, we propose DTIF (Delaunay Triangulation in Forests), a lightweight trunk-topology-based framework for forest loop closure detection and global registration. Tree trunks are first extracted as stable landmarks and encoded using a Delaunay topology for compact scene representation. Candidate submaps are then screened using edge-length and radius statistics, followed by edge--radius consistency verification and strong/weak vertex support aggregation to construct weighted vertex correspondences. Finally, topology-derived reliability weights are incorporated into a decoupled robust pose estimator that separately estimates yaw, horizontal translation, and elevation translation under gravity alignment. Experiments on simulated and real-world forest datasets demonstrate that DTIF achieves accurate registration with low computational overhead, providing a favorable balance among robustness, efficiency, and deployability on resource-constrained edge platforms.

</details>


### [53] [CRAG-MM-Diagnostics: Enabling Stage-Wise Analysis of Knowledge-Intensive VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21155)
*Hanseok Oh,Parishad BehnamGhader,Benno Krojer,Hyunji Lee,Paul Liang,Siva Reddy,Verna Dankers*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces CRAG-MM-Diagnostics, a stage-aware diagnostic benchmark for KI-VQA to isolate language grounding, object identification, and knowledge retrieval/reasoning; finds knowledge retrieval/reasoning as the main bottleneck and shows additional issues in grounding and object identification; proposes a grounded bimodal RAG pipeline that crops targets before image retrieval, improving GPT-5 and Qwen by 13.3 and 8.5 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KI-VQA benchmarks report only end-to-end accuracy, obscuring where failures occur. There is a need to dissect the entire KI-VQA pipeline (grounding, recognition, retrieval, reasoning) to guide targeted improvements and evaluation.

Method: Create CRAG-MM-Diagnostics with stage-wise annotations isolating (1) language-based grounding, (2) object identification, (3) knowledge retrieval and reasoning; evaluate fully parametric and retrieval-augmented VLMs; collect metadata (target ROIs, entity names, visual complexity); analyze failure modes; develop a grounded bimodal retrieval-augmented approach that first crops targets via visual grounding before image retrieval.

Result: Knowledge retrieval and reasoning emerge as the primary bottleneck; other components (object identification, embedding of textual cues by image retrievers) also show issues. Stage-aware evaluation exposes fundamental KI-VQA limits. The grounded bimodal RAG pipeline yields substantial gains: GPT-5 up 13.3 pp and Qwen up 8.5 pp.

Conclusion: Stage-aware evaluation is essential for diagnosing KI-VQA systems, and integrating a visual grounding crop step into the retrieval process can meaningfully boost performance, shaping future KI-VQA system design.

Abstract: Knowledge-Intensive Visual Question Answering (KI-VQA) benchmarks evaluate Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as multimodal knowledge assistants by requiring external information beyond a provided image to answer questions. KI-VQA involves multiple sub-problems -referring expression understanding, visual grounding, object recognition, knowledge retrieval, and reasoning-yet existing benchmarks typically report only end-task accuracy, obscuring where failures arise. To analyze the full KI-VQA pipeline, we introduce CRAG-MM-Diagnostics, a diagnostic benchmark with stage-wise data annotations that isolate 1) language-based visual grounding, 2) object identification, and 3) knowledge retrieval and reasoning. We evaluate fully parametric and retrieval-augmented VLMs, providing fine-grained analyses using newly collected metadata, such as target ROIs, entity names, and visual complexity scores. Our results point to knowledge retrieval and reasoning as the primary bottleneck, but also highlight issues in the other parts of the KI-VQA pipeline, such as the fact that VLMs struggle with target object identification or that image retrievers struggle to integrate textual cues. These findings expose fundamental limitations in current KI-VQA systems and motivate stage-aware evaluation. We, lastly, leverage these findings to propose a grounded bimodal RAG pipeline that integrates a visual grounding module to crop targets before image retrieval, boosting GPT-5 and Qwen's respective accuracies by 13.3 and 8.5 percentage points.

</details>


### [54] [Decoupling Cross-Modality Manifold Discrepancy: Leveraging Visible Diffusion Priors for Infrared Super-Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21174)
*Yunpeng Hua,Hongwei Yu,Jiawei Li,Qiankun Liu,Huimin Ma,Jiansheng Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A dual-path diffusion-based IR image SR framework (Shift-IISR) with GRM and LSR improves distributional and structural consistency while preserving diffusion capacity; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Infrared images suffer from low spatial resolution and require preservation of global distribution and structural information; existing methods are insufficient or overly intrusive, especially for diffusion-based models.

Method: Propose Shift-IISR, a dual-path diffusion-based framework comprising Global Representation Modulation (GRM) to extract modality-specific infrared cues and guide the diffusion model's global distribution toward ground truth, and Local Structure Refinement (LSR) to emphasize structural information at each denoising step.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate improved distributional and structural consistency with competitive super-resolution performance; ablation and comparative studies support effectiveness; source code available at the provided GitHub link.

Conclusion: Shift-IISR effectively balances distributional and structural fidelity with the generative capacity of diffusion models while maintaining competitive SR performance; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Infrared image super-resolution (IISR) mitigates the limitations imposed by low spatial resolution. Existing methods have recognized that IISR should preserve consistency in global distribution and structural information while enhancing image clarity. However, these methods are either insufficient or overly intrusive, a problem that becomes even more pronounced in diffusion-based models. To address these issues, we propose a dual-path diffusion-based framework for IISR, termed Shift-IISR. The proposed method is designed to improve the consistency of IISR results while preserving the generative capacity of diffusion models. Specifically, we develop a Global Representation Modulation (GRM) module to extract modality-specific information from infrared imagery and guide the global distribution of the diffusion model toward the ground truth. In addition, we introduce a Local Structure Refinement (LSR) module to encourage the model to focus on structural information at each step of the iterative denoising process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method effectively improves distributional and structural consistency while maintaining competitive super-resolution performance. The source code of the proposed Shift-IISR can be available at https://github.com/Assassink8/Shift-IISR.

</details>


### [55] [Out of Sight, Still in Mind: Token Compression for Omni-LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21179)
*Suho Yoo,Youngjoon Jang,Hyebin Cho,Joon Son Chung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A training-free framework, ReMo, compresses visual tokens in Omni-Modal LLMs by cross-modal token sharing and text proxies, achieving 54% input token reduction with no accuracy loss (and slight gains) on Qwen2.5-Omni.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Omni-LLMs suffer high input token cost due to unbalanced, redundant visual streams; reducing visual tokens without harming performance is crucial for efficient inference.

Method: Two-pronged approach: (i) align audio and video in a shared embedding space and remove visual tokens already explained by audio or other visual tokens; (ii) replace object-level visual tokens with compact textual proxies describing objects and their locations.

Result: On Qwen2.5-Omni (two model scales), ReMo removes 54% of input tokens with no accuracy loss; it slightly surpasses the full-token model, achieving 101.2% and 101.3% of its average accuracy across five audio-visual benchmarks.

Conclusion: ReMo is a training-free framework that significantly reduces input token cost for Omni-LLMs while preserving or improving accuracy, via cross-modal token sharing and text-proxy representations.

Abstract: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, a training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: a visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in a common embedding space, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with no loss in accuracy. Indeed, it slightly exceeds the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.3% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks.

</details>


### [56] [Physics-Informed Deep Learning Model for Cross-Modality Super-Resolution in Fluorescence Microscopy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21190)
*Mohammad Soltaninezhad,Elena Corbetta,Francisco Paez Larios,Paul M. Jordan,Oliver Werz,Christian Eggeling,Thomas Bocklitz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Physics-informed GAN for confocal-to-STED translation using microscope PSF priors improves structural fidelity and physics plausibility in cross-modality super-resolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Avoid outputs inconsistent with optical image formation in cross-modality super-resolution; embed optical priors (PSF) into the learning objective.

Method: A generative adversarial network trained with PSF information (simulated and measured PSFs) on a limited paired dataset of TOM20-labeled mitochondria in human primary M2 macrophages, evaluated across experimental days; includes reference-based and no-reference metrics and frequency/distribution analyses.

Result: PSF-guided models achieved closer agreement with STED references, improved structural fidelity, reduced local deviations, and better frequency-domain metrics compared to non-PSF baselines.

Conclusion: Incorporating optical priors via PSF information enhances the physical plausibility and structural fidelity of cross-modality super-resolution microscopy models.

Abstract: Cross-modality image translation offers a route to super-resolution fluorescence microscopy from low-resolution images while reducing phototoxicity and instrumentation demands. However, purely data-driven models can produce visually plausible outputs that are inconsistent with optical image formation. Here, we propose a physics-informed generative adversarial network for confocal-to-STED image translation that incorporates microscope-specific point spread function information into the training objective. Simulated and experimentally measured PSFs were evaluated using a limited paired confocal-STED dataset of TOM20-labeled mitochondria in human primary M2 macrophages acquired across different experimental days. Performance was assessed using reference-based and non-reference-based image-quality metrics, together with complementary frequency- and distribution-sensitive analyses. The no-reference metrics probed physics-relevant image properties, including spatial-frequency content, contrast, and signal-to-noise behavior. PSF-guided models improved structural fidelity, reduced local deviations, and achieved closer agreement with STED references than non-PSF baselines, particularly in frequency-domain analyses. These results demonstrate that optical priors can improve the structural fidelity and physical plausibility of generative microscopy models for cross-modality super-resolution imaging.

</details>


### [57] [Learning-based Seam Correspondence Reconstruction in Sewing Patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21213)
*Zhendong Wang,Jintong Wang,Chen Liu,Yao Jin,Ligang Liu,Huamin Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A graph-based framework reconstructs two-level sewing information (coarse panel connectivity and fine seam correspondence) from 2D panel geometry, using panel semantics and latent edge representations via graph neural networks to infer detailed seams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 2D sewing patterns are typically unlabeled with disparate panels, hindering automatic downstream 3D garment modeling. An automated method to recover stitching topology from geometry would reduce manual labeling and improve scalability.

Method: A two-stage graph-based approach. Coarse level infers panel connectivity by predicting panel semantics tied to anatomical body regions and garment conventions, enforcing structure consistency. Fine level learns latent edge embeddings on the panel graph via graph message passing to encode local seam geometry and global garment context, which are decoded into detailed seam correspondences, supporting many-to-one, intra-panel, and curved seams.

Result: The method achieves high stitching accuracy and strong generalization across garment styles, validating its ability to recover complex sewing topologies from 2D panel layouts.

Conclusion: A two-level, graph-based learning framework can automatically infer detailed stitching information from 2D sewing patterns, enabling scalable 3D reconstruction and design workflows by converting geometry into actionable seam annotations.

Abstract: Digital sewing patterns typically consist of disjoint 2D panels without explicit stitch annotations, making downstream 3D modeling reliant on labor-intensive expert specification. In this paper, we present a graph-based learning framework that reconstructs two-level stitching information, coarse panel connectivity and fine-grained seam correspondence, from 2D panel geometry alone. At the coarse level, panel connectivity is inferred by predicting panel semantics associated with anatomical body regions, enforcing consistency with body structure and garment design conventions. Based on the reconstructed panel graph, fine-grained seam correspondences between panel pairs are inferred by learning latent edge representations that jointly encode local seam geometry and global garment context through graph message passing. The resulting edge embeddings are subsequently decoded into detailed seam correspondences. Our method supports complex sewing-pattern topologies, including many-to-one correspondences, intra-panel seams, and curved seams. Experiments demonstrate high stitching accuracy and strong generalization across garment styles.

</details>


### [58] [DART: A Degradation-Aware Recurrent Transformer for Archival Film Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21219)
*Mikołaj Jastrzębski,Wojciech Kozłowski,Kamil Adamczewski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Degradation-aware recurrent transformer (DART) for archival film restoration that predicts and propagates a soft defect mask to guide temporal fusion and condition the restoration network on damage location and severity, improving no-reference perceptual quality and temporal coherence with a compact model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Archival film suffers multiple degradations (scratches, dust, blur, noise, flicker, photometric aging) and lacks clean reference videos; existing methods treat degradations implicitly, lacking explicit knowledge of where damage occurs or how severe it is.

Method: DART predicts and propagates a soft defect mask through time to supervise temporal fusion and condition the restoration network on damage location and severity; uses a degradation-aware recurrent transformer architecture to perform restoration.

Result: On real archival benchmarks, DART improves no-reference perceptual quality over prior restoration architectures while remaining compact and efficient, producing cleaner and more temporally consistent restorations of structured film damage.

Conclusion: Explicit degradation awareness via a predicted mask enhances archival film restoration; DART demonstrates effective, efficient restoration with better handling of complex, structured film damage and improved temporal consistency.

Abstract: Archival film restoration is a challenging problem because historical footage contains compound degradations such as scratches, dust, blur, noise, flicker, and photometric aging, while clean reference videos are unavailable. Existing video restoration methods largely treat these degradations implicitly, reconstructing frames without explicit knowledge of where damage occurs or how severe it is. We propose DART, a degradation-aware recurrent transformer for archival film restoration. DART predicts and propagates a soft defect mask through time, using it to guide temporal fusion and condition the restoration network on both damage location and severity. This makes the restoration process explicitly aware of film artifacts rather than relying only on reconstruction losses. Experiments on real archival benchmarks show that DART improves no-reference perceptual quality over prior restoration architectures while remaining compact and efficient, producing cleaner and more temporally consistent restorations of structured film damage.

</details>


### [59] [T-STAR: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Spatio-Temporal Panoptic Scene Graph Generation in Satellite Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21228)
*Linlin Wang,Xue Yang,Zhihuang Zhou,Zhenyu Zhong,Ruiyuan Zhang,Yansheng Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces spatio-temporal panoptic scene graph generation (TPSG) for satellite video, with the T-STAR dataset and a unified framework that jointly models identity-consistent masks and spatio-temporal relationships to benchmark dynamic geospatial understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Satellite video requires structured, dynamic scene understanding beyond object-centric perception. There was no dedicated TPSG dataset for satellite video, and existing TPSG methods on natural videos struggle due to small, occluded, weakly textured objects and strong temporal/spatial coupling.

Method: Define TPSG as generating triplets <subject, relation, object> with explicit temporal spans. Propose T-STAR, a large-scale dataset (~1.1M instance masks, ~3.8M spatio-temporal triplets) across 39 object categories and 70 relation categories. Develop a unified framework to improve cross-frame instance consistency and predict spatio-temporal relationships.

Result: Establishes a strong benchmark for TPSG in satellite video with extensive data and relationships. Experimental results demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness and the dataset’s significance, with code and data released for reproducibility.

Conclusion: TPSG in satellite video is feasible and valuable. T-STAR provides a resource enabling future research on structured satellite video understanding and dynamic geospatial scene reasoning.

Abstract: Structured understanding of satellite video is essential for advancing dynamic geospatial scene analysis from low-level perception to high-level cognition. To move beyond object-centric perception, this paper introduces spatio-temporal panoptic scene graph generation (TPSG) in satellite video as a new benchmark task. TPSG aims to generate a structured graph composed of a set of triplets <subject, relationship, object> with explicit temporal spans, thereby describing dynamic geospatial scenes by jointly modeling identity-consistent instance masks and spatio-temporal relationships among panoptic scene elements. However, there is still no dedicated dataset for TPSG in satellite video. Moreover, TPSG in satellite video is intrinsically challenging, as objects are often small and weakly textured, cross-frame association is easily disrupted by occlusion and background clutter, and relationship semantics are highly coupled with spatial structure and temporal evolution. Consequently, TPSG models developed for natural videos are not directly applicable to satellite video. This paper presents T-STAR, a large-scale benchmark dataset for TPSG in satellite video, comprising over 1.1 million instance masks and over 3.8 million spatio-temporal triplets across 39 fine-grained object categories and 70 fine-grained relationship categories. To enable TPSG in satellite video, we propose a unified framework to enhance cross-frame instance consistency and spatio-temporal relationship prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate the significance of T-STAR and the effectiveness of the proposed framework, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on structured satellite video understanding. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/linlin-dev/T-STAR.

</details>


### [60] [Stokes-Informed Diffusion for Robust Linear Polarization Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21239)
*Yidong Luo,Chenggong Li,Yuchao Feng,Boxin Shi,Junchao Zhang,Xin Yuan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GenPolar presents a Stokes-informed diffusion approach to recover polarization from a single RGB image by predicting S1,S2 from S0, deriving DoLP and AoP; uses two-stage training (physics-based diffusion then one-step generator with LoRA fine-tuning) and an observability-aware loss for AoP; achieves state-of-the-art DoLP fidelity and AoP stability across multiple datasets and improves downstream tasks like material detection and de-reflection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polarization cues are useful but require specialized hardware; AoP is especially unstable in weak polarization; single-image estimation is ill-posed; need physically grounded, robust methods.

Method: Stokes-based diffusion framework. Predict S1,S2 from S0; AoP and DoLP derived analytically. Observability-aware loss for AoP. Two-stage training: (1) multi-step conditional diffusion with physics-based loss; (2) distillation to a one-step generator with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) of VAE encoder to reduce domain bias.

Result: State-of-the-art DoLP fidelity and AoP stability across rotating-polarizer, DoFP, and hybrid datasets; improves downstream applications (material detection, de-reflection).

Conclusion: GenPolar demonstrates that incorporating Mueller/Stokes physics into diffusion-based single-image polarization estimation yields robust AoP and DoLP with practical downstream benefits; two-stage training plus model distillation and LoRA support efficient, stable inference.

Abstract: Polarization cues benefit applications such as material detection and de-reflection, yet acquiring them typically requires dedicated hardware. This motivates us to estimate the linear polarization from a single RGB image. However, the task is inherently ill-posed, with the Angle of Polarization (AoP) becoming particularly unstable in weak polarization regions, where the polarimetric signal is overwhelmed by noise, leading to erratic angle estimates. To address these limitations, we propose GenPolar, a Stokes-informed diffusion framework grounded in the Mueller formalism from an intensity observation. Specifically, GenPolar predicts channel-wise linear Stokes components (S1,S2) from intensity S0, from which degree of linear polarization (DoLP) and AoP are analytically derived; AoP is further supervised with an observability-aware loss. In addition, to enable efficient and high-fidelity inference, we adopt a two-stage training strategy. Firstly, a multi-step conditional diffusion model is trained with a physics-based loss. Subsequently, we distill it into a one-step generator, which further supports stable Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) of the VAE encoder to mitigate domain-specific autoencoding bias. Extensive experiments across rotating-polarizer, division-of-focal-plane, and hybrid datasets demonstrate that GenPolar achieves state-of-the-art performance in both DoLP fidelity and AoP stability. Crucially, these improvements translate to significant and consistent gains in downstream applications, including material detection and de-reflection.

</details>


### [61] [Detectors Learn the Wrong Thing: Shortcut-Resistant Adversarial Training Against Physically Realizable Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21243)
*Yuanhao Huang,Yilong Ren,Jinlei Wang,Xuesong Bai,Zheng Zhang,Haiyang Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: InsCAT is an instance-level contrastive adversarial training framework that prevents adversarial textures from acting as independent decision cues in detectors, improving robustness to physical texture attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical adversarial appearances undermine safety-critical perception; detectors may latch onto adversarial textures as evidence of object presence, causing false positives and poor generalization. A method is needed to suppress texture-only cues while preserving target-related evidence.

Method: Propose InsCAT with SICA (align adversarial and clean person features while separating texture-only negatives) and ROPO/Guard for online attack pressure and coordinated training. Trains on eight independently generated attack textures across rendered nuScenes, INRIAPerson, printed garments, and three detector families.

Result: InsCAT achieves an average attack AP of 82.3% on rendered nuScenes, outpacing the strongest baseline by 11.1 points. Texture FPR reduces from 46.9% (AT-Mix) to 7.3%. Physical tests yield F1 = 96.6% and FPR = 1.8%. Gains are consistent across detectors, showing applicability across architectures with direct inference.

Conclusion: Robust physical person detection hinges on preserving target-related evidence while preventing adversarial textures from becoming independent decision cues; InsCAT offers a practical, architecture-agnostic approach to reduce texture shortcuts in safety-critical visual perception.

Abstract: AI-enabled visual perception systems are increasingly deployed in intelligent transportation infrastructure and autonomous vehicle related applications. However, physically realizable adversarial appearances pose a significant reliability challenge for these safety-critical systems. Adversarial training is effective, but repeated co-occurrence between adversarial texture and positive person instances can cause detectors to treat the texture itself as evidence of object presence, forming a patch texture shortcut. The detector may then treat texture as evidence for the target, causing false detections on texture-only inputs and weakening cross attack generalisation. We propose InsCAT, an instance-level contrastive adversarial training framework that prevents detectors from using adversarial texture as an independent decision cue. SICA aligns adversarial person features with matched clean features and separates them from texture-only negatives, while ROPO and Guard maintain online attack pressure and coordinate training. We evaluate eight independently generated attack textures on rendered nuScenes, INRIAPerson, printed garments, and three detector families. InsCAT achieves an average attack AP of 82.3% on rendered nuScenes, exceeding the strongest baseline by 11.1 points.Relative to AT-Mix, texture FPR decreases from 46.9% to 7.3%. Physical tests yield an F1 score of 96.6% and an FPR of 1.8%. Consistent gains across separately trained detectors demonstrate applicability across architectures with direct inference. The findings show that robust physical detection depends on preserving target related evidence while preventing adversarial texture from becoming an independent decision cu

</details>


### [62] [Flash EQ-Linear: Accelerating Equivariant Linear Layers via Group-wise Discrete Fourier Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21271)
*Zhongchen Zhao,Jixin Wang,Qi Xie,Hui Lin,Lei Zhang,Deyu Meng,Zongben Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Flash EQ-Linear accelerates equivariant linear layers by modeling them as a circular convolution along the group dimension followed by a channel-wise linear transform, and accelerating via FFT-based convolution and real-DFT symmetry; achieves operator- and network-level speedups with code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address compute inefficiency in parameter-efficient equivariant networks caused by dense implementations, by exploiting structure to reduce FLOPs while maintaining accuracy.

Method: View EQ-Linear as circular convolution over the group dimension convolved with a channel linear transform. Use Fourier convolution theorem along the group dimension and leverage conjugate symmetry of the real DFT. Develop dedicated CUDA kernels for forward/backward passes in FP32/FP16. Complexity reduced from O(NDC) to O(NDC/T).

Result: Operator-level: up to 2× forward speedup over PyTorch's F.linear. Network-level: up to 1.7× end-to-end speedup over both equivariant and non-equivariant baselines. First to show equivariant networks can surpass non-equivariant baselines in accuracy, parameter efficiency, and inference speed. Code available at the provided GitHub.

Conclusion: Flash EQ-Linear enables practical, faster equivariant networks without sacrificing accuracy or parameter efficiency, representing a significant step toward more compute-efficient equivariant architectures.

Abstract: Equivariant networks embed geometric symmetries as structural priors through weight sharing, achieving remarkable parameter efficiency across vision tasks. However, this parameter efficiency does not translate into compute efficiency: existing implementations unroll the structured weights into dense matrices and dispatch them to generic dense kernels, so the FLOPs of an equivariant layer are no smaller than those of a non-equivariant counterpart. In this paper, we observe that the equivariant linear (EQ-Linear) layer---the most fundamental and frequently used module in modern equivariant architectures---is essentially a circular convolution along the group dimension composed with a linear transform along the channel dimension. Building on this observation, we propose Flash EQ-Linear, an exact acceleration algorithm that reduces the complexity from $\mathcal{O}(NDC)$ to $\mathcal{O}(NDC/T)$ by combining the Fourier convolution theorem along the group dimension with the conjugate symmetry of the real DFT. We further provide dedicated CUDA kernels for Flash EQ-Linear, covering both forward and backward passes and both FP32 and FP16 precision. At the operator level, Flash EQ-Linear achieves up to ${2\times}$ forward speedup over PyTorch's F.linear; at the network level, Flash EQ-ViT and Flash EQ-Swin achieve up to ${1.7\times}$ end-to-end speedup over both equivariant and non-equivariant baselines. To our knowledge, this is the first time equivariant networks strictly dominate their non-equivariant counterparts along all three axes simultaneously: accuracy, parameter efficiency, and inference speed.Code is available at https://github.com/zhongchenzhao/FlashEQLinear.

</details>


### [63] [Unlearning Under Imbalance: Benchmarking Fairness in Multimodal LLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21300)
*Lorenzo Orsingher,Thomas De Min,Massimiliano Mancini,Davide Talon,Elisa Ricci*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FAIRGET introduces a VQA benchmark to evaluate unlearning under unbalanced forget requests and FAUN provides a bias-aware activation steering method to forget identities while preserving fairness; experimental validation on FAIRGET and FIUBench shows improved unlearning quality and fairness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unlearning studies assume uniform forget requests, ignoring demographic imbalances that can bias model beliefs and outputs. There is a need for benchmarks and methods that account for fairness in unlearning.

Method: FairGET designs unbalanced forget scenarios across demographic groups for Visual Question Answering to evaluate unlearning. FAUN proposes bias-aware activation steering to remove information about forgotten identities while maintaining fairness across groups.

Result: FAIRGET and FIUBench experiments demonstrate improved unlearning quality and fairness compared to baselines; FAUN effectively forgets targeted identities without degrading fairness.

Conclusion: Accounting for unbalanced forget requests is essential; the proposed benchmark and algorithm address fairness in unlearning for MLLMs and show promise for safer, more equitable models.

Abstract: Machine unlearning has emerged as a tool for removing personal data from trained models to comply with recent AI regulations. To evaluate unlearning effectiveness in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), prior works fine-tune models on fictitious identities, simulating unlearning requests on subsets of these IDs, which are typically uniformly distributed. However, in realistic scenarios, people from different demographic groups may request to be unlearned at different frequencies, potentially altering the model's internal beliefs for these groups and leading to biased behaviors. To fill this gap, we propose FAIRGET, the first Visual Question Answering benchmark that evaluates unlearning under unbalanced, realistic, forget requests. These requests are designed to simulate multiple realistic scenarios, ranging from simple to challenging settings, that lead to biased unlearned models if fairness is not accounted for. Additionally, we propose FAUN, the first unlearning algorithm for MLLMs that forgets unlearning data while preserving model fairness. FAUN exploits a bias-aware activation steering mechanism to unlearn identities while accounting for the unbalanced nature of the forget data. Experiments on FAIRGET and the established FIUBench demonstrate our method's superiority both in unlearning quality and fairness.

</details>


### [64] [PC-Edit: Prompt-Contrastive Region Discovery and Region-Guided Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21318)
*Jian Zhang,Zhijun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A training-free MM-DiT editing framework, PC-Edit, uses prompt-contrastive attention to locate and control edit regions, enabling object replacement/addition with strong background preservation; achieves state-of-the-art performance on PIE-Bench and EditRegion-Bench without manual region cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current training-free editors either rely on terminal predictions with limited localization or reuse source features without explicit region discovery, leading to poor localization or background leakage.

Method: Contrast image-token attention outputs under source and target prompts to identify source-erasure and target-emergence regions; union of these regions guides edits. Then, during sampling, estimate edit region from earlier attention and inject cached source K/V features outside the region in subsequent blocks to protect background; achieves region-aware diffusion without user-specified masks.

Result: Empirical evaluation on PIE-Bench and EditRegion-Bench with human-annotated regions shows PC-Edit yields best editing quality and background preservation among training-free methods that do not require user-specified edit regions.

Conclusion: Prompt-contrastive, region-aware training-free MM-DiT editing significantly improves localization precision and content preservation, enabling effective multi-object edits without manual edit region specification.

Abstract: Replacing an object with one that differs in category or shape requires complete source removal, natural target formation unconstrained by the source silhouette, and preservation of unrelated content. Existing training-free editors either localize edits from terminal predictions under source and target prompts or preserve unrelated content through spatially unselective source-feature reuse without explicit region discovery. Before reaching the terminal predictions, prompt-induced semantic differences undergo additional network transformations that may obscure their spatial localization, reducing localization precision. Spatially unselective feature reuse forces a trade-off between edit completeness and background preservation. Therefore, we propose PC-Edit, a prompt-contrastive framework for training-free MM-DiT editing. PC-Edit contrasts the image-token attention outputs under the source and target prompts, capturing prompt-induced semantic differences directly where text-conditioned information is delivered to image tokens. The same contrast identifies a source-erasure region during inversion and a target-emergence region during denoising. Their union suppresses source remnants while allowing the target object to form naturally. PC-Edit further couples region discovery and background preservation within each sampling step by estimating the current edit region from preceding attention blocks and immediately injecting cached source K/V features outside it in subsequent blocks, thereby protecting unrelated content before the latent update. Experiments on PIE-Bench and our EditRegion-Bench, with human-verified edit-region annotations for single- and multi-object addition and replacement, show that PC-Edit achieves the best editing quality and background preservation among methods without user-specified edit regions.

</details>


### [65] [SlerpFlow: Spherical Trajectory Correction for Rectified Flow Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21326)
*Wenbin Duan,Yan Shu,Zhuoyuan Fu,Fangmin Zhao,Yan Li,Yaru Zhao,Binyang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SlerpFlow provides a zero-shot, geometry-driven correction for FLUX inversion, using Spherical Linear Interpolation (Slerp) to align velocity on the latent hypersphere, enabling high-precision inversion with first-order solvers and caching without extra training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inversion accuracy for Rectified-Flow-based diffusion transformers is limited by discretization errors of linear solvers; existing corrections (e.g., high-order Taylor) are complex and costly.

Method: Introduce SlerpFlow, which applies Slerp to rectify flow velocity directions on the latent hypersphere in accordance with the manifold hypothesis. The corrected velocity is cached for subsequent steps to preserve efficiency and enable high-precision inversion with a first-order Euler solver.

Result: Empirical evaluations on FLUX-based reconstruction and editing show improved reconstruction fidelity and stronger semantic alignment in editing, achieved without additional training; code released.

Conclusion: Zero-shot Slerp-based rectification leverages intrinsic curvature of the latent space to improve inversion fidelity and editing performance for FLUX, maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Rectified-flow-based diffusion transformers, particularly FLUX, have demonstrated outstanding performance in high-quality image generation. However, achieving fast and accurate inversion--transforming images back to latent noise for faithful reconstruction and editing--remains a challenging bottleneck due to the discretization errors of linear solvers. This paper introduces SlerpFlow, a straightforward yet highly effective zero-shot approach that unlocks the full potential of FLUX for high-fidelity inversion and editing. Unlike existing approaches (e.g., RF-Solver) that rely on complex numerical approximations such as high-order Taylor expansions to correct trajectory errors, we present a geometric view based on the Manifold Hypothesis: the empirically observed trajectory curvature is not a numerical artifact, but rather serves as a necessary "centripetal force" that constrains the flow to remain on the data manifold. Guided by this insight, SlerpFlow integrates Spherical Linear Interpolation (Slerp) to rectify flow velocity directions on the hypersphere, strictly adhering to the intrinsic curvature of the latent space. Crucially, by caching the corrected velocity for subsequent steps, SlerpFlow achieves high-precision inversion while maintaining the computational efficiency of a first-order Euler solver. Extensive experiments on FLUX-based reconstruction and editing tasks demonstrate that SlerpFlow improves reconstruction fidelity and achieves stronger semantic alignment in editing without requiring additional training. Code is available at https://github.com/0answer0/SlerpFlow.

</details>


### [66] [Quality-Aware Multimodal Fusion Reveals Implicit Identity in Valence-Arousal Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21347)
*Jisu Kim,Benjamin S. Riggan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Multimodal valence-arousal (VA) estimation via Quality-Aware Adaptive Fusion (QAAF) improves robustness and reveals VA dynamics as a complementary soft biometric to face recognition; per-sample modality reliability with soft gating and quality dropout yields strong CCC gains and resilience to missing modalities; VA-trained features also enhance identity verification with ArcFace.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional face recognition degrades with expression, occlusion, and poor lighting. Multimodal VA signals may carry identity-discriminative dynamics that are complementary to static appearance and require robust, quality-aware fusion to leverage in-the-wild video.

Method: Train a VA estimation model using QAAF to adaptively fuse audio-visual modalities. QAAF estimates per-sample, per-modality reliability and uses learned soft gating plus quality-dependent dropout. Evaluate with late fusion ensembles on Aff-Wild2 (CCC as metric); test robustness to missing modalities; probe identity potential by evaluating VA-trained features on AFEW-VA and YTF with ArcFace score-level fusion.

Result: On Aff-wild2, CCC=0.472 for QAAF (vs 0.415 baseline ensemble and 0.288 single backbone). Missing modalities cause only 7.5-34.4% relative CCC decrease. VA-trained features rank first among soft biometrics on AFEW-VA (67 actors) and YTF (1,595 subjects); ArcFace fusion reduces EER from 0.022 to 0.021 on AFEW-VA and 0.106 to 0.104 on YTF, correcting 68.2% of ArcFace’s false accepts on AFEW-VA.

Conclusion: Multimodal VA estimation with quality-aware fusion yields robust representations that complement conventional face recognition, providing both improved VA estimation performance and transferable identity-related cues without identity-specific training.

Abstract: Conventional face recognition relies on static appearance cues and degrades in unconstrained settings with expression variation, occlusion, and poor lighting. We hypothesize that audiovisual expression dynamics carry identity-discriminative information complementary to static appearance, and that extracting this signal requires multimodal representations robust to the variable input quality of in-the-wild video. To learn such representations, we cast multimodal valence-arousal (VA) estimation as a pretext task and propose Quality-Aware Adaptive Fusion (QAAF), which estimates per-sample, per-modality reliability and adapts each modality's contribution through learned soft gating and a quality-dependent dropout. For the problem of VA estimation, QAAF achieves an average Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) of 0.472 via late fusion ensembling on Aff-wild2, improving over a baseline ensemble under the same setting (0.415) as well as a single-backbone baseline (0.288). Furthermore, the proposed QAAF demonstrates greater resilience to unavailable modalities, with only a 7.5-34.4% relative decrease in CCC when one modality is missing. We then probe whether these VA-trained features encode identity without identity-specific training. On AFEW-VA (67 actors) and YTF (1,595 subjects), VA-trained backbone features rank first among evaluated soft biometric methods, and score-level fusion with ArcFace lowers EER on both datasets (0.022 to 0.021 on AFEW-VA, 0.106 to 0.104 on YTF), correcting 68.2% of ArcFace's false accepts on AFEW-VA. These findings establish multimodal VA estimation as a soft biometric modality complementary to conventional face recognition.

</details>


### [67] [Incremental Optimal Assignment for Real-Time Crowd Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21368)
*Ismail H. Toroslu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Incremental assignment for dense crowd tracking; achieves 3.7–6.5× speedup over Hungarian while yielding identical optimal matchings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce the O(N^3) bottleneck of the Hungarian algorithm in large-scale, dense-crowd tracking by exploiting block-sparse cost matrices.

Method: Incrementally build the N×N assignment by adding one detection/trajectory at a time. After step n−1, the dual potentials are exactly optimal for the (n−1)×(n−1) subproblem. Each new step uses a single augmenting path search from a certified optimal starting point, maintaining identical global optimum with an additional diagonal-reordering invariant to keep data compact.

Result: On benchmarks with N in [200,5000] organized into dense clusters, 3.7–6.5× speedup over Hungarian; speedup grows with N and remains stable beyond N=3000; provably optimal and identical to Hungarian.

Conclusion: The approach delivers scalable, exact, and cache-friendly matching for large-scale crowd tracking, making it especially suitable for stadium exits and mass events.

Abstract: Multi-object tracking in dense crowds requires solving a bipartite assignment problem between detections and trajectories at every video frame. The classical Hungarian algorithm solves this in $O(N^3)$ time, which becomes a bottleneck for large scenes with hundreds of people. We propose an \emph{incremental} assignment algorithm that exploits the block-sparse structure of crowd tracking cost matrices --- dense within each crowd cluster, near-zero between clusters. We compute the exact same optimal $N \times N$ assignment as the Hungarian algorithm, but via an incremental strategy: we add one person at a time, exploiting the fact that after step $n-1$ the dual potentials are \emph{exactly optimal} for the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ subproblem --- a strictly stronger condition than the intermediate feasibility maintained by the Hungarian algorithm during its $N$ outer iterations. Each new step therefore requires only a single augmenting path search from a certified optimal starting point. This avoids repeated full-matrix scans while guaranteeing an identical globally optimal result. A diagonal-reordering invariant keeps the data structure compact and cache-friendly. On realistic crowd benchmarks with $N \in [200, 5000]$ people organised into dense clusters, our algorithm achieves \textbf{3.7--6.5$\times$ speedup} over the Hungarian baseline while producing provably optimal matchings identical to those of Hungarian. The speedup grows with $N$ and remains stable beyond $N=3000$, making the method especially attractive for large-scale crowd scenes such as stadium exits and mass public events.

</details>


### [68] [ASTRA-Net: Anatomy-Specific Transfer and Representation Alignment for Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21370)
*Suhua Sun,Yuqiao Wang,Sheng Liu,Rui Fan,Jiajun Wang,Ruoyan Xu,Yixin Chen,Tao Li,Yan Yan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AstRA-Net uses synthetic, unlabeled virtual DISE frames to align features with scarce real annotations, enabling accurate plane-specific DISE segmentation with a two-stage process and limited real data; ensemble and alignment strategies yield high Dice/IoU and strong plane classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pixel-level DISE annotations are scarce, limiting quantitative assessment. A scalable approach leveraging unlabeled virtual endoscopy frames can provide robust, plane-specific segmentation with minimal real labels.

Method: Stage 1: align ConvNeXt-Base representations between 14,250 unlabeled virtual frames and real DISE frames using MMD and/or domain-adversarial objectives. Stage 2: fine-tune four independent UNet++ decoders on 401 real annotated frames with structured zero-mask supervision to constrain invalid outputs. Evaluate multiple alignment configurations (MMD, DANN, or both). Use a five-model ensemble for segmentation. A classification-enabled variant assesses four-plane top-1 accuracy on 100 hold-out frames.

Result: On a hold-out set of 100 frames, the five-model MMD-only ensemble achieved mean Dice 0.8927 (95% CI 0.8631–0.9160); mean IoU 0.8239. The classification-enabled variant reached top-1 accuracy 0.92 for four planes.

Conclusion: ASTRA-Net demonstrates that effective frame-level, plane-specific DISE boundary delineation is achievable with limited real annotations by aligning unlabeled virtual frames to real data and employing multi-stage, constrained segmentation with ensemble and optional plane classification.

Abstract: Quantitative drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) requires reliable airway boundaries at specific anatomical levels. Pixel-level DISE annotations are scarce, and manual contouring limits the scalability of quantitative assessment. To address this limitation, we developed ASTRA-Net for known-plane DISE segmentation with limited real annotations. Stage 1 aligned intermediate ConvNeXt-Base representations from 14,250 unlabeled virtual endoscopy frames derived from computed tomography and real DISE frames. Virtual images were used only for feature alignment. Stage 2 fine-tuned four independent UNet++ decoders on 401 real annotated frames. Structured zero-mask supervision constrained incompatible plane outputs and invalid frames. Six alignment configurations used maximum mean discrepancy, domain adversarial learning, or both objectives. On a hold-out evaluation set of 100 frames, the five-model MMD-only segmentation ensemble achieved a mean Dice of 0.8927, with a 95% image-level bootstrap interval of 0.8631 to 0.9160. The mean intersection over union was 0.8239. A classification- enabled variant of the same alignment configuration reached a restricted four-plane top-1 accuracy of 0.92 on the same hold-out frames. These results indicate that ASTRA-Net can support frame-level, plane-specific DISE boundary delineation when real annotations are limited.

</details>


### [69] [DINOde: Continuous Vision-Text Alignment for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21371)
*Sung-Hoon Yoon,Hoyong Kwon,Changgyoon Oh,Kuk-Jin Yoon*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DINOde introduces an ODE-based framework to align CLIP text embeddings with DINO's visual manifold for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, via Semantic Text Flow (STF) and Global Context Flow (GCF) with Velocity Tangent Projection to preserve hyperspherical geometry, achieving state-of-the-art results on OVSS benchmarks; code available at GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DINOv3 lacks native textual alignment for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, hindering cross-modal generalization. A continuous, geometry-preserving alignment between text embeddings and the DINO visual manifold can leverage textual semantics for OVSS.

Method: Two components: (i) Semantic Text Flow (STF) evolves text embeddings toward the DINO manifold through a continuous ODE trajectory; (ii) Global Context Flow (GCF) refines the holistic image representation carried by DINO's CLS token. Velocity Tangent Projection constrains the learned velocity field to the tangent space, preserving hyperspherical geometry and preventing manifold entanglement from discrete projections.

Result: Extensive experiments show that DINOde consistently outperforms existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple OVSS benchmarks.

Conclusion: DINOde enables robust, continuous cross-modal alignment for OVSS by modeling alignment as a continuous trajectory, avoiding discrete projection pitfalls; the method demonstrates strong empirical gains and provides code for replication.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) leverages textual semantics to segment objects beyond predefined categories. While the self-supervised model DINOv3 provides strong structured visual representations, its lack of native textual alignment hinders its direct application to OVSS. To bridge this gap, we propose DINOde, an ODE-based framework that continuously aligns CLIP text embeddings with the DINO visual manifold. Our approach employs two complementary components: (i) Semantic Text Flow (STF), which evolves text embeddings toward the DINO manifold through a continuous ODE trajectory, and (ii) Global Context Flow (GCF), which progressively refines the holistic image representation carried by DINO's CLS token. To preserve the hyperspherical geometry of the feature space during this evolution, we further introduce Velocity Tangent Projection, which constrains the learned velocity field to the tangent space. By modeling alignment as a continuous trajectory, DINOde avoids the manifold entanglement inherent in discrete MLP projections and yields more robust cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DINOde consistently outperforms existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple OVSS benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/yoon307/DINOde.

</details>


### [70] [When Are Reasoning-Based Guardrails Not Efficient? ResponseGuard: A Fast Vision-Language Guard for Real-Time Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21401)
*Dongbin Na*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A no-chain, single-pass vision-language guard (ResponseGuard) achieves strong performance and low latency on response harm detection, outperforming a larger reasoning-based guard while streaming, with the ability to stop harmful content sentence-by-sentence. It relies on a pooled representation of request, response, and image, and uses no chain-of-thought, though some limits appear in request-harmfulness and image-only cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce latency and compute cost of vision-language safety guardrails by removing the need for step-by-step reasoning, and to enable real-time, streaming screening of model outputs.

Method: Design and evaluate a 2B parameter ResponseGuard that outputs a harmfulness verdict from a single forward pass over a pooled representation of the user query, the generated response, and the image, without generating a chain of thought. The model is assessed on standard multimodal guardrail benchmarks and examined for streaming sentence-level screening and attention patterns.

Result: ResponseGuard outperforms a recent 3B reasoning-based guard on response harmfulness detection by about 150x faster time cost, despite having no reasoning. On request harmfulness, the reasoning guard retains a lead; gaps on both tasks are attributed to image-only encoder limitations and not the absence of reasoning. The reasoning guard tends to concentrate its attention away from image content during verdicts. ResponseGuard can perform sentence-by-sentence streaming screening and stop a harmful answer before it finishes. The work releases all code, models, and data.

Conclusion: Single-pass, non-reasoning guards can achieve strong safety performance and real-time gating for vision-language models, challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought reasoning is necessary for harm detection. However, image representation and encoder freezing influence gaps in certain scenarios, suggesting future work on better multimodal fusion or adaptable encoders.

Abstract: A vision-language AI assistant returns its answer as a stream of generated tokens. Therefore, a safety guard that watches that answer has to keep up with the stream and stop a harmful reply before a user reads it. Recent vision-language guardrails instead generate a chain of thought before they issue a verdict. They believe that step-by-step reasoning yields a safer guard. This design makes the guard heavy and slow, since the model must decode many tokens for harmfulness detection. We pose the question of whether a vision-language guard really needs to reason in order to screen a response. We answer with a guard that has no chain. ResponseGuard reads a harmful verdict from a single pooled representation of the request, the response, and the image in one forward pass. Across a standard multimodal guardrail benchmark, our 2B ResponseGuard outperforms a recent 3B reasoning-based vision-language guard on response harmfulness detection, without any reasoning and at about 150 times lower time cost. On request harmfulness the reasoning guard retains an overall lead, and the remaining gap on both tracks sits on the image-only cells. We observe that the gap may stem from the frozen vision encoders that both designs use rather than from the missing chain. We have also found the reasoning guard directs almost none of its verdict attention to the image. Based on a single-pass detection, ResponseGuard can screen an answer sentence by sentence as it streams and stop a harmful answer before it finishes. For guarding the response of a vision-language model, a calibrated single-pass label may provide a sufficient safety signal. We fully release all source code, trained models, and datasets at https://github.com/ndb796/ResponseGuard.

</details>


### [71] [Towards Privacy-Preserving Federated Prompt Tuning under Data Heterogeneity: A Subspace-Decomposed Expert Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21417)
*Yuhua Wang,Xiaodong Li,Yihao Guo,Yuxiang Jia,Qinnan Zhang,Yifan Sun,Hainan Zhang,Yongxin Tong,Zhiming Zheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedSEPT: Subspace-decomposed expert prompts for privacy-preserving federated prompt tuning, improving personalization-generalization balance with on-device fusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated prompt tuning (FPT) for vision–language models faces heterogeneity and privacy constraints. A single shared prompt can over-smooth diverse transferable knowledge, while multi-expert prompts (MEPs) improve expressiveness but raise DP noise and communication costs. There is a need for a privacy-preserving, communication-efficient design that captures diverse expertise.

Method: Subspace-decomposed Expert Modeling (SEM) parameterizes multiple prompt experts with shared low-rank factors, a fixed public basis, and private residuals, confining DP noise and communication to a compact factor space and enabling server aggregation in a common coordinate system. Instance-aware Expert Fusion (IEF) on-device routes among experts and performs logit-level fusion using cached expert-specific text features.

Result: Experiments on 11 heterogeneous benchmarks show FedSEPT achieves a better trade-off between local adaptation and global generalization under the same privacy constraints than strong baselines.

Conclusion: FedSEPT provides a privacy-preserving, communication-efficient, and robust multi-expert prompt-tuning approach for federated vision–language models, improving personalization without sacrificing generalization.

Abstract: Federated prompt tuning (FPT) enables collaborative adaptation of vision--language models (VLMs) using lightweight prompts. Existing methods often address heterogeneity and privacy through a split-prompt design under local differential privacy (DP), combining a shared prompt for global transfer with private prompts for local adaptation. However, a single shared prompt may over-smooth diverse transferable knowledge, weakening the balance between personalization and generalization. Multi-expert prompts (MEPs) can better capture this diversity, but enlarge the communicated space, increasing DP noise and communication cost while making robust expert composition more difficult. We propose FedSEPT, a privacy-preserving Fed}erated Subspace-decomposed Expert Prompt Tuning. Specifically, we employ Subspace-decomposed Expert Modeling (SEM) to parameterize multiple prompt experts with shared low-rank factors, a fixed public basis, and private residuals, thereby confining communication and DP perturbation to a compact factor space while enabling direct server aggregation in a common coordinate system. We further design Instance-aware Expert Fusion (IEF), which adaptively combines semantically complementary experts via on-device routing and performs efficient logit-level fusion using cached expert-specific text features. Extensive experiments on 11 heterogeneous benchmarks show that, under the same privacy constraints, FedSEPT achieves a better trade-off between local adaptation and global generalization than strong baselines.

</details>


### [72] [Adaptive Identity Anchoring: Closed-Loop Keyframe Placement for Synthetic Paired Supervision in Video Face Swapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21434)
*Logan Robbins*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Adaptive Identity Anchoring (AIA) and Reality-Referenced Texture Restoration are proposed to mitigate drift and over-smoothing in video face swapping by introducing adaptive identity anchors and texture matching with a feedback loop and spectral guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current unsupervised video face swapping typically relies on identity injection in only a couple of frames, causing long-range drift and artifacts; a mechanism to anchor identity and preserve micro-texture is needed.

Method: Generalize the synthesizer to arbitrary anchor sets within diffusion-forcing-style transformers; place anchors via a closed-feedback loop that scores each generated frame against the real identity and inserts the worst-scoring frame as an anchor until a threshold is met or the budget is exhausted; reuse the loop's verdict as an automatic data filter; pair with Reality-Referenced Texture Restoration: matched re-graining from non-face regions, band-split sub-texture transfer, and a spectral acceptance channel guided by the footage spectrum.

Result: No empirical results are presented in the abstract; the work outlines a framework and a set of falsifiable experiments.

Conclusion: AIA and Reality-Referenced Texture Restoration offer a controllable quality dial via anchor density and aim to reduce drift and over-smoothing; validation requires the proposed experiments to establish effectiveness and trade-offs.

Abstract: Video face swapping has no natural paired supervision: no real footage exists of one person's face performing another person's video. The strongest current answer, DreamID-V's SyncID-Pipe, mints pairs by replacing the identity in exactly two frames of a real clip -- the first and the last -- and regenerating the rest from a pose sequence alone. Pose carries no appearance evidence of the swapped-in identity, so over long clips, occlusions, and extreme pose excursions the synthesized identity has a long unanchored span on which to drift; no published ablation examines anchor count or placement. We propose Adaptive Identity Anchoring (AIA): (i) generalize the synthesizer to arbitrary anchor sets, architecturally natural for diffusion-forcing-style transformers where conditioning on a frame is clamping its tokens to zero noise; (ii) place anchors by a closed feedback loop that scores every generated frame against the real reference identity and inserts an image-face-swapped anchor at the worst-scoring frame until the pair passes a threshold or exhausts a budget; (iii) reuse the loop's verdict as an automatic data filter. A second pathology, the beauty-filter look of over-smoothed skin, has the same root cause: micro-texture, like identity, is priced by none of the pipeline's objectives. We therefore pair AIA with Reality-Referenced Texture Restoration: matched re-graining from each real frame's non-face regions, band-split transfer of sub-identity micro-texture from the real footage, and a second, spectral acceptance channel refereed by the footage's own spectrum. Identity-anchor density, we argue, is a controllable quality dial, and we specify falsifiable experiments -- drift-versus-gap curves, uniform-versus-adaptive placement at matched budgets, student training on AIA-minted data, and texture ablations with a human beauty-filter study -- that would validate or refute the proposal.

</details>


### [73] [DAPM: UAV Monocular Depth Estimation from Any Height, Pitch, Roll and FOV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21438)
*Tong Ling,Wenhui Diao,Yingchao Feng,Hanbo Bi,Zhongyan Hou,Xian Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes DAPM, a UAV-focused monocular depth estimation framework that jointly estimates camera pose and depth under continuously varying viewpoints, using IGD for dense pose supervision and PQB for robust depth quantization; introduces UAPD dataset; reports SOTA on depth and pose.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: UAVs exhibit dynamic camera poses (height, pitch, roll, FOV) leading to poor generalization of monocular depth methods across perspectives and depth scales. A geometry-guided approach leveraging the ground plane is proposed to stabilize depth estimation and pose inference across wide viewing conditions.

Method: Derives geometric relationships between UAV viewing angles and view distances with the ground plane as reference. Introduces Ideal Ground Depth (IGD) module for dense camera-pose supervision and depth feature enhancement, and a coarse-to-fine Progressive Quantization Bins (PQB) module to enable robust estimation under varied perspectives. DAPM is an end-to-end framework that jointly estimates depth and camera pose and is evaluated on the new UAV Any Perspectives Depth (UAPD) dataset.

Result: Experimental results on UAPD show state-of-the-art performance in both depth and camera-pose estimation metrics, demonstrating robust generalization across continuous pose distributions. The work provides source code and dataset.

Conclusion: DAPM advances monocular depth estimation for UAVs by integrating ground-plane geometry with pose-aware supervision and hierarchical quantization, enabling reliable depth and pose estimation under continuous viewpoint changes and expanding evaluative resources via UAPD.

Abstract: Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental prerequisite for 3D reconstruction and autonomous navigation in Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). In practical deployments, UAVs operate under highly dynamic camera poses characterized by continuous variations in height, pitch, roll, and field of view (FOV). Existing monocular depth estimation methods frequently fail to generalize across such diverse perspectives and the expansive scale of depth distributions inherent in aerial scenes. To address these challenges, we establish a quantitative representation of UAV viewing angles through rigorous theoretical analysis, deriving the geometric correspondence between viewing angles and view distances using the ground plane as a reference for observation. Building upon this, we propose Depth Estimation for Any Perspectives Model (DAPM), representing the first monocular framework specifically designed for UAV aerial imagery to jointly estimate camera pose and depth under continuously varying viewpoints. Specifically, we introduce an Ideal Ground Depth (IGD) module that leverages the derived geometric relationships between UAV perspectives and view distances to implement dense camera-pose supervision and enhance depth features. And we further develop a coarse-to-fine Progressive Quantization Bins (PQB) module. By incorporating progressive supervision and hierarchical quantization bins, the PQB module enables robust estimation in complex UAV aerial imagery. To evaluate the proposed framework, we present the UAV Any Perspectives Depth (UAPD) dataset, featuring comprehensive and continuous distributions of pose parameters. Experimental results on UAPD demonstrate that DAPM achieves state-of-the-art performance across both depth and camera-pose estimation metrics. The source code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/ThisIsLT/DAPM.

</details>


### [74] [GrainGS: Gradient-Decoupled Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Dynamic Novel View Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21448)
*Jiahao He,Yihua Shao,Zhengkai Zhao,Pan Gao,Fei Ma,Jingcai Guo,Hao Tang,Nicu Sebe,Qi Tian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GrainGS integrates a hierarchical anchor scaffold with per-Gaussian deformation to jointly model dynamic scenes: a static warm-up canonical frame, stop-gradient deformations, per-Gaussian temporal offsets, and a canonical-residual appearance model, yielding high-quality, real-time rendering with compact storage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To balance fine-grained dynamic motion modeling, structural stability, and compact representation in dynamic scene reconstruction, addressing the trade-offs of per-primitive flexibility versus anchor-based regularization.

Method: A static warm-up establishes a time-invariant canonical representation. During training, a stop-gradient path preserves canonical positions while still refining them via reconstruction loss. Each Gaussian independently predicts temporal offsets for position, rotation, and scale within a hierarchical anchor scaffold; a canonical-residual appearance decomposition handles frame-dependent photometry without deforming geometry.

Result: GrainGS achieves high reconstruction quality, real-time novel view synthesis, and compact storage on synthetic monocular and real-world multiview benchmarks. Synthetic PSNR is 36.98 dB, rendering at 435.6 fps, requiring 4.67 MB storage.

Conclusion: The proposed GrainGS framework effectively balances local motion detail and global structural constraints, delivering fast, high-quality dynamic scene reconstruction with efficient storage.

Abstract: Dynamic scene reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting requires a balance between fine-grained motion modeling, structural stability, and compact representation. Existing per-primitive methods provide flexible local deformation but often suffer from redundant primitive growth, while anchor-based methods improve spatial regularity at the cost of suppressing locally varying motion. To address these issues, we present GrainGS, a dynamic Gaussian framework that combines a hierarchical anchor scaffold with per-Gaussian deformation. A static warm-up stage first establishes a time-invariant canonical representation from observations across all timestamps. During joint training, a stop-gradient operation blocks the deformation-mediated gradient pathway to the canonical positions while preserving their direct refinement through the reconstruction objective. Each Gaussian then predicts independent temporal offsets for position, rotation, and scale, enabling detailed local motion within a structurally constrained scaffold. A canonical-residual appearance decomposition further models frame-dependent photometric changes without forcing them into geometric deformation. Experiments on synthetic monocular and real-world multiview benchmarks show that GrainGS achieves high reconstruction quality, real-time novel view synthesis, and compact storage. Under the synthetic benchmark setting, it reaches an average peak signal-to-noise ratio of 36.98 decibels, renders at 435.6 frames per second, and requires 4.67 megabytes of storage.

</details>


### [75] [SPDCN: Strip-based Deformable Convolutional Network for Steel Surface Defect Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21456)
*Zhongming Liu,Bingbing Jiang,Guangxin Wan,Xiang Zou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Two-stage SPDCN introduces FMCM and ADADC to address elongated steel defects, achieving high accuracy with compact parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial steel surface defects (cracks, scratches) are elongated and anisotropic; standard CNNs with isotropic receptive fields and rigid sampling fail to capture irregular, orientation-dependent boundaries, hindering segmentation performance.

Method: FMCM: fuzzy-enhanced multi-scale context via group-wise multi-branch convolutions and intuitionistic fuzzy channel attention. ADADC: decoupled horizontal and vertical strip convolutions in deformable conv to align sampling with defect orientation.

Result: On NEU-Seg benchmark, SPDCN achieves 89.60% mIoU with 3.54M parameters, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Code released at GitHub.

Conclusion: SPDCN effectively handles elongated defects by combining anisotropic deformable sampling with fuzzy multi-scale context, offering strong accuracy with low model complexity and good reproducibility.

Abstract: Steel surface defect segmentation is critical for industrial quality inspection, yet existing methods struggle with elongated, anisotropic defects such as cracks and scratches due to the isotropic receptive fields of standard convolutions and rigid sampling grids that cannot adapt to irregular defect boundaries. To address these limitations, we propose Strip-based Predictor for Deformable Convolutional Networks (SPDCN) with two key innovations. The \textbf{Fuzzy-enhanced Multi-scale Context Module (FMCM)} employs group-wise multi-branch convolutions with an intuitionistic fuzzy channel attention mechanism to adaptively capture multi-scale contextual information across varying defect sizes. The \textbf{Adaptive Direction-Aware Deformable Convolution (ADADC)} replaces the conventional offset predictor with decoupled horizontal and vertical strip convolutions, enabling the deformable sampling grid to anisotropically align with the principal orientation of elongated defects. Extensive experiments on public steel surface defect benchmarks demonstrate that SPDCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 89.60\% mIoU on NEU-Seg with only 3.54M parameters. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/DWlzm .

</details>


### [76] [CLUIE: Clustering-Aware Recurrent Propagation with Local Structural Compensation for Underwater Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21467)
*Kui Jiang,Zefan Feng,Laibin Chang,Yan Luo,Junjun Jiang,Xiaopeng Fan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CRWKV: a clustering-aware RWKV framework for region-adaptive underwater image enhancement; introduces CSDR for semantic-based dynamic token ordering and DMLP for local propagation control, achieving state-of-the-art results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater degradation is depth- and region-dependent, causing heterogeneous restoration needs; fixed, content-agnostic RWKV lacks adaptation for non-uniform scenes.

Method: Replace fixed recurrent path with content-adaptive token trajectory via CSDR, grouping tokens by semantic similarity and deriving dynamic traversal from inter-cluster relations; apply DMLP to maintain local continuity using depthwise convolution and a neighborhood-aware pseudo-dark response to modulate propagation.

Result: Experiments on multiple underwater benchmarks show state-of-the-art quantitative metrics and improved visual quality.

Conclusion: CRWKV successfully combines semantic-aware long-range modeling with local structural compensation to handle non-uniform underwater degradations.

Abstract: Underwater image enhancement remains challenging due to wavelength-dependent light absorption, scattering, and backscattering, which jointly cause color distortion, contrast degradation, and detail loss. Since these degradations vary with scene depth and imaging conditions, different regions within the same image often exhibit heterogeneous degradation patterns and thus require region-adaptive restoration. Although visual RWKV models offer an efficient linear-complexity solution for long-range dependency modeling, their predefined scanning orders are content-agnostic and therefore fail to adapt recurrent state propagation to spatially non-uniform restoration demands. To address this limitation, we propose a Clustering-aware RWKV framework, termed CRWKV, which reformulates the fixed recurrent propagation path of conventional RWKV into a content-adaptive token trajectory. Specifically, we introduce Clustering-aware Semantic Dynamic Reordering (CSDR), which groups tokens according to semantic feature similarity and derives a dynamic traversal order from inter-cluster contextual relations. This design enables WKV states to be accumulated along semantically correlated regions rather than fixed spatial or spectral orders. Since dynamic reordering may disrupt the local continuity of original spatial neighborhoods, we further propose Dark-response Modulated Local Propagation (DMLP), which extracts local structural responses via depth-wise convolution and adaptively modulates their propagation strength using a neighborhood-aware pseudo-dark response map. In this way, local structural cues are compensated before recurrent aggregation while preserving content-adaptive long-range modeling. Extensive experiments on multiple underwater image enhancement benchmarks demonstrate that CRWKV achieves state-of-the-art quantitative performance and superior visual quality.

</details>


### [77] [Future Rendering $\neq$ Future Surface: A Benchmark and Dataset for Dynamic Surface Reconstruction Beyond the Observed Window](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21471)
*Yukun Shi,Minglun Gong*

Main category: cs.CV
