TL;DR: A diagnostic benchmark and dataset (FutureSurf) for future-time surface reconstruction, evaluating how well methods predict surface geometry beyond the observed window using Chamfer distance, with controlled motions and falsification scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dynamic-scene benchmarks evaluate only within the observed window; deployment contexts (AR, robotics, anticipatory planning) require accurate future geometry, but there is no standardized benchmark for future-time surface reconstruction.

Method: Eight analytically defined controlled motions with exact per-frame ground-truth meshes and three falsification controls; train on the first 75% of sequences; evaluate future frames using Chamfer distance (primary metric: absolute future CD) and a future/observed gap; provide a ground-truth recoverability oracle; release split files, scoring code, benchmark card, and Croissant metadata; tested across two backbones (DG-Mesh and Deformable-3DGS) and additional animated scenes.

Result: Substantial future-surface gaps observed: 2.7–4.1x for DG-Mesh and 2.0–6.6x for Deformable-3DGS; four of five recoverable from observed motion by a fixed rule; falsification controls function as intended (surface-invariant motion shows no gap); future rendering quality metrics are decoupled from future-surface accuracy; future-error concentrates where the surface moves.

Conclusion: FutureSurf uncovers persistent, structured gaps in future geometry not captured by existing metrics, highlighting the need for dedicated future-time surface benchmarks; provides controlled data, tooling, and ground-truth mechanisms; resources announced on Hugging Face and GitHub.

Abstract: Dynamic-scene reconstruction is almost always evaluated inside the observed time window, yet deployment settings such as AR overlays, robot interaction, and anticipatory planning need the future surface: the geometry at times beyond those captured. No standard benchmark measures this. We introduce FutureSurf, a controlled diagnostic benchmark and dataset for future-time surface reconstruction that trades scene diversity for exact future ground truth and falsification controls. A method trains on the observed first 75% of a sequence; we score its extracted per-frame surface on the held-out future by Chamfer distance, reporting absolute future CD as the primary score and the future/observed gap as a diagnostic. The dataset contains eight analytically defined controlled motions, including three falsification controls, with exact per-frame ground-truth meshes. We also provide a ground-truth-side recoverability oracle. The release includes split files, scoring code, a benchmark card, and Croissant metadata. On the controlled motions, the DG-Mesh backbone leaves a 2.7-4.1$\times$ gap even for futures predictable in principle (four of five recoverable from observed motion by a fixed rule), while the falsification controls behave as designed (the surface-invariant motion shows no gap). Beyond the contributed dataset, the gap persists across six animated DG-Mesh asset scenes and a second backbone, Deformable-3DGS (2.0-6.6$\times$; both share a deformation-MLP temporal model). The benchmark also shows that future rendering quality and future-surface accuracy are statistically decoupled, so the novel-view-synthesis metrics the field reports do not track future geometry. The future error is structured, concentrating where the surface moves. The dataset, evaluation toolkit, and scoring code are available on Hugging Face and GitHub (https://github.com/Ricky-S/futuresurf).

</details>


### [78] [Recurrent Sinusoidal INRs for Efficient High-Fidelity Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21485)
*Hyunmin Cho,Jaejun Yoo,Kyong Hwan Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Sinusoidal recurrence enriches the spectral content of implicit neural representations by inducing a harmonic line spectrum; a shared sinusoidal block iteratively refines latent representations, yielding higher fidelity with fewer parameters and steps, with transfer to super-resolution, NeRF, and SDF.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: INRs often struggle with spectral efficiency and limited effective bandwidth. The work analyzes how sinusoidal activations and recurrence can expand the spectral support and provide a principled mechanism for spectral enrichment.

Method: Proposes a recurrent architecture using a shared sinusoidal block that iteratively refines the latent code. Provides spectral analysis showing the induced harmonic line spectrum. Empirically compares against feed-forward INRs, non-sinusoidal recurrent variants, and equilibrium-style sinusoidal models. Evaluates on RGB image benchmarks and cross-domain tasks (super-resolution, NeRF, SDF).

Result: Sinusoidal activations produce a harmonic line spectrum; recurrent unrolling expands spectral support. The proposed architecture achieves higher image fidelity than baselines with fewer parameters and fewer optimization steps, and transfers favorably to SR, NeRF, and SDF tasks.

Conclusion: Sinusoidal recurrence offers a principled spectral mechanism for enriching INRs, with practical gains in efficiency and cross-domain transfer. The approach warrants further exploration of spectral properties, stability, and broader 2D/3D representations.

Abstract: We study sinusoidal recurrence as an iterative mechanism for harmonic spectral enrichment in implicit neural representations (INRs). Our analysis reveals that sinusoidal activations induce a harmonic line spectrum, providing a spectral account of how recurrent unrolling enriches the effective spectral support. We realize this principle with a shared sinusoidal block that iteratively refines the latent representation. We empirically validate the resulting spectral behavior against feed-forward INRs, non-sinusoidal recurrent variants, and equilibrium-style sinusoidal models. Complementing this analysis, we evaluate the proposed architecture across image and 3D representation tasks. On RGB image benchmarks, our method achieves higher fidelity than feed-forward baselines with fewer parameters and fewer optimization steps, and it further transfers favorably to super-resolution, NeRF, and SDF tasks.

</details>


### [79] [Texture++: Elevating 3D Asset Texture Resolution with a Region-Aware Diffusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21504)
*Shuaiwei Wang,Shi Li,Jieting Xu,Yuchi Huo,Qi Wang,Wenting Zheng,Rengan Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Texture++ presents a diffusion-based texture super-resolution pipeline that operates across multiple rendered views in UV space, using adaptive view selection and a quadtree-based region merging to produce cohesive, high-resolution texture maps for 3D assets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many 3D assets are discarded due to low texture resolution. Existing SR methods focus on natural images and ignore texture maps, limiting reuse of aging assets in film and games. A generalizable texture SR model is needed to revitalize these assets.

Method: Reformulate SR in UV space as multi-view SR: render multiple views of the texture, perform SR for each view, and merge outputs. Use adaptive view selection to integrate textures across UV patches. Employ a quadtree-based region organization with masks to identify regions needing improvement. Apply a diffusion-based SR model to enhance the SR for masked regions and seamlessly blend with surrounding areas.

Result: Comprehensive evaluations show substantial improvements in texture detail and coherence compared with existing methods.

Conclusion: Texture++ delivers more complete, high-quality textures and demonstrates promising generalization across assets, enabling the revival of low-resolution textures for 3D assets.

Abstract: Numerous 3D assets are discarded due to low texture resolution, while current super-resolution models ignore texture maps and focus on natural images. An efficient and generalizable texture super-resolution model can revitalize a large corpus of aging yet valuable assets across industries such as film and video games. We present Texture++, a novel framework for texture super-resolution, which enhances the low-resolution textures of assets to produce high-resolution, high-quality results. Specifically, we reformulate the task of super-resolution in UV space into performing it across multiple rendered views and merging the outputs. Firstly, to achieve more complete and continuous textures in the view space, we propose an adaptive view selection strategy to integrate textures dispersed across UV texture patches. Furthermore, we introduce a quadtree-based texture region organization method for combining super-resolved textures from different viewpoints, providing masks to distinguish regions that require improvement. Finally, we design a diffusion-based super-resolution model that enhances the texture resolution for specified masked regions, seamlessly integrating with surrounding regions. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that our approach yields textures with substantially improved detail and coherence over existing methods.

</details>


### [80] [Boosting Robustness for All-Weather Self-Supervised Depth Estimation in Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21526)
*Mengshi Qi,Xiaoyang Bi,Xianlin Zhang,Huadong Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A self-training framework for robust depth estimation in adverse weather using uncertainty-aware multi-teacher distillation and camera-ray guided radar fusion (POV-BEV) to fuse camera and sparse radar data, achieving state-of-the-art results on all-weather datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-supervised depth estimation degrades under adverse weather due to distorted pixel correspondences and sparse radar fusion. The work aims to improve robustness and fusion by leveraging unpaired all-weather data and multi-sensor information.

Method: (1) Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Teacher Distillation: generate diverse teacher models with different adverse condition inputs; weigh the distillation loss with uncertainty estimates. (2) POV-BEV Radar Fusion: align camera POV and radar BEV via camera-ray constraints to utilize denser radar points and fuse perspectives.

Result: Extensive experiments show robustness and state-of-the-art performance on all-weather datasets; qualitative and quantitative results support effectiveness. Code and models released.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline addresses both deterioration of self-supervised supervision under adverse weather and sparse radar fusion, delivering robust depth estimation and effective camera-radar fusion with practical benefits.

Abstract: Self-supervised depth estimation is challenging for safe autonomous driving under various adverse weather conditions due to sensor perception degradation. These challenges arise from two main aspects. Firstly, adverse conditions can distort pixel correspondences and violate the assumptions embedded in the self-supervised loss function, leading to erroneous depth predictions. Secondly, while radar is a widely adopted sensor in adverse weather conditions, the sparse distribution of radar points in the Point of View (POV) poses challenges for self-supervised fusion. To address these issues, we introduce a novel self-training pipeline using unpaired real all-weather data through multi-teacher distillation and robust radar fusion. We propose the Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Teacher Distillation method to generate diverse teacher models with different adverse condition inputs, and then employ uncertainty modeling to weigh the knowledge distillation loss. Additionally, we design the POV-BEV Radar Fusion approach, which leverages camera-pixel ray constraints to establish connections between the camera's Point of View (POV) and the radar's Bird's-Eye View (BEV). This approach enables the utilization of denser radar points, effectively capturing the complementary perspectives of both POV and BEV. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the robustness of our proposed method on all-weather datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/MICLAB-BUPT/RobustDepth.

</details>


### [81] [ElasticTTT: Prior-Preserving Test-Time Tuning for Video Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21529)
*Yueyi Liu,Chi Zhang,Sen Cui,Miao Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ElasticTTT mitigates prior collapse in test-time tuning of pretrained diffusion models for video editing by preserving the generator's prior and elasticity via Target Distribution Regularization, Contrastive CFG, and Asynchronous Noise Schedule, achieving state-of-the-art one-shot video editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the mismatch between the distribution-mapping nature of generative models and the single-point optimization of standard Test-Time Tuning (TTT), which leads to Prior Collapse where text conditions and spatial latents are discarded or entangled.

Method: Introduce ElasticTTT: a framework with (1) Target Distribution Regularization to avoid sharp memorization minima, (2) Contrastive CFG to steer inference away from source biases, and (3) Asynchronous Noise Schedule to preserve unedited regions, all while maintaining and leveraging the base model's generative prior.

Result: The framework preserves the base model's generative prior, mitigates prior collapse, and achieves state-of-the-art performance for one-shot video editing, supported by extensive evaluations and theoretical analysis.

Conclusion: ElasticTTT reconciles the generative prior with one-shot editing tasks, preventing degenerate solution states and enabling robust, high-quality video edits without losing the model's distributional capabilities.

Abstract: Test-Time Tuning (TTT) on pretrained diffusion models has emerged as a powerful paradigm for video editing. However, there exists a foundational mismatch between the distribution-mapping nature of generative models and the single-point optimization of standard TTT. In this paper, we demonstrate that this mismatch triggers \textit{Prior Collapse}, a degenerate state where the model discards the text conditions and spatial latents, collapsing generations to the source video, or entangling the features of distinct regions. To resolve this, we propose \textbf{ElasticTTT}, a novel framework that preserves the prior generative distribution and rescues generative elasticity. Specifically, we propose \textit{Target Distribution Regularization} to prevent sharp memorization minima, \textit{Contrastive CFG} to guide inference away from source biases, and \textit{Asynchronous Noise Schedule} to preserve unedited regions. Extensive evaluations, supported by theoretical analysis, demonstrate that ElasticTTT successfully preserves the generative prior of the base model, achieving state-of-the-art performance on one-shot video editing.

</details>


### [82] [Towards Robust Iris Recognition Through Occlusion Identification and Conditional Diffusion-Based Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21545)
*Kamrul Hasan,Mylene C. Q. Farias,Oleg V. Komogortsev*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Occlusion-aware iris recognition framework with three modules: occlusion-type identification, diffusion-based reconstruction, and deep-learning-based recognition, using a residual CNN for occlusion type, a diffusion model for reconstruction conditioned on the mask and type, and a VGG19-HPMNet for recognition; evaluated on CASIA-Iris-Thousand with synthetic occlusions showing improved performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Iris recognition performance degrades when iris texture is occluded by eyelids, eyelashes, specular reflections, or other artifacts; existing methods either operate on degraded samples or rely only on visible iris regions, which is insufficient when substantial texture is corrupted.

Method: Three sequential modules: (1) occlusion-type identification via a residual 2D CNN to classify non-occluded vs specific occlusion categories; (2) diffusion-based reconstruction that takes the occluded image, binary mask, and predicted occlusion type to reconstruct the corrupted region; (3) recognition using VGG19-HPMNet (a modified VGG19 with horizontal pyramid mapping) to extract global and part-wise local iris features for classification.

Result: On CASIA-Iris-Thousand under a controlled synthetic-occlusion protocol, the framework improves iris recognition by identifying occlusion type, reconstructing masked areas, and re-evaluating restored samples.

Conclusion: An effective occlusion-aware iris recognition approach that combines occlusion-type identification, diffusion-based reconstruction, and enhanced feature extraction to improve robustness under synthetic occlusions.

Abstract: Iris recognition is a reliable biometric approach that identifies individuals using the distinctive and stable texture of the iris. However, recognition performance can degrade when discriminative iris texture is partially occluded by eyelids, eyelashes, specular reflections, or other acquisition artifacts. Existing approaches often perform recognition directly on degraded samples or rely only on the remaining visible iris region, which may be inadequate when substantial texture is corrupted. To address this limitation, we propose an occlusion-aware iris recognition framework with three sequential modules: occlusion-type identification, diffusion-based reconstruction, and deep-learning-based recognition. First, a residual 2D CNN-based network determines whether an iris image is non-occluded or belongs to one of the controlled occlusion categories. Second, the occluded image, binary mask, and predicted occlusion type condition a denoising diffusion probabilistic model to reconstruct the corrupted region. Finally, VGG19-HPMNet, a modified VGG19 model with horizontal pyramid mapping, extracts discriminative global and part-wise local iris features for recognition. Experiments on the CASIA-Iris-Thousand dataset under a controlled synthetic-occlusion protocol show that the proposed framework improves iris recognition performance by identifying the occlusion type, reconstructing masked regions, and re-evaluating the restored iris samples.

</details>


### [83] [UnDA: Unpaired Domain Alignment for Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21546)
*Rafsan Jany,Shadab Tanjeed Ahmad,Ahsan Bulbul,Tahsinul Islam,Md Azam Hossain,Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UnDA is an anchor-guided, backbone-agnostic unpaired cross-modal distillation framework featuring an Attention-based Alignment Module, Uncertainty-Weighted Optimal Transport (UCT-OT), and per-class ProtoNCE memories, yielding robust cross-modal knowledge transfer without paired data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-modal distillation faces large modality gaps and noisy supervision, while paired clinical data are scarce in real-world settings. A backbone-agnostic method that robustly transfers semantic structure across modalities without paired data is highly desirable.

Method: 1) Alignment Module: backbone-agnostic, uses attention-based pooling to extract semantically structured class tokens. 2) UCT-OT: dynamically weights feature-level alignment by prediction confidence to reduce noise in supervision. 3) ProtoNCE: per-class prototype memories enforce global discriminability across unpaired batches.

Result: In strictly unpaired segmentation benchmarks, UnDA consistently improves accuracy and boundary precision in the target modality, demonstrating effective structural knowledge transfer across heterogeneous data sources without paired datasets.

Conclusion: UnDA provides a robust, scalable approach to unpaired cross-modal distillation by combining anchor-guided alignment, uncertainty-aware optimal transport, and prototype-based contrastive learning, enabling meaningful cross-modality transfer without paired data.

Abstract: Multimodal based approaches often outperform single modality approaches in downstream tasks as the different modalities provide complementary information, yet acquiring paired clinical data remains a significant challenge in real world scenarios. While cross-modal knowledge distillation addresses this, existing methods often struggle with large modality gaps and the propagation of noise from uncertain source-domain predictions. To overcome these challenges, we propose UnDA, an anchor-guided framework for unpaired cross-modal distillation. Our approach introduces a backbone-agnostic Alignment Module that extracts semantically structured class tokens via an attention based pooling mechanism. To ensure robust knowledge transfer, we propose Uncertainty-Weighted Optimal Transport (UCT-OT), which dynamically weights feature-level alignment based on prediction confidence, effectively suppressing noisy supervision. Furthermore, a per-class ProtoNCE objective maintains stable prototype memories to enforce global discriminability across unpaired batches. Evaluations on representative segmentation tasks under strictly unpaired settings show consistent improvements in accuracy and boundary precision in the target modality, demonstrating that meaningful structural knowledge can be transferred across heterogeneous data sources without paired datasets.

</details>


### [84] [SANA-Video 2.0: Hybrid Linear Attention with Attention Residuals for Efficient Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21553)
*Junsong Chen,Jincheng Yu,Yitong Li,Shuchen Xue,Haozhe Liu,Jingyu Xin,Yuyang Zhao,Tian Ye,Zhangjie Wu,Zian Wang,Daquan Zhou,Ping Luo,Song Han,Enze Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A hybrid video diffusion transformer (SANA-Video 2.0) at 5B/14B scales generates 720p video on a single GPU by combining gated linear attention with periodic softmax anchors, augmented by AttnRes for depth propagation, trained from scratch, and accelerated with hardware-optimized back-end to achieve high quality with substantial speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce the quadratic cost and limited long-range modeling of full softmax attention in video diffusion, while preserving softmax-level expressiveness for long, high-resolution video generation on accessible hardware.

Method: Introduce Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention: gated linear attention for O(N)-dominated mixing plus periodic gated-softmax anchors at a 3:1 ratio; Block Attention Residuals (AttnRes) to propagate refreshed representations across depth; train from scratch to learn the hybrid directly; use reduced-resolution proxy studies to select 25% softmax as the optimum trade-off; 40-step sampling; optimize with full-stack Sol-Engine (kernel fusion, caching, sparse attention) to maximize hardware efficiency.

Result: Achieves up to 720p video on a single GPU; matches full-softmax video DiTs in quality; retains long-sequence benefits of linear attention; 25% softmax is the optimal quality-efficiency point; 40-step sampling yields VBench 84.30 at 480p in 13.2s on a single H100; compiled DiT forward is 3.2x faster than a full-softmax baseline at 720p/60s; Sol-Engine optimizations add 3.58x speedup, bringing 5B pipeline to 13.06s at 720p/5s and ~120x faster than Wan 2.2-A14B on one H100.

Conclusion: The hybrid design recovers softmax-level expressiveness at substantially reduced cost, enabling scalable long-range, high-resolution video generation with strong practical speedups and a path toward efficient deployment.

Abstract: We introduce SANA-Video 2.0, a hybrid video diffusion transformer instantiated at 5B and 14B scales under a unified architecture. Designed to generate high-quality video up to 720p on a single GPU, SANA-Video 2.0 matches full-softmax video DiTs in quality while retaining the favorable long-sequence scaling of linear attention. To avoid quadratic attention throughout, Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention combines gated linear attention for O(N)-dominated mixing with periodic gated-softmax anchors at a 3:1 ratio, restoring the full-rank token interactions that pure linear attention lacks. To propagate these refreshed representations across depth, Block Attention Residuals (AttnRes) route completed block summaries into later linear layers, enabling anchor-feature reuse and boosting deep-layer effective rank by ~12%. Through from-scratch training, SANA-Video 2.0 learns the complete hybrid directly rather than linearizing pretrained models, with reduced-resolution proxy studies establishing 25% softmax as the optimal quality-efficiency trade-off. With 40-step sampling, SANA-Video 2.0 achieves a VBench score of 84.30 in 13.2s at 480p on a single H100, remaining competitive with far larger softmax video DiTs at a fraction of the latency. Its compiled DiT forward pass is 3.2x faster than a matched full-softmax baseline at 720p/60s, a gap that expands with video duration. Furthermore, full-stack Sol-Engine optimization (kernel fusion, caching, and sparse attention) accelerates this hardware-friendly backbone by a further 3.58x, bringing the 5B pipeline to 13.06s at 720p/5s and making it 120x faster than Wan 2.2-A14B on one H100. Overall, our hybrid design recovers softmax-level expressiveness at substantially reduced cost, unlocking scalable long, high resolution video generation.

</details>


### [85] [Visual Contrastive Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21556)
*Yijun Liang,Yunjie Tian,Yijiang Li,Yuqi Jia,Furong Huang,Tianyi Zhou,Di Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VCSD is a purely input-conditioned on-policy self-distillation that uses a content-erasing control to create a contrastive learning signal from the same prompt, eliminating the need for external teachers or privileged information. It sharpens the teacher’s image-conditioned distribution within its plausible support and distills it to the student.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To remove all asymmetric information in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) by eliminating external teachers, privileged signals, and visual evidence, and test whether input conditioning alone suffices to provide a stronger learning signal.

Method: At each student-generated response prefix, an EMA teacher computes two next-token distributions for the same prompt/prefix: one conditioned on the original image and one conditioned on a content-erased control. The token-wise log-probability difference identifies tokens whose likelihood is increased by the visual content. This contrast is used to sharpen the teacher's original-image distribution within its plausible support, and this full-distribution target is distilled into the student. No external teacher, privileged answers, visual-evidence signals, reasoning traces, or extra inference-cost are required.

Result: On the ViRL39K dataset, VCSD consistently outperforms matched OPSD across Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 models. For example, on Qwen3-VL the seven-benchmark aggregate improves from 62.27% to 67.04% at 2B, 71.30% to 73.16% at 4B, and 72.51% to 76.26% at 8B.

Conclusion: VCSD demonstrates that a purely input-conditioned, on-policy self-distillation framework can outperform OPSD without external teachers or auxiliary signals, offering a simpler and cost-efficient approach for multimodal instruction-tuning.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is promising as it removes the external teacher required by on-policy distillation (OPD), yet it still needs asymmetric information between teacher and student to ensure that the self-teacher provides a stronger learning signal than the student. Existing methods create this asymmetry either through privileged answers or visual evidence. We ask whether both can be removed, yielding a simpler form of OPSD driven purely by input conditioning. For this purpose, we propose Visual Contrastive Self-Distillation, namely VCSD, which converts image-content removal into an on-policy self-distillation signal. At each student-generated response prefix, the EMA teacher produces two next-token distributions under the same prompt and prefix -- one conditioned on the original image and the other on a content-erased control. Their token-wise log-probability difference highlights candidates whose likelihood is specifically increased by the instance-level visual content. We use this contrast to sharpen the teacher's original-image distribution within its plausible support, and distill the resulting full-distribution target into the student. Using ViRL39K dataset, VCSD consistently outperforms matched OPSD across Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 models. For example, on Qwen3-VL, it improves the seven-benchmark aggregate from $62.27\% \rightarrow 67.04\%$ at 2B, $71.30\% \rightarrow 73.16\%$ at 4B, and $72.51\% \rightarrow 76.26\%$ at 8B. Furthermore, VCSD requires no external teacher, privileged answers, visual evidence signals, reasoning traces, or additional inference-time cost.

</details>


### [86] [Scene Parameter Saliency via Differentiable Light Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21562)
*Linas Beresna,Eugene Fiume*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Differentiable renderers enable metric-specific gradient fields (metric saliency maps) that reveal which scene elements most influence a scalar image-based metric, via backpropagation; saliency depends on the metric, not on the scene alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how scene parameters influence image-based metrics through the image formation process, enabling interpretable attribution similar to neural saliency but via light transport.

Method: Compute per-parameter gradients of a scalar metric with respect to scene parameters by a single reverse-mode pass through a differentiable renderer; generate metric saliency maps for multiple objectives (psychovisual glare indices, mean luminance, neural perceptual scores).

Result: Saliency rankings vary across metrics; parameters dominating one objective may be negligible for another; metric saliency is metric-specific; derivative images are informative about scene understanding akin to primal images.

Conclusion: Differentiable rendering yields informative gradient-based saliency (metric saliency maps) that reveal parameter dependencies for different objectives, enhancing interpretability of rendering-based optimization and analysis.

Abstract: Gradient-based saliency methods reveal which input features most influence a neural network's output, and are a standard tool for model interpretability. We observe that differentiable renderers, which are conventionally used for parameter optimisation, produce an analogous form of saliency: given any scalar metric evaluated on a rendered image, a single reverse-mode differentiation pass yields per-parameter gradients that identify which scene elements most influence the metric. We call these gradient fields metric saliency maps. Unlike neural saliency, which propagates attribution through learned weights, metric saliency propagates through the image formation process itself, including multi-bounce light transport, capturing parameter dependencies that are semi-opaque to manual inspection. We compute metric saliency maps for qualitatively different objectives: psychovisual glare indices, mean scene luminance, and neural perceptual scores. The saliency rankings differ substantially across metrics for the same scene, with parameters that dominate one objective being negligible for another. The saliency map is specific to the metric, not an intrinsic property of the scene. Our results suggest that differentiable renderers produce derivative images that are as informative for scene understanding as the primal images they were designed to generate.

</details>


### [87] [Self-Supervised Learning of Structured Dynamics from Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21576)
*Lukas Knobel,Andrew Zisserman,Yuki M. Asano*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SDM recovers structured, interpretable video dynamics by predicting future features and explicitly splitting camera-induced change from object motion, leveraging frozen ViT features and weak supervision from synthetic data; it outperforms simple baselines and competes with strongly supervised methods on ProbeMotion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motion in video mixes camera motion and object motion, and disentangling these factors is hard but valuable for robust video representations; prior work lacks effective supervision and structured latent dynamics.

Method: Freeze a pretrained image ViT; train Structured Dynamics Model (SDM) to predict future features, explicitly separating the dominant temporal change (likely camera motion) from residual dynamics; use self-supervision on real video plus weak supervision from synthetic Kubric data to guide the scene dynamics; evaluate on ProbeMotion with various motion types.

Result: SDM outperforms backbone baselines that use global CLS or average pooling; it also compares favorably to strongly supervised representations like VGGT on several probes, despite weaker supervision; demonstrates that pretrained models can yield structured, interpretable video dynamics.

Conclusion: Pretrained image models can be repurposed to yield structured, disentangled video-dynamics representations, providing a useful inductive bias for learning and analyzing latent motion dynamics.

Abstract: Understanding motion in video is a fundamental challenge for visual learning, as frame-to-frame change entangles two sources of dynamics: camera motion and object motion. This decomposition has remained underexplored in representation learning, partly because these factors are tightly coupled in natural videos and difficult to supervise separately. Yet recovering it is important for learning robust motion representations that separate meaningful object dynamics from camera-induced variation. We study whether such structured motion representations can be recovered from frozen features of a pretrained image vision transformer. We propose the Structured Dynamics Model (SDM), which explicitly separates the dominant source of temporal change from residual dynamics through future-feature prediction, rather than representing video change with a single entangled latent or with unstructured, spatially dense transition tokens. Training combines self-supervised learning on real video with weak supervision of scene dynamics on synthetic Kubric data. We evaluate SDM on ProbeMotion, a new evaluation suite spanning synthetic and real videos with camera motion, object motion, and combined dynamics. SDM outperforms backbone baselines using global CLS or average-pooled features, and compares favorably to strongly supervised representations such as VGGT on several probes, despite using substantially weaker supervision. These results suggest that pretrained image models can be readily repurposed into structured video-dynamics representations, providing a useful inductive bias for learning and analyzing latent video dynamics.

</details>


### [88] [Synthetic data generation framework for quality control automation in gravure printing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21577)
*Korota Arsène Coulibaly,Mohamed Hamlich,Khalid Hmali,Andrea Trombin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Synthetic data framework for rotogravure defect detection enabling RFDETR to reach 80.9% mAP on real tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world industrial defect datasets are scarce; manual inspection is slow and subjective; robust DL models require ample data; synthetic data can bridge the gap.

Method: Automated pipeline generates high-fidelity images of defects (creases, streaks, misregistration) with bounding boxes/annotations; dataset of 7,533 images; train RFDETR (state-of-the-art detector) on synthetic data; evaluate on real samples.

Result: Achieved mAP 80.9% on real industrial testing samples; demonstrates viability of zero-cost, rapid deployment without large manual data collection.

Conclusion: Synthetic-data-driven approach is practical for rotogravure QC and can accelerate deployment of automated defect inspection; potential limitations include generalization to unseen defects and variations; further validation across multiple lines and defect categories recommended.

Abstract: Quality control in printing, particularly in rotogravure printing, still depends on slow, costly, and subjective manual inspection. Automated surface defect detection is critical for maintaining high-quality standards in rotogravure printing. Deep learning models give prospects for automation. However, training robust deep learning models, such as YOLO or Vision Transformers, is heavily hindered by the extreme scarcity of real-world industrial defects images. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a novel synthetic data generation framework tailored for rotogravure printing quality control. The proposed pipeline automatically generates high-fidelity images of specific printing defects (creases, streaks, misregistration, etc.) and outputs corresponding bounding boxes and annotations. To validate the framework, a synthetic dataset of 7533 images was generated and used to train the state-of-the-art object-detection model RFDETR. Experimental results demonstrate that the model trained on our synthetic data achieves a Mean Average Precision (mAP) of 80.9\% on real industrial testing samples. This framework provides a zero-cost, rapid-deployment solution for automating defect inspection in printing lines without requiring massive manual data collection.

</details>


### [89] [GraphVid: Interactive Graph-Controllable Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21580)
*Vedant Shah,Onkar Susladkar,Tushar Prakash,Kiet Nguyen,Tianjio Yu,Adheesh Juvekar,Muntasir Waheed,Ismini Lourentzou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GraphVid introduces a graph-conditioned image-to-video generator and GraphVid-Bench dataset for structured, interaction-aware video generation; achieves strong controllability and quality with less data/parameters, outperforming Motion-I2V on FID/FVD/PSNR/SSIM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Controllable video generation is hard because text prompts or motion controls struggle to specify precise multi-object interactions; occlusion/overlap introduce ambiguity; structured interaction graphs offer flexible yet exact multi-subject control.

Method: Propose GraphVid, a graph-conditioned image-to-video generation model that uses structured interaction graphs to guide generation; curate GraphVid-Bench with relational annotations to enable training of interaction-aware video generation models; demonstrate data/parameter efficiency and improved metrics; compare to Motion-I2V.

Result: GraphVid achieves strong controllability and video quality, reducing FID by up to 39.9% and FVD by 37.6% relative to Motion-I2V, while improving PSNR from 9.87 to 15.98 and SSIM from 0.38 to 0.61.

Conclusion: Structured semantic interfaces via interaction graphs are a potent paradigm for controllable video generation; GraphVid demonstrates that structured representations can achieve higher quality with less data and fewer trainable parameters.

Abstract: Controllable video generation remains challenging due to the difficulty of specifying precise multi-object interactions using text prompts or motion-control inputs that primarily constrain pixel movement. In practice, trajectory-based control often requires users to draw accurate tracks for multiple objects, which scales poorly with scene complexity and becomes ambiguous under occlusion or overlap. To enable flexible yet precise multi-subject control, we introduce $\textbf{GraphVid}$, a graph-conditioned image-to-video generation model that enables interactive control through structured interaction graphs. We further curate $\textbf{GraphVid-Bench}$, a large-scale interaction-centric video dataset with structured relational annotations to enable training of interaction-aware video generation models. Despite using substantially less training data and fewer trainable parameters than prior motion-control methods, GraphVid delivers strong controllability and video quality. Compared with Motion-I2V, GraphVid reduces FID by up to 39.9% and FVD by 37.6%, while improving PSNR (9.87=>15.98) and SSIM (0.38=>0.61). Our results highlight the potential of structured semantic interfaces as a powerful paradigm for controllable video generation.

</details>


### [90] [Inference-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models via Progressive Seed Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21591)
*Rogerio Guimaraes,Pietro Perona*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PSP front-loads seed exploration in diffusion/flow-matching models to improve inference-time efficiency under a fixed compute budget by progressively pruning seeds based on intermediate denoised scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time seed sensitivity in diffusion/flow-matching models leads to inefficient compute; prior approaches maintain fixed memory while exploring seeds; need an effective, scalable method to balance exploration and denoising at inference.

Method: Progressive Seed Pruning (PSP): evaluate many seeds early, score intermediate denoised estimates, and progressively prune the candidate set so only the most promising trajectories are fully denoised; the total number of model evaluations remains fixed; demonstrated across diffusion and flow-matching backbones.

Result: PSP consistently improves reward-guided seed selection and GenEval (automated) scores, and outperforms best-of-N, importance sampling, and tree-search baselines at matched compute; also yields better human evaluation on prompt alignment.

Conclusion: Front-loading exploration with aggressive pruning is a practical inference-time scaling axis for diffusion/flow-matching models, enabling higher-quality outputs under a fixed compute budget.

Abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching models dominate conditional image generation, yet inference-time scaling for these models is far less developed than for autoregressive language models. Because final quality is highly sensitive to the initial noise seed, many approaches spend extra compute on seed search or resampling under a black-box reward, but typically maintaining a constant memory footprint throughout inference. We show that relaxing this constraint enables an underexplored inference-time scaling axis: by front-loading exploration, evaluating many seeds early, and pruning aggressively, we can use a fixed compute budget more effectively. \emph{Progressive Seed Pruning} (\PSP) scores intermediate denoised estimates and progressively narrows the candidate set so that only promising trajectories are fully denoised, while keeping the total number of model evaluations fixed. Across diffusion and flow-matching backbones, \PSP \ consistently improves reward-guided selection and achieves higher GenEval scores (automated) and better human evaluation on prompt-alignment than best-of-$N$, importance-sampling, and tree-search baselines at matched compute. Project page: https://www.vision.caltech.edu/psp. Code: https://github.com/rogerioagjr/psp.

</details>


### [91] [Unified Video Dense Prediction from Disjoint Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21592)
*Yihong Sun,Seoung Wug Oh,Jiahui Huang,Bharath Hariharan,Joon-Young Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniD is a unified video model that jointly predicts eight dense scene properties from disjoint, domain-specific datasets using distillation and diffusion-prior bridging to achieve strong generalization and temporal/cross-task consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome fragmented, non-overlapping annotations and the high cost of pseudo-labeling; enable joint prediction of geometry, appearance, and semantics from diverse sources.

Method: Per-task experts supervise a single unified backbone via lightweight task projectors; distillation step; leverages pretrained diffusion priors to bridge domain gaps; training on disjoint datasets for eight tasks.

Result: Competitive with per-task specialists and multi-task baselines; strong generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios; improved temporal and cross-task consistency; code/video results provided.

Conclusion: Diffusion priors enable robust transfer across disjoint training sources; UniD demonstrates effective unified dense scene understanding with reduced annotation requirements.

Abstract: Scene understanding requires simultaneous prediction about geometry, appearance, and semantics. However, existing task-specific annotations are fragmented across incompatible, domain-specific datasets. Current unified systems circumvent this by restricting training to fully co-annotated data, or by incurring the large computational cost of pseudo-labeling. To mitigate this, we introduce UniD, a unified video model that jointly predicts eight dense scene properties-depth, surface normals, semantic segmentation, boundaries, human parts, albedo, shading, and materials-all learned from disjoint, domain-specific datasets. We propose a simple yet effective distillation step in which per-task experts supervise a unified backbone through lightweight task projectors, eliminating the need for annotation overlap or pseudo-labeling. Our key insight is that the strong visual priors of a pretrained diffusion model are sufficient to bridge the domain gaps introduced by disjoint training sources, enabling robust generalization to scene-task combinations never seen during training. UniD achieves competitive performance against per-task specialists and multi-task baselines, with strong generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios and enhanced temporal and cross-task consistency. Code and video results are available at https://unid-video.github.io/.

</details>


### [92] [Streaming Multi-Agent Autoregressive Diffusion Model with World State Registers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21594)
*Sicheng Mo,Yuheng Li,Ziyang Leng,Krishna Kumar Singh,Bolei Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WorldWeaver (W^2) introduces explicit cross-agent world-state tokens to maintain persistent, shared state in multi-agent video diffusion, improving consistency and quality, validated on two-agent Minecraft tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive diffusion pipelines conditioned on past observations struggle to maintain coherent, shared world states across multiple agents and views; a persistent world-state mechanism is needed for robust multi-agent generation.

Method: A streaming multi-agent diffusion model augmented with cross-agent world state registers (learnable tokens) updated after each generated chunk; supervision signals for individual agent status, global/bird's-eye states, and scene text; Mixture-of-Transformers with separate weights for world state vs visual frame modeling.

Result: Explicit world-state modeling improves logical consistency and generation quality in two-agent Minecraft video generation.

Conclusion: Explicit, learnable world-state tokens enable better multi-agent coherence in diffusion-based video generation and are likely beneficial for broader multi-agent, multi-view tasks.

Abstract: Multi-agent interactive world models should not only generate consistent observations, but also maintain world states that persist across agents and evolve across views. Existing autoregressive video diffusion pipelines carry forward observation history as conditioning context, which makes shared state difficult to maintain in multi-agent and multi-view settings. We present WorldWeaver (W^2), a streaming multi-agent video diffusion model that augments rollout with cross-agent world state registers: learnable tokens that store shared world information, track individual agent status, and are dynamically updated after each generated chunk. We ground these registers with supervision signals spanning individual agent status, global state views including bird's-eye views, and scene text. We further improve the architecture with a Mixture-of-Transformers design that uses separate weights for world state modeling and visual frame modeling. Extensive experiments in two-agent Minecraft video generation show that explicit world-state modeling improves logical consistency and generation quality.

</details>


### [93] [3D-Aware VLMs with Implicit and Explicit Geometries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21595)
*Wenhao Li,Xueying Jiang,Quanhao Qian,Deli Zhao,Ran Xu,Shijian Lu,Gongjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RGB-only VLM-IE3D adds implicit (IGTs) and explicit (EGTs) 3D geometry tokens plus a 3D-aware adapter to fuse geometry with 2D cues, yielding strong performance on diverse 3D tasks without extra 3D inputs; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 2D-driven VLMs struggle with tasks that require fine-grained 3D spatial understanding. Injecting 3D inductive biases without extra 3D data is desirable. Propose a unified framework that learns both high-level (implicit) and detailed (explicit) 3D geometry from RGB videos.

Method: Introduce Implicit Geometry Tokens (IGTs) capturing high-level geometric priors from input videos and Explicit Geometry Tokens (EGTs) encoding detailed 3D structures from reconstructed attributes. A 3D-aware adapter fuses IGTs, EGTs, and 2D visual cues. Entire pipeline is RGB-only, avoiding additional 3D inputs.

Result: Empirically achieves superior performance across multiple 3D tasks—3D video detection, 3D visual grounding, 3D dense captioning, and spatial reasoning—demonstrating strong and consistent improvements. Code and models are released at the cited repository.

Conclusion: The framework effectively imparts 3D inductive biases to VLMs using both implicit and explicit geometry without 3D data, enabling robust fine-grained 3D reasoning and broad applicability across diverse tasks.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress, most existing vision-language models (VLMs) built from 2D visual inputs often struggle when handling various 3D tasks that require fine-grained spatial understanding and reasoning. To bridge this gap, we present VLM-IE3D, a unified framework that enhances the 3D spatial awareness of VLMs by equipping them with both implicit and explicit 3D geometries learned from RGB videos. Our VLM-IE3D introduces Implicit Geometry Tokens (IGTs) that capture high-level geometric priors from input videos, as well as complementary Explicit Geometry Tokens (EGTs) that encode detailed geometric structures from reconstructed 3D attributes. On top of that, VLM-IE3D comes with a 3D-aware adapter that effectively fuses the two types of geometric representations with 2D visual cues. This RGB-only design injects strong 3D inductive biases for fine-grained spatial understanding and reasoning without requiring any additional 3D inputs. Extensive experiments show that VLM-IE3D achieves superior performance consistently across various 3D tasks including 3D video detection, 3D visual grounding, 3D dense captioning, and spatial reasoning. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Vegetebird/VLM-IE3D.

</details>


### [94] [Deblurring in the Wild: A Real-World Image Deblurring Dataset from Smartphone High-Speed Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19445)
*Syed Mumtahin Mahmud,Mahdi Mohd Hossain Noki,Prothito Shovon Majumder,Abdul Mohaimen Al Radi,Sudipto Das Sukanto,Afia Lubaina,Md. Mosaddek Khan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A large, real-world deblurring dataset from smartphone slow-motion videos (42k+ blur-sharp pairs) enabling more diverse scenes (indoor/outdoor) and longer exposure realism; SOTA deblurring models degrade on it, establishing a challenging benchmark to promote robust, generalizable methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap between synthetic benchmarks and real-world blurred imagery, providing a large, diverse, realistic dataset that captures long-exposure blur from consumer devices to drive development of more robust deblurring models.

Method: Capture slow-motion video at 240 fps over 1 second per scene, generate blur by temporal averaging to simulate long-exposure blur, use the temporally centered frame as the reference sharp image, resulting in 42,000+ high-resolution blur-sharp pairs across ~8x more scenes than prior datasets (indoor/outdoor, varied motion).

Result: State-of-the-art deblurring models exhibit significant performance degradation on the dataset, highlighting increased realism and diversity; the dataset is about 10x larger and ~8x more scenes than existing datasets, posing a more challenging benchmark.

Conclusion: The dataset constitutes a challenging, realistic benchmark for image deblurring, intended to promote the development of robust and generalizable deblurring models suitable for real-world conditions.

Abstract: We introduce the largest real-world image deblurring dataset constructed from smartphone slow-motion videos. Using 240 frames captured over one second, we simulate realistic long-exposure blur by averaging frames to produce blurry images, while using the temporally centered frame as the sharp reference. Our dataset contains over 42,000 high-resolution blur-sharp image pairs, making it approximately 10 times larger than widely used datasets, with 8 times the amount of different scenes, including indoor and outdoor environments, with varying object and camera motions. We benchmark multiple state-of-the-art (SOTA) deblurring models on our dataset and observe significant performance degradation, highlighting the complexity and diversity of our benchmark. Our dataset serves as a challenging new benchmark to facilitate robust and generalizable deblurring models.

</details>

### [95] [Beyond Degree Four: Near-Orthogonal Planar Drawings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21305)
*Patrizio Angelini,Sabine Cornelsen,Giordano Da Lozzo,Seok-Hee Hong,Ignaz Rutter*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: NP-hard to minimize non-orthogonal faces in planar polyline drawings; the authors develop fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms for several parameters, plus a PTAS, and also obtain FPT results for the variable-embedding setting by treewidth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend orthogonal drawings (deg ≤ 4) to unrestricted degree graphs by allowing a bounded number of non-orthogonal faces, and study the computational boundaries and practical algorithms for constructing such drawings.

Method: Prove NP-completeness (even for triconnected graphs) for the decision problem; design fixed-parameter algorithms in fixed-embedding setting parameterized by outerplanarity or h; derive treewidth-based FPT results and a polynomial-time approximation scheme; in the variable-embedding setting provide an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth for biconnected graphs.

Result: NP-completeness for the decision problem with at most h non-orthogonal faces; linear-time FPT algorithms for fixed embedding with respect to outerplanarity index and h; FPT by treewidth and a PTAS in fixed embedding; in the variable-embedding setting, an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth for biconnected graphs.

Conclusion: Although the general problem is hard, there are several tractable regimes governed by natural parameters (outerplanarity, h, treewidth) and embedding settings, yielding a structured algorithmic framework for near-orthogonal planar polyline drawings.

Abstract: Orthogonal planar drawings constitute a classical and mainstream research topic in graph drawing due to their clarity and wide applicability. In an orthogonal planar drawing of a graph, each face is represented as an orthogonal polygon, that is, a polygon whose edges are either horizontal or vertical. Yet a planar graph admits such a representation if and only if its maximum degree is at most four.
  In this paper, we consider planar polyline drawings of graphs with unrestricted maximum degree. We focus on drawings that are ``close to orthogonal'', where closeness is measured by the number of faces that are not orthogonal polygons. We show that, even when the input graph is triconnected and thus has a unique planar embedding, the problem of testing whether there exists a planar polyline drawing with at most $h$ non-orthogonal faces is NP-complete. Motivated by this computational hardness, we study parameterized and approximation algorithms. In the fixed-embedding setting, we prove that the problem admits linear-time FPT algorithms parameterized by (i) the outerplanarity index and (ii) the natural parameter $h$. In addition, we provide an FPT algorithm parameterized by the treewidth and a polynomial-time approximation scheme. In the variable-embedding setting, we give an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth for biconnected graphs.

</details>

### [96] [AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20452)
*Vinil Pasupuleti,Shyalendar Reddy Allala,Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu,Shrey Tyagi,Srinivasateja Songa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AINTMA is a six-agent, cloud-native autonomous QA architecture that uses reinforcement learning for test prioritization and LLM-driven quality narratives, showing strong gains across 12 projects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contemporary software QA in cloud-scale environments demands autonomous, scalable decision-making to reduce cycle times and defects, beyond what traditional, manual test management can achieve.

Method: Six specialized agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, Cloud Security Monitor) operate via a secure multi-agent framework over a cloud-native microservices stack. RL uses MDPs with 47 features over a 36-month history; LLMs generate plain-language narratives and recommendations. Security via zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation.

Result: Evaluation on 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months: APFD 88.4% (vs 51.2% random; 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% reduction in test cycle time; defect escape rate from 8.3% to 2.1%; ROI 340% at 9 months; scalability to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400 ms responses; Generative Intelligence rated 4.3/5 for developer usefulness.

Conclusion: Agentic AI can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprises by combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative insights, and secure connectivity.

Abstract: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

</details>


### [97] [Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20462)
*Melanie Rieff,Robin Staab,Thibaud Gloaguen,Stefan Hegselmann,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Domain-specific evaluation reveals watermarking harms medical reasoning: despite robust general benchmarks, watermarking degrades clinical performance through lexical errors and hallucinations; need domain-tailored evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure safe deployment of watermarked LLMs in medicine by studying real-world clinical impact beyond general benchmarks.

Method: Benchmarked 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on unimodal and multimodal clinical tasks; developed human-expert-validated auditing pipeline to assess reasoning quality, terminology precision, and hallucinations; analyzed failure modes.

Result: Watermarking causes substantial degradation across multiple failure modes: lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, misattribution/omission of image findings; aggregate metrics hide domain-specific failures.

Conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is essential for safe medical deployment; current benchmarks mask clinically significant degradations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

</details>


### [98] [ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20463)
*Wojciech Michaluk,Tymoteusz Urban,Mateusz Kubita,Soveatin Kuntur,Anna Wróblewska*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI-driven browser extension detects clickbait using a hybrid model with transformer embeddings, linguistically informed features, and an XGBoost classifier, offering warnings and a spoiler with ~91% F1 on open data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate exposure to clickbait by delivering real-time, explainable detections and safeguards within the browsing flow.

Method: Hybrid architecture: transformer-based embeddings + linguistically motivated features + a custom baitness score; evaluation of vectorizers and LLM embeddings; XGBoost classifier; dataset: open combined; real-time warnings pre- and post- article; predictions explained via analyzed metrics; clickbait spoiler (1–2 sentence summary).

Result: F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset; capability to warn before and after article access; probability score and explanation for predictions; spoiler summarizing the article; demo video provided.

Conclusion: Demonstrates practical viability of an explainable, real-time clickbait detector integrated into a browser extension, with potential to improve user trust and media literacy; future work could include user studies and generalization assessment.

Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

</details>


### [99] [Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20464)
*Izhar Ali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-consistency provides per-question uncertainty but does not reveal cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether per-question variation from self-consistency reveals cross-question structure, by comparing it to cross-question signals revealed by a diverse ensemble using random-matrix tests.

Method: Two regimes on the same questions: (1) one model run 100 times at tau=1; (2) ensemble of 24 LLMs run once each at tau=0. Apply Marchenko–Pastur random-matrix tests to separate signal from noise on both sides; evaluate across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K).

Result: Within a single model, at most one eigenvalue rises above noise across the evaluated domains. Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge; a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null yields at most one in 500 Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency yields accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

Conclusion: Diversity in model ensembles is required to reveal cross-question structure and unknowns that self-consistency cannot expose.

Abstract: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

</details>


### [100] [JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20466)
*Arya Tschand,Charles Hong,Julian Walker,Nina Cai,Shangkun Wang,Suvinay Subramanian,Sundar Dev,Vijay Janapa Reddi,Amir Yazdanbakhsh,Sethu Sankaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JAXBench is a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs, enabling production-operator coverage and automated Pallas kernel generation; results show substantial gains from context-aware prompting and search-based generation, with open-source release.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of rigorous TPU-focused benchmarks and optimization targets analogous to GPU kernel benchmarks, enabling evaluation and improvement of AI-generated TPU kernels.

Method: Assemble 50 JAX workloads; extract 17 production operators from MaxText architectures, translate 33 operators from KernelBench with new problem sizes; evaluate four feedback-driven Pallas kernel generation methods on Gemini 3 Flash; include eight hand-tuned kernels; compare against XLA and Tokamax upper bound; release benchmark and evaluation harness.

Result: Curated TPU docs boost per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3%, solving 48/50 benchmarks at 1.28x geomean speedup; Autocomp with beam-search yields 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA; on eight hand-tuned kernels Autocomp achieves 1.60x over XLA, approaching Tokamax upper bound (2.08x) but missing specialized paged/ragged attention; overall demonstrates that target-specific context matters more than model scale in Pallas; high-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging; JAXBench and harness released open source.

Conclusion: TPU kernel optimization benefits from curated documentation and search-based, context-aware generation; JAXBench provides a reusable benchmark suite and evaluation framework to advance open-source TPU kernel optimization.

Abstract: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

</details>


### [101] [DC-Leap: Training-Free Acceleration of dLLMs via Draft-Guided Contiguous Leaping Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20467)
*Yanhua Jiao,Tianyi Wu,Xiaoxi Sun,Yulin Li,HuiLing Zhen,Libo Qin,Baotian Hu,Zhuotao Tian,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DC-Leap enables training-free acceleration of parallel decoding in diffusion LLMs by Dynamic Contiguous Verification to mitigate JPDE, plus draft-guided look-ahead decoding; achieves up to 53x-105x speedups with comparable quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: JPDE imposes conservative thresholds that cause redundant denoising and slow inference in dLLMs; a training-free method in moderate-confidence regime is desired to speed up decoding without sacrificing quality.

Method: Introduce Dynamic Contiguous Verification that enforces strictly-ordered causal constraints during parallel decoding, progressively validating token dependencies to neutralize JPDE; add draft-guided decoding to provide look-ahead context via drafts while preserving bidirectional attention.

Result: Substantial speedups reported on benchmarks, e.g., up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache, with comparable generation quality; code released.

Conclusion: DC-Leap offers a training-free framework for reliable acceleration of dLLMs by mitigating JPDE through dynamic verification and by leveraging draft-guided look-ahead, achieving large speedups with maintained quality.

Abstract: While parallel decoding is central to the efficiency of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs), current strategies are often hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds. These thresholds, necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), result in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. To overcome this, we propose DC-Leap, a training-free framework that enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in the moderate-confidence regime. DC-Leap introduces a Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process. By progressively validating token dependencies, this mechanism effectively neutralizes the JPDE, enabling reliable acceleration with comparable performance. Furthermore, DC-Leap incorporates the draft-guided decoding mechanism, where the draft helps extend the context by leaping forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context and retaining the structural benefits of bidirectional attention during inference. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DC-Leap achieves substantial speedups, up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache with comparable generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/ffh-wyls/DC-Leap .

</details>


### [102] [InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468)
*Jehyeok Yeon,Ben Rank,Maksym Andriushchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InferenceBench evaluates AI agents' ability to optimize a real-time LLM inference pipeline on a single GPU. Agents outperform a naive baseline but often underperform a straightforward hyperparameter search within the same time budget, suggesting memorized recipes—not genuine broad optimization—limit open-ended engineering gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether AI agents can perform genuinely novel optimization in open-ended engineering tasks, rather than relying on memorized recipes or narrow action spaces.

Method: 4 inference-bottleneck scenarios (prefill latency, decode latency, concurrency throughput, and a balanced mix) with a single H100 GPU, two-hour wall clock budget, and a target OpenAI-compatible LLM. 15 frontier agent configurations; compare against a naive PyTorch baseline, and a default-config vLLM, plus a simple hyperparameter search under identical time budget.

Result: Agents reliably beat the naive PyTorch baseline (up to 8.08x) and often match/exceed vLLM defaults (around 4.05x). Yet a straightforward hyperparameter search achieves up to 11.53x improvement within the same budget, outperforming the agent configurations. Qualitative analysis shows agents converge on a single inference framework and spend much budget on re-measurement/repair/hyperparameter tuning rather than exploring a diverse set of strategies.

Conclusion: The bottleneck is the agent’s ability to propose diverse, well-evaluated configurations and to search the space effectively under time constraints; memorized solutions provide limited gains in an open-ended AI-engineering setting, as demonstrated by InferenceBench.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

</details>


### [103] [DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20469)
*Zishan Shao,Lixun Zhang,Kangning Cui,Yixiao Wang,Ting Jiang,Hancheng Ye,Qinsi Wang,Zhixu Du,Yuzhe Fu,Fan Yang,Danyang Zhuo,Yiran Chen,Hai Helen Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Identify and intervention on a compact, task-general decode-time subspace (DecodeShare) shared across tasks; ablating it at decode-time significantly harms performance, more than prefill/random subspaces; enables clean separation of decode vs prefill channels and improves steering reliability; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand what task-general structure, if any, governs decode-time processing under KV caching, and establish a causal role for a shared subspace.
