Method: Compute a low-dimensional subspace in decode-time hidden states shared across tasks; perform causal interventions by removing that subspace during decoding only; compare with interventions on subspaces derived from prefill or random; evaluate impact on decisions; analyze activation steering directions and projection to separate components; assess decode-time signal vs prefill proxies; release code.

Result: Ablating the decode-time shared subspace degrades decision performance more than ablations of prefill-derived or random subspaces under equal budgets; steering directions overlap with the decode channel; projecting out the shared subspace cleanly separates decode vs prefill roles; decode-time signals provide more reliable guidance for deployment.

Conclusion: The shared decode-time subspace is a high-leverage, task-general causal channel for decoding in LLMs under KV caching; decoding-time interventions are informative for downstream deployment; the approach yields practical insights and a blueprint for activation steering.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

</details>


### [104] [PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20470)
*Jiacheng Wang,Weiyan Zhang,Guangya Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PlanE presents a planning framework to construct extractive-based LLMs with data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference, plus a DTI planner to choose the best base LLM and data-tuning-inference combos; results show efficiency gains and generalizability; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High annotation cost for instruction-tuning data and lack of methods to optimize task-specific LLM adaptation.

Method: PlanE framework integrating data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference; DTI planner for selecting base LLM and DTI configurations; experiments across datasets and base LLMs; validation of generalizability.

Result: Empirical evidence of effectiveness across different datasets with the same base LLM and across different base LLMs on the same dataset; DTI planner generalizes under different objectives; code available.

Conclusion: PlanE and DTI planner offer efficient, adaptable means to tailor LLMs to tasks, reducing annotation cost and enabling better matching of models to datasets; broader applicability and reproducibility via open-source code.

Abstract: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

</details>


### [105] [Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20471)
*Ashutosh Srivastava,Siddharth Yedlapati,Vinay Aggarwal,Yaman Kumar Singla,Shashwat Dixit,Jitendra Ajmera,Balaji Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Generative personalization is framed as a two-party Bayesian persuasion problem in sales. The paper introduces SDR-Bench/Arena, evaluates across frontier LLMs and agents, and finds a personalization plateau with limited ability to distinguish successful outreach; field validation shows moderate immediate usefulness and high expert agreement. Public release aims to enable reproducible study of personalized generation at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap between sender-side personalization benchmarks and real two-party persuasion where the receiver's action is the outcome. Leverage Bayesian Persuasion to model signaling and evaluation in generative agents for sales, with logged receiver actions to evaluate effectiveness.

Method: Adapt Kamenica and Gentzkow's Bayesian Persuasion to generative agents. Construct SDR-Bench (6,279 customer success stories, 22 industries, ~200 enterprises) and a temporally constrained simulation to prevent leakage. Evaluate across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents. Validate with a field deployment of 12 professional sales reps.

Result: Across models, observe a consistent personalization plateau: no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach in a Fortune 100 tech cohort. In field deployment, 48% of model-generated content rated immediately useful; senior-expert agreement on usefulness: Pearson r = 0.82. SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench released for reproducible study.

Conclusion: Public release of SDR-Arena/Bench enables reproducible study of generative personalization at scale; findings indicate current models struggle to achieve reliable two-party persuasion beyond sender-side signals, motivating further research and dataset expansion.

Abstract: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

</details>


### [106] [Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20472)
*Roman Belaire,Arunesh Sinha,Pradeep Varakantham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DCGS reframes adversarial dialogue as an MDp and uses per-turn intent inference with token- and utterance-level critics to reweight responses, improving safety robustness and transferring to frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambiguity in user intent in harmful queries; misclassify genuine users or be easily exploited; turn-by-turn trajectory is ignored by current safety methods that use contextual bandits.

Method: Model user intent at every turn with full dialogue history; learn value and regret-based critics at token and utterance levels; use an action-value critic to score candidate responses; inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting; formalization as an MDp.

Result: Outperforms strong baselines and frontier models on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, Harmbench; transfers to frontier models improving robustness without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Offers principled, theory-backed mechanism to adapt safety in multi-turn dialogues; ensures improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool; helps address trajectory-based adversarial intents.

Abstract: When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [107] [Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20473)
*Yeonjea Kim,Bumjin Park,Jaesik Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Formalizes incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) for LLMs, empirically characterizes when incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations, shows refusals are delayed until sentence termination, finds that retraining to refuse IPJs lacks generalization, and identifies two functional neurons (termination and continuation) suggesting neuron-level defenses for more robust IPJ mitigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs released with safeguards can still produce harmful continuations under incomplete prompts. There is a need for systematic understanding of IPJ phenomena and defenses that generalize across content and prompt attractor types.

Method: Systematic empirical analysis of incomplete sentence prompts. Characterization of attractor types, analysis of refusal timing, evaluation of parameter-tuning defenses, and identification of internal neurons (termination and continuation) involved in sentence completion to explore neuron-level intervention strategies.

Result: Demonstrates that LLMs systematically delay refusals until sentence termination, incomplete prompts can trigger harmful continuations, simple parameter-tuning to refuse IPJs fails to generalize across content domains and attractor types, and two functional neurons governing termination vs. continuation are identified, highlighting a potential path for fine-grained IPJ defenses.

Conclusion: Neuron-level understanding offers a promising avenue for robust IPJ defenses, but generalization across prompts and attractor types remains challenging; targeted interventions at the neuron level may enable more precise control over harmful continuations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

</details>


### [108] [VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20474)
*Sumaya Abdul Rahman,Seckhen Ariel Andrade Cuellar,Ghani Raissov,Mohammad Raza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSimpl uses simplification-based verification to improve NL-to-optimization translation via solver-generated diagnostic queries, enabling local reasoning and self-verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide correctness guarantees for NL-derived optimization formulations, ensuring the produced model aligns with the task description even when it can run without errors.

Method: Introduce a simplification-based verification paradigm: the optimization solver generates diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation; develop simplification strategies across constraints and decision variables to enable local reasoning under fixed global contexts; apply LLMs to reason about these simplified queries and the overall task.

Result: Demonstrates consistent accuracy gains over existing NL-to-optimization methods and introduces a high-precision self-verification signal.

Conclusion: VeriSimpl is effective for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization and provides a practical verification mechanism for LLM-based solvers.

Abstract: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

</details>


### [109] [SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20475)
*Pragaash Ponnusamy,Shivam Sahni,Jue Wang,Tri Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SonicSampler is a tile-aware Triton-based solution that vertically fuses the entire LLM sampling pipeline into a single, workload-aware kernel to support dynamic per-request decoding behaviors and CUDA Graph execution, achieving substantial speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches accelerate only parts of the pipeline, rely on multiple kernels, or assume homogeneous batch behavior, which hinders dynamic serving workloads and efficient CUDA Graph usage.

Method: Tile-aware Triton kernels that fuse the full sampling pipeline (logit processing, token selection, verification) into a single batched kernel. Supports per-request sampling options (grammar constraints, penalties, logit bias, temperature, top-k/top-p/min-p, repetition), speculative verification, and dynamic workloads. Introduces a hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm and exploits low-entropy output structure to scale to large vocabularies, all while remaining CUDA Graph-compatible.

Result: Up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines for top-k style operations; up to 16x speedup across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads compared to state-of-the-art baselines; supports dynamic per-request behaviors within a single kernel and full CUDA Graph compatibility.

Conclusion: SonicSampler delivers a unified, high-performance, CUDA Graph-friendly sampling pipeline for LLM inference that supports dynamic workloads and large vocabulary selection with significant speedups over prior approaches.

Abstract: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

</details>


### [110] [Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20476)
*Faizan Iqbal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Five LLMs fail to issue precautionary warnings when multiple sensors simultaneously exceed safe thresholds, while performing well on single-sensor violations; no benefits from structured tabular formatting; implies risk for multisensor safety monitoring systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess reliability and safety implications of large language models when interpreting multisensor physical hazard data, a critical task in safety-sensitive deployments.

Method: Evaluation of five LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) across 60 scenarios in three categories—multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation—using 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0. Metrics: accuracy of hazard warnings. Category A (multi-sensor) vs Category B (single-sensor) performance, plus comparison between structured tabular vs prose presentation.

Result: All models exhibit near-zero accuracy in Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) but near-perfect accuracy in single-sensor threshold violations (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Prose formatting yields significantly better results for ChatGPT-4o than structured tables (p = 0.001).

Conclusion: Multi-sensor fusion presents a significant blind spot for current LLMs under evaluation, raising safety concerns for physical hazard monitoring deployments. Prose-based evaluation can outperform tabular formats for some models; however, overall reliability depends on sensor fusion, model prompts, and presentation, underscoring the need for guardrails, sensor-data integration, and targeted red-teaming in safety-critical systems.

Abstract: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

</details>


### [111] [Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20477)
*Yurui Lai,Samir Moustafa,Renchi Yang,Tsz Nam Chan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A semi-supervised framework, ␀algo␀, using Wasserstein distance to scale Text-Attributed Graph (TAG) learning. It features a graph-text collaborative encoding with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) and collaborative self-training, plus a Wasserstein-distance-based graph sketching method and an LLM text-synthesis module that creates human-readable summaries via cluster-based keywords. It achieves state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs for both GNN- and LLM-based tasks on TAGs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TAGs fuse graph structure and textual data but face scalability bottlenecks with large language models and label scarcity in semi-supervised settings. There is a need to capture the interplay between modalities and to generate readable textual attributes for downstream LLM tasks.

Method: Propose ␀algo␀, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by Wasserstein Distance. Core components: (1) graph-text collaborative encoding with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) operating in a collaborative self-training loop to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse multi-modal features; (2) a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm to compress graph information; (3) a cost-efficient LLM text synthesis module that uses cluster-based keyword extraction to produce coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes.

Result: Extensive experiments on benchmark TAG datasets show that ␀algo␀ achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off for both GNN-based and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning and analytics.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates effective scalable TAG learning by integrating graph-text collaboration with Wasserstein-guided sketching and LLM-based synthesis, delivering strong performance while reducing resource demands for downstream tasks.

Abstract: {\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

</details>


### [112] [Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20479)
*Amr Moustafa,Max Feser,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Deception-detection probes for LMs are highly sensitive to dataset and training setup; no single probe or representation depth universally wins, and diverse deception types drastically affect detectability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse features, and lie typology affect deception-detection performance and transferability, addressing the transfer gap observed in prior work.

Method: Systematic evaluation of seven probe types across augmented training data that includes diverse deception types (fabrication, omission, exaggeration). Assessed factors: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations (dense vs sparse autoencoder features).

Result: Key findings: optimal representation depth is dataset-dependent; increased expressivity yields only selective gains over linear baselines; sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states; training data choice and lie typology substantially alter detectability, showing deception detection is highly representation-dependent.

Conclusion: Deception detection in LMs cannot rely on a single probe design or data setup; robust detection requires accounting for representation-dependent effects and diverse lie typologies, as dataset composition critically shapes detectability.

Abstract: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

</details>


### [113] [Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20480)
*Haoran Li,Lihao Mai,Muhao Guo,Jiaqi Wu,Yang Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A constrained inference framework refines a base utility topology using heterogeneous evidence under spatial and physical constraints, prioritizing consistency and scalability over reconstructing from scratch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Utility distribution grids suffer from unreliable topology records due to heterogeneous and imperfect data; existing methods relying on electrical similarity or metadata fail in dense feeders or under inconsistent data.

Method: Refine a provided base topology via constrained inference, detect inconsistencies, perform localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods, iteratively enforce physical feasibility, and use a falsification-driven reliability metric to gauge support for each inferred link.

Result: Achieves over 95% topology reconstruction accuracy on real feeders with >8,000 AMI meters; significantly reduces computation compared with global inference; shows correlation-based methods alone are ambiguous in dense urban feeders; combining electrical measurements with spatial/operational constraints yields robust topology recovery.

Conclusion: The framework offers scalable, operationally consistent topology estimation under realistic deployment conditions, enabling prioritized verification through a reliability metric and improving system observability.

Abstract: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

</details>


### [114] [Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20481)
*Evan Chen,Shiqiang Wang,Kevin S Chan,Su Wang,Christopher Brinton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Training-free routing: CARGO estimates local vs cloud trust using prompt-varied sampling and Bayesian early stopping, enabling adaptive local-cloud collaboration without trained routers; outperforms training-free baselines and often rivals supervised routers across diverse tasks and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce dependence on trained routers or finetuning for local-cloud LLM collaboration by leveraging the local model's own inference-time agreement signals.

Method: Prompt-varied sampling to measure agreement among local responses; Bayesian early stopping for efficient uncertainty control; lightweight deployment-time calibration to achieve arbitrary collaboration ratios; applicable to diverse local-model families and scales.

Result: CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and, in many cases, surpasses supervised learned routers across reasoning and QA tasks, various LLM families, and both pretrained and finetuned local models.

Conclusion: Effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can arise from the local model’s intrinsic response behavior without additional training, enabling a training-free, deployment-time routing solution.

Abstract: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

</details>


### [115] [PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20482)
*Seungbin Yang,Chaewoon Ki,Dohyun Lee,Jaegul Choo,ChaeHun Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: We present PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents and PACMem, a memory framework that decomposes browsing history into factual and preference memories; results show PACMem outperforms baselines in personalized navigation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agents struggle with underspecified prompts requiring inference from user browsing history; existing benchmarks do not capture personalization via history in web interactions.

Method: Introduce PersonaTrail benchmark using realistic browsing trajectories for user history; propose PACMem that splits raw histories into factual memories (session summaries) and preference memories (recurring behavioral patterns); at inference, retrieve relevant memories to guide navigation.

Result: PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both personalization and navigation tasks in extensive experiments.

Conclusion: Structured memory decomposition enables effective personalization by leveraging past browsing sessions, improving agent performance in open web tasks.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms. To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

</details>


### [116] [Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20483)
*Max Scribner,Antonio Vergari,Vaishak Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A method to constrain autoregressive LLM generation to satisfy LR(k) grammars in polynomial time, enabling syntactically valid outputs for code/data generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure syntactic validity of LLM-generated outputs (e.g., SQL/JSON) to enable reliable downstream processing in formal systems.

Method: Distill the LLM into a tractable probabilistic model and compute the probability that a generated string satisfies a given LR(k) grammar of finite duration in polynomial time; steer and mask generation using this containment probability to favor syntactically valid outputs.

Result: The satisfaction problem for any LR(k) grammar of finite duration can be solved in polynomial time, enabling efficient constraint-driven steering of LLM generation toward syntactically valid outputs, improving over prior exponential-time methods.

Conclusion: Provides a practical, scalable approach to enforcing formal syntactic constraints during LLM generation, with broad applicability to code and data tasks that require guaranteed syntactic validity.

Abstract: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

</details>


### [117] [The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20484)
*Yiheng Tao,Kaiwen Cheng,Yao Lu,Chang Liu,Jie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRSP introduces a non-invasive architectural regularization (Triangular Box with a length-aware gate) to balance spectral mixing and information capacity in LLMs, improving long-context performance without changing core attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address representation collapse in LLMs due to competing extremes (homogenization vs isolation) and the trade-off between spectral mixing (gap) and effective rank. A method is needed to preserve rank while enabling long-context information flow.

Method: Spectral analysis of attention dynamics; proposes Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP) with a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight length-aware gate; proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing; non-invasive integration that does not alter core attention.

Result: Significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks; on NoLiMa at 8x training length, TRSP retains 83% accuracy and outperforms Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by ~30 and ~50 percentage points, respectively; code released at the provided repository.

Conclusion: TRSP achieves spectral balance and improves general and long-context performance without modifying core attention, yielding a geometrically healthier transition operator with potential applicability to a broader range of architectures.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83\%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

</details>


### [118] [Expectation Alignment of Language Models for Real-World User Expectations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20485)
*Miaomiao Li,Yang Wang,Bin Liang,Shudong Liu,Zhiwei Zhang,Kam-Fai Wong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies real-world user expectations in LLM interactions, introduces ExpectBench based on real user data, and presents LENS, a framework to generate responses aligned with expected outcomes, showing misalignment in current models and improvement through expectation-aware generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation methods rely on heuristic metrics, expert rubrics, or user simulators that miss nuanced, real user expectations. There is a need for principled extraction of semantic user expectations and benchmarks grounded in real interactions to foster realistic human–AI alignment.

Method: 1) Propose a principled procedure to extract semantically rich user expectations from real LLM interactions. 2) Build ExpectBench, a benchmark derived from real user expectations. 3) Develop LENS, a lightweight latent-expectation-aware response generation framework that internalizes expectations to produce better-aligned outputs. 4) Evaluate across tasks to assess expectation satisfaction.

Result: Analyses show current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate user expectations, revealing a core misalignment source. ExpectBench captures diverse user expectations and exposes gaps in model behavior. LENS improves alignment by focusing on latent expectations, achieving consistent gains in expectation satisfaction.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling and internalizing user expectations is essential for realistic human–AI alignment. The proposed benchmarking (ExpectBench) and generation framework (LENS) provide a principled path to better align LLM outputs with user needs in real-world interactions.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, yet it remains largely unexplored whether they truly meet user expectations. Existing evaluation approaches, relying on model heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing models to appear competent while misaligning with what users actually seek. We present the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, proposing a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and introducing ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations. Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

</details>


### [119] [OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20486)
*Zhongzheng Li,Tiancan Feng,Wenhao Li,Qingsong Ran,Shikun Feng,Xiaoyuan Zhang,Yue Wang,Xiaoguang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPTScientist is a theory-guided multi-agent DSL-based framework for discovering optimizers; it leverages role-based collaboration, evolutionary search, and staged DSL Extensions to discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining; demonstrates automated optimizer science with theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current optimizer design is hard due to optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, and generalization; existing methods either explore unconstrained code spaces (uninterpretable) or stay within fixed families (limited novelty); need a framework combining theory, typing, and experimentation.

Method: Four agents (Theorist, Designer, Engineer, Reviewer) operate in a loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile/evaluate optimizers, and critique results. Uses a typed DSL with modules for direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, grouping; combines evolutionary search with a second-stage mechanism to extend DSL when bottlenecks arise; validates via compiler checks and closed-loop experiments.

Result: Discovery of RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining relative to strong baselines under the authors' evaluation protocol.

Conclusion:  Demonstrates a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation; hints at broader applicability of the framework and DSL-guided optimization discovery.

Abstract: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

</details>


### [120] [Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20487)
*Chendi Wang,Liam Cunningham,Tom Yishay,Jieying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reproducible framework treats LLM hallucinations in political QA as signals of ideological drift; across 21k expert-labeled U.S. articles, multiple models show left-leaning hallucinations, linked to high-entropy contexts, enabling audits and safeguards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand and quantify ideological bias/hallucinations in LLMs when handling political information, especially in election-relevant, high-stakes contexts, to inform auditing and safeguards.

Method: 1) Create article-specific questions; 2) obtain doc-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model; 3) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison; 4) classify ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier; 5) analyze output logits to relate uncertainty to hallucination and drift.

Result: Hallucination rates vary by model and concentrate on contentious topics; source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest; hallucination content shows robust leftward drift, including from right-leaning sources; entropy contexts correlate with hallucinations, and in some models uncertainty predicts leftward drift (uncertainty-to-guessing).

Conclusion: The framework supports auditing AI-mediated political information and guiding safeguards for election-relevant deployments, by linking hallucinations to ideological drift and token-level uncertainty.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

</details>


### [121] [Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20488)
*Bronislav Sidik,Chaya Levi,Nizzan Kimhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM) enables runtime restructuring of multi-agent LLM frameworks by detecting overload via a six-signal Bottleneck Index and factorizing overloaded agents into sub-agents, guarded by three safety invariants and privacy-aware routing; demonstrated large gains in task success and privacy with minimal latency; open-sourced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed team topologies limit runtime scalability and resilience; overload causes latency and errors; need dynamic, safe topology adaptation.

Method: Telemetry-driven overload detection using six-signal Bottleneck Index (queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, cross-agent wait time); threshold breach triggers factorisation into specialised sub-agents; hot-swaps parent to coordinator; privacy-level-aware memory routing; shadow validation before live traffic; invariants gate changes: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, shadow-before-live; evaluation on 720 DeepSeek-V3 tasks with ablations; live-tool probe; open-source.

Result: Factoriser increases code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%; memory privacy exposure events per task reduced from 2.0 to 0.0; overhead is under 500 microseconds p99 latency on hot-path; external validity via live Python tool probe; implementation and traces open-sourced.

Conclusion: ATM enables safe, low-latency runtime topology mutation for multi-agent LLM frameworks, improving performance and privacy, with empirical evidence and public availability.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality. The runtime rails carrying ATM's invariants add less than 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution is included as an external-validity check. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

</details>


### [122] [EvoSQL: Memory-Augmented Critic-Generator Co-Evolution for Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20489)
*Jiawei Zhou,Jianwei Wang,Chenyu Zhou,Chaojian Shi,Ming Dong,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoSQL introduces a memory-grounded co-evolution framework for Text-to-SQL that interleaves a generator and a critic, augmented by a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) stage, to improve multi-step reasoning and execution-aware accuracy; it yields consistent gains over Maj@16 baselines on Spider and BIRD, especially BIRD-Dev.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limit of one-shot generation in Text-to-SQL by incorporating iterative reasoning, execution feedback, and critique, thereby improving reliability and generalization across benchmarks.

Method: An iterative generator–critic loop with a contextualized candidate memory; verification of SQL candidates via execution signals and LLM-based critique; memory updated through utility-guided aggregation; SDPO fine-tuning injects execution-aware supervision into coding LLM backbones.

Result: Open-source models show consistent improvements over Maj@16 baselines on Spider and BIRD, with larger gains on BIRD-Dev (e.g., +1.37% for Qwen3-4B, +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B); SDPO initialization further boosts Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev.

Conclusion: Memory-grounded co-evolution is effective for building more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems; the authors provide code for replication.

Abstract: Text-to-SQL has advanced rapidly with large language models, but complex database queries still require reasoning beyond one-shot generation, including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. We present EvoSQL, a co-evolution framework that formulates SQL synthesis as an iterative interaction between a generator and a critic. EvoSQL maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates with both execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates its memory through utility-guided aggregation. To strengthen the underlying generator-critic pair, we further introduce a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones. Experiments on Spider and BIRD show that EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with particularly large gains on BIRD-Dev, ranging from +1.37% for Qwen3-4B to +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev. These results suggest that memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/EvoSQL.

</details>


### [123] [CRAWO: Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20490)
*Eugênio Santos,Daniel Maia,Stefano Loss,José Manoel Silva,Aluizio Rocha Neto,Thais Batista,Everton Cavalcante,Nélio Cacho,Eduardo Nogueira,Daniel Araújo,Frederico Lopes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRAWO is an architectural framework that enables adaptive, hardware-aware orchestration of AI pipelines across distributed edge environments using a control-loop model, CRDs, and a K3s-based microservices implementation; it improves workload distribution and reduces cloud reliance in latency-sensitive scenarios as demonstrated on license plate recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge AI deployment is hindered by heterogeneity and dynamic conditions; existing platforms focus on deployment rather than adaptive resource allocation, leading to inefficient utilization and latency. A control-loop approach with real-time metrics is needed to optimize placement.

Method: Proposes CRAWO framework with control-loop: allocation decisions, state management, inter-stage data flows; hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer; microservices architecture on K3s; domain modeling via CRDs; operator for state reconciliation; reference implementation.

Result: In a vehicle surveillance scenario for license plate recognition, CRAWO achieved improved workload distribution and reduced cloud dependency, yielding lower latency in edge processing.

Conclusion: CRAWO provides a practical, extensible approach for adaptive workload orchestration across heterogeneous edge infrastructures, enabling responsive AI pipelines with real-time metrics; demonstrated feasibility and benefits in latency-sensitive edge deployments.

Abstract: Edge Intelligence has emerged as a key paradigm for enabling real-time applications in smart cities by shifting computation from centralized cloud data centers to the network edge, thereby reducing latency and bandwidth consumption. However, deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures remains challenging due to the wide range of device capabilities, from low-power microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems. Existing edge orchestration platforms primarily focus on deployment automation and infrastructure management, but these approaches are often inefficient and limit the ability to adaptively allocate resources under dynamic conditions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces CRAWO (Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration), an architectural framework for coordinating AI pipelines across distributed edge environments. CRAWO follows a control-loop-based model that separates allocation intelligence from execution by managing placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows while instantiating services on edge nodes. The framework incorporates a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that leverages real-time infrastructure metrics to enable adaptive workload placement. The reference implementation adopts a microservices architecture deployed on a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation. Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.

</details>


### [124] [DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20491)
*Raffi Khatchadourian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A replay-based benchmark (DFAH-Bench) measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across tool-use, evidence contacts, and decision concentration. It reveals significant divergence in tool trajectories despite high outcome agreement and identifies three behavioral profiles, with related code and data released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard benchmarks capture only final decisions, not the stability of the decision-making process. There is a need to quantify how consistently agents use tools and gather evidence to reach decisions, especially in finance.

Method: A replay benchmark capturing three channels—tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration—without accessing hidden reasoning. It analyzes 8,127 replay episodes across 10 models and 3 financial tasks to compare outcomes with underlying tool paths, identifies trajectory profiles (pattern matchers, stable executors, trajectory divergers), and releases code, logs, and dataset.

Result: Outcome agreement among frontier models is high (about 95%), but same-tool-path usage occurs only ~77% of the time, yielding an 18-percentage-point gap not seen by outcome-only evaluation (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]). Over 55% of high-agreement cases show meaningful trajectory divergence. Three behavioral profiles are characterized: pattern matchers, stable executors, and trajectory divergers.

Conclusion: Evaluations should consider multi-channel observable behaviors to assess stability and reliability. DFAH-Bench provides a practical framework and accompanying resources to quantify and compare decision-making processes beyond final outcomes.

Abstract: Standard evaluation benchmarks measure what a tool-using agent decides, not whether it arrives at that decision through the same process each time. We introduce DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark that measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across three channels -- tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration -- none of which require access to hidden reasoning text. Across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks, we find that outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal: frontier models can agree on decisions 95% of the time while following the same tool path only 77% of the time -- an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) that outcome-only evaluation misses entirely. Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. We identify three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers that achieve near-perfect agreement by collapsing to a single output regardless of input, stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and trajectory divergers that reach the same conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts. The benchmark code, metric scripts, replay logs, benchmark card, dataset README, and release manifest are released in the accompanying repository.

</details>


### [125] [Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20493)
*Quentin Besnard,Nicolas Ragot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A continual time-series forecasting framework using an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention to adapt to non-stationary environments while preserving past knowledge, achieving maintained or improved accuracy with reduced retraining and data needs on benchmarks including a piezometric dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real-world settings, data distributions evolve over time, making static forecasting models brittle. Continual learning with a focus on stability (retaining prior knowledge) and plasticity (adaptation to new contexts) is needed under limited computational resources.

Method: Extend static forecasting models with an Experience Replay mechanism guided by Attention. The replay selectively revisits past experiences to adapt to new temporal contexts while using Attention to prioritize relevant past information, aiming to mitigate catastrophic forgetting under compute constraints.

Result: Empirical evaluation on standard forecasting benchmarks and a piezometric dataset with diverse temporal behaviors shows the method maintains or improves predictive performance over time and reduces retraining costs and data requirements.

Conclusion: The proposed Attention-guided Experience Replay framework provides an effective, resource-aware approach to continual time-series forecasting in dynamic environments, enabling sustained performance and easier deployment in real-world settings.

Abstract: Deep learning has led to remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, particularly in robotics, imaging and sound processing. However, a major limitation of neural networks remains their strong dependence on large and stationary datasets. In many real-world applications, these conditions are rarely met due to evolving and dynamic environments where data distributions change over time. Continual learning aims to address this challenge by developing models capable of adapting incrementally while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under computational constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for continual time series forecasting, designed to extend existing static forecasting models commonly used in the literature by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This approach allows the model to adapt dynamically to new contexts while preserving prior knowledge, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks as well as on a piezometric dataset exhibiting diverse temporal behaviors. Results show that our approach effectively increases or maintains predictive performance over time while reducing retraining costs and data requirements, thus facilitating the deployment of forecasting models in dynamic and real-world settings.

</details>


### [126] [Isolating LLM Alignment from Regex: Zero Coverage and Metric-Dependent Divergence Under Adversarial Mutation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20494)
*Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Disabling the regex filter reveals no additional coverage by alignment under a substring classifier, but an LLM-judge metric detects substantial refusals for adversarial prompts; alignment's benefit is metric-dependent and corpus-designed bypass challenges the regex pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether the previously claimed ceiling of regex-filter plus alignment holds when attackers craft corpora to bypass the regex, and compare substring-based coverage with LLM-judge refusals.

Method: Introduce L5-no-regex (identical to L4-real but with the nine-pattern filter disabled). Evaluate on N=45 adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified by Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ~1,555 probe-run pairs over N=5 replications. Use a primary substring classifier and a secondary LLM-judge metric (PAIR variants) to measure block rates and perform statistical tests.

Result: L5 shows 0% block rate under the substring classifier across all five OWASP Top-10 categories (p=1.00; Wilson upper bound <5%). The LLM-judge metric reports 56–100% block rates on PAIR variants (p<0.01), indicating alignment responds to adversarially-framed probes beyond the regex, but refusals are too nuanced for substring matching. Sub-corpus differential predictions are not supported (p=1.00).

Conclusion: Alignment’s contribution is metric-dependent: for natural-language harmful prompts, it adds no coverage beyond the regex; for adversarially-framed prompts, an LLM judge detects refusals the substring classifier misses. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

Abstract: Production LLM applications commonly stack a regex filter in front of model-side alignment; prior work found no measurable coverage gain from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. We ask whether that ceiling holds when the corpus is \emph{designed to bypass the regex}. We introduce $L_5$-no-regex -- identical to $L_4$-real (Gemini-2.5-flash, token-budget cap, rate limit, output scrub) but with the nine-pattern filter disabled -- and evaluate it against $N{=}45$ adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified by Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ${\sim}1{,}555$ probe-run pairs over $N{=}5$ replications. Under the primary substring classifier, H1 is refuted: $L_5$ block rate is $0,%$ across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories ($Δ\text{pp}{=}0$ vs.\ $L_0$, $p{=}1.00$; Wilson upper bound ${<}5,%$). A secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants shows $56$--$100,%$ block rates ($p{<}0.01$), revealing alignment does respond to adversarially-framed probes -- but produces refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is not supported ($p{=}1.00$). Alignment's contribution is \emph{metric-dependent}: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals the substring classifier misses. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

</details>


### [127] [Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20495)
*Anas Mohamed,Kaizan Haque,Azal Ahmad Khan,Chetan Sharma,Shuwen Ge,Ali Anwar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A workload-aware cache eviction approach for multi-agent DAG executions that uses recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency to prioritize valuable cached entries; demonstrates significant latency improvements and approaches unbounded caching under finite memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing eviction policies treat cached entries uniformly and ignore structural/workload signals available in agent-based DAG executions, leading to suboptimal reuse under memory constraints.

Method: Compute a unified score combining recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency to rank cached entries; evict lower-scoring entries under memory pressure; validate on three multi-agent benchmarks across diverse reuse regimes.

Result: Latency reduced up to 64.7% versus uncached baseline and about 31.1% on average versus the next-best finite-capacity baseline; performance near that of an unbounded cache and with accuracy comparable to or better than competing finite-capacity methods.

Conclusion: Workload-aware caching effectively leverages domain-specific signals (recomputation cost, DAG structure, and invocation frequency) to improve multi-agent pipeline efficiency and is complementary to other optimization strategies such as plan-level caching and parallel agent execution.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

</details>


### [128] [From Errors to Rules: Iterative Prompt Optimization for Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20497)
*Yueying Cui,Renhao Xue,Yi Zhang,Mukul Prasad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A comprehensive empirical study of three prompt-optimization paradigms for text classification (demonstration selection, exploration-based search, and error-driven diagnosis), introducing ERGO—an error-guided optimization method that diagnoses errors and prescribes rewrite rules. The study shows no single method dominates; ERGO excels on boundary-learnable tasks and offers interpretable rules, while other paradigms excel in coverage or many-class scenarios. A complementarity framework is proposed to guide paradigm choice by task characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically compare diverse prompt-optimization paradigms for text classification and to bridge gaps by proposing a method that leverages error patterns to generate targeted rules, thereby clarifying when each paradigm is advantageous.

Method: Conduct a large-scale empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (ranging from 2 to 150 classes). Compare demonstration-based ICL, exploration-based search, and error-driven diagnosis through quantitative metrics and qualitative tracing of optimization dynamics. Develop ERGO: iteratively process the full training set in non-overlapping batches to diagnose misclassifications and generate targeted decision rules via a diagnose–prescribe–rewrite loop. Evaluate on tasks with boundary-learnable errors (e.g., TREC, CLINC150), report accuracy, iteration counts, and interpretability of rules.

Result: ERGO attains best accuracy on boundary-learnable tasks (e.g., TREC: 90.0%; CLINC150: 94.4%), converging in 3–5 iterations and yielding interpretable decision rules. It does not top the overall average but complements other paradigms: demonstration-based ICL excels in coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search excels in many-class intents, and ERGO fills gaps where error patterns define learnable decision boundaries. A complementarity framework links task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection.

Conclusion: Task characteristics dictate the most effective prompt-optimization paradigm. ERGO provides a complementary, interpretable, error-driven option that performs best where error patterns define decision boundaries, and the study offers practical guidance for practitioners on selecting or combining paradigms based on task structure.

Abstract: Prompt optimization for text classification spans diverse approaches, from demonstration selection to exploration-based search to error-driven diagnosis, each with known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (2 to 150 classes) comparing these paradigms through both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces, revealing that each paradigm excels on structurally different task types and that no single method dominates. Guided by these insights, we propose Error-Guided Optimization (ERGO), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules through a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop.
