ERGO achieves the best accuracy on tasks where errors concentrate in specific confused label pairs (which we term boundary-learnable tasks): TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%, converges in 3-5 iterations, and produces interpretable decision rules. While ERGO does not achieve the highest overall average, it fills a complementary role: demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent, and ERGO wins where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns. We provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical guidance for practitioners.

</details>


### [129] [AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20498)
*Fanjin Zhang,Zhengyang Wang,Ruixuan Huang,Kefan Zhang,Amy Xin,Yuanchun Wang,Shu Zhao,Evgeny Kharlamov,Jie Tang,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AISE-Bench is a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs, featuring 1,133 QA pairs with complete API execution traces, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers; it reveals that even state-of-the-art multi-step, API-using LLM agents struggle with API planning/execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-using benchmarks rely on synthetic templates and narrow tasks, failing to capture realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, detailed parameterization, grounded references, and comprehensive process+outcome evaluation.

Method: Develop a real-world benchmark (AISE-Bench) with 1,133 QA pairs, annotated workflows that plan/execute/revise complex API pipelines; provide full API execution traces, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with references; implement an evaluation protocol assessing answer quality, grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success; evaluate 14 methods.

Result: Across 14 evaluated models, the strongest (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often fails at API planning/execution.

Conclusion: AISE-Bench supplies a challenging, quantitative testbed for assessing and improving stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning in multi-step API-using LLM agents; code and data are publicly available.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with tools are emerging as autonomous agents capable of using Web engine, APIs, and code to solve complex, long-horizon tasks. Current tool-using benchmarks for information seeking on academic graphs rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow tasks such as paper-centric tasks, leaving key challenges underexplored - realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling for APIs, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive evaluation of both the process and the outcome. We introduce AISE-Bench, a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs. AISE-Bench release contains 1,133 QA pairs, including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. To support high-quality annotation, we design a customized agent workflow to enable annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows efficiently. We develop a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Among the 14 evaluated methods, even the strongest model (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution. AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving the stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents. Our code and data are available at https://aise-bench.github.io/.

</details>


### [130] [ExecuGraph: A Multi-Agent, Execution-Grounded Framework for Reliable Backend Code Synthesis with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20499)
*Sai Deekshith Lekkala,Jothi Prabha Appadurai,Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu,Manpreet Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ExecuGraph introduces a six-agent, execution-validated backend-code synthesis framework that uses a typed, bounded-retry workflow to improve reliability and accuracy, especially with higher-capacity base models, and offers a single configurable codebase for ablations and controlled measurements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Guarantee correctness and runtime reliability of LLM-generated backend code, addressing the limitations of single-pass generation by incorporating execution-based validation and structured multi-agent collaboration.

Method: A multi-agent pipeline with six agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, Explainer) orchestrated by a typed directed workflow on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer. Execution is sandboxed with wall-clock timeouts. Evaluation across internal-30, HumanEval, and APPS-introductory sets, comparing against one-shot and execution-retry baselines, plus per-agent ablations, budget sweeps, and error taxonomies.

Result: On internal-30, differences between configurations are not statistically significant. On HumanEval, the multi-full configuration leads by +3.1 percentage points. Cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy rises from 57.5% (one-shot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp increase, supporting a scaling hypothesis where multi-agent decomposition benefits grow with base-model capability.

Conclusion: The work’s primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that can be configured as one-shot, execution-retry, or per-agent ablations, enabling controlled measurement of each lever. It reports per-agent ablations, retry-budget sweeps, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audits.

Abstract: Large Language Models generate plausible backend code, but a single-pass paradigm provides no guarantee of correctness or runtime reliability. We present ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework that places execution-based validation at the center of backend code synthesis. Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer) are coordinated by a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. We evaluate on a curated 30-problem DSA suite (internal-30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, contrasting ExecuGraph against a single-agent one-shot baseline and a single-agent execution-retry baseline (a Reflexion-style ablation that isolates the contribution of multi-agent decomposition). On internal-30, the three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (n=30; paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO, p=0.08 SR vs. SO); 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all pairwise mean differences include zero. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy improves from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump that supports a scaling hypothesis: the value of multi-agent decomposition grows with base-model capability. The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation conditions, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. A per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

</details>


### [131] [FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20500)
*Sizhe Tang,Guangyu Jiang,Yu Li,Rongqian Chen,Ioannis G. Kevrekidis,Tian Lan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlowEdit proposes an information-theoretic framework to enable branch-aware reasoning in LLMs for ill-posed open-world problems by generating multiple hypotheses and diverse alternative responses; it uses dual information-theoretic objectives to regulate internal reasoning and shows strong empirical gains and distinctive token entropy patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ill-posed/open-world problems create conflicting constraints with no valid single answer, exposing limitations of next-token LLM reasoning; need to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain multiple hypotheses, and produce alternative responses in parallel.

Method: FlowEdit imposes two dual information-theoretic objectives on internal reasoning representations: (1) maximize information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome; (2) minimize overlap/conditional dependence across sibling branches. Uses tractable variational bounds with boundary embeddings ε-sufficient to optimize conditional mutual information and generate a full set of alternative, hypothesis-consistent responses.

Result: FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, achieving a 68% improvement in exact-set-match accuracy and a 24% boost in overall response informativeness. Flow regulation manifests in the token stream as redistributed next-token entropy concentrated within branches, amplified at flow boundaries, and scaling with the number of required flows.

Conclusion: FlowEdit provides a principled, scalable approach to branching-aware reasoning for ill-posed problems, enabling explicit conflict handling and diverse response generation; theoretical framing via variational information bounds and empirical gains support its effectiveness.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

</details>


### [132] [MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20501)
*Jason Yoo,Rajarshi Saha,Shaowei Zhu,Tao Yu,Wei Tang,Youngsuk Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MKEvolve introduces a modular, co-evolving kernel synthesis framework that decomposes PyTorch modules and optimizes subkernels with LLM-driven search; it yields configurable, interpretable, and transferable kernels with improved correctness and speed, reducing LLM token usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The bottleneck in scaling ML workloads lies in crafting correct, efficient kernels for hardware accelerators; end-to-end kernel synthesis with LLMs is brittle, expensive in tokens, and hard to interpret. A modular, verifiable approach can improve correctness, performance, and adaptability.

Method: Iteratively co-evolve a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule. Refinement occurs by splitting/fusing submodules across iterations, while each subkernel is independently improved via LLM-driven beam search. The kernels are compositions of independently verified subkernels, enabling configurability, interpretability, and easy reuse across models.

Result: Empirical evaluation on Triton with KernelBench L2/L3 across multi-operator sequences and full model architectures shows improved correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines, and up to 35% reduction in LLM token usage.

Conclusion: Modular, composable subkernels with independent verification yield faster, more reliable kernel generation, with better adaptability to related model architectures and lower token cost, as demonstrated on Triton KernelBench benchmarks.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

</details>


### [133] [Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20502)
*Jan Speller,Malte Luttermann,Marcel Gehrke,Tanya Braun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a principled scheme to compare two probabilistic graphical models with non-identical variable sets by lifting them to a common measurable space using conditionally uniform extensions, preserving semantics while enabling distributional discrepancy measures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable principled, quantitative comparison of probabilistic graphical models defined over different variable sets by placing them on a shared measurable universe.

Method: Extend unmatched components via conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions so that joint distributions differ only by multiplicative constants and project to the original distributions. Prove invariance of the induced joint under projection. Provide a deterministic algorithm to minimally extend factor graphs to the smallest common measurable space and to a common graphical structure. Analyze structural and measure-theoretic properties and propose criteria for comparison methodologies.

Result: The extensions preserve probabilistic semantics, enable application of distributional discrepancy measures, and ensure the joint distribution is invariant under projection. A minimal structural extension to the smallest common space and a common graphical structure is obtained via a deterministic algorithm; structural and measure-theoretic properties are characterized, guiding comparison methodologies.

Conclusion: Lifting to a common measurable space via conditionally uniform extensions allows principled comparison of non-identical graphical models without distorting their semantics, and supports robust discrepancy-based methodologies through a well-founded, invariant joint representation.

Abstract: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

</details>


### [134] [LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20503)
*Lazar Milikic,Simon Guilloud,Khanh Nguyen,Viktor Kuncak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LeanFlow automates translating mathematical papers to Lean code via LLM agents; in two case studies it completes document-level Lean projects within limited call budgets and shows favorable token-efficiency; achieves 75.7% BEq+ on RLM25 PFR and solves ICML AI for Math TCS challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify runtime factors that influence completion, auditability, and efficiency in document-to-project formalization; current verifier-in-the-loop approaches lack systematic ablations of models, proof-workflows, and toolsets.

Method: Case studies on two unformalized theorems in number theory and measure theory; perform ablations across model (Kimi2.6 vs GPT5.5), proof-workflow, toolset; measure task outcome, API calls, input/output tokens; budgets: 2000 calls; evaluate both full-document and no-queue variants; replicate across two sources; assess BEq+ on RLM25 and ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenges.

Result: With Kimi2.6, full workflow finishes both document-level Lean projects within 2000-call budget; no-queue variants hit the budget limit. With GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete; lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost. LeanFlow achieves 75.7% BEq+ on RLM25 PFR slice and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in GPT5.5 runs.

Conclusion: LeanFlow demonstrates efficient, auditable translation of papers to Lean under multiple runtimes; supports scalable formalization with measurable resource usage; promising approach for document-to-project formalization; further validation on more papers and broader benchmarks is warranted.

Abstract: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

</details>


### [135] [Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20506)
*Houda Khrouf,Pedro Fillastre,Sebastiao Correia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GraphRAG-inspired reasoning over graphs and HyperGraphRAG over hypergraphs face issues: n-ary facts, error-prone extractions, and slow chunk retrieval. The paper proposes self-consistency prompting for better extraction and Personalized PageRank over the hypergraph for faster, more reliable chunk retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations in graph-based knowledge representations: GraphRAG struggles with n-ary facts; HyperGraphRAG offers richer semantics but hinges on unreliable LLM extractions and inefficient standard chunk retrieval.

Method: Introduce self-consistency prompting to stabilize LLM extraction of facts from hypergraphs and apply Personalized PageRank (PPR) on the hypergraph to prioritize relevant chunks during retrieval.

Result: Extraction accuracy is improved via self-consistency prompts; chunk retrieval quality and efficiency are enhanced by PPR on the hypergraph, leading to more robust, scalable reasoning over structured knowledge.

Conclusion: Combining self-consistent extraction with PPR-based retrieval on hypergraphs addresses the core weaknesses of GraphRAG/HyperGraphRAG, yielding more accurate and efficient knowledge reasoning with richer semantic graphs.

Abstract: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

</details>


### [136] [MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20507)
*Jingquan Chen,Jinghua Piao,Jie Feng,Shaogang Hu,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MiniCache is a reusable program caching framework that turns PoT programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reuse across structurally similar requests and reducing expensive target-LLM calls while maintaining task quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs incur high inference costs for program-aided reasoning and structured tasks. There is a need to reuse computation across similar requests to improve latency and throughput without sacrificing accuracy.

Method: Transform Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects. Use a small model to (1) extract semantic variables on cache-hit requests and (2) draft target-LLM content (speculative drafting) during generation, thereby enabling reuse and reducing target-LLM invocations while preserving quality. Evaluate on shopping-style datasets (WebShop), Formula, and CodeTAT-QA with parallel serving to measure latency, cache reuse, and accuracy.

Result: Experiments show up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving, with improved trade-offs between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy. Small models act effectively as interface models facilitating reliable reusable program caching without replacing large models.

Conclusion: Small models serve best as lightweight interface components that enable efficient, reusable program caching, augmenting large LLMs rather than replacing them.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

</details>


### [137] [Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20510)
*Dmitrii Khizbullin,Zaid Alyafeai,Abdelrahman Eldesokey,Nourah AlSultan,Raghad Alshalan,David R. Pugh,Bernard Ghanem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on real telecom data, with 100 QA tasks across English/Arabic, multi-hop reasoning over HTML/web content, a SQL database, and web archives, scored via deterministic exact-match in a Docker sandbox.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Create a rigorous, domain-specific evaluation framework for enterprise agents that integrates multiple modalities and sources, enabling objective, reproducible benchmarking without LLM-as-a-Judge.

Method: 100 human-verified QA tasks in English and Arabic requiring ~4.2-hop reasoning over three sources (static website snapshot with HTML/images/PDFs, a synthetic SQL database, external web archives) and multiple modalities (text, image, tabular); delivered in a sandboxed Docker environment with normalized exact-string scoring; evaluation spans 12 LLMs.

Result: Even strongest models solve up to 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, performance drops to ~40%; visually grounded categories lag with backend scores below 30%; document and image understanding show significant headroom.

Conclusion: Telco-GAIA provides a rigorous, reproducible enterprise testbed and offers a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks to assess tool-using agents.

Abstract: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

</details>


### [138] [SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20511)
*Keonhee Park,Gunhee Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SiGMA is a sign-guided framework that mitigates negative interference in multimodal continual instruction tuning by combining sign-guided adaptive tuning during training with sign-guided merging at inference, achieving superior performance over existing MCIT methods on UCIT and DCL; code is available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MCIT methods rely on Mixture of Experts or expansion-based approaches and primarily address catastrophic forgetting, but they exhibit negative interference during inference where new updates overwrite useful prior knowledge. A method that preserves prior knowledge while learning new tasks is needed.

Method: Introduce sign guided adaptive tuning to reduce collisions with past knowledge and minimize drift during training, and sign guided merging to selectively scale salient parameters at inference to preserve and amplify useful task-specific knowledge.

Result: Empirical evaluation on UCIT and DCL benchmarks shows that SiGMA substantially reduces negative interference and outperforms state-of-the-art MCIT methods.

Conclusion: SiGMA provides a simple yet effective approach to mitigate negative interference in multimodal continual instruction tuning, improving knowledge consolidation and task performance; code is released.

Abstract: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

</details>


### [139] [Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20515)
*Jingyi Huang,Ruohan Zong,Yujun Feng,Liran Ma,Lanyu Shang,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RGPO mitigates noisy human feedback in RLHF by estimating annotator reliability, inferring latent ground truth, and weighted training based on annotation consensus, yielding better LLM alignment than standard baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human feedback for RLHF is inherently noisy and subjective; treating all disagreements equally leads to overfitting and suboptimal alignment. A robust framework is needed to identify reliable signals and downweight inconsistent supervision.

Method: RGPO estimates annotator reliability, infers latent ground-truth labels from conflicting feedback, and applies reliability-aware consistency optimization that modulates the loss by the consensus level of annotations, prioritizing high-consensus supervision while mitigating noisy signals.

Result: Experimental results on LLM alignment benchmarks show RGPO reduces inconsistency and noise in the training data and achieves superior performance compared with widely used RLHF baselines.

Conclusion: RGPO provides a robust improvement to RLHF under noisy human feedback by leveraging annotator reliability and consensus-aware optimization; code and configurations are released.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

</details>


### [140] [CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20518)
*Xue-Jian Gao,Deng Pan,Yueming Su,Jiasheng Li,Bin Du,Fengming Zhu,Chengdi Ma,Junyi Fan,Qichen Liao,Chengqiu Hu,Xinxian Chen,Lingchao Zheng,Jun Li,Jiwei Yang,Yuwei Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANN Bench provides a three-axis benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei Ascend NPU, covering 53 operators and 1060 test cases, with multi-precision support and a three-dimensional composite score against baseline and HAP limit, aiming for reproducible, community-driven evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address lack of Ascend-relevant benchmarks; enable evaluation of AI agent code for low-level operators; ensure open, comparable yardstick across hardware ecosystems.

Method: 53 operators; 1060 test cases; four difficulty tiers; FP16, BF16, FP32, INT8; three-axis weighted composite score; compare to PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and hardware-anchored performance limit; resistant to reward hacking; versioned in CANN repository; community-driven.

Result: Provides principled, headroom-reflecting scores; robust evaluation framework; practical for benchmarking AI-driven kernel-authoring; enables long-term maintainability and adoption.

Conclusion: CANN Bench delivers a reproducible, scalable benchmark for Ascend operator generation, promoting ecosystem vitality and rigorous evaluation of AI-assisted kernel development.

Abstract: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

</details>


### [141] [Representation Robustness Under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20520)
*Sagnik Nath,Edith Aurora Graf,Liang Zhang,Diego Zapata-Rivera*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit representational brittleness in mathematical problem solving across story, word-equation, symbolic, and paraphrase variants; code-based reasoning helps some models but is not a universal fix; representation is a critical interface design variable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle reasoning errors from interface failures by systematically varying surface representations of the same mathematical problems and evaluating how LLMs respond, informing evaluation and deployment of AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

Method: Create a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems in multiple representations (story problems, word equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases). Evaluate five contemporary LLMs under direct answer generation. Add a code-augmented condition where models generate executable Python code validated by local execution. Analyze correctness across representations, track flip rates, and examine latency/cost and failure modes (reasoning errors, protocol violations, execution errors).

Result: Significant representational sensitivity: model correctness frequently changes across equivalent formulations; nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. Isomorphic reformulations degrade performance despite preserved math. Code-based reasoning reveals latent capabilities in some models but does not uniformly improve robustness; failures shift from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures, and representation sensitivity often persists even when reasoning succeeds. Overall, scaffolds improve some aspects but do not eliminate brittleness and introduce tradeoffs in reliability, latency, and cost.

Conclusion: Treat representation as a first-class interface design variable in evaluating and deploying LLM-based problem solving. Robust evaluation and tooling should account for surface representations, balancing correctness, reliability, latency, and cost in AI-assisted systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on mathematical problem solving, yet prior work often treats representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflates reasoning errors with interface failures. This paper investigates representation robustness in LLM-based mathematical problem solving by systematically varying surface representations of the same underlying problems, including story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Using a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems, we evaluate five contemporary LLMs under a direct answer generation condition. We find substantial representational sensitivity: models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations, with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. We also observe systematic regressions under isomorphic reformulations, showing that even subtle paraphrase-level changes can degrade performance despite preserved mathematical structure. We then evaluate a code-augmented condition in which models externalize reasoning as executable Python code that is run locally for validation. This interface reveals strong latent reasoning capability in some models that perform poorly under direct prompting, but it does not uniformly improve robustness. Instead, failures shift across interaction layers, from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Even when executable reasoning succeeds, representation sensitivity often persists. Overall, our results show that reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness, but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. We argue that representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, especially for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

</details>


### [142] [Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20524)
*Sagar Dangal,Manoj Shakya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mean cross-positional attention degradation in transformers shows a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern; however, increasing attention mass via biasing attention has limited or mixed effect on retrieval, suggesting function tokens influence via hidden states rather than attention scores. Interpretability claims based on cross-attention should be treated with caution, with implications for KV-cache eviction strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether mean cross-positional attention degradation causally limits contextual retrieval across diverse models, and assess the generality and interpretability of attention-based explanations.

Method: Six experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. Characterize short-term degradation (5-100 tokens) and layer-wise entropy; analyze function token anchoring; introduce strategic comma insertions; propose Relay-Aware Attention (RAA) to bias attention toward function tokens; use multi-fact retrieval probes.

Result: Observed an exponential-then-plateau degradation pattern whose rate decreases with depth; architecture-specific layer entropy signatures. Function-token anchoring varies: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversals at long distances. Comma insertion at clause boundaries reduces degradation in the 40-80 token window, linked to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. RAA increases attention mass by 16–24% but yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and mixed (near-zero net) effects on OPT-1.3B. Multi-fact retrieval probes indicate degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models.

Conclusion: Mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens influence predictions through their hidden states, not through the attention they receive. This challenges attribution based on cross-attention and has implications for interpretability methods and attention-score-based optimizations (e.g., KV-cache eviction).

Abstract: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

</details>


### [143] [Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20525)
*Yichen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Autonomous GPT-5.5 Pro agent reportedly produced seven correct proofs that the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture is false over R in eight trials; one trial left a gap. Proofs are diverse (units-based and L^p regions of algebraic integers); average ~132.4k reasoning tokens per trial; code and proofs released for reproducibility; claims data-contamination-free setup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess AI-driven automated mathematical proof generation for a long-standing open problem and evaluate the feasibility of a problem-agnostic, multi-stage prompting pipeline in producing rigorous proofs.

Method: Three-stage prompting pipeline: (1) proof-plan proposal, (2) proof construction, (3) review. Agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro; eight independent trials; explored diverse constructions, including unit-based and L^p regions of algebraic integers; measured and reported reasoning tokens; released code and intermediate outputs for reproducibility and contamination-free evaluation.

Result: In seven of eight trials, the agent generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over R; in the remaining trial, an unresolved gap was identified. Proofs are heterogeneous, with some aligning with existing unit-based approaches and others using algebraic-integer region constructions; average 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial.

Conclusion: Demonstrates AI potential for autonomous proof discovery and reproducible case-studies, but extraordinary claims require rigorous external verification. Key next steps include formalization, independent verification (proof assistants), and transparent data/code release to validate the counterexamples and gap analyses.

Abstract: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

</details>


### [144] [ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20526)
*Matthew ffrench-Constant,Daniel Yang,Xinmeng Huang,Sanyam Kapoor*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A calibration benchmark (ConfidenceBench) evaluates verbalized confidence in 15 frontier LLMs using Brier score on 200 private MC questions; results show some models calibrate well (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) with a 0.103 Brier score, outperforming calibrated-random baseline; accuracy and calibration diverge across models, indicating calibration is a distinct reliability axis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many applications, incorrect but confidently stated answers are costly; need to measure model's ability to express confidence truthfully; Brier score incentivizes honest probability reporting; enabling evaluation for closed and open models via prompting (no logits).

Method: Prompt-based elicitation of confidence without access to logits; 15 LLMs tested; 200 private MC questions across four categories (spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, unknowable); three independent runs; use Brier score as primary metric; comparison to calibrated-random baseline.

Result: Best models achieve Brier scores ~0.103 (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview); calibrated-random baseline 0.1875; Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite 0.367; accuracy and calibration diverge; an accurate model is not necessarily well-calibrated; several models underperform baseline despite reasonable accuracy.

Conclusion: Verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct, practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy evaluation; evaluating both accuracy and calibration is important for deployment decisions.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

</details>


### [145] [Evaluating and Guarding Citation Faithfulness in Agentic Scientific Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20527)
*Taewan Goo,Junsik Kim,Kyulhee Han,GwonYul Jo,Jong-Soo Kim,Tae-Hyung Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Demonstrates that reliability of citation checks in agentic LLMs is variable and not trustworthy across verifiers; proposes a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard using split-conformal bounds, validated on multiple models and benchmarks to enable bounded, reproducible evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the hidden unreliability of citation-verification checks in agentic LLM systems, which undermines trust and cross-paper comparability; establish a standard, auditable protocol and guard that produce calibration against human gold data.

Method: Introduce a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard. Use a swappable verifier and a deterministic BM25 re-attribution; apply split-conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample, distribution-free bounds on truly unsupported citations that slip past a flag rule; calibrate against human gold; validate across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA; provide open single-GPU kit.

Result: Found that the unsupported-citation rate on identical agent outputs ranges from ~3% to ~18% depending on verifier strictness; verifiers agree on which citations are supported but disagree on which to flag (low negative-specific agreement ~0.27–0.30); proposed protocol and guard produce a bound on missed unsupported citations that is valid on held-out gold; bound transfer to deployment depends on calibration challenges; demonstrated across four models and three pipelines with confidence intervals for key metrics.

Conclusion: Cross-paper comparison of citation-verification strategies is invalid without a named verifier and protocol. The paper offers a practical, auditable framework (gold-anchored protocol + conformal guard) that measures and bounds unsupported citations, enabling reproducible evaluation and deployment-ready safeguards, albeit with calibration challenges that must be addressed for real-world transfer.

Abstract: Agentic LLM systems such as OpenScholar and PaperQA2 read the scientific literature and return cited answers, and both they and their benchmarks already check whether those citations hold, with a fixed attribution model or human graders. Neither audits the reliability of that check itself. We show it is not reliable, and that this matters. On identical agent outputs the measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to about 18% depending only on the verifier's strictness, and although verifiers agree on which citations are supported, they disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27 to 0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy and cross-paper comparison is invalid without a named verifier and protocol.
  We present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that make this behavior measurable and bounded. The protocol validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates a guarantee against human gold rather than another model's verdict; the verifier is a swappable instrument chosen on cost (recall 0.94 on the supported class, held out), and re-attribution is a commodity step where a deterministic BM25 matches the best open generator. The guard adds a split-conformal layer placing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flagging rule, a guarantee on catch rate rather than conclusion correctness. The bound holds on held-out gold, and we identify and quantify the condition governing its transfer to deployment, calibration-negative difficulty, with a concrete recalibration recipe, left untested by prior conformal-factuality work.
  Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on public benchmarks (SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA), with confidence intervals on every headline number, the protocol and guard ship as an open single-GPU kit.

</details>


### [146] [PromptPack: Scaling LLM Annotation Agents for Online Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20528)
*Sebastian Koralewski,Merwan Barlier,Yulia Stolin,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A scalable, batched LLM annotation agent (PromptPack) reduces cost and increases throughput for ad-creative feature extraction without sacrificing AUC, using shared prompts, XML structure, and output correction; achieves 89% cost reduction and 2.5x throughput at batch size 20 in offline benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Per-creative prompting incurs high token costs and scalability limits; need high-throughput, deterministic multi-creative feature extraction.

Method: In-context batching with a shared system prompt, strict XML envelope, and an output correction layer to produce deterministic feature extraction; batch processing of multiple creatives; offline retrieval benchmark with logistic regression ranker; measure AUC and introduce VWAL metric.

Result: Cost reduced by 89%, throughput increased by 2.5x at batch size 20; AUC preserved; VWAL introduced; performance on offline benchmark.

Conclusion: PromptPack demonstrates scalable, cost-effective LLM annotation for ad creatives, preserving predictive quality while delivering substantial efficiency gains; suitable for production scaling.

Abstract: Online recommendation platforms increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract structured features from ad creatives. While deploying a single-call LLM annotation agent yields significant Click-Through Rate (CTR) improvements in our live production environment, per-creative prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale. The redundant system instructions sent in every request account for 94% of billed input tokens. To break this cost bottleneck, we introduce PromptPack, a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation agent. PromptPack achieves this scale via in-context batching, combining a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives simultaneously. We evaluate PromptPack via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker. To deeply profile the agent's behavior, we measure AUC and introduce Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), a novel metric capturing the signal quality of the generated features. Compared to our live, unbatched production baseline, PromptPack at batch size 20 cuts our LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x while fully preserving AUC.

</details>


### [147] [DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20531)
*Jerzy Kamiński,Ilya Galyukshev,Artem Kuznetsov,Sergey Chuprin,Kirill Redko,Aidar Shumbalov,Anna Kalyuzhnaya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DynamicMCPBench provides a reusable, live-evaluation framework for LLM agents on MCP servers, focusing on live task execution and effect-based scoring rather than final answers; large-scale study reveals current agents struggle with long, multi-step tool-use tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks score final answers or fixed tool lists, which are fragile on live, stateful data; a reusable, live, trajectory-based benchmark is needed to assess general agentic capabilities on real servers.

Method: Run live tasks on MCP servers with diverse models, generating realistic goals, recording successful trajectories, distilling them into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scoring based on reproducing those effects (pass^3). Scale: 24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks across 15 categories; three independent attempts required for success.

Result: Strongest agents solve ~50% of tasks; 31% of tasks unsolved by any model; longer tool chains reduce accuracy (39% to 13%); human validation shows scoring reliability (chance-corrected agreement = 0.76).

Conclusion: DynamicMCPBench is a practical, reusable benchmarking framework that highlights current agents’ poor performance on long, multi-step agentic tasks and enables practitioners to test on their own servers.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed "ground-truth" list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3: it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

</details>


### [148] [AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20536)
*Junzhi Chen,Harsh Trivedi,Jane Pan,Michael JQ Zhang,Tejas Srinivasan,Niranjan Balasubramanian,Ashish Sabharwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AppWorld-UL extends the AppWorld benchmark with 516 tasks across 9 apps to study user-in-the-loop tool-use; current LLMs struggle, highlighting the importance of correct user interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks miss the diversity of agent-user interactions and robust stateful reasoning; there is a need for larger, interactive benchmarks that incorporate ambiguities, constraints, and user confirmations.

Method: Extend AppWorld with ambiguities and constraints across 516 tasks and 9 simulated apps; simulate user behavior via an LLM constrained by designed knowledge boundaries for reliable interaction; evaluate using Claude Opus 4.7 on overall and compositional subsets.

Result: Claude Opus 4.7 achieves 48.6% overall success on AppWorld-UL, 35.7% on the compositional subset, and 21.3% on the scenario-level strict metric; findings indicate correct user interaction is crucial for success and highlight the benchmark's difficulty.

Conclusion: AppWorld-UL is a challenging, realistic benchmark that can drive progress in research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

Abstract: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a ``user-in-the-loop'' benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

</details>


### [149] [StrideDiffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Time-series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20545)
*Du Yin,Estrid He,Julián Jerónimo Bañuelos,Yang Yang,Feng Hu,Yuchen Luo,Hao Xue,Stephan Sigg,Flora Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StrideDiffusion is a training-free, spectral-aware sampler for time-series diffusion models that adaptively selects denoising stride by monitoring band-level activity (relative energy, log-power drift, phase velocity). It performs fine steps when high-frequency dynamics are active and larger jumps when coarse components dominate, leveraging a bandwise stability insight to justify step-size choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series diffusion models require many sequential denoising steps, causing slow inference. Time-series exhibit multi-band spectral dynamics with bands evolving at different rates, which fixed or generic timestepping fails to exploit.

Method: At each inference step, StrideDiffusion estimates band-level activity via relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to decide the next stride. It alternatingly uses small steps for rapidly varying bands and large jumps for stable, low-frequency components. The approach is training-free and is supplemented by a bandwise stability analysis showing that inactive frequency bands change linearly with jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing theoretical justification for using spectral activity as a step-size cue.

Result: Empirically, on six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, the method uses 14–66 function evaluations (instead of 500–1000) and achieves up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while maintaining or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it attains 5–14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy.

Conclusion: Spectral evolution is a practical and principled signal for fast sampling in time-series diffusion. The training-free, spectral-aware stride adaptation significantly accelerates inference with minimal loss (or gains) in quality, indicating broad applicability to unconditional and conditional time-series tasks.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become competitive generators for time series, but their practical use is limited by the large number of sequential denoising steps required at inference time. Existing fast samplers typically use fixed or generic timestep schedules, overlooking a distinctive property of time-series diffusion: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. We introduce StrideDiffusion, a training-free spectral-aware sampler that adaptively selects the denoising stride from band-level activity. At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to identify whether high- frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. It then takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps once only coarse components remain. A bandwise stability analysis shows that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing a local justification for spectral activity as a step-size indicator. Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 denoising steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it further delivers 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy. These results show that spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stridediff-ts.

</details>


### [150] [CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20553)
*Yubo Wang,Qiuyu Zhao,Zenghui Sun,Shichao Dong,Jinsong Lan,Xiaoyong Zhu,Haoyang Li,Bo Zheng,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes CMI-Mem, an RL-based, lightweight memory manager for agents that adds intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) as a valuation signal alongside downstream QA grounding, aiming to reduce reliance on QA-query sampling; releases code and a 4B checkpoint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory valuation heavily depends on sampled QA questions and the downstream reader, which can bias memory retention and underutilize information in new inputs. There is a need for a model-driven, information-theoretic signal that measures the intrinsic value of new inputs relative to the current memory state.

Method: Train a lightweight memory manager via reinforcement learning with a hybrid reward: (i) downstream QA correctness and (ii) intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) between the new input and current memory. CMI is computed without conditioning on any sampled QA query, providing an information gain measure that complements QA grounding.

Result: Proposes a complete framework (CMI-Mem) and provides open-source code and a 4B-parameter model checkpoint, illustrating the viability of combining QA grounding with CMI-based information gain for memory valuation.

Conclusion: CMI-Mem demonstrates that intrinsic information gain via CMI can complement QA-grounded valuation, enabling a more robust, RL-based memory manager; the authors provide code and a model checkpoint for reproducibility.

Abstract: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

</details>


### [151] [AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20554)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Simone Angelini,Emiliano Pallotti,Pierpaolo Salvo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A learning-to-optimise framework using a GNN to perform real-time multi-hop NR-V2X relay selection, trained on an offline MILP oracle; achieves near-optimal connectivity with orders-of-magnitude faster inference on SUMO–GEMV2 urban datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limitations of sparse RSU density, frequent NLOS conditions, and dynamic vehicular topologies hinder stable single-hop NR-V2X; MILP yields optimal relay decisions but is computationally prohibitive for real-time large-scale networks. A scalable, data-driven approach is needed to enable reliable, low-latency multi-hop connectivity in urban V2X.

Method: Model vehicular states as attributed graphs with CAVs and RSUs as nodes and candidate links enriched with propagation-aware features. Use an offline MILP oracle to generate optimal relay decisions, and train an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) to imitate the oracle, achieving near-constant inference latency for relay selection.

Result: On large-scale urban datasets generated by a SUMO–GEMV2 pipeline, the GINE-based L2O framework attains connectivity comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: The proposed L2O framework enables scalable, real-time NR-V2X relay selection in dense urban environments, leveraging existing vehicular assets to enhance urban V2X connectivity cost-effectively.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude. The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

</details>


### [152] [KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20556)
*Yan Zhu,Y. Chen,Rebecca Faust*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Keyword-based interaction (KeySI) enables feature-level feedback for domain-specific embedding adaptation by grouping extracted keywords into concepts, translating them into document-level supervision to tune pre-trained models with less labeling effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models often fail to capture domain-specific semantics and require extensive labeled data and complex training pipelines. Existing document-level feedback methods also necessitate inspecting whole documents. A keyword-centric interface could lower barriers to adapting embeddings.

Method: KeySI extracts representative keywords from a corpus, visualizes keywords and document embeddings, supports interactive grouping of keywords into concepts, and converts these groups into document-level supervision for iterative model tuning. A prototype implements curation, visualization, and refinement feedback loops.

Result: User studies, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrate that KeySI better captures user intent through keyword grouping and improves embedding alignment/conditioning compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Keyword-based concept specification can effectively steer embedding adaptation with reduced labeling and inspection burden, offering a practical pathway for domain-aware NLP in large corpora.

Abstract: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

</details>


### [153] [WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20638)
*Yichuan Liu,Daniel Cummings,Nick Vadlamudi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WaveformQA is an open-source LLM temporal reasoning benchmark for digital waveforms with 360 questions across 8 difficulty categories, showing context window limitations and benefit of an event-time JSON representation over VCD; framework supports extension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in evaluating LLMs on temporal reasoning over hardware waveforms, beyond HDL code generation, and provide reproducible grounding in real hardware behavior.

Method: Programmatically generate 360 questions with ground truth from open-source designs; eight categories including multi-signal correlation and event ordering; evaluate frontier LLMs; compare VCD vs event-time JSON; open-source framework to extend.

Result: LLMs perform reasonably on simple queries but struggle with complex temporal and multi-step questions due to context limits and reasoning challenges; event-time JSON improves reasoning accuracy relative to VCD.

Conclusion: WaveformQA is a practical, extensible benchmark for temporal reasoning over waveforms; supports rapid prototyping of experiments; demonstrates the value of structured representations for LLM reasoning.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

</details>


### [154] [NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20709)
