*Paul Furgale,Severin Klingler,James Nolan,Matt Staats,Gaia Di Lorenzo,Elisa Martinez Abad,Christian Schüller,Razvan Dinu,Alessio Devoto,Pascal Berard,Gal Kaplun,Elad Sarafian,Riccardo Roveri,Leon Derczynski,Ricardo Silveira Cabral*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NOOA presents a model-agnostic Python framework for building AI agents where the agent is a Python object: methods are actions, fields state, docstrings prompts, and type annotations contracts. Runtime completion of methods with ellipsis allows LLM-driven loops while standard bodies remain deterministic Python. The approach enables testing and maintenance like ordinary software and is supported by six model-facing ideas and validated on SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unify and simplify AI agent development by leveraging familiar Python programming abstractions, enabling testability, traceability, and software-engineering workflows for agent behaviors.

Method: Agent-as-a-Python-object programming model; use Python abstractions directly; expose agent capabilities (context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, validated LLM loops) via simple Python APIs; treat methods with '...' as runtime-augmented actions by an LLM-driven loop; six model-facing ideas: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events.

Result: Current models effectively use the interface in targeted capability tests and on agentic/reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3.

Conclusion: NOOA provides a unified, Pythonic framework that aligns agent development with standard software engineering practices, enabling reliable agent construction, testing, and iteration while integrating advanced LLM-driven loops and clear contracts.

Abstract: Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python. This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events. We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

</details>


### [155] [ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20764)
*Pavel Golikov,Evgenii Opryshko,Gennady Pekhimenko,Mark C. Jeffrey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARBIGRAPH is a benchmark generator that tests tool-assisted language agents on retaining, updating, composing, and discarding task-relevant context across extended reasoning graphs. It reveals failures not visible in single-task evaluation; code and data are open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-task benchmarks miss long-horizon reasoning failures; a controllable, verifiable benchmark with explicit task graphs and automatic verification is needed to probe context management in tool-assisted agents.

Method: Tasks are expressed as natural-language problems with executable Python solvers; tasks are linked via typed intermediate states (scalars and lists); graphs are configurable in length, dependencies, distractor count, and value types; instantiated across math, GSM-style word problems, and Python-tracing tasks; evaluated the Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent over four topologies.

Result: Isolated tasks yield high accuracy; performance drops significantly on dependent tasks, up to 33.3% on branching chains of math tasks, indicating vulnerabilities not captured by single-task tests.

Conclusion: ARBIGRAPH uncovers failure modes absent in single-task evaluations; the work provides code, datasets, and results at the linked GitHub repository, enabling broader benchmarking of context management in tool-assisted reasoning.

Abstract: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

</details>


### [156] [The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20781)
*Bonny Banerjee,Shreya Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an analytical HAT model capturing asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI scaling to determine when AI substitutes for humans, yielding a substitution principle and potential abrupt transitions, hybrid forms, and redesigned hierarchies within organizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To resolve when and how AI replaces human labor in hierarchical organizations, integrating automation economics with organizational design and governance.

Method: Analytical modeling framework that formalizes asymmetry between human and AI capability growth; derives risk-adjusted cost conditions, organizational depth, deployment scale; defines substitution criterion; explores transitions and organizational forms.

Result: Human–AI Substitution Principle; conditions for AI replacement; abrupt transitions; existence of hybrid teams, no minimum human fraction required; flatter hierarchies; middle-management vulnerability; skill-threshold effects; link to broader theory.

Conclusion: Unifies automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

</details>


### [157] [Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20791)
*Phillip Howard,Xin Su,Allen Roush,Manikandan Ravikiran,Amir Abdullah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: High-temperature sampling increases diversity but harms safety; proposes an efficient sequential decoding method to preserve refusal behavior at high entropy, achieving about 91-99% retention of greedy refusals with minimal latency across datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between high-entropy generation and robust safety refusals in LLMs; existing truncation/temperature methods degrade refusal behavior, necessitating a solution.

Method: Propose an efficient sequential decoding approach that preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures with minimal additional latency.

Result: Extensive experiments show preservation of 91-99% of greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets, without compromising high-temperature performance on safe prompts.

Conclusion: Refusal behavior can be maintained under high-temperature sampling with negligible latency, enabling safe high-entropy generation for applications that require diversity.

Abstract: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

</details>


### [158] [Can an AI System Be Creative? A Critical Perspective from Art and Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20796)
*Ivan Magrin-Chagnolleau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Using Boden's framework, the paper argues AI systems cannot possess creativity in its strongest sense. AI shows combinatorial creativity but is limited in exploratory creativity and essentially incapable of transformational creativity. It emphasizes the lack of serendipity and a subjective stance to welcome chance events. It proposes a practical, realistic model of human–AI collaboration for creative work, and demonstrates this via experiments—indeed the paper itself is produced through deliberate human–AI collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether AI can be truly creative, through the lens of Boden's taxonomy, and to reconcile engineering and arts/philosophy perspectives by clarifying limits and guiding practical collaboration.

Method: Theoretical analysis anchored in Boden's three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, value) and three processes (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational); argumentative essay supported by a methodological note and several concrete experiments illustrating human–AI collaboration; the paper itself is a demonstration of its thesis.

Result: AI exhibits combinatorial creativity but is constrained in exploratory creativity and fundamentally unable to achieve transformational creativity. The main limitation is the absence of serendipity and a subject-position to recognize and welcome chance events. A realistic, generative model of human–AI collaboration is proposed, supported by concrete experiments; the paper itself demonstrates the human–AI collaborative process.

Conclusion: Advocates a realistic, generative framework for human–AI collaboration rather than pursuing autonomous AI creativity; emphasizes phenomenology of creativity and practical collaboration; calls for further experiments and refinement of collaborative methodologies.

Abstract: This paper examines the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be creative, approached from the dual perspective of a researcher trained in electrical engineering, pattern recognition, machine learning, and neural networks, who has also spent most of his life engaged in the arts as actor, stage and film director, writer, composer, and visual artist, and in philosophy. Drawing on Margaret Boden's foundational framework, both her three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, and value) and her three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), the paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense. While they exhibit genuine capability in the domain of combinatorial creativity, they are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The paper further argues that the most important limitation of current AI systems is not the absence of novelty per se, but the absence of any mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, all of which play a central role in the phenomenology of creativity, and the absence of any subject position from which to recognize and welcome such chance events. The paper concludes by proposing a model of human, AI creative collaboration that is both realistic and generative, illustrated by several concrete experiments. The paper is itself a demonstration of the thesis it advances: it was composed through a deliberate human AI collaborative process, which is described in the methodological note that opens it.

</details>


### [159] [Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20806)
*Tomohiro Harada,Enrique Alba,Gabriel Luque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A PTME-based framework enables precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, exposing Pareto-optimal configurations under edge-resource envelopes and guiding deployment beyond proxy metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current efficiency evaluations for lightweight LLMs rely on proxy descriptors (e.g., parameter count, FLOPs) that do not capture task-precision or real hardware costs; a direct, precision-aware measurement framework is needed for edge environments.

Method: Develop a PTME-based experimental framework that directly measures Precision, Time, peak Memory, and Energy (hardware-level) during local inference. Apply to representative lightweight LLMs on a desktop platform under controlled edge-class constraints, using benchmarks in code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding.

Result: Static proxies approximate inference cost but fail to predict precision. Tightening resource envelopes raises cost without changing precision; time increases more than energy; larger models are penalized most. No single model dominates across PTME; Pareto analysis identifies non-dominated configurations that balance precision, time, memory, and energy. Relying on size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can misguide deployment; PTME profiling reveals configurations that maintain usable accuracy at lower physical cost.

Conclusion: PTME profiling provides a more nuanced, practical criterion for selecting lightweight LLMs, enabling Pareto-optimal deployment choices that traditional accuracy or efficiency metrics alone miss.

Abstract: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

</details>


### [160] [Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20814)
*Hai-Nam Duy Vuong,Duy-Anh Bui,Trong-Nghia Nguyen,Kim-Ngan Thi Nguyen,Trang Mai Xuan,Tien-Cuong Nguyen,Van-Dem Pham,Thien Van Luong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Guide-grounded multimodal ECG reporting: injecting a distilled ECG Interpretation Guide into prompts to anchor LLM-generated reports in diagnostic criteria, boosting semantic quality and consistency without sacrificing classification accuracy (PTB-XL).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limited interpretability and hallucination risk in CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM ECG report systems by anchoring outputs to established diagnostic criteria.

Method: CNN+Grad-CAM produce class probabilities and heatmaps; textbooks/guidelines are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide injected as a fixed knowledge block per sample; an LLM conditions on the image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the guide to generate structured, guideline-consistent diagnostic reports.

Result: On PTB-XL test set, guide grounding improves semantic quality and perceived consistency of reports while preserving competitive classification performance; average BERTScore of impressions increased from 0.818 to 0.953 compared to CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline.

Conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into multimodal prompting reduces hallucinations and enhances clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, aiding real-world deployment.

Abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

</details>


### [161] [Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20820)
*Christian Arzate Cruz,Stefanos Gkikas,Houshyar Asadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight temporal convolutional networks offer an efficient, interpretable alternative to graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition, nearly matching G-TSG performance with far fewer parameters and lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable real-time, interpretable body-based emotion recognition by reducing computational cost, addressing the heaviness of graph-based skeleton models.

Method: Evaluate a family of temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) on the DIEM-A dataset and compare them to a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Perform region-wise analyses with region-specific TCNs, zero-based occlusion, and gradient saliency of G-TSG.

Result: TCN-Base remains within 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points of G-TSG while using 79.18% fewer parameters and achieving ~12.5x lower classifier latency. Upper-body motion emerges as the strongest standalone cue; region usefulness varies across emotions, and different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior.

Conclusion: Lightweight TCNs can efficiently support body-based emotion recognition and provide practical insights into motion cue contributions and regional importance.

Abstract: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

</details>


### [162] [Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20827)
*Junchi Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Target-specific authorization auditing shows LLMs can be influenced by untrusted evidence; a quantified audit framework reveals nonzero unauthorized actions across tasks and models, highlighting vulnerability despite source-authority cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how mixed-context information (including untrusted sources) affects LLM decision-making and to enable precise auditing of which context factors drive actions.

Method: Introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors for each tool/argument target. Primary test fixes task, proposition, position, and policy while varying only the proposition's source authority; test robustness by weakening valid evidence and using context-subset interactions. Assess 450 controlled next-action tasks across multiple open-weight LLM families, comparing trusted vs. untrusted variants; include controlled degradation to study unauthorized competition.

Result: Trusted vs. untrusted variants diverge in 5.4% of competing cases and 1.7% of supporting cases. Under degradation, unauthorized competition remains at 2.4% (95% CI 2.1–3.0%). These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. Models respond to source-authority cues, but untrusted evidence can still influence actions.

Conclusion: The audit reveals that source-authority cues affect LLM decisions but do not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing actions; the framework enables precise localization of which context factors drive decisions and identifies residual susceptibility to unauthorized inputs.

Abstract: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

</details>


### [163] [Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20848)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A behavioral audit framework for evaluating medical LLMs' use of evidence in diagnosis, showing many evidence interactions are plausible and that accuracy can mask evidence-use failures; introduces role-aware audits separating evidence interaction discovery from failure assignment; evaluated across multiple datasets on open-weight LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnostic accuracy alone does not reveal whether models use clinical evidence properly; need to audit evidence use to detect reasoning failures and improve evaluation of medical LLMs.

Method: Decompose patient information into evidence units; score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets; mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins; separate interaction discovery from failure assessment; evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase; perform blinded five-reviewer, 130-item enriched review in DDXPlus to assess invalid/shortcut-like cases; analyze faithfulness of support and differential interactions.

Result: Most interaction strength is accounted for by faithful support or plausible differential diagnosis; characteristic interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures; invalid/shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and locally-specific evidence in the blinded review; shows accuracy can hide evidence-use failures.

Conclusion: Role-aware audits are needed for medical LLM evaluation; evaluation should separate evidence use from accuracy; flagged interactions should undergo clinical review, and frameworks should account for diagnosis-relative evidence and potential differential reasoning to improve robustness.

Abstract: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [164] [Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20852)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A monitor-red-teaming protocol (Code Monitor Red Teaming) tests whether weak verifiers can detect hidden bugs after code passes public tests; CodeMonitorBench experiments show substantial residual hidden bugs and limited detection, improved by scaffolding and model family but not fully; robustness tests reveal weaknesses under adversarial pressure; GLM-5.1 helps partly, but remaining misses relate to verifier and evidence limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public tests often fail to certify specification correctness for LLM-generated code. A deployment-like monitoring setup is needed to catch residual hidden bugs by using weaker verifiers and varying scaffolding and capability.

Method: Introduce a monitor-red-teaming protocol and instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench across function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Evaluate 71,000 generated candidates with public vs hidden tests, vary generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. Conduct robustness stress tests by public-test-overfit pressure. Use a GLM-5.1 verifier and perform an inferability audit.

Result: Out of 71k candidates, 43,677 pass public tests; 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family but miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates. GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary. Inferability audit shows remaining misses arise from verifier failures and M1 evidence limits.

Conclusion: Public checks alone are insufficient to certify correctness. A monitor-based red-teaming approach can reveal hidden bugs, and targeted improvements (scaffolding, stronger models) help but do not eliminate gaps. Residual misses are tied to verifier limitations and evidence-bound constraints (M1).

Abstract: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

</details>


### [165] [Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20891)
*Pengyu Zhu,Lijun Li,Longju Yang,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MisKnow-Agent framework shows that misleading knowledge can propagate into final reports in Deep Research workflows; corpus-level verification helps but does not stop workflow-level false conclusions; defenses mitigate but do not fully prevent, highlighting need for end-to-end evidence verification at both model and framework levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess reliability of Deep Research agents in open information environments and quantify risk that credible misinformation is integrated into long-horizon reports.

Method: Introduce MisKnow-Agent to generate 5,933 quality-controlled misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles; base on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks; evaluate across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents; test three defense configurations (pre-, post-, combined) and compare corpus-focused verification with workflow-level evidence use.

Result: Exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false conclusions in final reports even with limited exposure; corpus verification identifies misleading content but adoption persists in long-horizon workflows; all three defense configurations reduce but do not eliminate false-conclusion adoption; evidence verification and correction are needed at both model and framework levels.

Conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires integrated evidence verification/correction mechanisms beyond planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation improvements.

Abstract: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

</details>


### [166] [Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20913)
*Yi Xiong,Yuan-Yuan Cheng,Xiao-Ming Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A source-prior-guided selective adaptation method for fine-tuning diffusion models, using a static mask to pick parameters for downstream adaptation and applying structured updates, yielding a better adaptation–retention trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the trade-off between target-domain/style customization and retaining the model's broad generative capabilities, which is not adequately managed by existing full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods.

Method: 1) Observing that general-generative loss is unevenly distributed across pretrained parameters and that parameters with small impact on general capability are structurally inconsistent across layers/types; 2) Learn a static mask to identify parameters suited for downstream adaptation; 3) Apply structured update strategies on the selected subset.

Result: Empirical experiments show the proposed selective adaptation achieves a better adaptation–retention trade-off than strong existing baselines across diffusion-model fine-tuning tasks.

Conclusion: Selective, source-prior-guided fine-tuning with a learned parameter mask and structured updates provides an efficient way to adapt diffusion models to new domains or styles while preserving broad generative capabilities.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

</details>


### [167] [Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20916)
*Deyu Jing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Traceable Scholarship as the normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, introducing page anchors, citation-first generation, and a three-layer AIH-Infra to ensure traceability; demonstrates via a Kant knowledge-base case study that traceability enables retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fluency of LLM-generated scholarly text can mask lack of sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence; without traceable anchors, AI-assisted outputs risk being plausibly written but unverifiable. The paper situates traceability across print, digital, and generative AI knowledge infrastructures to preserve public, refutable scholarship.

Method: Define normative traceability constructs (page anchors, dual page numbers, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, Scope Contract), and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). Validate via a case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base to illustrate retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading.

Result: Articulates concrete traceability constructs and a reference architecture (AIH-Infra) and demonstrates their utility in a detailed Kant knowledge-base case study for improving verifiability, enabling corrections, evidence evaluation, and downgraded judgments when evidence is lacking.

Conclusion: Traceability is the essential condition for maintaining public, refutable scholarship in the era of generative AI; it transcends a mere software feature and should guide AI-assisted humanistic research across evolving knowledge infrastructures.

Abstract: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

</details>


### [168] [OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20918)
*Tong Zhao,Yuyang Hu,Reed Li,Yu Lu,Haibo Shi,Yutao Zhu,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPOD introduces On-Policy Omni Distillation, routing each student response to its modality-specific teachers (text, image, audio) and gating guidance to minimize cross-modal interference. It yields a balanced, high-performing omni-modal model that outperforms pooled multimodal training across 12 benchmarks on three backbone sizes, with a deployable single model after training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome performance clashes when training a single model on pooled multimodal data by leveraging modality-specialist teachers in a coordinated, on-policy distillation framework, thus preserving cross-modal balance in a unified model.

Method: For each student response, route to the matching text/image/audio teacher. Allow teacher guidance only when the teacher’s probability exceeds the student’s, and adjust the influence of each modality teacher independently during training. The routed teacher evaluates both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Training spans twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes; the modality-specific specialists are discarded after training to yield one deployable omni-modal model.

Result: OPOD achieves the best average performance across scales: 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2, surpassing the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points respectively. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a pooled multimodal post-training baseline on all twelve benchmarks and ranks first or second on eleven benchmarks, even when individual specialists are present.

Conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers through route-and-gate on-policy distillation yields superior, balanced omni-modal performance and produces a single deployable model without retaining the specialists.

Abstract: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

</details>


### [169] [Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20925)
*Shen Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a dual-signal, interpretable entity-importance representation (audience-evaluation and structural-authority) and empirically shows these signals are non-redundant; uses IMDb/Wikidata/Wikipedia in a movie-domain test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single scalar importance can discard distinctions needed for task-specific retrieval and reasoning; a minimal, interpretable multi-signal representation may improve task performance by preserving distinct signals.

Method: Define two dimensions per entity: audience-evaluation (IMDb rating-based ranking) and structural-authority (PageRank on Wikipedia hyperlink network; Wikidata for alignment). Evaluate on 482 entities with 13,690 directed relations. Compute Spearman correlation between dimensions and top-N overlap to assess redundancy and divergence.

Result: Weak but significant association (Spearman ρ = 0.2275, p < 0.001); top-10 overlap 10%, top-100 overlap 34%; divergent signals in both directions, indicating non-redundancy of the two dimensions.

Conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals; a single scalar notion of importance is insufficient for task-aware AI knowledge systems. The work provides a minimal, interpretable framework and empirical support for preserving multiple signals before context-specific selection or aggregation.

Abstract: AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

</details>


### [170] [SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20926)
*Yinhao Tang,Youqing Fang,Yanan Sun,Wenran Liu,Weiming Zhang,Bin Liu,Kuikun Liu,Wenwei Zhang,Kai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new benchmark, SciExplore, evaluates scientific information-seeking and reasoning for LLMs and agents across 103 tasks in 10+ disciplines, revealing notable gaps in current models, especially for complex structured synthesis tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address limitations of existing benchmarks that emphasize general-domain retrieval or static QA and to assess higher-level scientific information-seeking and reasoning found in realistic workflows.

Method: Four task types: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis; 103 expert-curated tasks spanning more than ten scientific disciplines; evaluation of 10+ state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents.

Result: Models exhibit substantial performance gaps; accuracy degrades as task complexity increases; extremely low accuracy on challenging structured synthesis tasks.

Conclusion: Current models/agents are limited for realistic scientific information-seeking; SciExplore provides a more realistic benchmark to drive progress in scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

</details>


### [171] [Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20937)
*Chinmaya Kumar Dehury,Boris Sedlak,Alaa Saleh,Ilir Murturi,Lauri Loven,Satish Narayana Srirama,Praveen Kumar Donta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), an intelligence-centric framework with a three-layer architecture to treat intelligence as a reusable, discoverable asset across edge and cloud.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing edge intelligence research focuses on AI for edge resource management or deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. There is no framework that treats intelligence as a first-class entity that can be described, discovered, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications.

Method: Proposes a three-layer CEI architecture and analyzes enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

Result: Provides a conceptual, vision-level framework with design considerations for CEI; outlines enabling technologies and research dimensions but does not report empirical results.

Conclusion: CEI aims to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity across the distributed edge–cloud continuum, encouraging standardization, interoperability, and lifecycle management, and prompting future research in inventories, clustering, and marketplaces.

Abstract: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

</details>


### [172] [From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20970)
*Weihan Zhang,Xuan Zhao,Yenwen Peng,Yuqi Chen,Jun Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reformulates time-varying INR training from dense coordinate sampling to per-location sequence-level supervision, improving reconstruction and reducing training cost, and can be extended with mixture-of-experts (MoE) for heterogeneous temporal dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense spatiotemporal sampling for implicit representations is computationally expensive and underutilizes temporal structure; a per-location temporal sequence view promises greater efficiency and better alignment with temporal evolution.

Method: Represent data as spatially indexed time series and train INRs with sequence-level supervision at each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples; this is compatible with existing INR architectures; includes a mixture-of-experts (MoE) instantiation.

Result: Consistent improvements in reconstruction quality and substantial reductions in training cost; the MoE variant yields further gains over both the base reformulation and prior MoE-based INR methods.

Conclusion: The reformulation is broadly applicable across INR architectures and enables stronger capacity allocation to handle heterogeneous temporal dynamics via MoE.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

</details>


### [173] [Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20972)
*Swapnanil Saha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a two-tier, harness-controlled memory architecture for long-running coding agents, where tacit, situational knowledge is stored outside the agent and reliably delivered through a cue-anchored memory channel. Empirically shows near-zero voluntary memory use, deterministic injections, and robust recall across compactions, highlighting delivery over storage as the key product.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agents rely on explicit, authored documents while tacit, situational expertise remains unwritten and is loaded only incidentally. This offloading is argued to be essential for long-term reliability and should be harnessed, not left to agent choice.

Method: Introduce a two-tier design grounded in cognitive theories of memory offloading and event-based prospective memory; define a cue-anchored memory model with trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary; deterministically evaluate the harness-driven memory channel in a real coding task; perform a repeated-compaction decay probe to test memory persistence and reconstruction.

Result: 1) Voluntary memory use is near zero even with pre-seeded stores (0 memory ops in 114 turns). 2) Deterministic injections in seeded runs with zero false alarms. 3) 39% of intra-session re-reads paid for previously stored content before compaction. 4) Ten facts held only in conversation vanish across first summary and most compactions, but can be reconstructed from harness files; facts from harness-owned store survive across all compactions. 

Conclusion: The reliable memory channel is delivery-focused: the harness-managed, cue-anchored memory system enables persistent, recoverable knowledge without requiring the agent to actively write or read it; true value lies in making memory usage transparent to the agent.

Abstract: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

</details>


### [174] [Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20981)
*Jay Gor,Karm Dave,Akshita Abrol,Rajesh Gupta,Sudeep Tanwar,Zhengkui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A survey synthesizing how efficiency techniques in multimodal LMs interact, highlighting that token compression, video management, caching, routing, and quantization are interdependent; introduces Temporal Routing Consistency diagnostic and outlines routing-aware design trade-offs and open directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient multimodal inference is constrained by hardware, memory, and energy, and improvements in one area can alter others. Independent optimizations can create bottlenecks; a unified, hardware-aware view is needed, especially for edge deployment and benchmarking.

Method: Review recent advances in vision-language and multimodal LLMs, organize literature around interactions among techniques (visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, MoE routing, quantization, etc.), introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic, and discuss design trade-offs and open research directions.

Result: Structured synthesis showing that efficiency techniques are interdependent (e.g., token compression affects routing; routing impacts quantization sensitivity; cache policies affect evidence retention). Provides a taxonomy, key design trade-offs, a diagnostic (Temporal Routing Consistency), and a roadmap of open research directions and benchmarking needs.

Conclusion: Calls for routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence, emphasizing end-to-end system considerations over isolated optimizations.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

</details>


### [175] [GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20982)
*Vishal Ishwar Naik,Chenyu Xu,Donna Dong,Hussein Hassan,Abhishek Pradhan,Ofer Mendelevitch,Tallat Shafat,Humayun Irshad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GuardianAgentBench (GABench) evaluates safety of autonomous LLM agents across 580 scenarios in six domains, using three production frameworks. It reveals persistent tool-use safety gaps, two failure regimes, and that runtime guardrails outperform prompts, achieving ~19.9% failure recovery at 0.5% false positives (best model at 74.8% accuracy).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess and quantify the safety and reliability of autonomous agents with tool usage in adversarial and varied tool-usage settings, and compare runtime guardrail interventions against prompt-based defenses.

Method: A 580-scenario benchmark (six domains) tested on LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara with six state-of-the-art models. Includes multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Analyzes tool-use behavior, tool-set size, and sequential turn depth. Compares runtime guardrails to system-prompt defenses by measuring accuracy and failure recovery (under controlled false positive rates).

Result: Best configuration achieves 74.8% overall accuracy. Two failure regimes observed: stronger models under-call required tools and weaker models mis-select/over-call tools. Performance declines as tool-set size and turn depth increase; long-horizon planning is a bottleneck. Guardrail interventions recover 19.9% of failures at a 0.5% false-positive rate, outperforming system prompts across all models.

Conclusion: Execution-time structural interventions can improve safety without harming correct agent behavior, suggesting runtime guardrails are a robust defense against tool-use-related failures in autonomous LLM agents.

Abstract: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

</details>


### [176] [Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20999)
*Zibin Lin,Shengli Zhang,Taotao Wang,Yihan Xia,Deen Ma,Guofu Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WML introduces a Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning framework to localize failures, attribute implicated mechanisms, and reuse third-party Skills through a Node–Mechanism Attribution component and a six-module WGSO loop. It achieves strong results on SpreadsheetBench (high hard accuracy) and WikiTableQuestions transfer, with efficient compiled execution on Compiler-Supported50; code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current optimizers fail to jointly identify where a workflow fails, which mechanism caused the failure, and how to reuse relevant Knowledge from Skills locally. The work seeks provenance- and scope-aware knowledge reuse and patching to improve reliability and efficiency of frozen LM agents.

Method: Node–Mechanism Attribution locates the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and the minimal valid edit; routes single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module WGSO loop selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory.

Result: Empirical gains include: SpreadsheetBench hard accuracy 90.33±1.53 (DeepSeek) and 74.67±3.51 (Qwen3.6-Flash); successful transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00±2.00 and 83.00±2.00 denotation accuracy without extra optimization. On Compiler-Supported50, WML achieves the highest hard-PASS rate and lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution reduces tokens and calls versus a direct SkillAgent while retaining most successful tasks.

Conclusion: WML enhances debugging, reliability, and efficiency of Skill-driven agents by localizing failures, attributing mechanisms, and curating provenance-aware knowledge via a structured optimization loop. The approach demonstrates strong cross-domain transfer and practical efficiency improvements; code is available for replication.

Abstract: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

</details>


### [177] [Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000)
*Hyuk Lim,Seunghyun Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Naju introduces a decoupled discrete recurrent unit that jointly achieves strong long-range memory retention and overwriting without stability regularization, outperforming Mamba baselines and maintaining linear-time/memory scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-sequence memory tasks require both near-lossless retention of bindings and the ability to overwrite stale information. Coupled single-gate designs constrain retention and write, while continuous-time SSMs add complexity; there is a gap for an efficient, stable recurrent cell that supports both demands.

Method: Factorize the recurrent update as x_n = f_n ⊙ x_{n-1} + i_n ⊙ (B_n u_n) with a discrete pole f_n in (0,1) (Schur-stable by construction), an independent write gain i_n, and input-dependent maps. Argue that decoupling f_n from i_n breaks the theoretical retention-write bound |r|+w ≤ 1 seen in coupled designs. Parameterize discrete transitions directly rather than via zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system. Evaluate on a diagnostic suite and standard benchmarks (WikiText-103, Long Range Arena, multi-query associative recall).

Result: Empirically, Naju remains strong on both retention and overwriting at long horizons—4× longer training length—whereas baselines often excel on only one aspect. Across WikiText-103, Long Range Arena, and multi-query recall, Naju consistently matches or surpasses Mamba baselines and remains competitive with Transformers while offering linear-time and linear-memory scaling.

Conclusion: Decoupling the write/read gates removes the anti-correlated retention-overwrite constraint observed in coupled recurrences, enabling robust long-range memory and efficient computation. Naju demonstrates strong generalization across language modeling and memory-heavy tasks, outperforming Mamba baselines and achieving competitive performance with favorable scalability.

Abstract: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

</details>


### [178] [Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21010)
*Vasudha Bhatnagar,Purnima Bindal,Vikas Kumar,Raj Kumari Bahl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM-based summarizers' stability in zero-shot settings, yielding a stability index across a stratified corpus; empirical results show inter-model variability and genre differences in stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the stochasticity and trustworthiness concerns of LLM-generated zero-shot summaries, particularly in educational contexts where reliability is critical.

Method: Level 1: document-level stability analysis with multiple zero-shot summaries produced under controlled conditions; compute a stability coefficient for each document by scoring semantic and factual alignment with the source. Level 2: aggregate observations over a stratified sample of documents to estimate an overall stability index (proxy for trustworthiness) of the LLM-summarizer.

Result: Found statistically significant differences in generation-level variability among three LLM-summarizers across three genres using multiple evaluation metrics, indicating a measurable stability problem.

Conclusion: The study highlights stability as a core issue in LLM-based summarization and motivates further work toward robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM-summarizers; introduces a two-level protocol and stability index as evaluation framework.
