Abstract: Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

</details>


### [179] [EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21013)
*Lihuang Fang,Yuchen Zou,kebin Jin,Jinghui Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces EmoAgent-R1, a reinforcement-learning framework for dynamic agent specialization in multimodal emotion recognition, with a cold-start phase and P-GRPO policy optimization; achieves stronger emotion reasoning and improved training stability on MER benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed prompts fail to capture dynamic, source-dependent emotions in multimodal inputs; there is a need for dynamic routing and specialization of agents within MLLMs to handle complex emotion reasoning.

Method: Cold-start training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data to bootstrap emotion recognition, reasoning, and routing; followed by reinforcement learning with a two-step workflow: agent selection and agent specialization; Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) combines group-relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to turn sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, addressing coarse credit assignment in GRPO.

Result: Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks show superior emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

Conclusion: Dynamic agent specialization via RL with P-GRPO enhances MER performance and stability; the framework effectively handles dynamic emotion sources in multimodal settings and offers a robust training strategy for MLLMs in MER.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

</details>


### [180] [HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21019)
*Wei Liu,Siya Qi,Linhai Zhang,Lorainne Tudor Car,Yulan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HiMe is a locally deployable, privacy-first platform enabling real-time, personalized health analytics from wearables via LLM agents, with the database treated as a first-class component and a focus on Pareto-optimal efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses limitations of rigid, non-personalized wearable analyses and the absence of open-source, privacy-preserving, real-time personal health platforms.

Method: Proposes HiMe architecture: privacy-first, real-time data processing, long-term user modeling, database-as-a-first-class citizen, and joint optimization of effectiveness and efficiency to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance; designed for compatibility with diverse wearable ecosystems.

Result: A concept/implementation of a locally deployable platform that processes personal health data in real time with privacy preservation, enabling continuous, personalized health monitoring via Personal Health Agents.

Conclusion: HiMe offers practical, adaptive health insights from wearables through privacy-preserving, real-time analysis and a platform design that foregrounds data ownership and efficiency.

Abstract: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

</details>


### [181] [Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21042)
*Muyang Du,Shuang Yu,Junjie Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Faster IndexTTS-2 optimizes all components of an autoregressive TTS stack (GPT, diffusion transformer, vocoder) with NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to enable streaming and batched inference, achieving up to 5x speedups (GPT) and 3.6x end-to-end on Seed-TTS with minimal quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To meet production latency requirements for autoregressive TTS, where IndexTTS-2 delivers high synthesis quality but is slow without streaming or batching.

Method: Port all neural components to NVIDIA TensorRT/TensorRT-LLM, implement streaming synthesis, and enable batched inference to maximize GPU utilization, evaluated on Seed-TTS for English and Chinese.

Result: End-to-end speedup up to 3.6x; autoregressive GPT component up to 5.0x; minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness.

Conclusion: Provides a practical blueprint for efficiently accelerating autoregressive speech models on GPUs, facilitating deployment in latency-sensitive applications and serving as a reference for similar architectures.

Abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

</details>


### [182] [Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21101)
*Jie Peng,Yanping Zheng,Zhewei Zhe,Bin Tong,Guan Wang,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SID-based generative recommender is compositional but not fully open-ended under a temporal strict protocol; unseen tokens and unsupported token paths hinder cold-start reach, prompting suggestions for separate token spaces and context-aware interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether semantic-ID (SID) based generative recommendations can support open-ended, cold-start items in an absolute-time setting and to diagnose token-level limitations.

Method: Seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing to assess reachability of new items; interpret SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing.

Result: Models can occasionally reach future items using observed tokens/prefixes but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths; SID generation is compositional but limited in open-endedness.

Conclusion: SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended; future directions include more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context to improve cold-start and open-world support.

Abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

</details>


### [183] [AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21106)
*Qinfeng Li,Yuntai Bao,Xinyan Yu,Hongze Chen,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An attribution-guided RL framework that adds token-level credit to memory-construction rewards, improving LLM memory management in long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory management in LLM agents is essential yet difficult: heuristic rules can misalign with downstream goals, coarse outcome rewards fail to identify which intermediate memory contents are helpful, and lack of ground-truth signals makes fine-grained credit assignment in RL challenging.

Method: AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer, guiding memory-construction decisions via reinforcement learning.

Result: AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL baselines on long-horizon dialogue QA, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, and stabilizes RL optimization.

Conclusion: AttriMem provides a principled, attribution-guided approach to memory construction for LLM agents, improving performance and transferability in long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Effective memory is crucial for LLM agents, yet constructing it effectively remains challenging. A memory-construction policy decides what information to extract, store, update, compress, or discard as interactions accumulate. Heuristic memory methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules, which can misalign with downstream objectives and limit cross-task adaptability. RL-based methods, by contrast, learn from task feedback but mainly use outcome- or module-level rewards. These coarse signals indicate task success but cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck. However, constructing such process feedback is prohibitively difficult because intermediate memory decisions lack unique ground-truth targets, while the appropriate credit varies with the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory and therefore cannot be specified in advance. We propose AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer. Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, stabilizes RL optimization.

</details>


### [184] [V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21151)
*Zhetong Zhang,Honghao Fu,Miao Xu,Yiwei Wang,Yujun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Video LLM safety: harmful videos paired with benign queries can bypass safeguards, yielding high attack success. A three-level diagnostic framework, V-DEAL, analyzes model behavior, understanding, and representations to diagnose this vulnerability, supplemented by a prompt-injection defense that substantially lowers attack success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify and understand a surprising safety vulnerability in Video LLMs where harmful video content is not effectively rejected when paired with benign queries, and develop practical defenses.

Method: Introduce V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework (behavior, understanding, internal representations); progressively rule out perception failures; quantify internal refusal tendency; conduct hidden-state analyses; evaluate on six Video LLMs across three benchmarks; also propose a prompt-injection intervention.

Result: Models correctly identify harmful content with >81% accuracy, yet attack success remains 48.33% under harmful video + benign query. Hidden-state analysis shows visual understanding triggers weaker refusal than textual understanding. Prompt injection reduces attack success by ~48.24 percentage points, comparable to fine-tuning methods.

Conclusion: V-DEAL provides a diagnostic lens into the mechanism behind the vulnerability; the proposed prompt-injection defense offers an effective, practical mitigation for safety risks in Video LLMs.

Abstract: As Video Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. Counterintuitively, we find that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with explicitly harmful queries. To understand the underlying mechanism of this vulnerability, we present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. By progressively ruling out perception failure and quantifying the model's internal refusal tendency, V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing the underlying mechanism of the observed vulnerability. We tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks and observed that models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81\% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33\% under the condition pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis further shows that visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a prompt injection intervention method that reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods, providing an effective and practical means to address such safety risks in Video LLMs.

</details>


### [185] [SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21156)
*Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti,David Gamez,Franco Such,Nik Kairinos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel assistant for elderly with frailty/dementia, using a travel-graph that combines route planning with predictive modelling. It generates failure scenarios with LLMs and Anticip8, proposes interventions, and estimates their impact to maximize the likelihood of reaching the destination. Evaluated on travel-graph generation and a 26-journey field study; results show Anticip8 + GPT-based intervention evaluation yields the most reliable performance; user feedback: improved confidence/safety but usability needs improvement; potential applications beyond travel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban mobility is hindered for over a million elderly with frailty or dementia; need for adaptive, proactive assistive systems that anticipate failures and prescribe interventions to maintain safe navigation to destinations.

Method: Proposes SafeStep with a novel travel-graph representation that integrates planning with predictive modelling. For each journey stage: (i) generate personalized failure scenarios using a combination of large language models (LLMs) and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine; (ii) propose targeted interventions; (iii) estimate impact on outcome probabilities. Select interventions to maximize probability of reaching the destination. Evaluation includes travel-graph generation experiments and a field study with 26 real journeys.

Result: Results indicate that combining Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most reliable performance. User feedback indicates increased confidence and perceived safety; however interface usability needs improvement for the target demographic.

Conclusion: SafeStep shows promise as a decision-support framework for elder mobility and could be extended to other domains such as mental health, career coaching, and addiction treatment; future work includes usability enhancements and release.

Abstract: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

</details>


### [186] [Safeguards for Speech2Speech LLM-Assistants: A Case Study in Automotive Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21180)
*Gregor Endler,Sebastian Kraus,Lukas Stappen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Two guardrail strategies for end-to-end speech-to-speech (S2S) automotive assistants—transcript-based and tool-based—are evaluated and found inadequate for industrial deployment due to prohibitive latency and non-determinism; the paper outlines open challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure domain-specific safety in S2S automotive assistants without compromising natural, humanlike dialogue, by evaluating guardrail architectures.

Method: Empirical evaluation of two guardrail approaches (transcript-based and tool-based) in S2S, measuring latency and reliability; assessment of feasibility for industrial deployment.

Result: Both approaches incur significant latency (0–1.4 seconds per answer) and technical issues (e.g., non-deterministic tool calls), limiting applicability in industry.

Conclusion: S2S guardrails in automotive settings remain challenging; the paper outlines open challenges and suggests that new strategies are needed to reconcile safety with responsive, natural interactions.

Abstract: Recent advances have introduced speech-to-speech (S2S) conversational assistants capable of producing natural-sounding interactions, including non-verbal cues like tonality and mood. In the automotive domain, this enables intuitive and humanlike in-car dialogue experiences. However, integrating these end-to-end assistants limits architectural options for programmable domain-specific safeguards. This paper discusses two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails: transcript-based and tool-based. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that both strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment in most cases due to prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks) and technical impediments (like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior). Finally, we outline open challenges for S2S guardrails in the automotive context.

</details>


### [187] [Explaining Weather Bulletins via ILP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21184)
*Enrico Santi,Alessandro Dal Palù,Agostino Dovier,Talissa Dreossi,Andrea Formisano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An ILP-based pipeline using FastLAS2 to learn interpretable hypotheses that explain weather bulletins by translating simulated meteorological data and official bulletins into ASP facts and deriving explanations for forecast pictograms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide transparent, symbolic explanations for meteorological forecasts, improving interpretability of bulletin symbols; leverage non-monotonic ILP capabilities to model complex weather reasoning.

Method: Pipeline: simulate data; extract ASP facts; create ILP examples; apply FastLAS2 to induce explanatory hypotheses; translate to natural language explaining forecast and symbol choices; approach is generic and region-independent.

Result: A hypothesis that explains the forecast and symbol choices; demonstrates interpretability and generality; no quantitative results reported in abstract.

Conclusion: The method is general, not region-specific; applicable to bulletins from various sources and regions; ILP with FastLAS2 yields human-understandable explanations for meteorological reasoning.

Abstract: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) originated within the Logic Programming community in the Nineties as a framework for combining symbolic learning with declarative knowledge representation. Nowadays, mature ILP frameworks exist and they are capable of learning complex, non-monotonic hypotheses, thus broadening both the modeling capabilities and the scope of real-world applications of ILP. This work is primarily based on the FastLAS2 framework and aims to generate simple, interpretable hypotheses to help clarify the weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG, the Regional Meteorological Observatory of the Italian region of Friuli Venezia-Giulia. In this paper we present a pipeline that, starting from simulated meteorological raw data and from OSMERs' bulletins (used as ground truth), extracts data as ASP facts and generates ILP examples. From such examples an explanatory hypothesis is then inferred via FastLAS2. Such a hypothesis (translated into natural language) explains the weather forecast issued by human experts, and in particular the rationale behind experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram (the symbol-annotated meteorological map of the forecast). The proposed approach is general, not specific to any particular region and it can equally be applied to bulletins from other sources and to different regions.

</details>


### [188] [Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21185)
*Akihiro Takemura,Katsumi Inoue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Matrix-based differentiable logic programming is proposed to reduce reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems by unifying rules and constraints in a single matrix, analyzing gradient-flow under fuzzy t-norms, and showing that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms mitigates shortcut phenomena on MNIST variants, with architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge to neural learning being crucial.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic systems risk shortcut reasoning where constraints are satisfied without addressing the task (constraint shortcuts) or data bias leads to semantically wrong mappings (cognition shortcuts). A unified, matrix-based logic framework aims to improve interpretability and generalization by better aligning neural and symbolic components and by examining training dynamics.

Method: Adopt a matrix-based differentiable logic programming framework that encodes rules and constraints in a single matrix; explore connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and analyze gradient flow properties; implement one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms to enforce crisp mappings; compare against soft-distribution baselines; evaluate on MNIST variant datasets to assess shortcut mitigation; analyze how architectural choices affect coupling of symbolic and neural parts.

Result: Empirical findings indicate that one-to-one grounding significantly reduces both constraint satisfaction shortcuts and cognition shortcuts compared to soft-distribution baselines; a unified matrix encoding of rules/constraints supports shortcut mitigation; gradient-flow properties vary with the chosen t-norm; architectural decisions in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning are critical for effective shortcut mitigation.

Conclusion: A matrix-based, unified encoding with crisp one-to-one grounding, together with careful architectural coupling, provides effective mitigation of shortcut reasoning in neurosymbolic systems. The results highlight the role of training dynamics and model architecture in achieving robust reasoning, suggesting broader applicability and further evaluation on diverse tasks.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems integrate neural networks with logical reasoning to achieve both generalization and interpretability, but recent work has shown they are susceptible to shortcut reasoning behaviors.  We propose a novel method using matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in two phenomena: constraint satisfaction shortcuts, where constraints are satisfied without achieving the intended task, and cognition shortcuts, where biased data leads to semantically incorrect concept mappings despite logically sound inference. Building on recent matrix-based logic programming semantics, we introduce design elements to mitigate shortcuts, including a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix.  We also identify connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and empirically compare their gradient flow properties. Through carefully designed experiments on MNIST variants, we show that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to previous methods that rely on soft probability distributions.  We then confirm that architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

</details>


### [189] [Identifying Good Rules for Efficient SAT Encodings of Single-Constant Multiplication Using Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21188)
*Chufeng Jiang,Neng-Fa Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Neuro-symbolic SCM encoding using a graph neural network to guide operator selection, pruning no-good choices in symbolic search, yielding large speedups and memory reductions while preserving near-optimal additions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single Constant Multiplication (SCM) is NP-hard; current dynamic-programming/SAT encodings are costly for large constants, hindering scalable hardware design.

Method: A graph neural network predicts promising operator types from constant decompositions and uses its confidence to prune non-promising choices in the symbolic search, forming a neuro-symbolic SCM encoding framework.

Result: On unseen 17–32 bit constants, achieves 10–100x reductions in encoding time (1–2 orders of magnitude), >97% memory reduction, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while maintaining near-optimal addition counts.

Conclusion: Learning-guided symbolic strategies substantially improve SCM encoding scalability and efficiency; code and data are publicly available.

Abstract: The Single Constant Multiplication problem is a fundamental NP-hard optimization task in hardware design, which seeks to decompose a fixed constant using only additions, subtractions, and bit-shifts. Although dynamic programming methods can produce near-optimal SAT encodings for SCM, their encoding cost remains high for large constants. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that accelerates SCM SAT encoding by identifying good rules for guiding operator selection during decomposition. Our approach employs a graph neural network model to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, and exploits the resulting confidence scores to prune no-good choices in the symbolic search. Experimental results on unseen 17-32 bit constants demonstrate one to two orders of magnitude reductions in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions. These results show that learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Chufeng-Jiang/SCM_MLDP

</details>


### [190] [Bound-Founded Semantics for Answer Set Programming with Difference Constraints: Preliminary Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21201)
*Pedro Cabalar,Jorge Fandinno,Nicolas Rühling,Torsten Schaub,Sebastian Schellhorn,Philipp Wanko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a many-sorted HTb framework to unify equilibrium-model semantics for ASP extensions with linear constraints, especially difference constraints, and applies it to clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo; formalizes numeric foundedness; provides a single foundation for reasoning about program simplifications and future semantic integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid ASP solvers with linear constraints use diverse semantic underpinnings; lack of a unified logical basis hampers rigorous comparison and integration.

Method: Define a many-sorted Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb); characterize equilibrium models across ASP with linear constraints; formalize foundedness for numeric variables; analyze influence of constraint atoms; instantiate for clingo[DL], clingcon, flingo.

Result: Semantic characterization of clingo[DL] within the HTb framework; a single, consistent formal foundation across different solvers; insights into why solvers justify constraint atoms; groundwork for program simplifications and future integration of differing semantic principles.

Conclusion: HTb provides a versatile, unifying foundation for ASP with linear constraints, enabling rigorous analysis of existing systems and guiding the design of future hybrids.

Abstract: While the integration of linear constraints has significantly expanded the reach of Answer Set Programming (ASP), existing hybrid solvers often rely on disparate semantic underpinnings that lack a unified logical foundation. We address this gap by introducing a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), providing a versatile framework capable of characterizing equilibrium models across a wide spectrum of alternative semantics for extensions of ASP with linear constraints. We apply this framework to the setting of difference constraints, focusing on the semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. Central to our approach is the formalization of foundedness for numeric variables. By investigating how different hybrid systems - such as clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo - justify constraint atoms, we uncover the semantic roots of their varying behaviors. This investigation results in a single, consistent framework that not only formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates the rigorous study of program simplifications and the future integration of diverse semantic principles.

</details>


### [191] [A New Well-Supported Semantics for Description Logic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21203)
*Spencer Killen,Jia-Huai You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a stricter well-supported semantics for Description Logic Programs that preserves NP-complete consistency, provides a reduct-based characterization and a fixpoint operator, and is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics. It is equivalent to the current semantics for a specific syntactic class.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current well-supported DL-program semantics increase the complexity of the consistency problem and lack a reduct-based characterization. A semantics that is strictly stricter on ontological atoms aims to retain NP-complete consistency and enable a logic-programming-like fixpoint and reduct framework.

Method: Introduce a stricter evaluation of ontological atoms; define a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation; prove complexity results; identify a syntactic class where the new semantics coincides with the current one; show that the new semantics is a strict subset of the existing well-supported semantics.

Result: Consistency remains NP-complete; the new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics; there exists a syntactic class where the two semantics are equivalent; a fixpoint operator and reduct-based transformation characterize the semantics.

Conclusion: The proposed semantics preserve the intuitive notion of well-supportedness from logic programming while enforcing a stricter interpretation of ontological atoms, facilitating a reduct-based treatment and maintaining desirable computational properties. It is a step toward aligning description logic programs with standard LP semantics.

Abstract: Description logic programs are a powerful formalism for combining rules with ontologies. The well-supported semantics for description logic programs ensures that no answer sets rely on cyclic dependencies. Most popular semantics for logic programming have this property of well-supportedness. We recognize two limitations of the current well-supported semantics for DL programs: its increased computational complexity for the consistency problem and its lack of a reduct transformation characterization.  In this work, we present a new semantics which evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the current semantics. This keeps the complexity of its consistency problem NP-complete, rather than increasing it to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Additionally, we identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which our new semantics is equivalent to the current semantics. We characterize our semantics using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. Our new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, so it maintains the prior notion  of well-supportedness while inducing its own stricter notion. We prefer our new notion of well-supportedness due to its similarities with logic programming.

</details>


### [192] [How Rules Represent Causal Knowledge: Causal Modeling with Probabilistic Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21208)
*Kilian Rueckschloss,Felix Weitkaemper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Extends Pearl's causal reasoning to probabilistic logic programming by defining a formal causal semantics for PLP with interventions, and showing equivalence with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs; non-stratified cases and other PLP formalisms may differ.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome Pearl's framework limitation to Bayesian networks and acyclic structures; to bring causal reasoning into probabilistic logic programming under a temporal-free, simultaneous-events view; to unify causal interpretation across PLP formalisms.

Method: Proposes a formal causal semantics for PLP, introduces interventions, provides an implementation, and analyzes its relationship to existing semantics. Shows that the PLP causal semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog; notes potential deviations for non-stratified cases and other PLP formalisms.

Result: The proposed causal semantics aligns with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs; possible differences arise in non-stratified cases and across other PLP formalisms; an implementation of the semantics is discussed.

Conclusion: The work extends Pearlian causality to probabilistic logic programming, establishing a compatible causal interpretation in the stratified ProbLog setting and highlighting limitations when generalizing beyond stratified or alternative PLP formalisms.

Abstract: Pearl famously argues that causal knowledge enables the prediction of intervention effects. By contrast, purely descriptive knowledge supports only conclusions drawn from observations. His theory of causality, however, is developed exclusively within Bayesian networks and causal models. Consequently, it is largely restricted to acyclic causal relationships, and transferring its ideas to other formalisms risks misinterpretation or inconsistency.
  This paper brings Pearl's approach to causality into probabilistic logic programming (PLP). To this end, such programs are aligned with philosophical foundations established in prior work that do not rely on temporal notions; that is, all relevant events are assumed to occur simultaneously. A formal causal semantics for these programs, together with a notion of intervention and an implementation, is proposed. It is shown that this semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while the two may differ in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms.

</details>


### [193] [ICAE-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Interactive Project Builders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21217)
*Zhongyuan Peng,Dan Huang,Chuyu Zhang,Caijun Xu,Changyi Xiao,Shibo Hong,David Lo,Lin Qiu,Xuezhi Cao,Jiyuan He,Yixin Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICAE-Bench: an interactive project-building benchmark for coding agents anchored to real repos with a grounded User Agent and multi-dimensional evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridging the gap between static benchmarks and dynamic, exploratory coding tasks that require planning, clarification, tool use, and repository-level construction.

Method: Three design pillars: (1) ambiguity derived from precise executable repos to avoid unconstrained fuzziness; (2) User Agent Data to ground interaction and reveal hidden constraints; (3) standardized black-box tests plus multi-dimensional diagnostics: functional correctness, semantic/API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, interaction quality.

Result: Abstract presents benchmark design; no empirical results reported.

Conclusion: ICAE-Bench provides a realistic, evaluable framework for vibe-coding workflows and interactive project-building; enables fair, multi-faceted assessment of coding agents in open-ended tasks.

Abstract: The recent emergence of vibe-coding workflows is changing what coding agents are expected to do. Instead of merely completing code under fully specified instructions, agents are increasingly expected to transform incomplete product intent into working software by combining various abilities including planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction. Yet existing benchmarks have not fully caught up with this shift, evaluating agents on static, fully specified tasks.
  In this paper, we introduce ICAE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings. The basic idea is to start from a fuzzy product requirement, simulating the dynamic paradigm with an automated User Agent. To make this setting both realistic and evaluable, ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs. First, to avoid the ambiguity of unconstrained fuzzy requirements, each task derives ambiguity from a precise real open-source repository with executable behavior. Second, to ensure high-quality and reproducible user simulation, ICAE-Bench grounds interaction through User Agent Data, allowing the User Agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts. Third, to evaluate open-ended repositories fairly, ICAE-Bench uses standardized black-box tests together with multi-dimensional diagnostics, including functional correctness, semantic and API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

</details>


### [194] [Logic Programming Semantics for Causal Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21233)
*Felix Weitkämper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Stable models of positive logic programs map to the eventual states of causal processes starting from a neutral state; supported models map to eventual states from arbitrary starting points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address modelling challenges in the life sciences by linking logic programming semantics with the causal states of processes, and to add a temporal perspective to causality interpretations.

Method: Theoretical analysis establishing correspondences between stable/supported model semantics and the evolution of causal processes. It distinguishes starting conditions (neutral versus arbitrary) and treats logic programs as causal rule languages with an explicit temporal dimension.

Result: Proves that stable models correspond to eventual states from a neutral initial condition, while supported models correspond to eventual states from arbitrary starting points, and situates these results within a causal-temporal interpretation of logic programming semantics.

Conclusion: Contributes a temporal, causal interpretation of stable and supported model semantics, enriching the view of logic programming as a causal rule language and guiding future semantical and modelling work in life sciences.

Abstract: Motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, we investigate the relationship between logic programming semantics and the eventual states of causal processes compatible with those logic programs. More precisely, we show that while stable models of positive logic programs correspond to the eventual states of processes commencing from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed indefinitely, supported models describe the eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points. This also contributes to the discussion of the appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language, adding a temporal perspective to recent interpretations of the stable and supported model semantics from an explanatory viewpoint of causality.

</details>


### [195] [BasketEvent: Understanding Who Did What and When in Basketball Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21267)
*Yu Zhang,Jiayuan Rao,Haoning Wu,Weidi Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces BasketEvent, a basketball dataset with player-grounded event labels and a subset with precise temporal intervals, and PlayNet, a player-centric framework for event reasoning with temporal evidence in basketball videos; demonstrates superior performance over baselines and will release data, code, and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the disconnect between spatial perception and semantic recognition in sports video understanding by grounding events to responsible players and localizing temporal evidence within complex team dynamics.

Method: BasketEvent provides player-grounded event labels and a subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals. PlayNet tracks entities, assigns player identities, and reasons about events via player–player, player–ball, and global court interactions, using gated pooling to aggregate sparse temporal evidence.

Result: PlayNet outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, validating the effectiveness of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding; data, code, and models will be publicly released.

Conclusion: Player-centric modeling with grounded events and temporal evidence localization is superior for comprehensive basketball video understanding, enabling precise attribution of actions to players and temporal localization of key evidence.

Abstract: Comprehensive basketball video understanding requires resolving not only what event occurs, but also who is responsible and when the key evidence appears. However, exist- ing methods typically treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint their temporal boundaries within complex collective dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce BasketEvent, a player- centric basketball event understanding dataset curated from real NBA broadcasts. In BasketEvent, event labels are grounded to the responsible players, and a manually an- notated subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals is provided to evaluate tem- poral evidence localization. Based on this data, we propose PlayNet, a player-centric reasoning framework that maps basketball videos to player-level event predictions with temporal evidence. Concretely, PlayNet tracks key entities, associates player identities, and reasons about events by modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court inter- actions, while aggregating sparse temporal evidence via gated pooling. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, proving the superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding. Our data, code, and models will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [196] [An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21292)
*Ari Luna Rueda,Eike Cramer,Klaus Hellgardt,Mehmet Mercangöz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A structured LLM-driven workflow decomposes automated multivariable control design into constrained code-generation steps with iterative validation and Bayesian-optimization-based tuning; demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater; yields a physically consistent decentralized PI with executable tuning, achieving ~26.5% improvement in a composite performance objective; highlights feasibility and need for broader validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automate and render reproducible multivariable control design from dynamic process models using structured LLM-based code generation, integrating validation loops and automated tuning to produce executable control-design workflows.

Method: Propose a workflow that splits design tasks into: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and Bayesian-optimization-based tuning. Artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks; failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. Demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics, yielding a decentralized PI with feedforward and an executable tuning environment.

Result: The workflow generates a physically consistent decentralized PI controller and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed-loop objective by ~26.5% relative to the initial workflow-generated controller, mainly via improved pressure-loop transient performance. This improvement pertains to automated tuning rather than a comparison with a manually designed controller. The work demonstrates feasibility of structured LLM-based code generation for executable control-design workflows but calls for broader validation on larger plant-wide benchmarks.

Conclusion: Structured LLM-driven code generation can construct executable control-design workflows and enable automated tuning, but generalization to larger plant-wide systems requires further validation.

Abstract: We present a structured large-language-model-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design from dynamic process models. The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

</details>


### [197] [Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21302)
*Gong Gao,Weidong Zhao,Xianhui Liu,Ning Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) for online RL by deriving expert priors online via Q-guided CVAE from the replay buffer, with EPG and PGC to stabilize learning, achieving higher sample efficiency and stability across robotics and industrial control benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcomes reliance on static offline datasets for policy priors in BPRL, which suffer from low diversity and suboptimal quality, hindering exploration and stability.

Method: Introduce Q-guided CVAE to model expert policies from online replay; Expert Policy Guidance (EPG) to select actions from a generative support set; Policy Gradient Correction (PGC) to align Q-guidance with expert supervision; integrate into online RL.

Result: Empirical results on Gym/PyBullet and DMControl show superior sample efficiency and more stable convergence compared with state-of-the-art online RL baselines.

Conclusion: EBP enables online RL to leverage immediate, high-value expert priors learned from experience, improving exploration, stability, and efficiency without pre-collected expert data.

Abstract: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

</details>


### [198] [Regulating autonomous and agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21345)
*Chris Reed,Alex Austria,Anmol Bharuka,Pragnitha Mandava,Khushiya Mujawar,Luka Shakhkulashvili*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Four-regime comparative analysis showing the need for new proactive governance of autonomous AI, highlighting cross‑supply‑chain regulation and shifting from reactive to proactive oversight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous and agentic AI disrupts traditional regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control, necessitating governance that covers the AI supply chain and new systemic risks.

Method: Analytical comparison of four regulatory systems (UK content-platform regulation, data protection, UK financial services, EU AI Act cross‑sectoral regime) to identify challenges and propose regulator-facing solutions.

Result: Identification of regulatory challenges posed by AI autonomy and a set of potential regulator strategies to move from reactive to proactive oversight and to address systemic risks across the supply chain.

Conclusion: Regulatory models must be redesigned for active risk management; cross‑regulatory and supply‑chain inclusive approaches, illuminated by the four systems, offer pathways to govern autonomous AI effectively.

Abstract: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act\'92s cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

</details>


### [199] [SPORD: A Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose Approach for Supply Chain Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21354)
*Jiayin He,Yutong Pan,Sen Yang,Ningxuan Kang,Yongzhi Qi,Jianshen Zhang,Wei Qi,Zuo-Jun Max Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SPORD, a decoupled simulation-then-optimization framework (NetSim) that addresses fragmentation, combinatorial scale, and trust barriers in e-commerce supply-chain planning, delivering large performance and sustainability gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supply chain planning at scale suffers from bespoke models, combinatorial complexity, and lack of executive trust; need a unified, tractable, and auditable planning workflow.

Method: Simulation-Propose-then-Dispose (SPORD): simulation enumerates all operationally valid candidate paths incorporating idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program selects the globally optimal subset. Implemented with matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU-accelerated simulation, a list-scheduling step to reduce coupled-order processing, and an intelligent diagnosis engine forming a closed loop; deployed as JD.com’s NetSim platform.

Result: 10–100× speedups for simulation over serial methods; hours-to-minutes reduction in coupled-order processing; NetSim optimized end-to-end services for >20,000 suppliers; cross-regional fulfillment rate reported to drop from 6.1% to 4.9%; monthly carbon reduction ~5,745 tCO2e.

Conclusion: SPORD moves simulation into active planning, delivering transparent outputs that engage executives and a modular architecture that enables future planning with configuration rather than rebuilding from scratch.

Abstract: For years, supply chain planning at e-commerce firms has operated as a collection of isolated projects. Each planning task from static network planning to dynamic warehouse assortment planning requires analysts to spend weeks building models from scratch, calibrating and persuading executives to act on outputs they cannot verify. Three barriers drive this: bespoke models proliferate because standardization is difficult (operational fragmentation); once unified, the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and intricate routing logic exceeds what solvers can handle within a tight window (computational intractability); and a mathematically optimal solution still fails to be implemented if the executives do not trust it (implementation hurdle). To bridge this gap, we propose and implement the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose method, deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform. The central insight is decoupling: simulation proposes by generating and evaluating the full set of operationally valid candidate paths-absorbing all idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computationally, matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation achieves a 10-100 times speedup over serial methods, and a list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Operationally, we establish a closed loop via an intelligent diagnosis engine. Since 2025, NetSim has optimized end to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers, the cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and the average monthly carbon reduction is approximately 5,745 tCO2e. SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning. The transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures that the next planning requires just configuration, not reconstruction.

</details>


### [200] [Towards Faithful Graph Explanations with Synergistic Edge Effects via Granular Balls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21381)
*Jiancu Chen,Shuyin Xia,Guan Wang,Degang Chen,Fan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SeeExplainer is a parameter-free instance-level explainer for GNNs that captures edge synergistic effects via a granular-ball graph refinement to form a structural graph; explanations are generated by perturbing nodes and edges; outperforms baselines on graph classification tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge-level explanations often miss synergistic interactions among edges; existing perturbation-based methods perturb edges individually and may fail to capture interactions, necessitating a synergy-aware, parameter-free approach.

Method: Introduce granular-ball graph refinement to decompose the input graph into disjoint granular-balls of variable size; treat these granular-balls as nodes to build a structural graph. Perturb nodes and edges in this structural graph to produce explanatory subgraphs according to their contributions; the method is parameter-free.

Result: Empirical experiments on multiple graph classification datasets across different networks show SeeExplainer achieves superior explanatory performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: SeeExplainer provides accurate instance-level GNN explanations by modeling edge synergistic effects through a granular-ball structural graph and targeted perturbations, eliminating the need for tuned parameters while improving interpretability.

Abstract: Instance-level explanations aim to reveal the rationale behind a model's decisions for a specific graph. Previous methods explain graph neural networks (GNNs) by selecting important edges to induce subgraphs, where edge importance is assessed by perturbing each edge and observing changes in the model predictions. However, they often neglect the synergistic effects among edges, which are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance. To address this issue, we propose SeeExplainer, a parameter-free explainer to interpret GNNs. Specifically, we first introduce a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into several disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size, and utilize them as nodes to construct a structural graph. This process can better capture the synergistic effects among edges. Then, we perturb nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [201] [Multimodal Pretraining for Generalizable EEG Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21384)
*Targol Bakhtiarvand,Jugal Kalita,Adham Atyabi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multimodal EEG foundation model enables robust, cross-dataset seizure detection with a shared embedding space across raw EEG, time-frequency, and text, achieving state-of-the-art results on CHB-MIT and supporting LOSO generalization and localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG seizure models often overfit to specific datasets or tasks; foundation models and self-supervised learning promise adaptable backbones that generalize across datasets and settings.

Method: A multimodal foundation model comprising: (1) a raw signal encoder based on Mamba, (2) a ViT-style time‑frequency encoder, and (3) a lightweight text encoder, all projected into a shared embedding space. Pretraining uses masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses on unlabeled data, followed by fine-tuning on seizure detection benchmarks. Evaluations include standard CHB‑MIT splits and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols across multiple datasets.

Result: On CHB-MIT, best single model AUROC = 0.874; ensemble AUROC = 0.878 (state-of-the-art on this benchmark). LOSO mean balanced accuracy = 0.558 across 19 subjects, highlighting challenges of patient-independent detection. Overall, the model shows robust detection across datasets and settings and supports interpretable seizure localization.

Conclusion: The proposed multimodal EEG foundation model delivers strong cross-dataset and LOSO performance, facilitates easy adaptation to new seizure scenarios, and enables interpretable localization of seizures.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) models used for epilepsy are often limited to specific datasets and tasks. This limited approach can make it challenging to apply these models across different datasets or in various situations. However, recent studies in foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest that an adaptable EEG backbone could support a range of EEG related tasks. In this study, we have developed a multimodal EEG foundation model that combines a raw signal encoder based on the Mamba architecture, a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and a lightweight encoder for text, all within a shared embedding space. The pretraining process relies on several innovative techniques, such as masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. These methods are designed to create rich, seizure-relevant representations without requiring labeled data. To assess the efficacy and generalization of our pretrained model, we fine-tuned it on the canonical CHB-MIT seizure detection benchmark and additional seizure detection datasets, and conducted extensive experiments comparing different model variants. On the standard CHB-MIT split, our best single model achieved an AUROC of 0.874, and an ensemble variant reached 0.878 AUROC, representing state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark. In addition to standard train-test splits, we evaluated performance under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, which is rarely reported in prior EEG seizure modeling work and highlights the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection, with a mean LOSO balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects. Across datasets and evaluation settings, our multimodal foundation model enabled robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

</details>


### [202] [MSBraM: A Multi-scale Self-supervised Brain Foundation Model for Hierarchical EEG Dynamics Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21402)
*Tao Zhou,Jing Han,Lingyu Shu,Zixing Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSBraM introduces a two-stage, multi-scale SSL framework for EEG that learns hierarchical representations via a multi-scale neural tokenizer and curriculum masking, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 12 datasets and 10 downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG signals exhibit rich multi-scale temporal structure; existing models struggle to jointly capture local patterns and long-range dependencies, limiting cross-task generalization.

Method: Stage 1: multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG into semantic codes at multiple temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Stage 2: pretrain to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy that progressively combines fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. Pretraining on ~2,400 hours of EEG data.

Result: MSBraM outperforms current state-of-the-art pretrained models and demonstrates strong generalization and transferability across diverse downstream tasks and datasets.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is crucial for effective EEG foundation models and enhances cross-task transferability.

Abstract: Self-supervised foundation models have recently shown strong potential for electroencephalogram (EEG)-based analysis. However, existing approaches struggle to capture the inherently multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals, where local neural patterns and long-range dependencies jointly encode task-relevant information. This limitation hampers cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose MSBraM, a Multi-Scale self-supervised Brain foundation Model designed to learn hierarchical EEG representations. MSBraM follows a two-stage pretraining framework. First, a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG signals into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Second, the model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. We pretrain MSBraM on over 2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluate it across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets. Extensive experiments show that MSBraM achieves superior performance on other state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability. These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for effective EEG foundation models.

</details>


### [203] [Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21412)
*Bartolomeo Bogliolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Euclid-MCP provides a deterministic, Prolog-backed reasoning server with an intermediate representation (Euclid-IR) for Horn clauses, offering a standardized, tool-augmented interface (translate-run-inspect-repair) and exact inference, contrasting with LLM-only approaches and semantic RAG for rule enforcement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the unreliability of LLMs in multi-step, safety-critical reasoning and the lack of standardized interfaces for tool-augmented agents; provide a reusable, open-source reasoning substrate that can serve both RAG-based and agentic systems.

Method: Develop Euclid-MCP MCP server using SWI-Prolog with Euclid-IR as an engine-agnostic Horn-clause representation. Provide a compact translate-run-inspect-repair loop interface for LLM clients, expose proof traces and derivation logs, and evaluate on IT security/compliance use case.

Result: LLMs alone hallucinate on larger knowledge bases; Euclid-MCP yields exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs, delivering deterministic reasoning, proof traces, and scalable performance; improved reliability over naive LLM approaches.

Conclusion: Semantic RAG is inadequate for enforcing rules; Euclid-MCP can act as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems; the approach is open-source and can standardize tool-augmented reasoning workflows.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

</details>


### [204] [Logical Regression for Planning with Axioms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21414)
*Connor Little,Christian Muise*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Approximate logical regression in axiomatic domains by restricting to minimal partial states, avoiding axiom recomputation; embedded in execution monitoring; achieves substantial variable reduction and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logical regression with axioms is computationally hard; need robust execution monitoring and compact policies; partial-state approximation avoids expensive axiom handling while preserving useful generalization.

Method: Compute minimal partial-state regressions for actions in domains with axioms, avoid rechecking/recomputing axioms, integrate regression into execution monitoring to assess plan feasibility under non-determinism.

Result: Partial states generalized across multiple domains; up to 70% fewer variables required for execution monitoring; monitor recovers >50% of the time in environments with unexpected changes.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a scalable, robust regression approach in presence of axioms, with practical benefits for execution monitoring and planning under uncertainty.

Abstract: In automated planning, logical regression is an operation that returns the most general condition necessary for an action to achieve a particular formula. It has many applications, such as allowing for more robust plan execution and providing compact policies for non-deterministic planning. Although relatively simple to calculate in basic planning settings, logical regression becomes significantly more complex when additional factors, such as axioms, are present. We introduce a methodology for approximating the logical regression of an action in a domain that includes axioms; an approximation that limits conditions to partial states. Our method produces minimal partial states while avoiding the recalculation of axioms. To demonstrate the impact of our methods, we embed our form of regression in an execution monitoring context, a well-established setting that can benefit greatly from logical regression. Our results show that this form of regression can dramatically generalize partial states across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70%, and demonstrate that the resulting execution monitor is robust enough to recover frequently in an environment with unexpected changes: several domains recover over 50% of the time in our tests.

</details>


### [205] [PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21419)
*Yipeng Shi,Zhipeng Ma,Yue Wang,Qitai Tan,Yang Li,Peng Chen,Zhengzhou Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pats reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold for long-horizon LLM agent RL, turning policy rollouts into evidence cards and adaptively adjusting context to guide learning; it improves performance and reduces token usage while discarding scaffold at deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weak policies produce repetitive failures and uninformative trajectories; existing skill-centric methods don't adapt training-time support to policy evolution.

Method: Policy-centric training paradigm; Pats converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards; task-specific evaluation modulates subsequent rollout context; provides concrete guidance; reduces reliance on explicit guidance as policy improves; standard RLVR for environment rewards; scaffold discarded at deployment.

Result: ALFWorld and WebShop: up to 18.6% gains over strong baselines; across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks: competitive with 32.1% fewer prompt tokens.

Conclusion: Pats offers an adaptive, policy-driven scaffold that enhances learning efficiency in long-horizon LLM agent RL, by coupling evidence-based guidance with evolving rollout context; promising improvements with token-efficiency; generalizes across domains with varying task structures.

Abstract: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts. Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

</details>


### [206] [Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21421)
