*Michael Romei de Socio,Gian Luca Pozzato,Alessio Merlo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Post-sampling symbolic constraints improve structural admissibility of diffusion-generated graph trajectories; hard filtering yields high validity with ~84% retention, while soft weighting preserves samples but offers limited validity gains; complexity increases inadmissibility, driven mainly by dependency constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical plausibility of generative trajectories does not imply structural feasibility under graph-structural constraints; assessing how post-sampling symbolic constraints affect reliability is essential for dynamic graph-structured systems.

Method: A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations. An external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. Evaluation on two synthetic regimes (compact graph and medium-complexity dependency graph) with metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. Family-level analysis identifies constraint sources.

Result: In the compact regime, invalid probability mass is 0.002996 (near-complete admissibility). In the medium-complexity regime, invalid mass increases to 0.155929. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples. Soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields limited validity gains. Dependency constraints explain nearly all observed inadmissibility.

Conclusion: Statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties; symbolic constraint handling gains importance with increasing graph-structural complexity.

Abstract: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples, whereas soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity gains. Family-level analysis shows that dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. These results indicate that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties and that symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases.

</details>


### [207] [Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21437)
*Nooshin Maghsoodi,Amoon Jamzad,Robert Policelli,Mohammad Farahmand,Dilakshan Srikanthan,Martin Kaufmann,Kevin Y. M. Ren,Shaila Merchant,Sonal Varma,Ross Walker,Doug McKay,John Rudan,Gabor Fichtinger,Parvin Mousavi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent-Guided Concept Discovery learns data-driven concepts for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment without predefined labels, using a reasoning agent to refine concepts and a biochemical knowledge graph for grounding. It improves robustness, accuracy, and reduces false positives in intraoperative settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To close the generalization gap of deep learning models trained on ex vivo spectral data when applied to noisy, unlabeled intraoperative spectra, and to address interpretability by mapping measurements to human-understandable concepts.

Method: Train an unsupervised concept discovery framework where a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of learned concepts and adaptively weights them by diagnostic relevance. Ground concepts with a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure metabolic consistency. Evaluate on Skin and Breast Cancer REIMS datasets and assess intraoperative case performance.

Result: The framework improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over baselines on Skin and Breast Cancer datasets and reduces false positives in a representative intraoperative case, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

Conclusion: Agent-guided concept discovery with knowledge-grounded concepts enhances generalization and interpretability of REIMS-based surgical margin assessment, showing promise for intraoperative deployment.

Abstract: Deep learning models can effectively use Rapid Evaporative Ionization Mass Spectrometry (REIMS) data for surgical margin assessment. However, their clinical adoption remains challenging due to limited generalization to operating room conditions. This difficulty arises because models are typically trained on labeled spectra collected from resected tissue samples, while they must operate on noisy, unlabeled data acquired directly during surgery. In addition, the black-box nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to understand and systematically improve their behavior. Concept-based learning offers a promising way to address these challenges by mapping raw measurements to human-understandable concepts. However, supervised concept-based approaches rely on concept annotations, which are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows. We propose Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns meaningful concepts directly from data without requiring predefined concept labels. During training, a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of the learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weight based on diagnostic relevance. These concepts are further grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships. Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, our model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

</details>


### [208] [Detecting LLM-Generated Tokens in Human--LLM Coauthored Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21458)
*Yangjun Lu,Hongyi Zhou,Fabian Spill,Kai Ye,Chengchun Shi,Jin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Token-level localization of LLM-generated content via adaptive smoothing of token scores with a Lepski-type bandwidth rule; training-free, with theoretical MSE guarantees and strong empirical performance, plus a public demo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Document-level detectors fail to localize generated content within mixed-authorship texts. There is a need for fine-grained, token-level detection that can identify which portions are LLM-generated, leveraging existing token-level scores without requiring labeled data.

Method: Apply smoothing to token-level detection scores to reduce variability. Use an adaptive Lepski-type bandwidth selection that tunes smoothing locally according to authorship structure. The approach is simple to implement and does not require token-level labeled data for training.

Result: The method achieves favorable mean square error in estimating the underlying signal and shows strong empirical performance against a broad set of baselines on synthetic and realistic datasets. A publicly accessible website implements the method.

Conclusion: The proposed token-level smoothing with adaptive bandwidth delivers effective, training-free localization of LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents, with theoretical guarantees and practical demonstration via a public demo.

Abstract: The rise of human-AI collaborative writing has created a growing need for fine-grained detection methods that support localizing likely LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents. Existing methods for detecting LLM-generated text mainly focus on document-level classification and cannot identify which parts of the text are generated by LLMs. This paper introduces a new method to address this urgent need. Our method operates at the token level, the natural unit of modern language models, and builds on existing token-level detection scores. The key idea is to smooth adjacent token scores to reduce their variability, while using an adaptive Lepski-type rule to select the bandwidth according to the local authorship structure. Our method is simple to implement and does not require token-level labeled data for training. Theoretically, we characterize this trade-off and show that the proposed method achieves favorable mean square error performance in estimating the underlying signal. Empirically, we demonstrate strong performance of our method against a wide range of baselines in both synthetic datasets and a realistic dataset. We deploy a publicly accessible website that implements the methods as well.

</details>


### [209] [AREX: Towards a Recursively Self-Improving Agent for Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21461)
*Shuqi Lu,Chaofan Li,Kun Luo,Zhang Zhang,Hui Wang,Hongwang Xiao,Zheng Liu,Lei Xiong,Jiahao Wang,Sen Wang,Xiyan Jiang,Wanli Li,Yuyang Hu,Hongjin Qian,Bingyu Yan,Ziyi Xia,Yingxia Shao,Kang Liu,Zhicheng Dou,Di He,Chaozhuo Li,Qiwei Ye,Zhongyuan Wang,Zheng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AREX introduces Recursively Self-Improving agents that alternate inner evidence gathering with outer constraint-wise auditing, plus an autonomous context-update tool, trained via RL on synthetic tasks, achieving strong results across reasoning benchmarks and competitive with larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address discovery-verification asymmetry in complex research tasks and enable long-horizon problem solving by recursively improving answers using partially verified evidence and compressed history.

Method: Inner loop gathers evidence and constructs provisional answers; outer loop audits constraints, identifies unresolved claims, and launches targeted follow-ups; autonomously updates context with a compact representation of history; trained via agentic pretraining and long-horizon RL; evaluated on BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, HLE, etc.; uses 4B dense model and 122B-MoE variant.

Result: AREX outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with models with substantially larger activated parameter counts across multiple benchmarks.

Conclusion: RSI-based research agents with a self-improvement loop and a context-update mechanism can substantially improve long-horizon reasoning and tool-use performance while maintaining efficiency.

Abstract: Deep research requires agents to find answers that jointly satisfy multiple constraints. Discovering such answers is costly, whereas verifying a candidate can often be decomposed into tractable constraint-wise checks. This discovery--verification asymmetry suggests that a research agent should do more than simply search longer: it should recursively improve its current answer by verifying intermediate results and using the partially verified state to guide subsequent refinement. We introduce AREX, a family of Recursively Self-Improving (RSI) deep research agents. AREX alternates between an inner research loop that gathers evidence and constructs a provisional answer, and an outer self-improvement loop that audits the answer constraint-wise, identifies unresolved claims, and launches targeted follow-up research. To sustain RSI over long horizons, AREX learns an autonomous context-update tool that compresses growing interaction history into a compact improvement state preserving verified evidence and unresolved constraints, without relying on an external model. We train AREX on verified synthetic tasks and high-quality trajectories through agentic mid-training and long-horizon reinforcement learning. To mitigate sparse final rewards during long horizon learning, we emphasize key steps where decisive evidence is acquired or erroneous research directions are corrected. We instantiate a dense 4B model and a 122B-A10B Mixture-of-Experts model. Across BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and other reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, AREX substantially outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with models using substantially more activated parameters.

</details>


### [210] [Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21482)
*Mack Nixon,Liam Wright,Yevgeniya Kovalchuk,Alison Fang-Wei Wu,Martin Danka,Andy Boyd,David Bann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-weight LLMs evaluated for AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research.
A new open-source framework RRBench benchmarks 20 data-prep tasks (102 variables) using six-wave British cohort data, focusing on clean/R code and outputs. State-of-the-art 31–35B models nearly saturate the benchmark (avg task completion ~87.9%), and open-weight models on consumer hardware show promise for local, privacy-preserving use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings by using locally deployable open-weight LLMs, avoiding data transmission to external services, and to establish a benchmark for evaluating such models on longitudinal cohort data tasks.

Method: Develop RRBench: a framework with a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts for six sweeps of a British cohort study), task definitions (e.g., category harmonization, multi-wave merging), and automated evaluation of LLM-generated R code and outputs. Benchmark across consumer-grade deployment for 20 data-prep tasks (102 variables).

Result: Current state-of-the-art 31–35B parameter models achieve high performance, with average task completion around 87.9%, nearing saturation of the benchmark. Open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware show promising viability for AI-assisted data preparation under governance constraints. The framework and baseline results are publicly available at RRBench repository.

Conclusion: Open-weight LLMs deployed locally can be a viable path for AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research, enabling privacy-preserving automation. The RRBench framework provides a standardized benchmark and dataset for evaluating such models on longitudinal data tasks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now widely used tools in code development, with data typically sent to third-party cloud-based models. Their adoption in research using personal data is constrained by governance requirements that typically prohibit data transmission to external services. Locally deployable open-weight models offer an alternative since sensitive data never leave the local environment. We introduce an open-source framework for evaluating the efficacy of AI agents powered by open-weight LLMs on one of the most persistent bottlenecks in research on longitudinal population studies: data preparation. The framework comprises: a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts preparing six sweeps of data from a British cohort study), task definitions encompassing tasks such as category harmonization and multi-wave merging, and automated routines for evaluating the LLM-produced R code and outputted data. We benchmark LLMs across the (consumer grade) deployment spectrum to assess their efficacy in 20 data preparation tasks (creation of 102 variables). Current state-of-the-art, 31-35B parameter models almost saturated our benchmark ("average task completion" up to 87.9%). The performance of open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware shows promise of a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings. Our framework is publicly available at: https://github.com/UCL-ARC/RRBench.

</details>


### [211] [Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21495)
*Natan Levy,Harel Berger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational AI agents to mitigate reliability degradation caused by democratized development; includes dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance; validated via an initial auditor prototype and scenario-based assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Democratization of AI agent creation by non-engineers introduces a reliability gap: agents can degrade silently due to evolving models, tools, data sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, or external services after deployment, without user changes.

Method: Proposes a continuous-assurance framework combining dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance; provides an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment to translate taxonomy into concrete checks and remediation guidance.

Result: An initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment demonstrating practical checks and remediation guidance derived from the taxonomy; establishes feasibility and a concrete path to operationalize reliability assurance for citizen-created agents.

Conclusion: A lightweight, actionable framework that enables ongoing operational readiness of democratized AI agents, enabling organizations to monitor and remediate reliability risks in deployed agents.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly created inside organizations by non-engineering users through low-code, no-code, and conversational development environments. This democratization enables rapid local innovation, but it also creates a reliability gap: agents that appear to users as simple productivity artifacts may depend on changing models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, and external services. These dependencies can cause silent degradation long after deployment, even when no user directly modifies the agent. This paper identifies the reliability challenge created by democratized AI agent creation and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational agents. The framework combines dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess whether an agent remains operationally ready under expected conditions. We also present an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment showing how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

</details>


### [212] [Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21503)
*Gaurav Dadhich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agentic Context Management (ACM) reframes context handling for production AI as a lifecycle, not merely storage. It defines five primitives—architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation—and demonstrates that validated context compaction enables linear token costs with preserved fidelity, unlike naive accumulation or crude summarization. A reference implementation, Maximem Synap, is proposed and evaluated (92% LongMemEval; 93.2% LoCoMo). The work highlights new benchmarks (latency, token efficiency, context-rot resistance) and broader organizational implications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production AI agents accumulate histories, prompts, tool definitions, and outputs, causing time- and token-cost growth and memory-related failures. Treating context management as a storage problem is insufficient; a lifecycle perspective across organizational scope is needed to decide what to remember, how to structure it, and how to compact without losing provenance or relevance.

Method: Proposes Agentic Context Management (ACM) decomposed into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. Implements these in a reference system, Maximem Synap, as a multi-tenant service. Evaluates performance on LongMemEval and LoCoMo under a detailed configuration, and analyzes cost-accuracy trade-offs of different context-management strategies.

Result: Empirical claims include 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo for Maximem Synap under the paper’s configuration, supporting the effectiveness of validated context compaction over naive accumulation or crude summarization.

Conclusion: ACM offers a structured discipline for in-memory context management with organizational applicability. It opens new benchmarking dimensions (latency, token efficiency, context-rot resistance) and points toward future work in decision-level and organization-level context management.

Abstract: Production AI agents' failures are less often due to an inability to reason well and more often because they cannot manage what is in their reasoning context: conversation histories, large prompts, large tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. Agents drown in their own accumulating history while paying a token cost that grows every turn, producing missing recalls within and across conversations. The incumbent response treats this as a storage-and-retrieval problem. We argue that framing is too narrow. Actively managing what an agent holds in mind is a lifecycle, not merely a store: it spans deciding what to remember, extracting and structuring it, choosing the right store per data type, consolidating and forgetting while preserving provenance, deciding what is relevant now, anticipating what is needed next, and compacting context to a budget without losing what matters. In serious production this operates not over a single user but across an organizational scope hierarchy. We name this discipline Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decompose it into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. We then make the economic case: naive context accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost at the price of an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity. We describe a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, that realizes the five primitives as a multi-tenant service and reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the configuration detailed in Section 6. We close with dimensions existing benchmarks do not yet capture, latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance, and the frontier of decision-level and organization-level context the category points toward.

</details>


### [213] [Same Dangerous Objective, Opposite Advice: Direct Exposure versus Multi-Agent Mediation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21518)
*Linjun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Direct exposure to a dangerous objective can misalign advice with the target when unmediated, while downstream transformations bias the user-facing model toward the target; reveals a compositional safety gap in multi-stage LLM workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how objective manipulation and multi-stage composition affect safety alignment in high-capability LLMs and whether user-facing components can inherit or veil upstream intents.

Method: Empirical evaluation using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol with 25 mirrored trade-off profiles, comparing raw objective exposure (Id/Censor) against transformed versions and a downstream Superego component that preserves the target direction while obscuring the raw objective and provenance; analysis of resulting advisory directions and upstream leakage.

Result: Direct exposure yielded advice opposite to the target; transformed versions yielded advice aligned with the target, indicating a reverse shift. Demonstrated a compositional safety gap: a high-capability model can serve as the user-facing element of a multi-stage workflow that preserves the target direction while hiding the raw objective, manipulation clauses, and provenance; endpoint-only users cannot inspect upstream messages.

Conclusion: Highlights the need for stronger provenance, prompt exposure controls, and auditing in multi-stage LLM systems to prevent leakage of objectives and manipulation through orchestration layers. Calls for defensive design, such as transparent upstream prompts, restricted access to raw directives, and monitoring for misalignment when composing models.

Abstract: Even a current high-capability LLM can appear safer when shown a dangerous objective directly than when other agents transform and relay its direction. Using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol model alias, we test 25 pre-specified mirrored trade-off profiles. Direct exposure to an objective authorizing concealment, fabrication, and pressure produced advice net opposed to its target. After an Id and Censor transformed the same objective into affect and a constraint-rewritten, target-bearing intention, the user-facing Superego---which saw the preferred direction but not the raw objective, its manipulative clauses, or its source---produced advice net aligned with the target.
  This behavioral reverse shift is consistent with the model recognizing or distrusting the manipulative motive, although we do not identify its internal mechanism. The second result exposes a compositional safety gap: a current high-capability model can be used as the user-facing component of an automated, multi-stage workflow serving an explicitly manipulative objective. The workflow can keep the raw instruction, its manipulation-authorizing clauses, and its provenance outside the downstream model's context while preserving the objective's target direction. A user with endpoint-only access likewise cannot directly inspect those upstream messages including the objective.

</details>


### [214] [The Boundaries of Automation: A Theory of Persistent Human Participation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21547)
*Fares Fourati,Hinrich Schütze,Eyke Hüllermeier,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reframes automation limits by showing that human participation can persist even with highly capable AI due to technical complementarity, developmental value of participation, and emergence-driven targets, treating human–AI co-construction as a lasting feature rather than a fallback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenge the dominant view that automation should replace human labor as AI improves; ask where conceptual limits to automation lie and explore why humans remain involved even with capable AI, with implications for design, evaluation, and ethics.

Method: Conceptual analysis and theoretical framing that synthesizes three grounds for persistent human involvement (technical/complementarity, normative/developmental, and emergence-based) and argues for a co-construction view of human–AI work.

Result: Identifies three distinct bases for ongoing human participation in AI-enabled tasks and shows that in some activities, the target emerges through interaction, making human input constitutive; frames a persistent co-construction perspective with design/ethics implications.

Conclusion: Emphasizes that automation limits are not merely technical barriers but include the nature of objectives and human agency; advocates rethinking design, evaluation, and ethics of AI systems to accommodate enduring human–AI co-production.

Abstract: The rapid progress of AI has intensified the long-standing pursuit of automation: replacing human participation with algorithms wherever possible. Implicit in this pursuit is the assumption that humans remain in the loop only because current AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. This paper challenges that assumption. Rather than asking how far automation can extend, we ask where its conceptual limits lie and argue that human participation may persist even with highly capable AI systems for three distinct reasons. Technical or complementarity grounds arise when humans contribute capabilities or perspectives unavailable to AI. Normative or developmental grounds arise when participation itself is valuable for human agency or learning. Most importantly, emergence grounds arise from target emergence: in some activities, the target is not fully specified in advance but instead emerges through the interaction itself. In these cases, human participation is not merely a means of improving execution but is constitutive of the target being produced. Human--AI co-construction, understood as the joint production of outcomes by humans and AI systems, is therefore not simply a temporary response to imperfect AI, but a persistent feature of activities whose objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems.

</details>


### [215] [MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21552)
*Wen Ye,Yuxiao Qu,Aviral Kumar,Xuezhe Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multiview reasoning in geometry QA: dataset and RL-based MIRROR to leverage text, image, and combined views for improved multimodal reasoning with cross-view supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs lag in visual reasoning; different modalities reveal distinct reasoning paths; need dataset and training method to exploit complementary views.

Method: Create ODA-Data with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined views for geometry problems; propose MIRROR: evaluate all views, select best as teacher, train others via reverse-KL to align to teacher.

Result: MIRROR outperforms standard RL on geometry benchmarks, delivering higher accuracy and more consistent multimodal behavior across modalities.

Conclusion: Modality-informed reciprocal reasoning effectively leverages complementary views, suggesting cross-view self-supervision as a viable route to improve multimodal reasoning in geometry tasks.

Abstract: Unlike large language models (LLMs) that exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with visual reasoning, even on geometry problems that admit equivalent text, diagram, and combined diagram+text views. We show that these views often elicit different behaviors: a model may solve a problem from text but fail on the corresponding diagram, or succeed visually while failing textually. This inconsistency suggests that different views expose complementary reasoning paths and failure modes that standard multimodal post-training does not fully exploit. To study and exploit this phenomenon, we construct ODA-Data, a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined image+text views of the same problems, together with splits for training and evaluating modality-dependent reasoning behaviors. We then develop Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization (MIRROR), a reinforcement learning approach for improving multimodal reasoning via self supervision. For each problem, MIRROR evaluates the model under all views, selects the best-performing view as a teacher, and trains other views with a reverse-KL objective towards the teacher. Across reasoning benchmarks that evaluate on geometry problems, MIRROR improves over standard RL and yields more accurate and consistent behavior across modalities

</details>


### [216] [OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21557)
*Xiao Yu,Baolin Peng,Ruize Xu,Hao Zou,Qianhui Wu,Hao Cheng,Wenlin Yao,Nikhil Singh,Zhou Yu,Jianfeng Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OpenForgeRL decouples training from inference for harness-based agents by introducing a lightweight proxy and a Kubernetes-based orchestrator, enabling end-to-end RL training across diverse harnesses and environments; it achieves strong benchmark performance and reveals that harness choice affects learnability and that RL improves reliability but some abilities (e.g., error recovery) remain weak.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current inference harnesses (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) enable powerful multi-turn reasoning but hinder end-to-end training with standard RL stacks due to stateful, multi-process inference that is not natively expressible in SFT/RL pipelines.

Method: Introduce a lightweight proxy that records harness model calls as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL) and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container. This decouples training from inference, enabling harness-based agents to be trained end-to-end across diverse environments. The framework supports multiple harnesses and environments and facilitates training on real harnesses and deployment contexts.

Result: Empirical results across harness-based agents and GUI browser/CLI tasks: OpenForgeClaw achieves 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval; 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI achieves 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. In general, outperforming open baselines of similar size; GUI results match or surpass models several times larger. Analyses show harness choice influences learnability; RL improves agentic reliability (self-verification, tool coverage, multi-step planning) but critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

Conclusion: OpenForgeRL enables end-to-end training of harness-based agents across diverse environments by decoupling training and inference with a proxy and containerized rollout orchestration. Harness choice significantly affects learnability; RL improves several reliability aspects but not all, pointing to future work in improving error recovery and other robustness aspects.

Abstract: Modern AI agents rely on elaborate inference harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw to drive multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and access to external systems. While powerful, these complex harnesses also make agents hard to train end-to-end with open infrastructure, whose SFT/RL stacks cannot natively express stateful, multi-process harness inference. To address this, we present OpenForgeRL, an open-source framework for training harness-based agents end-to-end in diverse environments. OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale. By decoupling training and inference, OpenForgeRL allows researchers to easily train, study, and improve agents directly in the real harnesses and environments they are deployed with. We validate our framework across diverse, complex harnesses and environments, spanning tool/claw-based agents and multimodal GUI browser- and computer-use agents. Using only hundreds to a few thousand tasks, OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks, and in the GUI setting match or surpass models several times larger. Beyond benchmarks, we analyze how harness choice (e.g., ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, Codex) and RL shape agent behavior. We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

</details>


### [217] [Beyond Sycophancy: Structured Resistance and Compliance in LLM Moral Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21558)
*Baihui Wang,Bernard Koch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic study of how large language models revise judgments under social influence, identifying three key factors—distance to the incoming view, source attribution, and coalition structure—that shape receptivity and distinguish constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond merely reducing sycophancy and develop a principled framework for when models should incorporate others' perspectives while preserving well-grounded moral judgment.

Method: Three studies examining judgment revision in large language models; experiments manipulate the proximity of incoming views, how the view is attributed (as own prior judgment or otherwise), and the coalition/power structure behind the view to observe effects on model updating.

Result: Models are generally more receptive to nearby positions, more influenced when views are framed as the model's own prior judgments, and variably influenced by group pressure; suggests sycophancy is an expression of broader judgment-updating guided by social influence.

Conclusion: The proposed framework distinguishes constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance and provides a principled basis for better alignment in morally consequential interactions.

Abstract: Building socially calibrated large language models, which can learn from others without simply yielding to them, requires more than reducing sycophancy as a one-dimensional failure mode. Models must distinguish when to incorporate others' perspectives from when to maintain a well-grounded moral judgment. We study the broader resistance-compliance process governing this distinction. Across three studies, we show that models' judgment revision is structured along three dimensions that parallel classic phenomena in human social psychology: the distance between an incoming view and the model's initial position, the source attribution of that view, and the coalition structure supporting it. Models are generally more receptive to nearby positions, more influenced by views presented as their own prior judgments, and differently responsive to group pressure. These findings recast sycophancy as one expression of a broader judgment-updating process shaped by social influence. Our framework provides a principled basis for distinguishing constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance, thereby supporting better alignment in morally consequential interactions.

</details>


### [218] [Unsupervised Consensus-Based Anomaly Detection for Spatiotemporal Malaria Incidence in Ghana](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21559)
*T. Ansah-Narh,Y. Asare Afrane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A spatial-temporal consensus anomaly detection framework reveals distinct patterns of malaria transmission in Ghana (2014-2023), showing that high-burden areas are not the same as high-anomaly areas, with persistent hotspots and region-specific dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address incomplete understanding of malaria transmission by separating anomalies from overall burden to improve surveillance and targeting.

Method: Apply a consensus anomaly detection framework to monthly malaria surveillance data across regions in Ghana (2014–2023); analyze spatial-temporal structure of anomalies; quantify anomaly burden (cumulative cases during anomalous periods) and anomaly frequency (persistence of unusual transmission); compare anomalous months to normal months using effect sizes (Cohen's d).

Result: Anomalies are highly structured in space and time; Ashanti and Northern Regions show most recurrent anomalies; persistent hotspots at Tamale, Kumasi, and Accra; Tamale has highest burden during anomalies; anomaly rates highest clustered in Ashanti; high-burden vs high-frequency mismatch; anomalous months have much higher counts (Cohen's d = 3.252) and large seasonal deviations (d>1.2) vs normal months.

Conclusion: Malaria burden alone is insufficient; distinguishing where malaria is prevalent from where transmission behaves unusually improves surveillance, prioritization, and targeted control.

Abstract: A consensus anomaly detection framework was applied to monthly malaria surveillance data from Ghana (2014-2023) to identify atypical transmission patterns. Anomalies were highly structured in space and time. Ashanti and Northern Regions accounted for most recurrent anomalies, with persistent hotspots at Tamale, Kumasi, and Accra. A key finding was the spatial distinction between anomaly burden (cumulative cases during anomalous periods) and anomaly frequency (persistence of unusual behaviour). Tamale had the highest burden during anomalies, whereas the highest anomaly rates clustered in Ashanti districts, showing that high-burden areas are not necessarily those with the most frequent anomalous transmission. Anomalous months formed a statistically distinct group, with much higher case counts (Cohen's $d = 3.252$) and large seasonal deviations ($d > 1.2$) compared with normal months. Malaria burden alone provides an incomplete picture of transmission dynamics. By distinguishing where malaria is most prevalent from where transmission behaves most unusually, this framework can strengthen surveillance, prioritise investigations, and support targeted control strategies.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [219] [DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20465)
*Hao Liang,Qifeng Cai,Yibo Lin,Jianzhuo Du,Qifeng Xia,Sizhe Qiu,Linzhuang Sun,Meiyi Qiang,Zhaoyang Han,Xiaochen Ma,Bohan Zeng,Ruichuan An,Conghui He,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DataPrep-Bench provides a unified benchmark to evaluate end-to-end LLM-driven data preparation across data construction and data quality evaluation, introducing Data-Construction-Skill and Distributional Alignment Score (DAS); shows strong cross-model performance and correlations across six domains and multiple base models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No unified, downstream-grounded benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows prepare training data end-to-end for downstream tasks.

Method: Two complementary capabilities are evaluated. Data construction: identical raw sources are transformed into supervised data; models are fine-tuned on the outputs jointly with Dolly-15k. Introduces Data-Construction-Skill, an agent that improves the Dolly baseline by ~20 points (absolute) on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and competes with strongest methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. Data quality evaluation: scoring functions predict downstream performance from candidate datasets. Introduces Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy; cross-model correlation is strongest in four of six domains and achieves r>0.70 in Math, Science, and Medical. Six-domain, multiple-base-model setting with a shared candidate pool for evaluation.

Result: Data-Construction-Skill lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and matches leading agent/DataFlow baselines in several domains. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric achieving r>0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality, diversity, and heuristic evaluators.

Conclusion: DataPrep-Bench demonstrates a unified, downstream-grounded framework to assess both data construction and data quality evaluation as co-equal targets in LLM-driven data preparation, with a practical metric (DAS) showing robust cross-model validity and an agent (Data-Construction-Skill) delivering substantial gains.

Abstract: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

</details>


### [220] [PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20492)
*Rana Muhammad Usman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Structured-output constraints induce rampant fabrication across LLMs; the proposed PhantomFill benchmark quantifies this with Coerced Fabrication Rate (CFR) and Escape Utilization Rate (EUR); a simple schema fix shows promise but overall model supply chain remains vulnerable to format pressure in production contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In production systems, LLMs are asked to fill structured fields (JSON, enums, arrays). The study investigates whether the format itself causes hallucination, revealing systemic reliability issues when models must conform to schemas rather than provide honest, unconstrained responses.

Method: The authors compare 13 models on identical questions, varying only the answer format. Inputs are crafted to be unanswerable (e.g., a viral post with no replies, a support ticket with no transcript). Free-form text yields honest responses; when a required JSON sentiment field exists, models fabricate. The study examines explicit 'insufficient evidence' options, and direct instructions (e.g., 'do not infer sentiment') across model sizes. They also introduce PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable metrics, and test a one-line schema fix.

Result: Across ten of thirteen models, required fields coerced fabrication to 100% in many cases. Nine open-weight models ignore the 'insufficient evidence' option; four of six models are overridden by explicit instructions embedded in the schema. Effects do not strictly correlate with model size within a family. The authors report a robust pattern of schema-induced fabrication, identify the exact failure points (required enums/minimum-count arrays), and show that honesty is not preserved under format pressure. PhantomFill yields two metrics (CFR and EUR) to quantify these failures, and demonstrates that a single schema tweak can mitigate but not eliminate the problem across models.

Conclusion: Schema-level constraints are a major source of systematic hallucination in production LLM usage. The PhantomFill benchmark provides a deterministic way to measure and compare resilience to format pressure, and a minimal schema fix is proposed as a practical remedy. The work highlights the need for schema-aware training and evaluation to prevent coerced fabrication in real-world deployments.

Abstract: Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

</details>


### [221] [The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20512)
*Yufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Orthogonalization via Newton-Schulz iteration is the main driver of Muon’s faster grokking threshold; spectral-norm constraints alone offer no reliable speedup. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations speeds up training but harms stability; five iterations provide a robust, learning-rate–robust solution. Spectral scaling can be dropped without cost. A stability-aware metric (first-crossing and sustained grok) is essential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To isolate which mechanism underlies Muon’s grokking speedup (spectral-norm constraints vs orthogonalized momentum) and to understand how orthogonalization influences generalization and stability across learning rates.

Method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps; ablation comparing orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz) vs spectral-only components; mechanistic analysis of spectral-norm, embedding movement, and norm of converged solutions; experiments varying Newton-Schulz iteration count (1 vs 5); evaluation of first-crossing vs sustained grok times; testing on modular-arithmetic grokking relative to AdamW; reproducibility via released code.

Result: Ablation shows the speedup stems from orthogonalization; spectral-only approaches are no faster than AdamW and unreliable. Orthogonalizers reach generalization at ~3× lower spectral norm and settle into a lower-norm solution when movement is accounted for. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from 5 to 1 speeds up threshold but increases fragility, with stability dependent on learning rate; 5 iterations remain the robust, LR-robust default. Spectral scaling can be dropped without measurable cost.

Conclusion: Under a stability-aware metric, faster claims about grokking optimizers can invert; reporting both first-crossing and sustained grok times is essential. The work provides reproducible code to support further investigation.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

</details>


### [222] [Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20516)
*Tolgay Atinc Uzun,Radu Timofte,Dmitry Ignatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaling the closed-loop LLM-based channel-configuration search to 250 candidates per cycle improves accuracy and parameter efficiency; reveals non-power-of-two widths and structured channel-allocation patterns, suggesting the search signal transfers under denser sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether the channel-search optimization observed in sparse evaluations generalizes to a denser sampling regime and to uncover additional architectural regularities that emerge with more generated networks.

Method: Replicate the prior search setting across 8 cycles with 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle, yielding 2000 generated candidates and 462 CIFAR-100 evaluations after filtering; evaluate per-cycle mean accuracy, top-k frontier, and parameter counts; analyze channel-width distributions and block-level channel allocations.

Result: Per-cycle mean accuracy shows a positive linear trend (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043). Best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676; the top-5 and top-10 cycle means also rise. The best model uses 11.8M parameters versus 166.5M for an earlier high-performer. Non-power-of-two channel widths appear in 41.8% of verified candidates; strongest models exhibit structured channel-allocation patterns with moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks.

Conclusion: The channel-search signal transfers to the denser sampling regime, achieving higher accuracy with greater parameter efficiency and revealing architectural regularities that were not evident in sparser samples; this supports scalability of the approach and informs future design biases.

Abstract: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

</details>


### [223] [Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20517)
*Takato Yasuno*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion retrieval-augmented generation system for heterogeneous PDFs, combining dense text embeddings, BM25, knowledge-graph filtering, and image similarity to enable robust multi-hop retrieval in disaster-domain documents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG over multimodal, domain-specific, and multi-hop retrieval across dispersed evidence is challenging; lexical bias and noisy PDFs degrade retrieval unless structured, multi-axis fusion and efficient filtering are used.

Method: Four-axis fusion architecture integrating dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity; builds a multimodal index from 2,403 blocks over 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs with hybrid OCR and LLM-based captioning; extracts 11,414 OpenIE triples indexed with FAISS for sub-second triple lookup; uses a HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume → chapter → block); Bayesian optimization over fusion weights (alpha_triple = 0.44) to balance contributions; image-to-lesson pipeline with a vision LLM.

Result: On a 457-pair benchmark, Retrieval Recall = 0.9909; 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries; triple-filtered fusion improves structured reasoning on noisy PDFs; demonstrates applicability to visual inputs via an image-to-lesson pipeline.

Conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for robust, structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework extendable beyond the disaster-domain context.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

</details>


### [224] [Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20519)
*Andrei Cristian Popescu,Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This work reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, showing that fixed-prior depth supervision and simple post-hoc readouts often match or outperform learned gates, and that failures arise mainly from trajectory induction rather than gate capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle the conflation between exit decisions (halting policy) and training-time supervision in looped Transformers, which can obscure the true sources of adaptive-compute performance.

Method: Systematic diagnostic evaluation across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale checkpoints (Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B). Compare fixed-prior depth supervision, post-hoc confidence readouts, and learned gates (including gates fitted on frozen trajectories). Analyze trajectory formation and exit readout separately and quantify latency/Pareto efficiency.

Result: Fixed-prior depth supervision shapes trajectories that yield useful stopping signals; simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or exceed learned linear/MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes failure to the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than gate expressivity. In Ouro evaluations, pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal; latency reductions correlate with reduced average exit depth, confirming practical inference-time savings.

Conclusion: Adaptive depth should be viewed as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout rather than gate learning alone; distinguishing trajectory effects from gate capacity reveals where adaptive compute gains actually come from, guiding more effective design of looped Transformers.

Abstract: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

</details>


### [225] [Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20521)
*Lei Cao,Sihang Feng,Jixin Yan,Tao Sun,Naichen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GBF replaces fixed observation models with CVAE-based generative likelihoods and uses score-based sampling for online Bayesian filtering, improving accuracy and robustness in nonlinear, high-dimensional, multi-mode systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical filters rely on simple observation models (e.g., linear-Gaussian) that fail to capture nonlinear, heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor data; there is a need for flexible observation models and robust uncertainty quantification.

Method: Train conditional generative models (CVAE) to represent p(y|x, mode) as a flexible likelihood; perform sequential Bayesian prediction-update; cast the measurement update as a posterior sampling problem combining dynamical priors with CVAE-induced likelihood; convert to score-based sampling; use ensembles for uncertainty estimation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic data and real-world tasks shows GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness compared with baseline filtering approaches.

Conclusion: GBF offers a flexible, uncertainty-aware filtering framework by integrating pretrained conditional generative models into the observation model, enabling better handling of nonlinear/high-dimensional dynamics and latent mode switching.

Abstract: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

</details>


### [226] [Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20522)
*Larry Richards*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Falsification of the semantic-concentration prediction: holonomy concentrates on active SAE feature planes in Gemma 2 2B is not supported; active-feature planes show less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls. The result is a narrow auditable reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. Common support issues and transport distortion emerge as confounds. Area-law checks partially support measurements on a small validation subset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether holonomy-targeted measures of representation align with a semantic-concentration hypothesis, by testing active sparse-autoencoder feature planes vs controls in a concrete model (Gemma 2 2B); preregistered design to examine causality between feature engagement and holonomy.

Method: Measure holonomy across layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by transporting a local frame around small loops using restricted-Jacobian transport; correct/normalize rotation by enclosed area; preregistered and frozen design; compare active-feature planes against mixed-feature and random planes; magnitude-matching controls; three-way ordering assessment; post-freeze diagnostics including area-law validation on a small subset, paired regression for center displacement, and identification of transport distortion as a potential confound.

Result: Adjusted log contrast = -0.29439; 95% CI [-0.43989, -0.14889]; active-feature planes carry less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls; magnitude-only explanation unsupported; three-way ordering undefined at matched magnitude due to lack of common support; post-freeze checks support area law on a small validation subset; transport distortion identified as live mechanism/confound.

Conclusion: The finding constitutes a narrow, auditable reversal rather than evidence that semantic content suppresses holonomy; the underlying cause remains unresolved, with several plausible alternatives (activation-strength geometry, feature engagement degree, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, transport shear) warranting further causal investigation.

Abstract: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

</details>


### [227] [Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20529)
*Jiawei Zheng,Jiazhen Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uncertainty-aware trust estimation for multi-LLM ensembles using Cooke-style log weighting to calibrate expert reliability, robust in heterogeneous and contaminated settings on MMLU benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address unreliability and differing uncertainty quality across heterogeneous LLMs; move beyond equal-trust aggregation.

Method: Adapt structured expert judgment with context-aware calibration questions; apply Cooke-style log weighting to weigh experts by calibration and informativeness; evaluate on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels.

Result: Cooke weighting yields better accuracy-reliability balance under heterogeneity and contamination, maintaining robustness when unreliable experts are present; similar performance to baselines in homogeneous settings.

Conclusion: Uncertainty calibration is essential for robust multi-LLM aggregation; Cooke-style trust weighting improves resilience to unreliable models, suggesting broader applicability of uncertainty-aware aggregation.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

</details>


### [228] [CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20530)
*Léa Billet,Louise Travé-Massuyès,Elodie Chanthery,Alexandre Gaffet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLOE is a scalable semi-supervised anomaly detector that uses an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction and a Christoffel Function–based detector in latent space, with a CF-informed loss, principled thresholding, and a single hyperparameter to tune.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the poor scalability of Christoffel Function–based methods in high dimensions and reduce hyperparameter tuning in lightweight anomaly detectors by leveraging representation learning.

Method: Train an autoencoder to obtain latent representations; apply a Christoffel Function–based detector in latent space; introduce a loss that uses the Christoffel Function to steer the encoder toward preserving the support of normal data; propose a principled thresholding procedure and an efficient strategy to tune the remaining hyperparameter.

Result: Empirical evaluation on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks shows CLOE outperforms existing methods while maintaining the lightweight, low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function–based approaches.

Conclusion: CLOE provides a scalable, low-tuning semi-supervised anomaly detection framework by integrating dimensionality reduction with CF-based detection, with strong empirical performance on high-dimensional data.

Abstract: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

</details>


### [229] [Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20532)
*Nadine Chang,Maying Shen,Jialiang Wang,Rafid Mahmood,Jose M. Alvarez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a proactive test-driven maintenance paradigm for open-ended AI systems, introducing a 'test space' to map feedback to task objectives and proving, theoretically, that this approach scales better and requires fewer iterations than reactive flywheels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reactive maintenance often misses broader system objectives and struggles with long-tail, open-world errors, leading to inefficiency and many iterations. A proactive approach aims to anticipate edge cases and align maintenance with global objectives.

Method: Introduce a 'test space' concept that maps feedback data to task objectives, transforming maintenance from reactive to proactive via a test-driven flywheel. Provide a mathematical proof that the proactive approach achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive alternative.

Result: A theoretical framework asserting that a proactive, test-driven flywheel yields superior long-term scaling and requires fewer iterations, supported by a mathematical proof. No empirical validation reported in the abstract.

Conclusion: Advocate shifting from reactive to proactive maintenance by formalizing a test space and proving scaling benefits, to build more generalizable AI systems.

Abstract: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive.
