We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

</details>


### [230] [Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20533)
*Marcos Florencio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural predicates generate probabilistic views for Black-Litterman by processing structured data into P, q, Omega; provides data-driven, interpretable, end-to-end differentiable framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address subjectivity and scalability in eliciting views and uncertainties in Black-Litterman; leverage neural predicates to automate view generation with uncertainty.

Method: Use a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates processing structured financial data; outputs are distributions that map to P, q, Omega; view confidence derived from predicate distributions; end-to-end differentiable.

Result: Proposed framework yields distributions for views; potential interpretability via traceability; data-driven uncertainty handling; end-to-end learning though specifics are not provided in abstract.

Conclusion: Offers an interpretable, differentiable alternative to subjective view elicitation in Black-Litterman, enabling scalable, data-driven portfolio optimization.

Abstract: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

</details>


### [231] [A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20535)
*Alicia Tierz,Icíar Alfaro,David González,Elías Cueto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zero-Shot Digital Twins: a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed framework using Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Networks (TIGNN) with real-time perception and data assimilation to generalize to unseen geometries and regimes without retraining, achieving ~25 ms/frame.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the rigidity and retraining dependence of traditional predictive digital twins when the physical domain or boundary conditions change; enable real-time, physically consistent simulations across unseen geometries.

Method: Introduce Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture based on metriplectic thermodynamic formalism to enforce energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally via graph message passing. Use an auxiliary GNN to infer unobservable fields from sparse initial boundaries; employ continuous closed-loop data assimilation with deep segmentation and sparse optical flow to correct the autoregressive simulation and suppress drift.

Result: Showcase strong generalization to two disparate regimes—large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid—without any case-specific retraining, operating in real-time (~25 ms per frame) and enabling AR projection of latent mechanical variables.

Conclusion: A geometry-agnostic, physics-informed predictive framework that harmonizes perception, theory-guided inference, and data assimilation to deliver zero-shot, real-time simulations across diverse physical domains, reducing or eliminating the need for retraining.

Abstract: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

</details>


### [232] [ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20537)
*Huei-Chung Hu,Hsin-Tai Wu,Koyo Kobayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReliableTableQA introduces a ten-category reliability taxonomy and a data-efficient training pipeline that labels the statistical reliability of tabular QA results. The key finding is that small, schema-stratified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffices to achieve near-perfect reliability annotation and eliminates UCAR; reinforcement GRPO adds little once SFT is adequate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In enterprise analytics, syntactically correct SQL can produce results based on too-small samples, wide confidence intervals, or confounding factors. Merely answering whether a query is answerable is insufficient; there is a need to identify when computed results are statistically unreliable and avoid confident but unreliable outputs (UCAR).

Method: Develop a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10). Build a programmatic data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits. Conduct controlled studies comparing SFT and GRPO under varying data regimes, including in-distribution and out-of-distribution (held-out H&M) evaluation.

Result: With a small, schema-stratified SFT set (as few as 200 examples), reliability-flag F1 rises from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, UCAR is driven to zero, and Rel-F1 on held-out H&M reaches 0.997. GRPO provides marginal gains only when SFT is under-trained and offers no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, confirmed across hard compound-flag slices, strict exact-match metrics, and OOD evaluation.

Conclusion: Reliability annotation for tabular QA can be treated as a data-efficiency problem. Reinforcement fine-tuning (GRPO) has limited value once a sufficient SFT baseline is established, and the approach generalizes to unseen retail domains. The work clarifies when RLHF/GRPO pays off and sets precise expectations for reliability labeling in enterprise analytics.

Abstract: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

</details>


### [233] [Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20538)
*Yitao Jiang,Yaoqing Yang,Luyang Zhao,Muhao Chen,Devin Balkcom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Codec-Gauge adds a post-training, cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing KV-cache compression backends to improve fidelity of long-context Transformer inference without modifying model weights. It employs a frequency-aware objective (DCT spectral-centroid loss and a smooth rate proxy) to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency layouts, achieving substantial reductions in KL divergence (avg. 44% with zfp) and better preservation across multiple quantization schemes and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context transformers rely on KV-cache compression/quantization, which can distort model behavior. There is a need for post-training mechanisms that improve compression fidelity without retraining model weights, altering attention semantics, or changing backend rules.

Method: Introduce Codec-Gauge: a post-training cache-coordinate layer that applies small orthogonal channel transforms around compression backends. Optimizes a combined frequency-distribution objective: a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss plus a smooth rate proxy to bias energy toward low-frequency, codec-friendly layouts. Evaluate across six models at 3, 4, and 6 bits/value; compare against random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls; test on 27B model and long-context prompts; assess via measured bytes, rolling compressed-history score, quality metrics, and timing/serialization.

Result: Gauges learned with Codec-Gauge reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average versus raw coordinates, outperform multiple baselines (random, Hadamard, DCT, PCA/KLT). They improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Reproduces trend on a 27B model and long-context prompts; serial storage and timing measurements validate compressed-cache paths.

Conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry is a practical post-training variable to improve compression fidelity for KV-cache in long-context Transformers without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

Abstract: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

</details>


### [234] [Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20539)
*Kyunghoon Hur,Eunjung Jeon,Hyun Woo Kim,Gyubok Lee,Seongjun Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two priors to inject ODE knowledge into neural nets for bioprocess data are substitutable; simulation pre-training on ODE curves matches architecture-embedded decoders, enabling data-efficient DL under scarcity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bioreactor data are scarce and costly; biokinetic ODE models exist but are rarely integrated into DL; need systematic study of how to inject this knowledge.

Method: Compare a data-level prior (pre-train a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves) with an architecture-level prior (embed the ODE inside the decoder); evaluate on 11 datasets across 7 microbial species; baseline comparisons.

Result: Both priors outperform no-prior baselines; central finding: they are substitutable; a simulation-pretrained decoder matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data.

Conclusion: Simulation pre-training provides a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning in bioprocess contexts with scarce data; the data-level prior can replace architecture-level encoding.

Abstract: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

</details>


### [235] [From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20540)
*Luca Ambrogioni,Giulio Franzese,Alberto Foresti,Gabriel Raya,Bac Nguyen,Georgios Batzolis,Yuhta Takida,Naoki Murata,Chieh-Hsin Lai,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a principled, asymptotic framework for allocating diffusion-noise levels during training. Finds that, in the fully coupled setting, optimal schedules are finite-support (atomic). In an independent-learner (decoupled) regime, the optimal sampling density is linked to the square root of the forward-process entropy rate. Empirically, finite-support schedules emerge in controlled tests (Dirac mixtures, manifolds, MNIST), with the entropic proxy tracking the optimum and square-root entropy scheduling improving training efficiency, especially on discrete domains and remaining competitive on continuous images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models currently rely on heuristic or tuned noise schedules for training. A principled, asymptotic understanding of optimal noise-level allocation could improve efficiency and performance, particularly across discrete and continuous domains, and inform schedule design beyond empirical heuristics.

Method: Develop a general statistical framework for asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation. Analyze a fully coupled regime (information can propagate across time) under convexity/Polyak-Lojasiewicz conditions, showing the optimizer has an atomic (finite-support) schedule. Specialize to an idealized independent-learner regime with a feature-noise decoupling condition; perform a random-matrix analysis to derive an information-theoretic proxy where the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the sqrt of the forward-process entropy rate. Validate via controlled experiments (Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, MNIST) and larger-scale tests where possible.

Result: The optimized schedules in controlled settings are consistently finite-support. The entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural networks and only fails in the fully coupled parametric case as theory predicts. On larger-scale problems, square-root entropy scheduling improves efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

Conclusion: A square-root entropy-based scheduling principle offers a principled and effective approach to noise-level allocation, particularly for discrete domains, with strong alignment to the atomic optimum in coupled settings. While less reliable in fully coupled parametric regimes, the framework provides actionable guidance and aligns with empirical improvements in efficiency; future work could extend to broader model families and more scalable optimization of schedules.

Abstract: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

</details>


### [236] [HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20541)
*Dimitrije Ždrale,Cassie An Jeng,Katie Wang,Sonia Vanier,Alexandre Bayen,Hossein Nick Zinat Matin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HypNO: a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws that enforces upwinding and entropy near shocks; achieves accurate snapshot predictions and shock capture on LWR and ARZ traffic-flow models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Operator-learning methods struggle with hyperbolic PDEs featuring global transport and discontinuities; there is a need for physics-informed architectures that respect causality and entropy to reliably predict shocks.

Method: Constructs a space-time graph of finite-volume cells; uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to enforce upwinding and entropy admissibility; operates directly on the space-time graph to forecast solution snapshots.

Result: HypNO accurately predicts solution snapshots across varied initial conditions and captures shocks and discontinuities; validated on LWR and ARZ traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods.

Conclusion: Graph-based neural operators with physics-informed upwinding and entropy constraints provide a robust approach for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws, demonstrated on traffic-flow models.

Abstract: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

</details>


### [237] [Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20542)
*Angel Tsai-Hsuan Chung,Jatu Abdulai,Patrick Bayoh,Lawrence Sandi,Francis Smart,Hamsa Bastani,Osbert Bastani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decision-aware ML with multi-task learning and catalytic priors improves essential medicines allocation in LMICs; Sierra Leone deployment increased consumption by ~19% in treated districts and scaled nationwide to ~2M women/children under five.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address scarce essential medicines and limited high-quality data in LMICs; traditional data-driven methods struggle; need sample-efficient, equitable allocation.

Method: Proposes a decision-aware ML framework; uses multi-task learning for sample efficiency; catalytic priors to promote equity; deployed as decision support tool; staggered nationwide deployment with government collaboration.

Result: Econometric evaluation reports 19% higher consumption in treated districts; nationwide scale to ~2M beneficiaries; suggests improved access at low cost.

Conclusion: Shows potential for ML to improve efficiency of essential medicines allocation in resource-constrained settings; combination of ML with policy priors and evaluation enabling scalable impact.

Abstract: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

</details>


### [238] [When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20543)
*Todd Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diagnostic framing for pass@k inversion in RLVR; introduces Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) to preserve base-solvable prompts, improving robustness against boundary prompt loss; suggests safety considerations for post-training optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and mitigate the observed mismatch where verifiable rewards improve one-shot accuracy but degrade performance under multiple samples, by diagnosing the mechanism and proposing a simple mitigation.

Method: Two-mode account (absence-of-evidence). Propose PBA as a proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with frozen-base evidence and anchor risky prompts to base distribution. Evaluation across three seeds on Omni-MATH-Test with MATH500, plus a 3000-prompt diagnostic study; use mathematical verifiers as controlled testbed; discuss generalization to vision-language agents with external verifiers.

Result: PBA yields improvements in Pass@1 and high-budget coverage over GRPO; diagnostic study shows ordinary GRPO loses boundary prompts solvable by base but PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories; results consistent with the proposed diagnostic signature.

Conclusion: Reasoning post-training should consider not just optimization strength but safety of optimization; inversion risk exists and can be mitigated by anchoring to base evidence; PBA is a simple proof-of-concept enabling verifier-guided optimization to operate safely.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

</details>


### [239] [Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20547)
*Esrat Farhana Dulia,Syed Arbab Mohd Shihab,Caleb Adams,Ruben Del Rosario*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Deep Q-Network-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework enables decentralized conflict resolution for heterogeneous AAM in a 3D corridor, with a 14-action policy per aircraft category; evaluated under degraded surveillance revealing safety-capacity trade-offs via Pareto-optimal configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safe Advanced Air Mobility requires maintaining separation despite noisy, delayed, or missing surveillance; scalable, decentralized conflict resolution for mixed fleets in confined corridors.

Method: Multi-agent reinforcement learning with a Deep Q-Network; separate policies for two aircraft categories; local observations; 14-action space (course, turn, vertical maneuver, landing, speed); simulation includes dynamics, energy, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty; 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds; Pareto analysis.

Result: Loss-of-separation frequency and duration increase with traffic density and separation requirements, though most events resolve within 1 s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of the time. In conflicts, actions: turning 33%, maintain 29%, speed control 25%, vertical maneuvers 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations show trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity.

Conclusion: The framework enables simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance and supports identifying Pareto-optimal designs balancing safety and corridor capacity.

Abstract: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

</details>


### [240] [SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20548)
*Mikail Khona,Aditya Vavre,Boxiang Wang,Deyu Fu,Hao Wu,Mike Chrzanowski,Bryan Catanzaro,Dheevatsa Mudigere,Jeff Pool,Michael Lightstone,Mohammad Shoeybi,Mostofa Patwary,Nima Tajbakhsh,Tijmen Blankevoort*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Higher-order optimizers (SOAP, Muon) outperform AdamW for large-scale LLM pretraining when augmented with per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning; a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM is proposed to address memory/communication, enabling stable training up to multi-billion-parameter models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address numerical stability and computational efficiency barriers of preconditioned, higher-order optimizers at scale to enable faster convergence in large LLM pretraining.

Method: Identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes; add per-step QR orthogonalization and enhanced preconditioning; conduct unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, AdamW with update-RMS matching; assess Muon orthogonalization; develop a layer-wise distributed optimizer for Megatron-LM; implement system-level improvements to accelerate the layer-wise approach; release codebase of emerging optimizers.

Result: SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at tested scales, maintaining stability and training quality at batch sizes up to 100M tokens where AdamW degrades; introduced a memory-efficient, non-approximate layer-wise optimizer suitable for Megatron-LM; system-level optimizations further speed up training; code released for community.

Conclusion: Higher-order optimizers can be practical for large-scale LLM pretraining with proper stabilization (QR orthogonalization, preconditioning) and system design (layer-wise distributor); the study supports adoption at scale and provides actionable tooling.

Abstract: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

</details>


### [241] [SevDiff: Severity-Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Tail Conflict Trajectory Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20549)
*Eni Solomon Laughter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion model for generating vehicle interaction trajectories conditioned on a target minimum Time-to-Collision (TTC).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the extreme data imbalance in ADAS evaluation where genuine V2V conflict events are rare; previous generative approaches condition on scene properties but cannot target a specific TTC.

Method: A diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that takes a scalar TTC target as conditioning input and generates paired interaction trajectories. Trained on 468 interaction windows from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing).

Result: Achieves high hit-rates for TTC targets: ~100% within ±0.5 s for 0.5–1.5 s TTC; ~97–99% for 2.0–2.5 s; ~39% for 5.0 s. Kinematic features are physically plausible (max out-of-range 4.7%; >96.5% no negative speed/gap). Degradation of hit-rate aligns with conditioning signal strength relative to training prior, indicating a precise generator characterization.

Conclusion: SevDiff provides a controllable, precision-aware generator for V2V conflict scenarios with tunable severity via TTC conditioning, addressing data imbalance in ADAS evaluation while yielding physically plausible trajectories; performance degrades gracefully as TTC targets become more extreme than training distribution.

Abstract: Trajectory datasets used in ADAS evaluation are heavily biased toward routine driving; genuine vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events are rare, and the rarer the event, the higher the cost when an ADAS system fails to handle it. Existing generative approaches address this imbalance by conditioning on scene-level properties - spatial goals, agent structure, or natural-language adversarial objectives - but none can accept a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value as input and be held to producing it within a measurable error. This paper introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that accepts a requested minimum TTC value as a scalar conditioning signal and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories whose realized conflict severity matches the request, evaluated through a hit-rate metric. Trained on 468 interaction windows extracted from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing), SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s and 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s, with graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematic features are physically plausible, with a maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features and no negative speed or gap values in more than 96.5% of samples. The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the strength of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, making it a precision characterization of the generator rather than a pass/fail result.

</details>


### [242] [Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20550)
*Tianming Han,Zhijie Pan,Wenchi Ge,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Geometric deep learning enables polypharmacology in structure-based drug design by modeling 3D geometry, multi-target binding, and de novo ligand generation; survey of architectures, applications, and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: One-drug-one-target paradigms fail for multifactorial diseases due to compensatory signaling and drug resistance; non-Euclidean molecular geometry and multi-target interactions require advanced representations and generative strategies; GDL offers invariant/equivariant learning and diffusion-based generation to tackle these challenges.

Method: Systematic survey of GDL architectures (invariant graph neural networks, SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models), multi-target fusion on heterogeneous graphs, structure-conditioned generation via diffusion with reinforcement learning, integration of multimodal omics data, and the establishment of specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures.

Result: Critical analysis across three core dimensions: (i) shared binding pocket geometry via geometric embeddings, (ii) multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, (iii) de novo generation of dual-target ligands; emphasis on diffusion-based, structure-conditioned generative methods and RL to resolve inter-site geometric conflicts; discussion of multimodal omics integration and benchmarking frameworks; provides a structured, roadmap-style guide for rational polypharmacology in drug design.

Conclusion: Geometric deep learning can drive a paradigm shift from serendipitous to rational, structure-driven polypharmacology; the review outlines key methodological advances and a clear path toward next-generation therapeutics.

Abstract: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

</details>


### [243] [SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20551)
*Tianming Han,Li Zhang,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SenCos-GEM introduces an explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that uses a law-of-cosines-based geometric consistency loss, SE adapters, and FiLM+SENet dual-modulation to achieve state-of-the-art performance on 3D conformation-sensitive tasks and robust stereoisomer discrimination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of explicit physical constraints, vulnerability to geometric noise from coarse empirical force fields during large-scale SSL pre-training, and catastrophic forgetting during downstream adaptation in 3D GNN-based molecular representation learning.

Method: A physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity 3D priors; lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation modules as backbone adapters; a dual-modulation prediction head combining FiLM and SENet for dynamic feature recalibration.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on MoleculeNet, notably on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks (FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, QM9) with relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE); enhanced capability to distinguish stereoisomers and detect conformational perturbations.

Conclusion: Explicit physical constraints and dynamic adaptation via geometry-aware priors and auxiliary modules enable accurate molecular property prediction and robust geometric modeling, representing a significant advancement in SSL-based 3D molecular representation learning.

Abstract: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

</details>


### [244] [Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20552)
*Chitraansh Pandey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a thermodynamics-inspired diagnostic (CV) for attention to predict grokking; introduces CvAdamW, an online, energy-injecting regularizer that uses Cv peaks to guide weight decay; demonstrates improved generalization timing on modular arithmetic with a cold-start variant and scale-invariant z-score reformulation; shows statistically significant yet small-to-moderate effects across seeds; code/data are public.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking (delayed generalization) remains inefficient and unpredictable. Building on the isomorphism between Transformer attention and a thermodynamic system, the work seeks early precursors of the generalization transition and an online intervention to enable generalization within a fixed compute budget.

Method: Define Cv as the variance of attention logits (treated as a heat capacity). Develop CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that scales weight decay dynamically when Cv indicates a phase transition. Identify three failure modes (initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, slingshot blinding) and mitigate them with a memorization gate and EMA shock absorber. Evaluate on the modular arithmetic task (a+b mod 97), showing grokking within budget where baseline does not. Propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation to remove task-specific hyperparameters, tested over 10 paired seeds.

Result: Cv peaks before grokking; CvAdamW enables grokking within budget where baseline fails. Cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 6.0% (257 epochs; median 166), p=0.049, d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489], across 8 of 10 seeds. All seeds show Cv peaking before grokking on this task. Code and data are public.

Conclusion: Neural networks may exhibit detectable precursors to impending generalization transitions, and a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate timely generalization within fixed compute budgets.

Abstract: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

</details>


### [245] [Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20555)
*Bryce A. Christopherson,Jack Baretz,Darian Colgrove,Salah Dandan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Double-scoring augments the edge-popup framework with an enlarged score space, replacing layerwise sparsity search with optimization over augmented scores. Theoretical result: fixed-density masks in augmented space preserve access to all original masks and equate to edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. Empirically, it improves strong-ticket extraction over baselines, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enhances rewound sparse-training performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable reliable extraction of strong lottery tickets in overparameterized random networks by addressing the bottleneck of layerwise sparsity selection, thereby enabling subnetworks accurate from initialization without training.

Method: Introduce double-scoring: an augmented score-space parameterization that enlarges the score tensors and optimizes over them, effectively performing edge-popup in a richer space. Prove that fixed-density masking in augmented space can realize any original-coordinate mask. Interpret as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. Validate via controlled experiments against fixed-density edge-popup, pruning-at-initialization, and rewound sparse-training baselines; conduct ablations.

Result: Substantially improves strong-ticket extraction compared with fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines; yields better performance than rewound sparse-training topologies; exhibits lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations indicate the gains arise from augmented score-space competition rather than simply more trainable scores, as it induces effectively the original sparsity.

Conclusion: Augmented score-space optimization effectively mitigates the layerwise sparsity bottleneck in strong ticket extraction, enabling more reliable and robust identification of strong lottery tickets with theoretical backing and empirical gains.

Abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

</details>


### [246] [Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20557)
*Hesen Chen,Xinyu Su,Xiaomeng Yang,Yuetan Lin,Zixiong Yang,Junyi An,Fenglei Cao,Yifeng Jiao,Yunqi Zhang,Yuan Cheng,Zhiyu Tan,Hao Li,Libo Wu,Yuan Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified scientific multimodal model (MKB) with a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored heads achieves cross-domain understanding and native-output generation across six domains, using a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum; results show competitive benchmarks and native outputs with public code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address fragmentation in scientific AI: current systems are domain-specialized or rely on text tokenization, hindering cross-domain reasoning, multi-modal integration, and modality-native outputs; motivate a unified model that can handle diverse scientific inputs and outputs.

Method: MKB uses a shared Transformer backbone with modality-specific encoders/adapters/decoders. It covers six domains (DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, medical images) and supports native outputs (biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, segmentation masks). Training follows a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality components with the frozen backbone, Stage 2 consolidates with the language backbone using mixed science/general corpora.

Result: MKB achieves competitive performance on biological/molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely preserves the general capabilities of the Qwen3-VL backbone.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of a shared-backbone, modality-tailored framework for cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration, and the approach provides a foundation for future cross-domain AI in science; code and model are publicly available.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

</details>


### [247] [StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20558)
*Emma Kondrup,Zachary Yang,Anne Imouza,Reihaneh Rabbany*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StabilityBench converts static, single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn interaction histories using realistic user simulations to probe LLM stability, revealing robustness gaps; StabilityBench-Mini offers a cost-efficient diversification variant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static benchmarks miss real-world contextual variability and user dynamics; a general, model-agnostic test operator is needed to assess LLM behavior in high-stakes settings.

Method: Transform single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn histories by injecting realistic users via demographic proxies and sycophantic bait while preserving task intent; apply to four benchmarks across math, health QA, and safety; evaluate nine LLMs; introduce StabilityBench-Mini as a smaller, diversified sampler.

Result: LLMs exhibit instability under user-injection perturbations with notable degradation on most benchmarks; static evaluations underestimate risk; StabilityBench-Mini enables diversified evaluation without increased cost.

Conclusion: Highlights the need for realistic, context-aware evaluation in high-stakes LLM deployment; the StabilityBench family provides a general, model-agnostic framework and a scalable mini-version for broader, cost-effective testing.

Abstract: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent. We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

</details>


### [248] [Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20559)
*Aditya Dutt,Paul Gader,Aditya Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deep learning pipeline (JuGAAD) fuses census, geospatial, and NSSO survey data to produce high-resolution socioeconomic indicators. It uses village-cluster tessellations for scale alignment, an autoencoder for latent NSSO representation, and a regression step to map upscaled census/geospatial features to that latent space, yielding fine-grained predictions validated against district-level NSSO data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developers aim to overcome scale mismatches between census coverage (geographic detail) and infrequent, coarse NSSO surveys, enabling accurate, high-resolution poverty and food-security indicators in developing nations; India 2001/2011 serves as a case study.

Method: Three-step process: (1) aggregate census and geographic data into intermediate village-cluster tessellations to reduce noise and stabilize boundary changes; (2) apply an autoencoder to compress high-dimensional NSSO data into a low-dimensional latent representation; (3) use a regression model to map upscaled census and geospatial features to the latent NSSO representation and generate high-resolution predictions when applied to fine-grained census data.

Result: High-resolution socioeconomic indicator predictions show strong accuracy when validated against ground-truth district NSSO indicators.

Conclusion: The JuGAAD framework demonstrates the feasibility of deriving fine-scale socioeconomic indicators from coarse-scale survey data by combining tessellation-based data regularization with representation learning and regression, enabling scalable, policy-relevant insights in India and potentially other settings.

Abstract: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

</details>


### [249] [Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20560)
*Muntaser Syed,Marius Silaghi,Sheikh Abujar,Sharun Akter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A three-layer neuro-symbolic RAG framework (Chronofy/TLDA) embeds temporal validity into representation, retrieval, and reasoning to curb temporal hallucination, with principled data re-acquisition triggers and improved grounding on temporal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address temporal hallucination in retrieval-augmented generation caused by treating retrieved facts as time-invariant; demand explicit temporal provenance to ensure factual relevance. 

Method: Layer 1: introduce a dedicated temporal subspace in Matryoshka embeddings to structurally separate fact age. Layer 2: embed learnable exponential decay in graph-based retrieval; decay coefficient β_j grounded in Bayesian theory as 2× mean-reversion rate. Layer 3: apply Signal Temporal Logic robustness to assess temporal validity of retrieved knowledge; enforce possibilistic weakest-link so output confidence is bounded by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain.

Result: Preliminary evaluation on temporal knowledge graphs, TimE temporal QA, and domain sensitivity analysis shows that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

Conclusion: Explicit temporal decay modeling in representation, retrieval, and reasoning yields temporally grounded RAG with safer, more reliable outputs and a mechanism to trigger re-acquisition of data when needed.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation. Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

</details>


### [250] [CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20561)
*Keumseo Ryum,Joonhyuk Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CT-Merging is a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that develops a common basis from average task subspace projectors and uses RMS-based task-level coefficient scales to merge adapters, improving multi-task performance on DC-Merge CLIP benchmarks for ViT models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA adapters offer efficient task specialization but require per-task adapters; merging multiple adapters into a single multi-task adapter is attractive, yet existing SVD-based merges rely on original task magnitudes that may not align with a fixed merged basis. CT-Merging seeks to build consensus directions and scale coefficients to better align tasks within a shared basis.

Method: CT-Merging constructs a common basis by repeatedly selecting shared support across task SVD subspaces and computing average task subspace projectors to derive consensus directions. It assigns task-level RMS scales to the final update, reducing dependence on the magnitudes from rank-wise SVD while preserving directionality.

Result: On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves higher average normalized accuracy than state-of-the-art merging methods and improves DC-Merge baselines by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

Conclusion: CT-Merging provides a robust, geometry-based approach to LoRA merging that improves multi-task performance by aligning task directions within a common basis and using RMS-based coefficient scaling, with demonstrated gains across ViT variants and KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

Abstract: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

</details>


### [251] [AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20577)
*Mengda Xing,Jean-Marie Lagniez,Alejandro Franco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Swin3D Transformer-based deep learning surrogate predicts spatiotemporal lithium-ion battery discharge dynamics from volumetric data, using Gaussian Positional Encoding and Temporal Encoding to improve spatial-temporal modeling; outperforms point-cloud baselines and is computationally efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-based LIB simulations are computationally expensive, hindering high-throughput design. There is a need for accurate, fast surrogates that can handle electrode microstructure geometry and non-linear time evolution.

Method: A Swin3D Transformer operating on volumetric electrode data; introduces Gaussian Positional Encoding to better capture geometry; includes a Temporal Encoding module to model non-linear time dynamics; trained/validated on an Electrochemical Simulation dataset; benchmarked against point-cloud baselines.

Result: The pipeline achieves higher prediction accuracy than state-of-the-art point cloud baselines on ES dataset and reduces computational overhead by orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: The proposed surrogate enables scalable, efficient high-throughput battery design and optimization by providing accurate spatiotemporal predictions with much lower computational cost.

Abstract: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

</details>


### [252] [Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21488)
*Gil Lifshits,Igal Bilik,Gilad Katz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPS: a hierarchical MARL framework where a central Master proposes a compact proto-plan embedding that guides decentralized Worker agents to coordinate at unsignalized intersections; shows improved travel time, collision-free navigation, and strong zero-shot generalization in HighwayEnv.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the combinatorial action spaces and reliance on privileged information in MARL for multi-vehicle coordination at intersections; enable scalable coordination via a global, continuous coordination embedding.

Method: A centralized Master agent outputs a compact continuous proto-plan embedding encoding global coordination; decentralized Worker agents fuse this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control. This decouples strategic intent from tactical execution and permits independent optimization of each module. Evaluation on 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv.

Result: MAPS achieves collision-free navigation and reduced average travel time, outperforming baselines. Proto-plans demonstrate robust generalization, achieving 94% success when transferred zero-shot from 3-agent to 5-agent scenarios.

Conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning is a promising framework for scalable, generalizable multi-vehicle coordination in MARL, enabling efficient global-to-local coordination with strong zero-shot transfer.

Abstract: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

</details>


### [253] [Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20578)
*Vu Khac Ky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces primal and inverse Fisher Gaussian widths on a statistical manifold and analyzes their complementary roles in learning and sparse recovery; proves a fundamental product lower bound with Euclidean width and characterizes the effect of Fisher anisotropy on statistical complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how Fisher information geometry governs statistical complexity in estimation and recovery, and quantify the interplay between local fluctuations (primal width) and anisotropic measurements (inverse width).

Method: Define w_G(T)=w(G^{1/2}T) and w_{G^{-1}}(T)=w(G^{-1/2}T) using Gaussian width on the metric induced by Fisher information G. Derive learning-scale bounds on Fisher balls for Fisher-regular losses; analyze inverse-Fisher geometry for sparse recovery, obtaining a two-sided bound on the statistical dimension and posteriorly sensitive recovery guarantees; prove a universal product inequality w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)≥w(T)^2 on common compact sets.

Result: Main results include: (i) w_G(H_r)/√n is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls for Fisher-regular losses; (ii) inverse-Fisher width captures anisotropic Gaussian measurements and depends on the position of active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum, with a two-sided statistical-dimension estimate and support-sensitive recovery; (iii) a sharp inequality w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)≥ w(T)^2 on common compact T, establishing a trade-off that Fisher anisotropy can transfer complexity but not reduce it below Euclidean baseline.

Conclusion: Fisher anisotropy mediates a transfer of statistical complexity between the primal and inverse geometries without beating the Euclidean complexity in both directions. The framework unifies learning and sparse-recovery analyses under Fisher geometry and suggests connections to curvature and spectrum of the Fisher information.

Abstract: We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

</details>


### [254] [Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20582)
*Frederik Hauke,Patrick Wienholt,Christiane Kuhl,Dyke Ferber,Jakob Nikolas Kather,Sven Nebelung,Daniel Truhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MC dropout-based epistemic uncertainty improves error-detection in a multi-task chest X-ray classifier; using a binary uncertainty flag reduces confident misdiagnoses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
