It achieves a high-probability l_infty error bound close to vanilla Q-learning, with an additive term that scales with the corruption fraction; it is the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under such corruption and is minimax-optimal in the reward-only case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning deployed in harsh environments where an adversary can perturb both rewards and state observations. The work aims to provide theoretical robustness guarantees under the Huber contamination model for Q-learning, including asynchronous settings.

Method: BR-Async-Q is epoch-based and batch-oriented. The online data stream is partitioned into batches to reduce variance, and robust estimators of the Bellman optimality operator are constructed using batched data to withstand corruption in rewards and observations.

Result: The paper proves a high-probability l_infty error bound for BR-Async-Q that matches vanilla Q-learning up to a small additive term that scales with the corruption fraction. It provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under joint reward and state corruption. When corruption affects only rewards, the bound is minimax-optimal with respect to the corruption fraction.

Conclusion: BR-Async-Q demonstrates robustness of asynchronous Q-learning to adversarial data corruption with rigorous performance guarantees. The batching-based approach for robust Bellman estimation enables resilience in harsh environments and lays groundwork for further robustness analyses in RL.

Abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning in harsh environments, we consider the problem of learning an optimal policy subject to adversarially corrupted feedback. Specifically, at each time-step, an adversary can perturb both the reward and state observations of the learner following the Huber contamination model. To defend against such data corruption, we propose {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}}: a novel, epoch-based, robust \(Q\)-learning algorithm built upon two key ideas: (i) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using such batched data. We prove a high-probability $\ell_\infty$ error bound for {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}} that matches that for vanilla \(Q\)-learning, up to a small additive term that scales with the fraction of corrupted samples. To our knowledge, this provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous \(Q\)-learning subject to both reward and state corruption. Furthermore, when only rewards are corrupted, the dependence of our algorithm's bound on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal.

</details>


### [280] [Beyond Heavy Log Curation: Perplexity-Based APT Detection via Unsupervised, Context-Augmented Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20832)
*Shoya Otsu,Kei Suzuki,Toshiaki Koike-Akino,Jing Liu,Ye Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAPTAIN is a perplexity-based detector that uses general pre-trained language models with minimal domain-specific preprocessing to detect APT-related activity in long log entries. It encodes recent history with an encoder and a Q-Former-style bridge, injects compact context tokens into the decoder input so perplexity reflects temporal context, and applies smoothing to the perplexity time series. It achieves competitive performance against strong baselines while reducing preprocessing and engineering costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: APT campaigns are hard to detect because only a small fraction of large-scale logs are attack-related. Traditional ML pipelines require heavy domain knowledge and curated data; there is a need for robust, scalable detection with reduced preprocessing and engineering effort.

Method: CAPTAIN leverages general, pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing. It encodes recent history with an encoder, uses a Q-Former-style bridge to generate compact context tokens, and injects these into the decoder input so perplexity incorporates temporal context. Perplexity time series are further stabilized with smoothing filters.

Result: On APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN competes with strong baselines and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs, reducing development and operational costs for advanced log preprocessing.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates the viability of context-augmented perplexity-based detection for APT logs, offering competitive performance with lowered domain-specific preprocessing and associated engineering costs; future work could explore broader datasets and parameter sensitivity.

Abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) remain difficult to detect because only a small fraction of events in large-scale logs are attack-related, and investigation is expensive and hard to scale. Prior machine-learning approaches can reduce analyst workload, but they often rely on heavily curated training data and sophisticated preprocessing pipelines. Building and maintaining such pipelines require substantial domain expertise and engineering cost. Motivated by insights from a study of a strong APT detection baseline, we propose CAPTAIN (Context-Augmented Perplexity-based Threat Activity log detectIoN), a perplexity-based detector that leverages general, pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing, enabling robust scoring of long, minimally processed log entries. CAPTAIN encodes recent history with an encoder model and a Q-Former-style bridge, then injects the compact context tokens into the decoder input so that perplexity reflects temporal context. To improve stability, CAPTAIN additionally applies smoothing filters to the perplexity time series. Across APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs, that reduces the development and operational cost of advanced log preprocessing.

</details>


### [281] [Offline RL with Hierarchical Action Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20834)
*Ahad Jawaid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HiQC (Hierarchical Implicit Q-Chunking) introduces offline goal-conditioned RL with dual horizon compression: high-level latent planning plus low-level action chunking, enabling unbiased k-step value backups. It yields a tighter error bound and state-of-the-art results on OGBench, especially for long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline goal-conditioned RL struggles with value estimation errors propagating over long horizons. Hierarchical approaches help by subgoal decomposition but rely on low-level controllers that can be myopic and biased. A dual decomposition that compresses horizon at planning and execution is needed to improve long-horizon performance and estimation reliability.

Method: HiQC combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking. The low-level critic conditions on temporally extended action sequences, enabling unbiased k-step backups. The approach provides a theoretical bound on value error that is tighter than standard hierarchical or flat chunking baselines, under a bounded per-backup error model. Empirically evaluated on the OGBench suite.

Result: Theoretical: tighter bound on value error under a bounded per-backup error model, compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking. Empirical: achieves the highest aggregate performance among compared methods on OGBench, with the largest gains on long-horizon navigation tasks (e.g., humanoid-giant).

Conclusion: HiQC effectively combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking to compress the horizon at both planning and execution levels, yielding improved offline goal-conditioned RL performance and more reliable value estimates for long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning general-purpose policies from static datasets. However, scaling these methods to long-horizon tasks remains a challenge due to the curse of horizon, where value estimation errors can compound through long chains of bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical approaches mitigate this by decomposing tasks into subgoals, yet they often rely on low-level controllers that suffer from myopic execution and biased value estimates. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Implicit Q-Chunking (HiQC), an offline goal-conditioned RL algorithm that combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking. By conditioning the low-level critic on temporally extended action sequences, HiQC enables unbiased k-step value backups, compressing the horizon at both the planning and execution levels. We theoretically demonstrate that this dual decomposition results in a tighter bound on value error under a bounded per-backup error model compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking alone. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance among the compared methods on the OGBench suite, with its largest gains on long-horizon navigation tasks such as humanoid-giant.

</details>


### [282] [Multilevel Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing with Scale-Aware Neural Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20857)
*Amirhossein Nouranizadeh,Sarang Rajendra Patil,Alan John Varghese,Varsha Narayanan,Amit Chakraborty,Mengjia Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GWCS compresses graph signals offline by sparse spectral graph wavelet coefficients, using a multilevel importance sampler and a scale-aware GNN to reconstruct. Evaluated on synthetic band-limited graphs and four PDE mesh datasets; achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression versus benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce data preparation and training cost in scientific ML methods (neural operators, PINNs) by compressing graph signals without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

Method: Nonparametric multilevel importance sampling retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale under a target compression ratio; a scale-aware graph neural network reconstructs the signal from sparse wavelet coefficients.

Result: Demonstrates high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines across synthetic and PDE mesh datasets (Turblulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, Dynamic Stall).

Conclusion: GWCS provides an interpretable, energy-preserving sparse representation in the spectral graph wavelet domain and effective offline compression for graph signals, enabling efficient use of data in data-hungry scientific ML pipelines.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning methods such as neural operators and physics-informed neural networks have advanced engineering applications and inverse problems, but their training typically requires large volumes of simulated data. This makes data preparation and model training expensive. We propose Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing (GWCS), a learning-based framework for offline compression of graph signals by representing them as sparse, interpretable wavelet-domain representations using the spectral graph wavelet transform. The framework combines a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler, which retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio, with a scale-aware graph neural network that reconstructs the signal from the sparse coefficients. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic approximately band-limited graph signals over random graphs and four PDE simulation datasets over meshes, which include Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, and Dynamic Stall. We compare against graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to existing benchmarks.

</details>


### [283] [Position Bias is Hidden Behind Ceiling Effects: A Permutation Diagnostic for LLM Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20864)
*Hiroki Tamba*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exhaustive permutation-based measurement of position bias in MC-LLM evaluation using an open-source tool (inspect_permute); demonstrates bias is detectable only in a Goldilocks band of base accuracy (~60–95%), with two underlying signal types; provides reproducible pipeline (MIT) and preregistration, clarifying when absence of signal implies not measurable rather than unbiased.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation can confound cross-model capability comparisons. Prior work used single-order shuffles, conflating content noise and sampling stochasticity. Exhaustive order permutations with statistical testing enables verifiable detection and interpretation of bias signals across models and tasks.

Method: Extend inspect_ai with inspect_permute to run exhaustive answer-order permutations per question; compute chi-squared and Cramer’s V to quantify position bias; bootstrap confidence intervals. Experimental setup: 4 vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3); 5 MMLU subjects; 24,000 API calls at temperature 0; preregistered falsifier predictions via public SHA-256 hash before half data observed.

Result: Position bias is detectable only within roughly 60–95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below this band, processing-load dominance swamps signal; above it, ceiling effects compress variance below chi-squared resolution. Two detectable mechanisms: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load) in low-tier models and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity) in a narrow capability band. Frontier-tier models (standard MMLU) lie above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. The work, together with arXiv:2606.26185’s ceiling effect characterization, brackets the detectable region for position-bias measurement and supports verifiability; package, data, and preregistration released under MIT.

Conclusion: This study delineates the detectable region for position-bias signals in MC-LMM evaluation, enabling researchers to interpret null results correctly and to plan reproducible experiments. It provides a concrete methodology and release for open verification.

Abstract: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is widely cited as a confound in capability comparisons, but published measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles whose results confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. I introduce inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports the chi-squared / Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. I apply the tool across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, with falsifier predictions pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed. Position bias turns out to be statistically detectable only within a roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress the variance below the chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells separate into two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. Together with the ceiling-effect characterisation in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and makes the field central question askable in a verifiable form. Package, data, preregistration under MIT.

</details>


### [284] [TwistedMerge: Certified Higher-Order Diagnostics and Abstention for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20887)
*Ting Gong,Shitan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TwistedMerge provides a conservative, certification-driven framework for merging independently trained models via descent theory, demanding inverse-consistency, centrality, and closure; embraces abstention when obstructions persist, with the claim that many natural merges cannot be certified.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the mismatch between pairwise alignability and global consistency in model merging; provide a falsifiable certification framework.

Method: Formulate as finite descent; local checkpoints, transitions, cycle residuals; fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, central obstruction, nonabelian holonomy; promote residuals to cohomology classes after a sequence of tests; abstain otherwise; prove theorems; apply to synthetic and natural data; audit with low-rank adapters; compare to GLr representations; analyze cycle residuals.

Result: Constant-edge no-go result; three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems; refinement test; planted defect removal; behavior of controlled central systems; noisy estimates yield abstention; stability of global factor synchronization; naive averaging sensitivity; cycle residuals not predictive; no natural central/class certified.

Conclusion: Descent theory can serve as a falsifiable certification/abstention framework for model merging.

Abstract: Model merging combines independently trained or fine-tuned models, but pairwise alignability does not imply globally consistent alignment. We formulate merging as a finite descent problem in which checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge is a conservative certification pipeline that separates fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a specified comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains and returns an ordinary or synchronized fallback. We prove a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, showing that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover the predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior, while noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on the tested controls. A trained low-rank-adapter audit shows that naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoint collections, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified. The results position descent theory as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework.

</details>


### [285] [Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20890)
*Hyeong-Gun Joo,Songnam Hong,Dong-Joon Shin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Efficient, information-theoretically secure on-device aggregation for sign-based FL using MV polynomial and single-round secure multiplication, achieving major communication/latency reductions and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protect gradient signs from inference attacks in sign-based FL while keeping low communication/computation overhead; enable secure aggregation under honest-majority; ensure robustness to dropouts and adversaries.

Method: Compute the majority-vote (MV) polynomial securely with single-round secure multiplication; apply inverse-form exponent reduction to lower the polynomial degree; employ MDS-code-based decoding for dropout/adversary robustness; reveal only the final aggregated sign to the server, achieving end-to-end information-theoretic security under honest-majority.

Result: Online communication reduced by up to 99.5%; latency reduced by up to 85.7%; accuracy gains up to 20.65% (dropouts) and 10.74% (adversarial behaviors); scalable to large-scale FL with low latency.

Conclusion: Presents a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL, combining efficiency techniques with robustness guarantees.

Abstract: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

</details>


### [286] [HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20896)
*Kritanu Chattopadhyay,Soumya Chatterjee,Ondrej Krejcar,Debotosh Bhattacharjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A dual-graph neural framework HierarchicalDAEW for predicting spatial gene expression from H&E; domain-aware edge weighting on spot graphs plus gene-level PPI-informed graph; evidential uncertainty yields calibrated intervals; outperforms baselines across six Visium tissues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the high cost and technical barriers of spatial transcriptomics and the lack of tissue-structure-aware, trustworthy predictions suitable for clinical use; incorporate explicit tissue architecture and reliable uncertainty quantification.

Method: Spot graph uses a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolution to learn separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, treating tissue heterogeneity as a structural signal. A second gene-level graph fuses STRING-DB protein-protein interaction priors with tissue-specific co-expression via learned attention gating. Reliability is provided by evidential uncertainty estimation, yielding calibrated confidence intervals. Evaluations span six human Visium sections (breast, colorectal, prostate, cerebellar) against thirteen baselines, with ablations confirming necessity of domain-aware edges and hierarchical depth.

Result: HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression across six tissue types and thirteen baselines; performance remains robust under multi-seed reproducibility and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations show both domain-aware edge typing and hierarchical depth contribute to improvements. Calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions suitable for pathologist review.

Conclusion: The approach effectively integrates tissue architecture and prior biological networks to improve accuracy and reliability of predicted spatial transcriptomes from histology, with practical clinical implications owing to calibrated uncertainty that flags unreliable predictions.

Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

</details>


### [287] [Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20908)
*Quazi Ishtiaque Mahmud,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Ali Jannesari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CudaPerf extends RL-based program optimization by adding verifiable execution rewards and structural, program-parallelization-aware rewards, with offline ranking and online RL phases, plus a new GPU-focused dataset; achieves substantial speedups and correctness gains over strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL-based reward signals rely mainly on outcome-based feedback (e.g., correctness, speedup) and ignore key structural properties that govern GPU performance. Incorporating parallelization-aware, code-structure signals can guide generation toward more efficient CUDA code.

Method: A two-stage framework: (1) offline pairwise ranking via contrastive learning to distinguish strong vs weak candidates; (2) online RL training that jointly optimizes correctness, performance, and structural-efficiency rewards. It uses iterative refinement with execution feedback and evaluates on a dataset of 2.9k C→CUDA and 1k PyTorch→CUDA programs with diverse inputs and multiple CUDA implementations.

Result: CudaPerf outperforms strong baselines (e.g., Qwen-3-32B for C→CUDA and CUDA Agent for PyTorch→CUDA), achieving up to 5x speedup and 3.32x speedup, with improvements in correctness of 17% (C→CUDA) and 7% (PyTorch→CUDA).

Conclusion: Integrating verifiable execution rewards with structural, code-aware rewards enables more effective RL-based code generation for GPU targets, and the accompanying dataset facilitates evaluation across translation directions and optimization strategies; iterative feedback further enhances learning.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capacity of LLMs for optimized code generation. However, existing RLVR approaches primarily rely on outcome-based signals such as correctness and speedup, overlooking performance-critical structural properties of programs that are essential for generating optimized code. In this work, we propose CudaPerf, a reflective RL framework that incorporates both verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards derived from parallelization features (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy, Arithmatic Intensity, and synchronization patterns). CudaPerf operates in two stages: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong and weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through a unified reward signal. To further enhance learning, CudaPerf utilizes iterative refinement using execution feedback enabling progressive improvement of generated candidates. We also introduce a dataset comprising 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs, each paired with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations encompassing diverse optimization strategies. CudaPerf is evaluated across multiple benchmarks comprising both C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations. Empirical findings suggest that CudaPerf significantly outperforms strong baselines, including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA) by achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively.

</details>


### [288] [Three-Pronged Spectral Control for Federated Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20914)
*Shiva Raj Pokhrel,Dipsan Bhattarai,Anwar Walid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRISHUL: a spectral-control approach for federated PEFT that uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases and nuclear norm shrinkage to align subspaces across non-IID clients, enabling robust, low-overhead aggregation and improved convergence across vision and language tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated PEFT with LoRA can suffer from spectrally misaligned, locally useful updates due to client non-IID data, leading to high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. A method that robustly aggregates compact updates without extra communication or privacy guarantees is needed.

Method: TRISHUL employs shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to enable algebraically exact aggregation of core updates. It applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress high-rank spectral components before uploading updates. Adaptation heads are allocated non-uniformly across layers via a concave water-filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. The approach adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication beyond the base multi-head PEFT protocol.

Result: Empirical evaluation across vision (CIFAR-100, SVHN) and NLP/IR benchmarks (20 Newsgroups, MRQA, GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B) shows TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with larger gains under stronger heterogeneity.

Conclusion: TRISHUL delivers a robust, communication-efficient federated PEFT framework that mitigates non-IID heterogeneity via spectral control, achieving consistent gains across diverse tasks with minimal overhead; privacy guarantees are not provided by the method itself.

Abstract: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables communication-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models on decentralized edge data, but it remains fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity. In low-rank adaptation (LoRA), different clients may learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, causing high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. We propose TRISHUL, a spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT. TRISHUL follows the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting but does not itself provide formal privacy guarantees. TRISHUL uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to obtain algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Because shrinkage is performed only on small core matrices, TRISHUL adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication over the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. Across vision and language benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.

</details>


### [289] [Best-of-Evidence: Best-of-N Selection under Partial Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20950)
*Cenwei Zhang,Teng Fang,Yuxia Wang,Derek Li,Bryan Dai,Lei You*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Best-of-Evidence (BoE) extends bootstrapped, best-of-n (BoN) sampling by using a fixed pool and partial, reusable evidence to guide the final decision; it formalizes partial verification via a signed candidate–factor graph and shows theoretical and empirical gains under limited evidence budget, especially in medical VQA, while highlighting limits due to evidence capacity and channel quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BoN relies on evaluating full candidate responses, but many tasks provide only partial, verifiable evidence. Conflicting observations across candidates further complicate selection. BoE aims to enable evidence-driven reweighting within a fixed candidate pool, leveraging partial signals to improve decision quality.

Method: Introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE): keep BoN pool fixed, model reusable claims with a signed candidate–factor graph, and allocate a budget to evidence actions that can influence the final choice. BoE includes a score-based controller and reduces to BoN when budget is zero; theoretical results show residual evidence capacity bounds on improvement and a log(K) vs K query advantage with shared factor queries in a factor-code model.

Result: Theoretically, residual evidence capacity bounds any improvement; shared factor queries yield O(log K) vs Θ(K) query separation. Empirically on four medical VQA datasets, BoE improves fixed-pool selection and rescues some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant; it also reveals channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that cap universal gains.

Conclusion: BoE generalizes BoN to partial verification, providing a practical controller and framework for evidence-driven selection. Its benefits materialize under favorable evidence conditions, while fundamental limits (evidence capacity and evidence quality) constrain universal gains.

Abstract: BoN improves model outputs by sampling several candidates and selecting one with a proxy score, but it assumes that complete candidates can be evaluated reliably. Many vision-language tasks instead provide only partial verification: a finding, span, value, region, or relation may be checkable even when no dependable whole-response verifier exists. Moreover, the same claim may recur across candidates with opposing stances, allowing one observation to support part of the pool and contradict another. We introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE), an inference-time selection framework that keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims with a signed candidate--factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can change the final choice. BoE formalizes selection under partial verification and provides a practical score-based controller, with the zero-budget case recovering the underlying BoN decision. Theoretically, we show that residual evidence capacity limits any evidence-driven improvement and that shared factor queries can achieve an O(log K) versus Θ(K) query separation in a factor-code model. Common-ledger experiments on four medical VQA settings show that BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant, while also revealing the channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that prevent universal gains.

</details>


### [290] [The Weight of Silence: A Causal Case for Weights Over the Scratchpad in Latent Chess Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20952)
*Ishan S. Kshirsagar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL-enhanced chess model shows latent reasoning acts mainly as a training-time parameter-shaping mechanism; robustness to thought perturbations increases after RL, challenging the view of latent thoughts as an inference-time scratchpad.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether latent reasoning is used as an inference-time scratchpad after RL, extending prior causal analyses from math/logical tasks to a strategic domain (chess) and comparing before/after RL.

Method: Train a chess model via staged latent-reasoning curriculum; then apply reinforcement learning. Use six-condition causal intervention suite, perturbing latent thought vectors (noise, ablations, exact-zero). Compare performance pre- and post-RL on legality and checkmate confabulation.

Result: Post-RL legality 61% vs 48% pre-RL; checkmate confabulation eliminated; exact-zero perturbations cause collapse (1% pre-RL vs 9% post-RL), showing a robustness gap; most perturbations have little effect; RL increases robustness to disruption more than reliance on latent thoughts.

Conclusion: Latent reasoning likely shapes model parameters during training rather than serving as an active inference-time scratchpad; demonstrates RL gains in chess and suggests a general mechanism of latent reasoning improving training-time representations rather than inference-time computation.

Abstract: Latent, or silent, reasoning lets language models carry out intermediate computation in continuous vector space instead of words, and is widely assumed to function as an internal scratchpad the model actively consults during inference. Whether that assumption survives reinforcement learning has not been tested directly: existing causal analyses of latent reasoning are confined to math and logic tasks, and compare a model's reliance on its thoughts within a single checkpoint, never before and after an RL stage. We train a chess-playing model through a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by reinforcement learning, and find legality climbs monotonically to 61% (from a 48% pre-RL baseline) while checkmate confabulation is eliminated entirely. To locate this gain, we run a six-condition causal intervention suite on the same model before and after RL: substituting or adding matched noise to the latent thought vectors leaves performance unchanged, ablating them causes only mild degradation, and only exact-zero vectors cause collapse. This robustness gap is itself the finding: under exact-zero corruption, legality collapses to 1% pre-RL versus 9% post-RL, a gap that survives correction for testing across the full battery; milder conditions trend similarly without independently reaching significance. RL appears to add robustness to disruption, not reliance on thought content. These results push back against the field's default assumption that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad, and instead indicate latent reasoning's principal effect here is shaping the model's parameters during training. We also demonstrate a working RL gain in chess, a domain outside the math and logic settings where multiple groups report the same latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipe failing to improve accuracy over SFT.

</details>


### [291] [ADABORD: a novel AdaBoost approach for ordinal classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21003)
*Rafael Ayllón-Gavilán,Francisco José Martínez-Estudillo,David Guijo-Rubio,César Hervás-Martínez,Pedro A. Gutiérrez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ADABORD extends AdaBoost for ordinal classification by using ordinal Gini splitting and absolute ranked probability score, achieving significant gains over seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO benchmark, especially with five or more classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ordinal Classification tasks have ordered classes; traditional approaches treat the problem as nominal, underutilizing ordinal information. There is a need to integrate ordinal structure into both the base learner and the boosting weight scheme to improve performance.

Method: Proposes ADABORD, an AdaBoost-based framework for OC. The base estimator uses decision trees with an ordinal Gini splitting criterion. The weight update function and the final classifier weights use the absolute ranked probability score, capturing order and class distance.

Result: Empirical evaluation against seven state-of-the-art OC methods on the TOC-UCO repository shows ADABORD significantly outperforms competitors, particularly as the number of classes grows to five or more. Statistical analyses support the significance of improvements. The authors provide source code and experimental protocols for reproducibility.

Conclusion: Incorporating ordinal information into both the weak learner and the boosting weight scheme yields tangible performance gains in ordinal classification. ADABORD is a competitive and reproducible approach for OC, with pronounced advantages on more class-rich problems.

Abstract: Ordinal Classification (OC) deals with classification tasks where the classes follow a natural order. Despite the progress in OC, many existing approaches fail to fully leverage the ordinal information, treating the problem as nominal classification and thereby losing performance potential. In this work, ADABORD, an AdaBoost framework specifically designed for ordinal classification problems, is introduced. The ordinal nature of the classes is incorporated into two key components of the well-known AdaBoost algorithm: 1) the base estimator, where decision trees with the ordinal Gini splitting criterion are proposed; 2) the error function used to update sample weights at each stage and the weights of the classifier in the final ensemble model, given by the absolute ranked probability score, a measure that accounts for both the ordering and the distance between classes. ADABORD is extensively compared against seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository, the largest benchmark collection for OC to date. The experimental results, supported by statistical analysis, show that ADABORD significantly outperforms competing methods, particularly on datasets with five or more classes, where the ordinal structure becomes more pronounced. Source code, along with all experimental protocols, is publicly available to ensure reproducibility and facilitate future research in OC.

</details>


### [292] [Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21005)
*Xiaolong Li,Zhangchen Zhou,Zhi-Qin John Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces weight-norm criticality: instability in deep nets arises from the interaction of normalization-induced scale invariance and weight decay, causing loss spikes as scale-invariant norms shrink and sharpness rises; explains limitations of strong regularization and offers testable predictions with empirical validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address training instability beyond the well-known learning-rate Edge of Stability by incorporating the role of weight decay on scale-invariant components created by normalization.

Method: Theoretically analyze how scale-invariant weight subspaces interact with weight decay to alter sharpness and norms; derive testable predictions; conduct empirical experiments on networks with scale-invariant components to observe loss spikes and stability boundaries.

Result: Identify a distinct weight-norm criticality: increasing weight decay drives scale-invariant weight norms toward zero while the loss sharpness rapidly increases, leading to instability and abrupt loss spikes; provide empirical evidence and predictions that align with networks featuring scale-invariant components.

Conclusion: Proposes a mechanistic framework for loss spikes grounded in weight-norm criticality; explains why weight penalties improve generalization only up to a limit, and offers testable predictions and practical guidance for regularization in networks with normalization-induced scale invariances.

Abstract: Most explanations of training instability focus on \emph{learning-rate criticality}, typically characterized by the Edge of Stability, beyond which optimization becomes unstable. We argue that, in practical deep neural network training, there is an additional and often overlooked \emph{weight-norm criticality}. This criticality is induced by the interaction between normalization (which introduces scale-invariant components) and weight decay (which persistently shrinks parameter norms). As the weight decay coefficient increases, the norms of scale-invariant weights are progressively driven toward zero. Meanwhile, the sharpness of the loss landscape increases rapidly, destabilizing the optimization dynamics and resulting in abrupt loss spikes. This perspective provides a rationale for why weight penalties can improve generalization yet cannot be made arbitrarily strong: excessive decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary and destabilizes training. Our work provides a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through the lens of \emph{weight-norm criticality}. Moreover, \emph{weight-norm criticality} yields testable predictions that we validate empirically in networks with scale-invariant components, providing empirical support for the proposed mechanism.

</details>


### [293] [Regularized Optimization on Grassmann Manifold: Theory, Algorithm and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21039)
*Zhuan Liang,Zheng Zhai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Robust estimation of rank-K projection matrices via Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) on the Grassmann manifold improves spectral subspace recovery under noise and perturbations, with efficient Riemannian optimization and improved clustering/community detection performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spectral methods are sensitive to noise, outliers, and model perturbations. There is a need for robust, sparse, and interpretable estimates of spectral subspaces (rank-K projections) for reliable clustering and community detection.

Method: Formulate RPMA as an optimization problem on the manifold of rank-K projection matrices, exploiting the equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. Derive first- and second-order optimality conditions, analyze local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize landscape stability under small regularization. Solve with a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search and a Cayley–Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury (Cayley–SMW) gradient method to avoid repeated eigendecompositions.

Result: RPMA improves recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering in noisy environments, as demonstrated on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Conclusion: Regularized projection estimation on the Grassmann manifold yields robust, sparse, and interpretable rank-K projections, with provable local stability and practical efficiency, leading to superior performance in noisy spectral tasks.

Abstract: Spectral methods are among the most widely used techniques for community detection, clustering, and graph learning. Their performance, however, critically depends on the accurate estimation of the underlying spectral subspace and can deteriorate substantially in the presence of noise, outliers, or model perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) framework for robust estimation of rank-$K$ projection matrices. RPMA extends classical spectral projection by incorporating a regularization term, producing projection estimates that are more robust, sparse, and interpretable. We formulate the proposed model as an optimization problem on the manifold of rank-$K$ projection matrices and exploit its geometric equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. Based on this manifold characterization, we derive the first- and second-order optimality conditions, establish the local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize the stability of the critical-point landscape under sufficiently small regularization. To efficiently solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search, together with a more efficient Cayley--Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury (Cayley--SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves the recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.

</details>


### [294] [Counterfactual Explainability Framework With CycleGAN And Counterfactual-Classifier Alignnment Score for Retinal Disease Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21068)
*Kritanu Chattopadhyay,Sayanjit Singha Roy,Soumya Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces CounterFundus, a CycleGAN-based counterfactual XAI framework for retinal disease detection that translates diseased fundus to healthy, uses difference maps to localize pathology, and proposes CCAS to quantify alignment with classifier saliency; shows spatially consistent explanations and improved classification with counterfactual augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explainability gaps in deep learning for retinal disease detection; standard post-hoc saliency methods often do not align with clinically meaningful retinal regions. Counterfactual explanations via disease-to-normal translation aim to provide more plausible, clinically relevant insights.

Method: EfficientNet-B5 classifier for retinal disease detection augmented with a CycleGAN that generates disease-to-normal (healthy) fundus translations. Difference maps between input and counterfactual highlight disease-related changes. The Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) merges Spearman correlation, IoU, and pointing accuracy to assess spatial alignment with classifier saliency (using EigenCAM for localization). Ablation studies assess CCAS impact on downstream performance.

Result: CounterFundus yields counterfactual explanations that are spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across CCAS dimensions. CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves downstream classification performance. Ablation confirms the importance of CCAS components.

Conclusion: CounterFundus provides a clinically grounded, explainable AI framework for retinal disease detection, leveraging plausible disease-to-normal translations to localize pathology. It couples counterfactual explanations with a unified alignment metric, and demonstrates potential to enhance classification via counterfactual augmentation. Future work should address generalization, artifact risk, and validation across diverse datasets.

Abstract: Automated detection of vision impairing retina-based ocular conditions from fundus images is important for early screening, timely referral and reducing dependency on specialist-only assessment, for which neural network-based deep learning (DL) models have been widely utilized. However, explainability of the DL frameworks remains a major bottleneck for clinical adoption, particularly when model decisions are not linked to retinal regions that are clinically meaningful. To address this issue, this study presents CounterFundus, a novel CycleGAN-driven counterfactual explainability framework, integrating EfficientNet-B5-based retinal disease detection with visually interpretable disease-to-normal fundus image translation. For each pathological image, the counterfactual yielded by the CycleGAN generator represents an estimated healthy counterpart and the resultant difference map is utilized to localize disease-associated retinal changes. Unlike conventional post-hoc saliency methods, CounterFundus provides counterfactual explanations through visually plausible disease-to-normal retinal translation. Thereafter, to quantify the spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and classifier saliency, the Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) is introduced, embedding Spearman correlation, binary IoU and pointing accuracy into a single assessment protocol. To this end, EigenCAM-aligned evaluation demonstrates that the generated counterfactual explanations remain spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Along with that, ablation studies further confirm that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves the downstream classification performance in fundus images, establishing CounterFundus as a clinically-grounded, explainable artificially intelligence (XAI) framework for retinal disease detection.

</details>


### [295] [From Evaluation to Optimisation: Hierarchy-Aware Training Signals for CWE Prediction in Python](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21069)
*Muntasir Adnan,Manile Srun,Carlos C. N. Kuhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hierarchical ALPHA penalty can train models to reduce CWE-level vulnerability penalties, with reinforcement learning (GRPO) outperforming supervised methods under distribution shift; the best policy substantially reduces penalty and matches a much larger zero-shot teacher, highlighting the importance of penalty delivery directness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether the ALPHA taxonomy-aware penalty used for evaluation can also serve as an effective training signal for vulnerability prediction in Python, and compare how different training paradigms leverage it under distributional shift.

Method: Compare three delivery mechanisms for the ALPHA penalty-based signal: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalized ALPHA penalty. Evaluate on SVEN using Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, with greedy and sampled decoding (p=0.005).

Result: Supervised approaches regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while the GRPO reinforcement learning approach succeeds. The best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty by 27.9% under greedy decoding and 25.5% under sampled decoding (p=0.005, Welch’s t-test), achieving statistical parity with its 4.5× larger zero-shot teacher.

Conclusion: The effectiveness of the hierarchical ALPHA penalty as a training signal hinges on how directly and effectively its feedback is delivered to the model during learning.

Abstract: The original ALPHA benchmark introduced a taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python and proposed that the penalty could theoretically also serve as a training signal. This paper provides that validation. We compare three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalised penalty. We find that supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeds. Our best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset by 27.9% under greedy decoding, and by 25.5% under sampled decoding(p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher. We conclude that the value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery.

</details>


### [296] [Spectral Transformation for Layer-wise Global Rank Discovery in Federated LoRA for Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21074)
*Hariharan Ramesh,Jyotikrishna Dass*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpecTraL introduces a principled spectral approach to federated ViT fine-tuning with LoRA, discovering layer-wise global ranks without dense updates or hyperparameter tuning, yielding better accuracy-communication trade-offs and lower server computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated LoRA-based fine-tuning of Vision Transformers suffers from cross-term aggregation errors when naïvely averaging adapters, and methods that preserve ranks incur high server-side costs or require reinitialization. A unified, low-overhead mechanism to discover and apply global ranks is needed.

Method: Server-side stacking of client-local LoRA modules, followed by orthonormal Householder transformations in the low-rank space. The global rank per layer is analytically inferred using the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory to separate consensus signal from non-IID noise. Padding-aware initialization aligns new residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging into the base model, allowing consistent subsequent-round participation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 across DomainNet and NICO++ shows improved accuracy-communication efficiency, reduced server computation, and eliminates the need for hyperparameter search for rank selection.

Conclusion: SpecTraL provides a unified, principled framework for Fed-Lora aggregation that avoids dense global updates and auxiliary refinements, enabling scalable, adaptive, and communication-efficient federated ViT fine-tuning with automatic per-layer rank discovery.

Abstract: Fine-tuning Vision Transformers (ViTs) with low-rank adapters (LoRA) promises better communication efficiency under federated setup, yet existing aggregation strategies face fundamental limitations. Independently averaging these LoRA factors is mathematically inconsistent, introducing cross-term aggregation error. In contrast, approaches that preserve heterogeneous client ranks by concatenating local adapters on the server substantially increase download cost and often require merging global LoRA updates into pretrained weights on the clients, causing reinitialization lag and unstable convergence. Other approaches further increase server-side overhead by reconstructing dense weight updates or training auxiliary models to refine aggregation error. In this work, we propose SpecTraL, spectral transformation for layer-wise global rank discovery, that resolves these challenges within a unified design. SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation of the stacked adapters directly in the low-rank latent space, eliminating dense reconstruction of the global update and any auxiliary refinement on the server. By leveraging the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, SpecTraL analytically separates the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without manual hyperparameter tuning. To match local ranks in subsequent rounds, we introduce a padding-aware initialization framework that lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pre-trained base model. Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL

</details>


### [297] [Nipping the Butterfly Effect in the Bud: Self-Output Fine-Tuning for Autoregressive Weather Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21080)
*Yun-Ye Cai,Hsuan-Tien Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Autoregressive DLWP forecasts suffer rapid long-horizon error growth due to a feedback loop where small output errors expand and shift input distributions; a plug-and-play Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT) using the model's own one-step predictions calibrates the first-step input, yielding stronger long-horizon forecasts and reduced distributional mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon weather prediction with autoregressive deep learning shows error amplification; understanding and mitigating distribution shift caused by the model's own outputs is crucial for reliability.

Method: The paper combines theoretical analysis and empirical experiments to characterize how output errors interact with input distribution shifts in autoregressive DLWP. It identifies that distributional drift begins at the first inference step and proposes SOFT, a plug-and-play fine-tuning technique that uses the model's one-step predictions to recalibrate the initial input distribution. Extensive experiments validate improved long-horizon performance and reduced distributional discrepancy.

Result: SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy.

Conclusion: Reexamining the DLWP pipeline with SOFT demonstrates a critical advance for atmospheric science by addressing early-stage distribution shift and error feedback, improving reliability of long-horizon forecasts.

Abstract: Long-horizon weather forecasting is a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science, for which autoregressive Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) has emerged as the primary paradigm. Although the autoregressive pipeline is highly scalable and flexible, its prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. In this work, we study this error growth phenomenon from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis reveals that the growth is driven by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. Specifically, the autoregressive process amplifies small initial output errors, which progressively corrupt subsequent input distributions, echoing the butterfly effect in atmospheric science and ultimately deteriorating forecasting accuracy over longer horizons. Furthermore, we show that this distributional shift originates at the earliest stage of inference, with out-of-distribution signatures detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT)}, a plug-and-play strategy that leverages the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental pipeline of deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

</details>


### [298] [CASC: Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Spatiotemporal Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21088)
*Francis Ndikum Nji,Vandana Janeja,Jianwu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes CASC for evolving latent regimes in spatiotemporal data using causal subspace preservation and dynamic temporal subspace evolution, integrated with U-Net adversarial clustering, FAConvLSTM, and graph-attention self-expression; introduces two causal/temporal losses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep subspace clustering relies on self-expressiveness and static subspaces, often missing causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics in nonstationary spatiotemporal systems.

Method: CASC combines a U-Net–inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial/temporal structure; uses a graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network to model local/global/spatial/temporal dependencies; introduces two losses: (1) Causal Subspace Preservation Loss aligning self-expression with latent causal relations, and (2) Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss capturing evolving subspace structures and regime transitions.

Result: Not specified in the abstract; no empirical results described.

Conclusion: The framework advances deep subspace clustering from correlation-driven methods to causal-temporal regime discovery for evolving spatiotemporal subspaces.

Abstract: Deep subspace clustering plays a critical role in applications involving multivariate spatiotemporal data, such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and tracking neuro-degeneration over time. Despite recent advances, existing methods primarily rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and often fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework for discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. CASC integrates a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial and temporal structure while learning robust latent representations. A graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network is introduced to jointly model local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions. Furthermore, we propose two new learning objectives: (1) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, encouraging clusters to reflect underlying causal processes rather than simple feature similarity, and (2) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions in nonstationary environments. Together, these components transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework.

</details>


### [299] [Training Large Language Models for Self-Explanation Faithfulness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21090)
*Yeoktatt Cheah,María Pérez-Ortiz,Noah Y. Siegel,Oana-Maria Camburu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An RL-based method to directly optimize faithfulness of self-explanations by turning faithfulness metrics into a training reward; demonstrates improved Phi-CCT scores on Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B using random-word and user-bias insertions; exhibits cross-intervention transfer in Llama but not consistently in Qwen; discusses safeguards against reward gaming; suggests scalable path to reduce unfaithful reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap that prior work evaluates faithfulness post-hoc or uses prompting frameworks without directly optimizing model parameters for faithful explanations; enable models to detect and disclose factors influencing decisions.

Method: Transform faithfulness metrics into RL objective; two intervention types (random-word insertions and user-bias insertions); per-sample reward using Phi-CCT correlation; RL fine-tuning on Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B.

Result: Phi-CCT faithfulness improved from near-zero to up to 0.664 in-distribution and up to 0.691 out-of-distribution (StrategyQA); cross-intervention generalization weaker but observed transfer for Llama; Qwen did not replicate transfer; analysis claims no reward gaming.

Conclusion: Models can learn to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them; provides scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

Abstract: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method to directly optimize the faithfulness of self-explanations - the extent to which a model's generated reasoning accurately reflects its internal decision-making process. While existing work focuses on evaluating faithfulness or using inference-time prompting frameworks to improve an LLM's self-explanation's tractability, these approaches do not provide a mechanism to directly optimize a model's parameters to generate faithful self-explanations. We bridge this gap by modifying existing faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective. We investigate (1) if models can be trained to accurately detect factors that affect their decisions, and (2) whether RL can directly optimize for the disclosure of these factors thereby improving LLM self-explanations' faithfulness. We experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions, using a per-sample reward derived from the Phi-CCT correlation metric. RL fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show substantial improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric, with in-distribution scores rising from near-zero to as high as 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reaching up to 0.691 on held-out tasks such as StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but more interesting: a priori we would not expect a model trained only on random word insertions to generalize to user-bias phrases, yet Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer in this direction. The reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, indicating model-dependent and setup-dependent effects we cannot yet explain. Lastly we analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming behaviors that often plague RL training. Ultimately, we show that models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

</details>


### [300] [A Polynomial Architecture-Attribution Co-Design Framework for Exact Aumann-Shapley Attribution in GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21094)
*Bizu Feng,Zhimu Yang,Shuming Wang,Shaode Yu,Yuan Cheng,Xiaojun Qian,Zixin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APEX enables exact Aumann-Shapley path attributions for a class of GNNs by designing PolyGIN to preserve polynomial form, making path integrals exactly computable via Gauss–Legendre quadrature with a small, deterministic set of evaluation points; this yields high attribution fidelity with lower computational cost, preserving predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide reliable, axiomatic attributions for GNN explanations. Path-integral methods (e.g., Integrated Gradients) rely on numerical approximations that trade off accuracy and efficiency in deep GNNs. An exact, efficient path attribution would improve interpretability.

Method: Introduce PolyGIN—a GIN-like GNN whose message passing, normalization, and transformation preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar scores. For an L-block PolyGIN, the derivative along the attribution path has degree ≤ 2^L − 1, enabling Gauss–Legendre quadrature to compute the Aumann–Shapley path integral exactly up to floating-point precision with 2^{L−1} evaluation points. Compute feature-level attributions and aggregate to node-level scores while preserving completeness.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world graphs shows PolyGIN retains competitive accuracy while APEX achieves higher attribution fidelity than baselines and dramatically reduces the number of path-integral evaluations.

Conclusion: APEX provides an exact (within FP) path-attribution framework for polynomial GNNs, enabling complete, efficient feature- and node-level explanations. The approach trades off generality for exactness within the polynomial family but yields substantial gains in interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance.

Abstract: We study feature-level and node-level explanations for graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of Aumann-Shapley attribution. Path-integral methods such as Integrated Gradients provide an axiomatic formulation of attribution, but their practical use in deep GNNs typically relies on finite-sample numerical approximations to the path integral, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This paper proposes APEX, a model-attribution co-design framework that makes the attribution integral exactly computable under a polynomial GNN architecture. The key component is PolyGIN, a GIN-style graph network whose message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar model scores, such as pre-softmax logits. We show that, for a PolyGIN with $L$ polynomial transformation blocks, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most $2^L-1$. Therefore, Gauss--Legendre quadrature can evaluate the Aumann--Shapley path integral exactly, up to floating-point precision, with $2^{L-1}$ deterministic evaluation points. The resulting attributions can be computed at the feature level and then aggregated into node-level scores while preserving completeness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks show that PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance, while the complete APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than the compared baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations required for path integration.

</details>


### [301] [Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21098)
*Michele Bellomo,Riccardo Ramaschi,Alberto Dolara,Tomaso Aste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Parametrize the conditional intensity function (CIF) directly as a non-negative linear combination of B-spline basis functions, with coefficients produced by a neural network; enables exact NLL evaluation, parallel training, CIF smoothness regularization, and improved efficiency and accuracy compared with neural TPP baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of neural TPPs that model the compensator or impose architectural constraints, which impede exact NLL computation, flexibility, and training efficiency.

Method: Model CIF(t) = sum_j c_j B_j(t) with non-negative coefficients c_j predicted by a neural network; enforce non-negativity (e.g., via softplus). Compute NLL exactly, including the integral of CIF, and apply regularization based on the integrated squared second derivative of CIF to promote smoothness.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy over a reference neural TPP baseline.

Conclusion: Direct CIF parametrization with B-spline basis offers a flexible, efficient, and accurate neural TPP framework, enabling exact likelihood evaluation and smoothness control without constraining network architectures.

Abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) provide a general and flexible framework for modeling sequences of events in continuous time. Neural networks have been successfully employed to model TPPs in a highly expressive and data-driven way. Neural TPPs are typically trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which depends on both the conditional intensity function (CIF) and its integral over time, the compensator. Recent neural TPP approaches enable exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration. However, these methods typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose constraints on the neural network architecture, and are computationally expensive during training, as event contributions to the NLL are evaluated sequentially rather than in parallel. In this work, we propose a novel neural TPP model that directly parametrizes the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions, whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This formulation enables exact evaluation of the NLL, preserves full flexibility in the neural architecture, allows efficient parallelization during training, and naturally supports CIF smoothness regularization through the integrated squared second derivative. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.

</details>


### [302] [TOUR: A Trajectory-Level Unlearning Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21111)
*Chaofan Pan,Lingfei Ren,Xiangyu Jiang,Yanhua Li,Xuemei Cao,Xiangkun Wang,Hao Yu,Wei Wei,Xin Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR) is a benchmark for evaluating trajectory-level deletion/unlearning in offline RL, using matched non-member controls, retraining references, and multi-attack privacy auditing to reveal that deletion effectiveness is environment-dependent and cannot be adequately summarized by a single score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address evaluation challenges for trajectory-level data deletion in offline RL, where a low membership score can result from deletion, memorization, or policy collapse; thus requiring a robust, multi-faceted auditing framework to assess true unlearning and privacy leakage.

Method: Introduce TOuR benchmark combining trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Evaluate across D4RL locomotion tasks and AntMaze; compare deletion baselines (e.g., GA+Refit, TrajDeleter) and perform diverse attacks (reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, query-limited) to assess deletion quality and retained utility.

Result: TOUR reveals environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior for common deletion baselines; retraining and fine-tuning often outperform uniform GA+Refit as retained-utility references; TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but not uniformly strongest; a single likelihood-based score overstates deletion quality; conclusions about offline RL unlearning are not stable under single-score auditing and depend on non-member construction, retraining calibration, attack family, retained utility, and diagnostic scope.

Conclusion: A robust evaluation of offline RL unlearning requires multi-faceted auditing with matched non-members and retraining-relative calibration; reliance on a single-score metric is insufficient; the TOUR framework and diverse attack types should guide future unlearning research and benchmarking.

Abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are trained on fixed behavioral trajectories, which makes trajectory-level deletion important when selected data must be removed after training. Evaluating such deletion is difficult because a lower membership score can reflect trajectory removal, residual memorization visible to another attack, or policy collapse that destroys useful behavior.
