We introduce Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR), a benchmark that combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Across D4RL locomotion experiments and an exploratory AntMaze extension, TOUR shows that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit, while TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but is not uniformly stronger under the same audit. Reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks further show that a single likelihood-based membership score can overstate deletion quality. In the evaluated settings, conclusions about offline RL unlearning are therefore not stable under single-score auditing. They depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

</details>


### [303] [GlucoTune: A Unified Framework for Blood Glucose Preprocessing, Forecasting, and Benchmarking in Diabetes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21117)
*Davide Marelli,Giorgia Rigamonti,Mirko Paolo Barbato,Paolo Napoletano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GlucoTune provides an end-to-end, reproducible framework for preprocessing and modeling blood glucose time-series, with YAML-config pipelines, dataset wrappers, and a benchmarking leaderboard for fair cross-dataset evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In diabetes time-series research, preprocessing variability and data-sharing restrictions hinder reproducibility and fair comparison; a standardized, extensible toolchain is needed.

Method: Modular framework with YAML-defined preprocessing pipelines, public-dataset wrappers, curated models for glucose prediction and time-series forecasting, and a benchmarking leaderboard to compare configurations across datasets.

Result: Demonstrates effectiveness through comprehensive experiments and a user study, showing improved reproducibility and evaluation transparency.

Conclusion: GlucoTune enables reproducible experiments, easy extension to new datasets/models, and privacy-conscious evaluation without distributing sensitive preprocessed data.

Abstract: Preprocessing blood glucose time-series data is a critical yet often overlooked step in developing data-driven methods for diabetes management, particularly for type 1 diabetes. The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols hinders reproducibility and complicates fair comparison across studies. These challenges are further exacerbated by data-sharing restrictions, as privacy and licensing constraints often prevent the redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. To address these limitations, we present GlucoTune, a comprehensive and extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data. The framework standardizes the entire experimental workflow, from preprocessing to model evaluation, enabling reproducible experiments directly from the original datasets. Reproducible preprocessing is achieved through configurable pipelines defined in portable YAML configuration files, ensuring consistent data handling without distributing sensitive preprocessed data. Beyond preprocessing, GlucoTune provides a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models. The framework integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers and provides a curated collection of state-of-the-art blood glucose prediction and general time-series forecasting methods, while remaining readily extensible to additional datasets, preprocessing strategies, and forecasting models. To promote transparent and consistent evaluation, GlucoTune includes a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods, enabling systematic comparison of experimental settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GlucoTune through comprehensive experiments and assess its usability in a user study.

</details>


### [304] [Relative Value Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21120)
*Marc Höftmann,Jan Robine,Stefan Harmeling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Relates to learning value differences directly via a pairwise, antisymmetric operator; establishes contraction to true value differences; derives targets and R-GAE; shows competitive Atari performance with PPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Since only value differences drive control, learning relative values can be more principled and stable than absolute value critics; aim to produce unbiased policy gradients and robust learning.

Method: Define Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j) with an antisymmetric pairwise Bellman operator; prove γ-contraction with unique fixed point; derive 1-step, n-step, and λ-return targets; reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to yield R-GAE; integrate RV with PPO.

Result: The operator is a γ-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to true value differences; well-posed targets are derived; unbiased policy-gradient estimator R-GAE is produced; RV-PPO achieves competitive Atari performance across 49 games compared to standard PPO.

Conclusion: Relative value learning offers a viable alternative to absolute critics, delivering effective policy gradient estimates and competitive performance when combined with PPO.

Abstract: In reinforcement learning, critics typically estimate absolute state values $V(s)$, estimating how good a particular situation is in isolation. However, it turns out that only differences in value are relevant for control. Motivated by this, we propose Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that learns value differences directly via an antisymmetric function $Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. We introduce a pairwise Bellman operator and prove it is a $γ$-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, derive well-posed $1$-step, $n$-step and $λ$-return targets and reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Beyond theoretical results, we integrate RV with PPO and achieve competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, indicating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.

</details>


### [305] [Demographically-Informed Heat-Mortality Risk Curves via Risk Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21131)
*Alex O. Davies,Eunice Lo,Rui Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RGNN enhances DLNM-based heat-mortality modeling by integrating granular census features via a hierarchical GNN, improving calibration while preserving interpretable exposure-response curves.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DLNMs capture exposure-response but ignore demographic/geographic heterogeneity in heat vulnerability; need models that improve predictive calibration and reflect context while preserving interpretability.

Method: Introduce Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs): a hierarchical GNN encoder that leverages granular census features to optimize DLNM coefficient vectors and produce interpretable risk curves; evaluate on 10 regions of England and Wales across two extreme heat years; compare against standard DLNM baselines; analyze calibration and predictive performance.

Result: RGNN variants show lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave (when baselines struggled); improved calibration while retaining interpretable risk curves.

Conclusion: Incorporating granular demographic/geographic context via a hierarchical GNN into the DLNM framework improves predictive performance and calibration without sacrificing interpretability, demonstrating robustness across regions and extreme heat events.

Abstract: Estimating heat-related mortality risk is a core task in environmental epidemiology, typically addressed with Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs); interpretable exposure-response surfaces fitted to temperature-mortality time series. DLNMs are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, despite well-established relevance to heat vulnerability. We propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while substantially improving predictive calibration. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse.

</details>


### [306] [Agree on the Model, Verify the Inference: GKR Protocols for HND-Based Transformer Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21162)
*Xiaolong Liang,Juanjuan Li,Rui Qin,Yisheng Lv*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GKR-HND introduces a verifiable outsourced inference protocol for Homomorphic–Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers (HND). A retained verifier checks the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings while costly public computations are delegated to an assigned worker. Under honest-verifier and non-colluding, signed, request-bound responses from the worker must agree with the proof claims. Empirical results validate the proof path and delegated public computation without dense-matrix replay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outsourced transformer inference risks model substitution and incomplete execution and can negate delegation benefits if verification is weak; the work aims to provide cryptographic guarantees while preserving efficiency via delegation.

Method: Propose a registered-model protocol (GKR-HND) where the verifier retains the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings; external heavy public computations are performed by a worker who signs the response; verification requires consistency between the worker’s response and the proof claims under non-collusion assumptions.

Result: Experiments with pretrained HND models validate the proof path and the delegated public computation, avoiding dense-matrix replay.

Conclusion: The approach offers a verifiable outsourcing framework for HND transformers, balancing delegation efficiency with cryptographic verification under plausible trust assumptions; it relies on non-collusion and honest verifier/prover-woker behavior.

Abstract: Outsourced Transformer inference exposes clients to model substitution and incomplete execution, while direct replay removes the computational benefit of delegation. We present GKR-HND, a registered-model protocol for verifying the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic--Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers. The retained verifier checks the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings, but delegates expensive public evaluations to an assigned computation worker. Assuming an honest retained verifier and prover--worker non-collusion, the verifier accepts only when the worker's signed, request-bound response agrees with the proof claims. Experiments with pretrained HND models validate the proof path and the delegated public computation without dense-matrix replay.

</details>


### [307] [Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21173)
*Irena Girshovitz,Dan Zeltzer,Ran Gilad-Bachrach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ARA introduces an AI-driven, protocol-first workflow that uses SCM-based synthetic data and adversarial validation to reveal invalid causal assumptions, not just compute estimates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address silent failures in automated causal inference where analysis code runs but causal assumptions are invalid, ensuring validity and transparency of automated science.

Method: ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation via Structural Causal Models with known ground-truth effects, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline; it translates natural-language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code, evaluated against the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark by testing identification strategies, causal quantities, and variable mappings under controlled assumption violations.

Result: Compared to standard LLM generation, protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates; however, they shifted failure modes from silent numerical errors to surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations; synthetic data supports development under restricted data access and aids transparency.

Conclusion: Validity-first automated-science systems should be evaluated by their ability to indicate when causal claims are unwarranted, not solely by numerical accuracy; ARA demonstrates that adding design-checks changes failure modes toward more transparent diagnostics.

Abstract: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

</details>


### [308] [Filter Learning for Subgraphs: Algebras and Performance Risk Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21263)
*Purui Zhang,Feng Ji,Yanan Zhao,Bihan Wen,Wee Peng Tay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Subgraph filter learning (SFL) provides a framework to approximate ambient graph filters using subgraph-supported operators under partial observations, with a distance-aware Laplacian-based algebra and statistical learning guarantees, showing empirical improvements over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In practice, full graph topology is often unavailable. A data-dependent approach that learns operators on subgraphs can approximate ambient filters from partial observations while offering theoretical guarantees.

Method: Formulate SFL as a statistical learning problem; develop a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacians to define a structured, controllable filter class; derive least-squares risk bounds for the learned operator's approximation to the restricted ambient mapping.

Result: Experiments on real-world datasets show the proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines in SFL tasks.

Conclusion: A principled, data-dependent subgraph operator framework can effectively approximate ambient graph filters from partial observations, with theoretical risk guarantees and practical empirical gains.

Abstract: Graph signal processing tasks that leverage spectral information typically assume access to the complete graph topology, which is often unavailable in practice. We propose a systematic framework for subgraph filter learning (SFL), where subgraph-supported operators approximate ambient graph filters under partial observations. We formulate SFL as a statistical learning problem in which optimal subgraph operators are inherently data-dependent. To address the difficulty of directly estimating such operators, we develop a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacian constructions, defining a structured and controllable class of filters for effective approximation. We further establish performance risk bounds under the least squares loss, quantifying how well the learned operator approximates the restricted ambient mapping. Experiments real-world datasets show that, for SFL tasks, the proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines that attempt to recover the underlying structure from data.

</details>


### [309] [The Dark Room in the Reward Channel: Dense Prediction Rewards Collapse GRPO-Trained LLM Agents -- and What Actually Works](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21273)
*Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dense per-step prediction rewards under group-normalized RL catastrophically collapse policy behavior (dark room pathology) in Qwen LLM agents on ALFWorld. Removing GRPO's std normalization eliminates the collapse, revealing a variance-profile interaction: z-scoring amplifies within-group variance in all-fail groups, making dense rewards unsafe. A two-line proposition and a controlled signal-delivery matrix generalize the finding; reward channels are at best neutral while auxiliary-loss channels gain ~20 points, with shuffled-gold controls supporting label-robust conclusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To diagnose why dense per-step supervision (predicting the next observation) fails under group-normalized RL and whether reward shaping can reliably guide long-horizon LLM agents without inducing pathological collapse.

Method: Empirical study across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on the ALFWorld benchmark. Implemented a potential-based prediction reward under GRPO; performed ablations, notably removing GRPO’s standard deviation normalization; formulated a two-line proposition explaining the mechanism; conducted a controlled signal-delivery matrix experiment varying only the consumption mechanism; included a shuffled-gold placebo and preregistered endpoints (single-seed) to assess label robustness; preregistered group sizes and seed replication in progress.

Result: Under GRPO, the prediction reward drives all runs into a degenerate absorbing state: prediction accuracy → 1.0, task success → 0, episode length pinned at horizon (the dark room). Removing the std normalization converts this catastrophic outcome to baseline parity. The two-line proposition explains why: in all-fail groups, the z-scored advantage is invariant to the shaping coefficient, producing unbounded pressure from bounded rewards; annealing cannot mitigate. The variance-profile criterion captures and retrodicts collapses and aligns with preregistered predictions for unobserved arms. A controlled signal-delivery matrix shows the reward channel is at best neutral while the auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points; shuffled-gold placebo matches the true-gold arm, indicating label robustness. Single-seed endpoints; seed replication and group-size preregistrations in progress.

Conclusion: A variance-profile-based criterion explains when dense per-step supervision in GRPO is dangerous, predicting collapses and guiding safe designs: avoid z-scored, all-fail amplification; when dense signaling is necessary, rely on orthogonal channels (e.g., auxiliary losses) and robust labeling controls. The reward channel alone is not reliably beneficial; proper evaluation with label controls and preregistered designs is essential.

Abstract: Dense per-step supervision is an appealing remedy for sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agents: reward the agent for predicting its next observation, and memory should follow. We show that under group-normalized RL (GRPO), this recipe does not merely fail -- it destroys the policy. Across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on ALFWorld, a potential-based prediction reward drives every run into a degenerate absorbing state (prediction accuracy -> 1.0, task success -> 0,episode length pinned at the horizon): the "dark room" pathology, built automatically by the optimizer. A single-factor ablation localizes the cause -- removing only GRPO's std normalization turns the same reward from catastrophic (0%) into baseline parity -- and a two-line proposition explains why: in all-fail groups the z-scored advantage is invariant to the shaping coefficient, so bounded rewards become unbounded pressure and annealing cannot help. Our central insight generalizes this: what z-scoring amplifies is a dense signal's within-group variance while all-fail groups dominate, so signals whose variance decays by mastery are structurally amplifier-safe.This variance-profile criterion retrodicts our collapses, carries preregistered predictions for arms that had not yet run, and is consistent with published reward-channel successes (a compatibility check, not an independent test). Finally, a controlled signal-delivery matrix (identical signal, varying only the consumption mechanism) shows the reward channel is at best neutral while the auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points -- and a shuffled-gold placebo matches the true-gold arm, so the gap survives without correct labels. Endpoints are single-seed; seed replication and group-size controls are preregistered and in progress.

</details>


### [310] [Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Prediction from Video Game State with Transfer Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21290)
*Jonas Peché,Aliaksei Tsishurou,Alexander Zap,Günter Wallner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-task learning with a shared multimodal model improves generalization and efficiency for endpoint prediction in a team-based game, handling multiple data modalities and transfer across maps, with attention to loss weighting and gradient conflicts and benefits under limited data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exploit related supervision signals in game telemetry to improve prediction while reducing training/inference cost; handle heterogeneous modalities and structured environments in multi-agent game settings.

Method: Adapt a multimodal endpoint-prediction architecture to a multi-task setting using rasterized vision, global match context, and per-unit state, combined via an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling; compare single-task vs multi-task training; experiment with loss weighting strategies, gradient conflict handling, pre-training/fine-tuning under limited data; assess cross-map transfer.

Result: Empirical evaluation on a large proprietary World of Tanks dataset shows when multi-task training is used, generalization can improve and training/inference cost decreases relative to separate models; loss weighting and gradient-conflict strategies affect performance; pre-training/fine-tuning and cross-map transfer are feasible, with positive transfer observed under limited data.

Conclusion: A shared multimodal multi-task framework effectively leverages related signals to improve predictive performance and efficiency in complex game environments, with careful handling of losses and gradient conflicts; cross-map transfer extends utility across structured environment shifts.

Abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a promising approach for prediction tasks derived from video game state data, as modern game telemetry provides multiple related supervision signals from the same structured observations. We study whether a shared model trained jointly across tasks in team-based multiplayer games can improve generalization while reducing training and inference cost compared to specialized single-task models. We adapt a multimodal architecture for endpoint prediction to a general multi-task setting that combines rasterized vision inputs, global match context, and per-unit state information through an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling. Experiments on a large proprietary World of Tanks dataset compare single-task and multi-task training, evaluate weighting strategies for mixed losses and conflicting gradients, and test pre-training/fine-tuning under limited target-data regimes. We also examine within-game transfer across game maps under structured environment shift.

</details>


### [311] [AI Assistants Overassist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21306)
*Verona Teo,Raghav Jain,Tobias Gerstenberg,Max Kleiman-Weiner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Int-Bench: a simulation-based benchmark to study how LLM tutors intervene during learning and how these interventions affect problem-solving performance and generalization; LLMs tend to intervene too often and provide full solutions rather than targeted hints, unlike humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in understanding how AI tutoring interventions influence student reasoning and long-term learning, moving beyond task success to cognitive engagement and transfer.

Method: A paired 'student' and 'teacher' simulation where an LLM-based teacher monitors reasoning and decides when/how to intervene; evaluation across code debugging, mathematics, and brain teaser tasks; metrics include intervention frequency/timing, immediate task success, and generalization to new problems; comparison with human tutors.

Result: LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans and tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints; as a result, they may optimize for short-term success at the expense of deeper reasoning and transfer.

Conclusion: Current LLM tutoring often prioritizes short-term task completion over fostering reasoning processes essential for durable learning, indicating a need for intervention strategies that promote cognitive engagement and generalization.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

</details>


### [312] [M$^3$-Gen: Interpretable Multimodal Generation of Gene Expression Profiles Using Clinical and Imaging Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21343)
*Francesca Pia Panaccione,Carlo Sgaravatti,Marco Venere*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MultiModal Molecular Generation (M^3-Gen) generates gene expression profiles conditioned on histopathology images and clinical metadata using a GAN with a unified latent representation learned via contrastive learning; incorporates an attention-based mechanism for explainability linking image regions to gene outputs; validated on TCGA showing realistic, functionally meaningful data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gene expression data are expensive and privacy-sensitive, hindering multimodal AI research; need synthetic, biologically coherent gene expression data aligned with other modalities.

Method: Train a GAN whose generator is guided by embeddings from clinical data and H&E images; learn a unified latent space via contrastive learning across modalities; use attention to map image regions to gene outputs, enabling interpretation.

Result: On TCGA, generated gene expression profiles are realistic and functionally meaningful; attention mechanism provides intrinsic explanations by identifying image regions influencing specific genes.

Conclusion: M^3-Gen enables integrated multimodal generation of gene expression with interpretable conditioning, potentially reducing data collection costs and privacy concerns while supporting multimodal disease understanding.

Abstract: Integrating heterogeneous biomedical data, including clinical metadata, histopathology images, and molecular profiles, is crucial for comprehensive disease understanding. However, gene expression data acquisition remains constrained by high costs and privacy concerns, limiting its use in multimodal research and AI-driven applications. We present MultiModal Molecular Generation (M$^3$-Gen), a novel framework for the generation of gene expression profiles by conditioning a Generative Adversarial Network on histopathology images and clinical metadata. M$^3$-Gen learns a unified latent representation from the clinical variables and the images, leveraging contrastive learning, and exploits the embeddings of the two modalities to guide a generative model in producing biologically coherent gene expression profiles. Evaluations on the TCGA dataset demonstrate that M$^3$-Gen generates realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression data. Importantly, by integrating multiple modalities in an attention-based mechanism, M$^3$-Gen provides intrinsic explainability: it allows the identification of which regions of the histopathology images most strongly influenced the generation of specific gene expression profiles, making the model's decisions interpretable by design.

</details>


### [313] [How Many Bits Can an Adapter Write? Measuring the Capacity and Memorization of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21351)
*Kaizhen Tan,Heqing Du,Yang Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A LoRA adapter writes only a few bits per trainable parameter into a frozen model, and where those parameters sit (e.g., attention vs MLP) critically determines capacity and privacy leakage. Extending compression-based memorization analysis to frozen-base settings yields a quantitative, design-guiding metric for fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify how much a LoRA adapter imprints information into its frozen base, in bits, and how this memory depends on architecture choices, with implications for privacy and security of fine-tuned models.

Method: Extend compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting. Measure, in bits, how much a LoRA writes into a model it does not modify. Analyze the distribution of writes across architecture (attention vs MLP), and the effect of removing the base structure. Apply the method to realistic Qwen2.5 fine-tunes. Compare privacy leakage against bits written and contrast supervised vs reinforcement learning.

Result: Adapters store a couple of bits per trainable parameter, below a full fine-tuning budget. Memory capacity depends more on where the parameters sit than on their nominal count: shifting budget from attention to MLP increases capacity; removing the base structure almost eliminates capacity. Privacy leakage grows with the bits written by the adapter; supervised fine-tuning tends to copy secrets verbatim, while an adapter trained with verifiable rewards (RL) does not record them.

Conclusion: Measuring what fine-tuning writes (in bits) provides a quantitative design target to mitigate privacy risks and guide adapter placement. This reframes fine-tuning analysis from post-hoc attacks to proactive design against information leakage.

Abstract: A LoRA adapter is a few megabytes that almost everyone treats as a skill rather than a record of the data behind it. We put that assumption on a scale. Extending compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting, we measure directly, in bits, how much a low-rank adapter writes into a model it never changes. The answer is both smaller than full fine-tuning and less lawful than parameter counting would predict. Adapters store a couple of bits per trainable parameter, well short of a full model's budget, but that figure turns less on how many parameters an adapter carries than on where they sit. Move the same parameter budget from attention into the MLP and it holds nearly twice as much; strip the frozen base of its structure and the capacity all but disappears. Applied to realistic fine-tunes of Qwen2.5, the same instrument shows privacy leakage rising with the bits an adapter writes rather than the parameters it nominally has, and it draws a clean line between supervised and reinforcement learning: the secrets that supervised fine-tuning copies down verbatim, an adapter trained on verifiable rewards never records. Measuring what fine-tuning writes, rather than attacking it after the fact, turns a piece of folklore into a quantity one can design against.

</details>


### [314] [Gradient Concentration, Not Weight Saliency, Explains Representation-Level Class Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21353)
*Billel Habbati,Alessio Merlo,Luca Verderame,Meriem Guerar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Saliency-based masking in SalUn does not enhance representation-level forgetting; gradient energy concentrates in final layers, making masking less impactful and similar to random masks; effective unlearning likely requires latent-representation objectives rather than selective weight updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether saliency-based weight selection is essential for representation-level forgetting and unlearning, by performing a controlled ablation of SalUn’s masking mechanism.

Method: Matched-compute ablation on CIFAR-10/100 using ResNet-18. Compare saliency-based masking, random masks with equal sparsity, and unconstrained updates, keeping the unlearning objective, optimization schedule, and computational budget fixed. Evaluate representations with linear probing, prototype recovery, and layer-wise CKA.

Result: All three configurations show statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability. Forget gradients are highly concentrated in final layers (≈92% of squared gradient energy on CIFAR-10) prior to masking, placing masking within the same representational subspace. Saliency masks exhibit limited class specificity (specificity index ~0.09–0.11) and select highly overlapping parameter subsets across forget classes.

Conclusion: Representation-level forgetting appears governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry rather than the specific identity of saliency-selected weights. Supports broader view that effective unlearning requires objectives acting directly on latent representations rather than sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data while preserving model utility. Many state-of-the-art approaches pursue this goal by restricting the forgetting update to a subset of parameters selected through gradient-based saliency. Although such methods are widely adopted, the actual contribution of saliency-based weight selection to representation-level forgetting remains unclear. In this work, we perform the first controlled ablation of the saliency masking mechanism used by SalUn. Using a matched-compute experimental design on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, we compare saliency-based masking against random masks of equal sparsity and unconstrained updates, while keeping the unlearning objective, optimization schedule, and computational budget fixed. Across multiple representation-level evaluations, including linear probing, prototype recovery, and layer-wise CKA, the three configurations exhibit statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability. We find that forget gradients are strongly concentrated in the final network layers (approximately 92% of the squared gradient energy on CIFAR-10) before any mask is applied, causing all masking strategies to operate within the same representational subspace. Furthermore, saliency masks show limited class specificity (specificity index 0.09-0.11), selecting highly overlapping parameter subsets across different forget classes. Our findings suggest that, in the studied setting, representation-level forgetting is primarily governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry rather than by the specific identity of saliency-selected weights. More broadly, the results support a growing body of evidence indicating that effective representation-level unlearning requires objectives that act directly on latent representations rather than on increasingly sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

</details>


### [315] [Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21356)
*Mohammed Suhail B Nadaf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is driven by a shared low-rank persona subspace that exists before fine-tuning. Projecting this subspace out of the residual stream during fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment; injecting it into an untuned model induces misalignment. The effect is dose-dependent and domain-spanning; weight-gradient projections and post-hoc edits have limited or nuanced effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain why a narrow lesson generalizes to unrelated tasks, identify the latent structure enabling emergent misalignment, and assess interventions that prevent or induce misalignment to reveal causal mechanisms.

Method: From a frozen Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct model, extract per-domain persona subspaces via contrastive teacher forcing. Find four unrelated domains sharing a low-rank core (approximately 657 dimensions) outside a matched-diversity style core. Analyze the first optimization step of fine-tuning on insecure code vs. educational framing. Project the subspace out of the residual stream during fine-tuning; compare with a matched-rank random subspace (no effect). Inject the subspace into a never-fine-tuned model to induce misalignment; assess via margin changes up to 45.4%. Assess projection of the weight gradient and perform three post-hoc weight edits to see persistence. Distribute a fixed budget of bad data across domains and compare to other interventions. All experiments use a single 14B model; extraction from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint leaves provenance open; the same intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow behavior.

Result: Identification of a shared low-rank persona subspace across four domains that drives broad misalignment when engaged by fine-tuning. Projection of this subspace from the residual stream prevents misalignment (reducing judged generations to 0%), while injecting it into an untuned model reproduces misalignment (up to 45.4%). The subspace is largely outside a style core and is not affected by weight-gradient projections; post-hoc edits can suppress but not erase the behavior, with the structure re-forming inside the subspace after edits. A distributed bad-data regime across domains yields stronger misalignment than other accounts.

Conclusion: Broad misalignment stems from a persistent latent persona subspace learned before or during initial alignment. Targeted interventions that remove or desaturate this subspace can prevent emergent misalignment, supporting a causal role for latent representations rather than solely the training data distribution.

Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.

</details>


### [316] [Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366)
*Hossein Mobahi,Peter L. Bartlett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HOPE reframes neural network compression in Hilbert space, modeling neurons as rank-1 Hilbert–Schmidt operators to unify pruning and neuron merging via low-rank projections, with macro-block eviction for multi-layer structures; data-free and hyperparameter-free; proof-of-concept on compression and fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address scale symmetries and architectural biases in standard compression heuristics and seek a unified, architecture-agnostic framework to analyze and deconstruct learned representations.

Method: Represent individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert–Schmidt operators in a Hilbert space; reinterpret pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projections; extend to macro block eviction to cover multi-layer structures like residual pathways; operate in a data-free, hyperparameter-free setting.

Result: Proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning illustrating the practical potential of the theory (qualitative demonstrations without detailed quantitative benchmarks).

Conclusion: HOPE offers a unified, continuous-space framework for deconstructing representations and making architecture-agnostic compression decisions across layers, with potential benefits for both compression and transferability.

Abstract: Deep neural networks encode complex representations, but deconstructing this internal knowledge remains a challenge. Given the link between learning and compression, network compression offers a promising lens to analyze this knowledge. However, standard compression heuristics often suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases. To resolve these, we introduce Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE), a mathematical framework to gradually deconstruct the representations in trained network weights.
  HOPE shifts network compression from the discrete domain into a Hilbert space of continuous functions. By modeling individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators, HOPE unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection. Extending this formulation, HOPE introduces macro block eviction to encompass multi-layer structures like entire residual pathways under the same unified metric. This unified approach enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers with different types and sizes. HOPE is a data-free and hyperparameter-free framework. We present proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning to highlight the practical potential of our theory.

</details>


### [317] [Mean-to-Score Discrete Diffusion: Posterior-Mean Denoisers for Score Entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21372)
*Jingyuan Li,Xiaoyi Jiang,Yixuan Jiang,Wei Liu,Yi Zhu,Zuoqiang Shi,Pipi Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEDD's unconstrained score ratios can violate Bayes realizability; projecting scores to the bridge polytope fixes negative weights; M2S maps clean-token posterior means to scores via a kernel-dependent linear map; achieves improved generative metrics and overall superiority across scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure Bayes realizability of posteriors in discrete diffusion models and eliminate non-Bayes-realizable scores that degrade sampling efficiency and quality; improve external generative perplexity (PPL) and downstream metrics.

Method: 1) Project raw scores onto the bridge polytope to enforce Bayes realizability and remove negative pre-normalization weights; 2) Mean-to-score (M2S): map clean-token posterior mean to score through an exact kernel-dependent linear transformation; applicable to any coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) with a mild support condition; for uniform corruption, maps the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, recovers MD4 exactly; validated on CIFAR-10 with a 28.4M-parameter model; a 170M-parameter M2S model trained on ~262B OpenWebText token slots; compares with pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints.

Result: Projection eliminates all negative pre-normalization weights; external PPL improves from 203.6 to 175.1 without changing the sampler. In CIFAR-10, M2S reduces test BPD from 3.173 to 3.129 and improves FID-50k (values shown in abstract). The 170M M2S model achieves PPL 143.3 at 128 steps vs 183.6 for the strongest pure-uniform baseline, outperforming baselines at every tested budget.

Conclusion: M2S provides a general, exact, kernel-aware mapping from posterior means to scores for CTMC-based diffusion models; projecting scores onto the bridge polytope ensures Bayes realizability and eliminates negative weights, enabling substantial performance gains across scales and corruption types; the approach yields state-of-the-art or competitive results on CIFAR-10 and large-scale OpenWebText settings, suggesting broad applicability to discrete diffusion models.

Abstract: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) parameterizes discrete reverse processes with unconstrained positive score ratios. While positivity guarantees nonnegative reverse jump rates, it does not ensure Bayes realizability: ratios at a noisy state need not be jointly induced by any clean-token posterior under the forward kernel. The score-entropy loss has the correct population optimum but does not enforce this constraint away from it. In a trained pure-uniform SEDD checkpoint, roughly one quarter of complete score vectors violate the coordinate box, while more than half lie inside it yet remain materially incompatible with any valid posterior. Such violations can produce negative pre-normalization weights in finite-step sampling. Projecting raw scores onto the bridge polytope removes all observed negative weights and improves external generative PPL from $203.6$ to $175.1$ without changing the sampler. We introduce \emph{mean-to-score} (M2S), which predicts a clean-token posterior mean and converts it to the score through an exact kernel-dependent linear map. The construction applies to any known coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) satisfying a mild support condition. For uniform corruption, it maps the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, the resulting objective recovers MD4 exactly. In a controlled 28.4M-parameter CIFAR-10 comparison, M2S lowers test BPD from $3.173$ to $3.129$ and FID-50k from $\CifarSEDDFID$ to $\CifarMtwoSFID$. A 170M-parameter M2S model trained on about 262B OpenWebText token slots outperforms the evaluated pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints at every tested sampling budget, reaching generative PPL $143.3$ at 128 steps versus $183.6$ for the strongest pure-uniform baseline.

</details>


### [318] [A Diffusion-Model Subpopulation Digital Twin for Mobile Health Deployment: A Case Study on the HeartSteps Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21403)
*Ziping Xu,Yuyi Chang,Chenshun Ni,Nithin Sugavanam,Asim H. Gazi,Pedja Klasnja,Emre Ertin,Susan A. Murphy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JITAI-Twins are digital twins of a target subpopulation to evaluate online health-behavior algorithms before deployment, using a conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent. The method supports three-stage updating (pre-train, fine-tune, calibration) and is validated on the HeartSteps HeartSteps v2–v4 deployments, outperforming simple simulators in reproducing temporal and between-participant structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile-health interventions risk disengagement if algorithm choices are poorly designed. Realistic simulators are needed to vet online decision rules before live deployment.

Method: A conditional time-series diffusion model ensures temporal consistency (future actions do not influence past). The framework updates in three steps: (1) pre-train on a large observational dataset, (2) fine-tune on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, (3) inference-time calibration to the next target population using domain-scientist expertise.

Result: The JITAI-Twins reproduce the target subpopulation's temporal dynamics and inter-individual structure better than simpler simulators and can simulate a deployment before it occurs, informing online algorithm design decisions.

Conclusion: JITAI-Twins provide a practical, validated approach for pre-deployment evaluation of JITAI algorithms, reducing risk and guiding algorithm development.

Abstract: Mobile-health interventions increasingly use online learning and decision making algorithms to personalize when to nudge users toward healthier behavior, but a poorly designed algorithm can burden and disengage participants. New algorithm design decisions should therefore be vetted against realistic simulated users before each real-life deployment. We propose a method to develop ``JITAI-Twins'': digital twins of a target subpopulation for comparing candidate online algorithms before a just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) deployment. The method builds on a conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent (future actions do not affect the generated past), and it supports repeated updating from three sources of information, in three steps: pre-training on a large observational dataset, fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and inference-time calibration to the next target population from domain-scientist expertise. We validate the twin at each pre-deployment stage of the long-running HeartSteps series (v2 through v4) of physical-activity suggestion intervention deployments, treating each successive deployment as an upcoming study. The proposed method reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators. These results suggest that our twin can be used to simulate a target deployment before it runs, the prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions.

</details>


### [319] [Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21426)
*Ahmad Halimi Razlighi,Maximilian H. V. Tillmann,Edgar Beck,Bho Matthiesen,Armin Dekorsy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A semantic-aware task clustering framework for cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) uses two stages: (1) clustering semantically aligned tasks with hierarchical density-based clustering after a brief pretraining, and (2) intra-cluster end-to-end CMT-SemCom training, yielding accuracy gains by mitigating destructive cooperation and negative transfer compared with unclustered/multi-task baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Negative transfer and destructive cooperation hinder performance in cooperative multitask semantic communication. Promoting constructive cooperation requires identifying semantically related tasks and isolating them for training.

Method: Two-stage optimization: (i) semantic clustering via hierarchical density-based clustering (e.g., HDBSCAN) to form groups of semantically aligned tasks; (ii) intra-cluster end-to-end CMT-SemCom learning within each cluster.

Result: Simulation results show mitigation of destructive cooperation and negative transfer, with accuracy gains over unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

Conclusion: Semantic-aware clustering enables constructive cooperation in CMT-SemCom and improves task performance by restricting joint training to semantically aligned groups, reducing cross-task interference.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

</details>


### [320] [Context-weighted Discrete Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21427)
*Daniil Cherniavskii,Daniel Severo,Karen Ullrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Context-aware CTMC modifications for discrete flow matching improve sampling and training efficiency, achieving strong perplexity gains and competitive generation quality with flexible autoregression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard factorized objectives mix targets of varying difficulty; token uncertainty correlates with local context density, motivating a context-aware approach to balance training signals and improve sampling.

Method: Introduce a context-weighted sampler within the CTMC and a scaled cross-entropy loss that reweights token losses based on local context information, enabling better handling of high- vs. low-uncertainty tokens.

Result: Improved generation quality with negligible overhead; up to 63% perplexity reduction on OpenWebText; matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while preserving generation in any order.

Conclusion: Local context is a key factor in discrete generative modeling; simple context-aware modifications can substantially improve sampling and training efficiency without sacrificing flexibility.

Abstract: Discrete flow matching provides a flexible framework for generative modeling on discrete structures. However, the standard factorized training objective exposes the model to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned, predictable tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. We empirically demonstrate that the uncertainty over the value of each token is closely related to the density of available context in its neighborhood. Motivated by this observation, we propose a simple modification to the underlying continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) that incorporates local context information. Our context-weighted sampler improves generation quality with negligible computational overhead, while our scaled cross-entropy loss function reweights the training signal from different tokens and reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. Moreover, our approach matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while retaining the ability to perform generation in any order. These results highlight the role of local context as an important factor in discrete generative modeling and show that simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency.

</details>


### [321] [KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21446)
*Yann Bouquet,Alireza Khodamoradi,Kristof Denolf,Mathieu Salzmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KroQuant introduces a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform for 32-element activation blocks in post-training quantization of diffusion transformers to W4A4. It reduces parameter and online computation costs compared to per-channel scaling and Hadamard transforms, enabling faster, more accurate quantization with offline Calibrated LoRaQ weight calibration. It achieves closer FP references and preserved/improved image quality on several diffusion benchmarks/datasets, with reported speedups on MI350 GPUs.



<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PTQ for diffusion transformers (DiTs) at extremely low precision (W4A4) degrades outputs due to activation outliers and the need to apply a transform online during denoising. Prior options trade quantization quality for inference cost (per-channel scaling, fixed Hadamard, full dense invertible transforms). A structured, efficient transform could retain accuracy while reducing compute and parameter count.

Method: Apply a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element activation block. This block-local structure enables small tensor-core GEMMs. Store fewer than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. Use offline LoRaQ to calibrate residual per-weight quantization error. Evaluate on PixArt-Σ, SANA, FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2) and compare to SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI.

Result: KroQuant achieves faster kernel performance (up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant kernel on MI350) and produces outputs closer to FP references than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on key diffusion benchmarks, while preserving or improving image quality.

Conclusion: A Kronecker-structured invertible transform offers a parameter-efficient, online-friendly alternative to existing PTQ transforms for DiTs, delivering quantization quality comparable or superior to state-of-the-art methods with reduced compute and memory footprints. Offline LoRaQ calibration complements the approach, enabling robust W4A4 quantization on real-world datasets.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

</details>


### [322] [Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21453)
*Rajiv Shailesh Chitale,Rahul Madhavan,Taneesh Gupta,Deepanway Ghosal,Aravindan Raghuveer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TTEL enables token-level error localization at test time to maximize reuse of valid prefixes, achieving superior efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs in sequential reasoning tasks; demonstrates Pareto dominance across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard inference-time strategies lack token-level credit assignment, leading to wasted computation; need to reuse prefixes and isolate where errors occur.

Method: During inference, compare conditional probabilities with feedback against a null-context baseline to locate the first erroneous step; truncate trajectory there, then branch a new generation; reuse valid prefix; evaluate against pass@k vs generated tokens on LiveCodeBench and math benchmarks; uses Qwen models.

Result: TTEL yields strictly dominating Pareto frontiers; pass@64 71.0% on LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-8B; about 360k generated tokens vs 735k baseline; outperforms test-time baselines on AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 for multiple models.

Conclusion: Error-localized test-time scaling substantially improves efficiency without sacrificing performance; generalizes to complex reasoning/math tasks.

Abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

</details>


### [323] [Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21475)
*Peng Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deterministic KV-cache eviction is non-identifiable; randomized eviction with Poisson-tail and Hájek correction enables per-step error certificates and better attribution, at the cost of potential accuracy trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether cache-level eviction decisions leak or distort the true attention output, enabling safe recomputation scheduling in serving LLMs.

Method: Theoretically prove non-identifiability for deterministic eviction; introduce randomized eviction with Poisson-sampled tail and known inclusion probabilities; apply Hájek correction inside softmax via a logit offset; derive a survey-sampling variance estimator over retained tokens; validate with real workloads across seven pre-registered claims; measure attribution and calibration.

Result: Deterministic eviction cannot bound true attention-output error; randomized eviction yields 0.97 empirical coverage for the error certificate; attribution performance (AUC 0.73–0.75) surpasses output-confidence baselines (AUC 0.47–0.54); three of seven pre-registered claims were lost; certificate improves scheduling of recomputation.

Conclusion: Randomization restores identifiability and enables per-step error certificates that separate cache-induced from inherent failures; attribution improves decision-making and recomputation scheduling; randomization trades some predictive capability for better diagnostic power; output log-probability is less predictive than the certificate; certificate-gated budgets have no advantage in some settings.

Abstract: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the Hájek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

</details>


### [324] [Finite-Sample Coverage Audits for High-Recall Candidate Generation: Certification and Learning-Theoretic Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21480)
*Martin Anthony,Kaveh Salehzadeh Nobari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Characterizes the label complexity and finite-sample guarantees for auditing missed relevant mass in a high-recall initial stage. Shows excluded-pool sampling is necessary and minimax-rate-optimal in the zero-miss regime; offers an exact finite-sample toolkit (binomial/hypergeometric inversion) to certify missed mass, convert to recall, and evaluate pre-specified generator families under fixed-design auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In high-recall screening pipelines, unrecovered relevant items are potentially lost. The paper seeks finite-sample guarantees on the missed mass and the label complexity required to certify it, addressing the insufficiency of using only included-pool labels.

Method: Theoretical analysis establishing a lower bound: any audit that certifies miss mass with high probability in zero-miss case must sample from the excluded pool, yielding a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Develops an exact finite-sample toolkit using binomial and hypergeometric inversion, enabling certification of missed mass, conversion to recall via a two-pool design, simultaneous certification for nested candidate generators, and stress-test certificates against perturbations. Assumes fixed candidate generator/family and a fixed audit rule before labeling.

Result: Proves excluded-pool auditing is minimax rate-optimal for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime; provides non-asymptotic, exact certificates for missed mass and derived recall, plus design principles to compare pre-specified generators under strict fixed-design conditions; yields stress-testing capabilities.

Conclusion: Finite-sample, fixed-design auditing of excluded-pool labels offers robust, minimax-rate-optimal guarantees for missed mass in the zero-miss setting, enabling principled selection of generator families under bounded labeling effort and providing versatile certificates and stress tests.

Abstract: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

</details>


### [325] [Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535)
*Alagappan Valliappan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Windowed-MTP accelerates speculative decoding by sliding-windowing the draft's attention (attention sink) and reclaiming unread KV, maintaining target verification while reducing draft cost by 28–44% at 1M context across multiple architectures; training-free, drop-in, with negligible quality impact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: At very long contexts, a built-in MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the KV cache at each draft step, causing the draft read to dominate cost. This bottleneck worsens with draft length and blocks benefits of speculative decoding, especially with hybrid/linear attention.

Method: Introduce StreamingLLM-style sliding window and an attention sink on the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP). Bound the draft's KV working set to a constant, drop ~99% of KV entries at 1M context. Reclaim unread draft KV via a compact ring buffer. No training required; preserves acceptance decisions and target output distribution.

Result: Per-decode-step cost on 1M context reduced by 28% to 44% across three architectures (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) on a single GPU in SGLang. End-to-end latency improves by the same amount under matched acceptance. Unread draft KV (~7.7–11% of total KV at 1M) reclaimed with no cost to acceptance or quality.

Conclusion: Windowed-MTP offers a practical, training-free, lossless acceleration for speculative decoding in long-context LLMs by constraining the draft's attention to a sliding window and reclaiming unused KV, improving latency without affecting the verified output.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

</details>


### [326] [Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21542)
*Yakun Wang,Leyang Wang,Song Liu,Taiji Suzuki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel two-sample test (ZF2ST) based on zero-flow discrepancy that learns a data-driven witness to detect distribution differences while preserving calibrated type-I error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve high power for detecting distributional differences in high-dimensional or structured data, using flexible neural witnesses without sacrificing statistical validity.

Method: Introduce zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD) as the test statistic. Learn a witness that captures local misalignment between samples from two distributions, using either regression-based or power-maximized training. Separate witness learning from hypothesis evaluation to retain valid calibration, enabling neural networks within a two-sample testing framework. Provide a practical procedure, ZF2ST, that computes a test statistic and p-value under the null.

Result: Prove the validity of ZFD and develop ZF2ST with two witness-learning strategies. Demonstrate well-calibrated Type-I error and strong testing power for structured distributional changes on synthetic and image datasets.

Conclusion: ZF2ST offers a flexible, calibrated, high-power two-sample test leveraging learned witnesses through neural networks, with distinct learning strategies and solid empirical performance on structured distributional changes.

Abstract: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

</details>


### [327] [X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21550)
*Dongjie Fu,Di Cao,Xize Cheng,Zihan Zhang,Wenxu Jia,Yifu Chen,Shengpeng Ji,Yu Zhang,Tao Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes X^3-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning from a text teacher to an audio-language student, aided by a three-tier symmetric corpus (text-to-speech, audio-event reasoning in acoustic scenes, spoken-dialogue reasoning) to improve audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while maintaining capabilities under domain shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data and the lag of audio-language models in deep reasoning compared to text LLMs by enabling cross-modal transfer of reasoning from a powerful text teacher.

Method: X^3-OPD framework: a student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its acoustic perception; a text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers; training uses a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning with paralinguistic cues.

Result: Empirical evaluation on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR shows substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality, with the model largely preserving existing capabilities under domain shift.

Conclusion: Cross-modal distillation extends reasoning beyond text to non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context; the X^3-OPD framework effectively transfers reasoning capabilities and yields robust improvements across audio-language benchmarks.
