Abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

</details>


### [328] [Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21561)
*Aaron Feller,Kris Deibler,Maxim Secor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EnsembleEGNN encodes conformational ensembles via shared EGNN layers plus a set-attention pooling, pretrained on a cyclic-peptide ensemble dataset, and outperforms sequence-only baselines for cyclic-peptide property prediction; co-training with a sequence encoder further boosts performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of using a single molecular conformation for property prediction by leveraging thermodynamically informed ensemble representations.

Method: Encode each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers; pool conformer representations with a Set Attention Block to form an ensemble embedding; pretrain on CREMP with multi-task self-supervised objectives (masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, pairwise distance reconstruction); evaluate on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB; also experiment with end-to-end co-training with a BERT sequence encoder.

Result: From-scratch training on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB fails (R^2=0.005). Pretraining yields R^2=0.477 and Pearson r=0.699, beating sequence-only BERT (R^2=0.439, r=0.667). End-to-end hybrid with BERT improves to R^2=0.538 and r=0.737.

Conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into a single, thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction and can surpass sequence-only approaches; leveraging ensemble information is beneficial for molecular property tasks.

Abstract: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

</details>


### [329] [Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21573)
*Hongnan Ma,Yiwei Shi,Mengyue Yang,Weiru Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TimePNS is a two-stage, necessity-aware explanation framework for time-series classifiers that combines sufficiency-oriented masking with counterfactual interventions to identify both sufficient and necessary subsequences, improving explanation quality over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sufficiency-centered explanations may highlight spurious subsequences that suffice for a prediction but are not essential. There is a need to identify subsequences that are causally necessary for the model’s decision in time-series data.

Method: Two-stage design: Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process jointly with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, guiding a temporal gate that suppresses non-essential components and emphasizes counterfactually necessary ones.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

Conclusion: TimePNS offers a principled, necessity-aware framework for explaining time-series models by combining causal generation with counterfactual interventions, reducing reliance on spurious subsequences and yielding explanations that align with temporally necessary features.

Abstract: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

</details>


### [330] [Expanding Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21585)
*Sophia Tang,Pranam Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows) and Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs) to enable generative models that grow the output dimensionality and handle variable-length outputs, by decomposing maps into an expand operator and a transport map; unifies fixed-canvas flows as a special case and extends to discrete simplex for graphs/sequences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of flow-based models to fixed dimensionality or fixed sequence length; enable controllable, variable-size outputs and cross-modality (continuous and discrete) generation; improve efficiency by few-step generative maps.

Method: Introduce an expanding interpolant that grows state by adding conditional noise; define EFMs that factor the timestep map into (1) an expand operator adding new coordinates/tokens conditioned on current state and (2) a transport map advancing the expanded state along the interpolant; compose these operators to get a single expanding-denoising map; show that fixed-canvas flows are recovered when the expand operator is identity; extend the framework to the discrete simplex for variable-size graphs and variable-length sequences.

Result: A unified framework (EFlows/EFMs) for variable-dimension generative modeling across continuous and discrete domains; allows variable output sizes and provides a path to efficient few-step inference; shows special-case recovery of fixed-canvas flows.

Conclusion: EFlows and EFMs deliver a principled, generalizable approach to learnable output size in flow-based models, unifying existing fixed-dimension methods and enabling flexible generation in both continuous and discrete settings (including graphs and sequences).

Abstract: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

</details>

### [331] [HERMES: Heterogeneous Edge-Relational Multi-Head Embedded SSM Attention for Traffic Conflict Prediction at Signalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20505)
*Md Monzurul Islam,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HERMES is a heterogeneous edge-relational GNN for traffic safety assessment that models multi-agent interactions as a temporal heterogeneous scene graph, achieving state-of-the-art detection of traffic conflicts with strong transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SSM evaluation often flattens scenes or treats interactions pairwise, losing heterogeneous topology and temporal evolution; there is a need for a model that preserves interaction structure and scene-level risk across sites.

Method: Introduce HERMES, a heterogeneous edge-relational GNN with SSM-informed multi-head attention. Represent vehicles and pedestrians as heterogeneous nodes; encode relation-specific edges (vehicle-vehicle, vehicle-pedestrian, pedestrian-pedestrian) with continuous kinematic and surrogate-safety descriptors. Use relation-specific attention, dynamic updates, safety-aware graph pooling, and temporal sequence learning to estimate scene-level conflict probability.

Result: Evaluated on 109,028 trajectory-derived sequences from a signalized urban intersection and tested on an independent comparable intersection. Enhanced HERMES achieved AUC-ROC 0.9898±0.0013, AUC-PR 0.9412±0.0067, F1 0.8449±0.0103. At 5% false-alarm rate, detected 95.7% of conflict sequences, outperforming strongest Transformer baseline and XGBoost. In zero-shot external evaluation, AUC-ROC 0.9752 and AUC-PR 0.7829. Joint source-target training improved target-site performance with limited data.

Conclusion: Preserving heterogeneous interaction topology, safety-informed edge semantics, and short-term temporal evolution improves scene-level conflict classification and supports transferable roadside safety monitoring at signalized intersections.

Abstract: Surrogate safety measures (SSMs) enable proactive traffic safety assessment, but many existing methods evaluate pairwise interactions independently or flatten multi-agent scenes into fixed feature vectors, limiting their ability to represent heterogeneous interaction structure and evolving scene-level risk. This study formulates traffic conflict assessment as temporal heterogeneous scene-graph classification and proposes HERMES, a heterogeneous edge-relational graph neural network with SSM-informed multi-head attention. Vehicles and pedestrians are represented as heterogeneous nodes, while vehicle-vehicle, vehicle-pedestrian, and pedestrian-pedestrian interactions are encoded as relation-specific edges with continuous kinematic and surrogate-safety descriptors. Relation-specific attention, dynamic node-edge updates, safety-aware graph pooling, and temporal sequence learning are jointly used to estimate scene-level conflict probability. HERMES was evaluated using 109,028 trajectory-derived sequences from a signalized urban intersection and tested on an independently collected comparable intersection dataset. Enhanced HERMES achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9898 +/- 0.0013, an AUC-PR of 0.9412 +/- 0.0067, and an F1 score of 0.8449 +/- 0.0103. At a 5% false-alarm rate, it detected 95.7% of conflict sequences, outperforming the strongest Transformer baseline and XGBoost. In zero-shot external evaluation, HERMES achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9752 and an AUC-PR of 0.7829. Joint source-target training further improved target-site performance with limited target-site data. These findings show that preserving heterogeneous interaction topology, safety-informed edge semantics, and short-term temporal evolution improves scene-level conflict classification and supports transferable roadside safety monitoring at signalized intersections.

</details>


### [332] [PhysCoRe: Physics-Corrected Residual World Models for Material-Aware Deformable Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20653)
*Haocheng Yin,Shuohan Tao,Yongsheng Chen,Lu Gan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PhysCoRe merges a differentiable MPM simulator with a material refinement module and a residual dynamics module to learn per-particle elasticity from visuals and correct simulation biases, enabling online material identification and uncertainty-guided exploration for deformable-object manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deformable-object manipulation is hindered by slow, object-specific parameter fitting and poor generalization of end-to-end models; physics-grounded, adaptable models are needed to capture object-specific material behavior and biases.

Method: A physics-corrected residual world model that combines a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) simulator with two neural nets: Material from Motion (MfM) estimates per-particle elasticity from visual data; Residual from Dynamics (RfD) learns discrepancies between the simulator and real dynamics to provide corrections and absorb system biases; supports online material identification and uncertainty-driven exploration.

Result: Real-deformable-object manipulation experiments show PhysCoRe surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in prediction accuracy; the model’s predictive uncertainty yields a reliable confidence distribution across the object’s geometry, guiding exploration.

Conclusion: PhysCoRe provides a physics-grounded, adaptive framework for predicting deformable-object dynamics, enabling online material identification on new objects and offering uncertainty-aware predictions to drive future exploration.

Abstract: Predicting how deformable objects evolve under robotic manipulation is a longstanding challenge. Existing approaches typically rely on per-object optimization to fit material parameters, which can be slow and cannot generalize, while end-to-end learned alternatives extrapolate poorly and often violate basic physical structure. We present PhysCoRe, a physics-corrected residual world model that couples a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) simulator with two feed-forward neural networks. A material refinement module, Material from Motion (MfM), infers per-particle elasticity from visual observations, grounding the simulator in object-specific physics. A residual correction module, Residual from Dynamics (RfD), learns the discrepancy and predicts corrections to the simulator's internal dynamics, absorbing systematic biases that the analytical model cannot capture. This design also supports online material identification on novel objects. MfM adapts from limited interactions, and its predictive uncertainty steers further exploration toward the regions where its estimate is least confident. Experiments on real deformable-object manipulation sequences show that PhysCoRe outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in prediction accuracy, and that its predicted confidence forms a reliable distribution across the object's geometry, providing a natural signal for future confidence-guided exploration.

</details>


### [333] [Scalable Low-Cost Laboratory Automation: A Digital Twin-Integrated Robotic Platform for Autonomous Liquid Handling (RAINBOTTM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20662)
*Mohamed Rami Ayeche,Souhil Sid,Ahyen Mostofa,Rehaan Hussain,Ali Shayesteh,Fadwa El Mellouhi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An open-source, low-cost liquid-handling robot (RAINBOT) built by converting a consumer Cartesian 3D printer; features a G-code-driven XYZ gantry with a pipette and two actuators; browser-based digital twin enables remote supervision; validated by color-mensor mixing with MAE ~2% and an inverse-design loop via CEID; hardware cost under $1300, about 10x cheaper than entry-level commercial systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial liquid-handling systems are expensive, proprietary, and lack transparent remote supervision. There is a need for accessible, reproducible platforms to accelerate discovery and enable self-driving laboratories.

Method: Replace the printer's extruder with a precision single-channel pipette mounted on the printer's XYZ gantry. Use two compact linear actuators for plunger and tip eject, controlled via Python. Implement a browser-based digital twin to synchronize real-time kinematics and pipetting states with the physical platform, enabling remote monitoring, intervention, and emergency stop. Validate with sequential dye exchanges and a color sensor to quantify mixtures, and integrate with the CEID inverse-design framework to guide experiments.

Result: Demonstrated accurate mixing behavior (RYB) with mean absolute error of two percentage points. Achieved bidirectional real-time synchronization between hardware and digital twin; remote monitoring/intervention capabilities; total hardware cost about $1.3k (roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than commercial liquid handlers).

Conclusion: Shows a feasible, open, low-cost hardware–software stack for self-driving laboratory automation, coupling a physical platform with an inverse-design framework to enable remote supervision and iterative discovery at significantly reduced cost.

Abstract: Laboratory automation accelerates discovery, yet its adoption is constrained by the high cost, proprietary design, and limited remote supervisability of commercial liquid-handling systems. This work presents RAINBOT\textsuperscript{TM}, a low-cost, openly reproducible liquid-handling robot built by converting a consumer-grade Cartesian 3D printer (Elegoo Neptune 4 Max). The printer extruder is replaced by a precision single-channel pipette actuated through the printer's own G-code-driven X--Y--Z gantry, with plunger and tip-eject motions effected by two compact linear actuators under Python control. To make experiments transparent and remotely supervisable, a browser-based digital twin is implemented to synchronise bidirectionally with the physical platform, mirroring kinematics and pipetting states in real time and exposing remote monitoring, intervention, and an emergency stop from any web browser. As a proof of concept, RAINBOT\textsuperscript{TM} performed sequential exchanges of differently coloured aqueous solutions while an integrated colour sensor quantified the resulting mixtures; measured red, yellow, and blue (RYB) responses agreed with expected mixing behaviour to within a mean absolute error of two percentage points, validating correct execution and real-time tracking. Closing the loop, the platform is coupled to the CEID\textsuperscript{TM} (Cooperative Explorer for Inverse Design) framework, which recasts experimentation from iterative manual guessing into a goal-directed inverse-design search while keeping a human in the loop. The complete hardware costs under US\$1300, which is roughly an order of magnitude below entry-level commercial handlers, thereby establishing an accessible physical--virtual framework for self-driving laboratory automation.

</details>


### [334] [Safe and Scalable Multi-Drone Payload Transport via CBF-based Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20665)
*Jaeyoun Choi,Oswin So,Songyuan Zhang,Cooper Taylor,Chuchu Fan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A learning-based, distributed framework for safe and scalable multi-drone payload transport using a 2D abstraction and domain randomization, trained with Discrete Graph Control Barrier Function Proximal Policy Optimization (DGPPO) to enable robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and generalization across team sizes and dynamic environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the complex, coupled dynamics of multiple drones, cables, and payloads that hamper safety and scalability, especially in dynamic and unstructured environments; enable robust, generalizable policies that transfer from simulation to real-world multi-drone teams.

Method: Introduce a minimal 2D abstraction that preserves task-relevant drone-payload coupling; train a fully distributed policy via Discrete Graph Control Barrier Function Proximal Policy Optimization (DGPPO) with domain randomization over team size and physical parameters to support zero-shot sim-to-real transfer; evaluate on both single and multi-group hardware scenarios with moving obstacles.

Result: The learned policy demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, generalizes across varying team sizes and task scenarios, and operates safely in dynamic environments with moving obstacles, as validated by extensive real-world experiments including multi-group hardware tests.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient, safe, and scalable multi-drone payload transportation with strong generalization to complex real-world conditions, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for large-scale learning.

Abstract: Multi-drone payload transportation has emerged as a promising research paradigm with potential applications in construction, logistics, and disaster response. However, the complex coupled dynamics among drones, cables, and payloads pose significant challenges, and existing approaches remain limited in safety and scalability, particularly in dynamic and unstructured environments. In this work, we propose a learning-based framework for safe and scalable multi-drone cooperative payload transport. We introduce a minimal 2D abstraction that preserves the task-relevant drone-payload coupling required for coordination and safety, while remaining computationally efficient for large-scale learning. Using domain randomization over team size and physical parameters, we train a fully distributed policy via Discrete Graph Control Barrier Function Proximal Policy Optimization (DGPPO), enabling robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning. Extensive real-world evaluations demonstrate that a single learned policy generalizes across varying team sizes and task scenarios. Furthermore, multi-group hardware experiments show that the same policy can safely operate in dynamic environments, where other drone teams act as moving obstacles. These results indicate that the proposed framework enables efficient, safe, and scalable multi-drone payload transportation with strong generalization to complex real-world conditions.

</details>


### [335] [Towards Capability-Aware Traversability Navigation for Unstructured Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20679)
*Gianluca Capezzuto,Felipe Tommaselli,Matheus P. Angarola,Ricardo V. Godoy,Marcelo Becker*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Capability-Aware Traversability (CAT) embeds robot embodiment into the spatial feature space using per-robot traversability vectors and SPADE conditioning, improving ranking metrics on diverse datasets and enabling real-time embodiment-aware obstacle avoidance on legged and wheeled platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traversability must be conditioned on robot embodiment because terrain that is traversable for one platform may be unsafe for another; existing methods rely on late-stage trajectory filtering rather than representation-level constraints.

Method: An interactive annotation pipeline grounds dense supervision masks in physical trajectories; Spatially-Adaptive Denormalization (SPADE) blocks modulate semantic terrain maps with per-robot traversability vectors; uses per-robot prototypes for capability specificity; evaluated on human-annotated and trajectory-aligned datasets; deployed on a legged quadruped and a wheeled skid-steer for real-time obstacle avoidance on embedded hardware (4.8 Hz).

Result: CAT achieves leading performance on ranking metrics: AUROC improves by 11.0% on physically executed trajectories and AUPRC by 15.8% on human traces over the strongest baseline; ablations indicate the importance of spatial conditioning and per-robot prototypes for capability sensitivity beyond generic path prediction.

Conclusion: Embedding embodiment constraints directly into the spatial feature space yields embodiment-aware traversability estimation with strong empirical gains and feasible real-time deployment across diverse platforms.

Abstract: Estimating traversability in unstructured environments requires conditioning on robot embodiment, as the same terrain can be traversable for one platform and unsafe for another. Existing methods often transfer predictions across morphologies through late-stage trajectory filtering rather than encoding platform constraints in the learned representation. We propose Capability-Aware Traversability (CAT), a framework that embeds physical limits directly into the spatial feature space. CAT grounds dense supervision masks in physical trajectories through an interactive annotation pipeline and modulates semantic terrain maps with robot-specific traversability vectors through Spatially-Adaptive Denormalization (SPADE) blocks. Across human-annotated and trajectory-aligned datasets, CAT leads all ranking-based metrics, improving AUROC by 11.0% on physically executed trajectories and AUPRC by 15.8% on human traces over the strongest baseline. Ablations show that spatial conditioning and per-robot prototypes produce capability sensitivity beyond generic path prediction. Deployments on a legged quadruped and a wheeled skid-steer demonstrate embodiment-aware obstacle avoidance on embedded hardware at 4.8 Hz.

</details>


### [336] [FELT: Generating Tactile Signals from Vision for Visuo-Tactile Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20683)
*Zinan Li,Yiyang Ling,Yuming Gu,Binghao Huang,Chenhao Liang,Sharfin Islam,Hisham Bedri,John Chirikjian,Yunzhu Li,Stefanos Nikolaidis,Daniel Seita*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FELT synthesizes per-finger tactile signals from RGB using a frozen visual encoder and separate per-finger decoders, enabling tactile augmentation of vision-only policies with either generated tactile images or latent features, reducing tactile data needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile data are scarce and costly due to fragile, specialized sensors; combining vision and touch helps manipulation, but acquiring tactile data is a bottleneck. A way to synthesize tactile signals from RGB can enable training robust visuo-tactile policies with less real tactile data.

Method: A learning-based framework with a large frozen visual encoder and a lightweight query decoder that predicts tactile signals in a single forward pass. Left and right tactile sensor panels are decoded through separate branches to reflect their physical topology. At inference, only RGB is required; training can use real tactile data to supervise the synthesis, and the outputs can be used as generated tactile images or as latent tactile features.

Result: In four contact-rich manipulation tasks, both generated tactile images and latent tactile features improve policy success over vision-only baselines. The latent features, in particular, require no real tactile sensor during training or deployment.

Conclusion: FELT effectively reduces reliance on tactile data by synthesizing tactile signals from RGB, enabling visuo-tactile policy learning with either generated tactile data or latent representations; latent features offer a sensor-free deployment advantage.

Abstract: The sense of touch is central to manipulation, especially when vision is occluded or ambiguous. Although combining vision and touch improves manipulation, learning robust visuo-tactile policies requires substantial tactile data. Such data remains scarcer than visual data, because tactile sensors are fragile, specialized, and hard to standardize. To address this, we present Feature-Extracted Latent Tactile (FELT), a learning-based framework that synthesizes per-finger pressure tactile images from RGB observations, reducing the need for tactile-equipped data collection. FELT uses a large frozen visual encoder and a lightweight query decoder to predict tactile signals in a single feed-forward pass. To respect the physical topology of dual-finger tactile sensors, FELT decodes the left and right tactile sensor panels through separate branches, capturing the asymmetric contact patterns during interactions such as wiping, insertion, and in-hand rotation. At inference time, FELT only requires RGB data, allowing us to augment existing vision-only data with tactile observations, either as generated tactile images or as latent tactile features. Experiments on four contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that both generated tactile images and latent tactile features improve policy success over vision-only baselines, with latent feature requiring no real tactile sensor during policy training or deployment. Supplementary material is available on our anonymous website: https://felt-tactile.github.io/.

</details>


### [337] [Decentralized UAV Swarms for Ground Target Protection in GPS- and Communication-Denied Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20710)
*Dimitria Silveria,Paulo Ricardo Marques de Araujo,Tiago Nascimento,Sidney Givigi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A decentralized, GPS-denied UAV swarm framework for ground-target protection that detects, encircles, and intercepts hostile UAVs using onboard sensors and relative measurements, with Kalman-based state estimation and a decentralized encirclement strategy; validated on real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern warfare with UAV threats and limited GPS/communications motivates autonomous, sensor-based swarm defenses capable of operating without external positioning or links.

Method: Develop Kalman filters to estimate unknown target states and swarm UAV positions using only relative measurements; design a decentralized swarm encirclement strategy that adapts to target motion; implement a pipeline for detection, encirclement, and interception in GPS-denied conditions; validate with real robots.

Result: The approach effectively detects, encircles, and intercepts hostile UAVs, demonstrated through experiments on real robots.

Conclusion: A viable sensor-based, decentralized UAV swarm defense method for protecting ground targets in GPS-denied environments, capable of tracking and countering moving threats with autonomous coordination.

Abstract: The presence of UAVs in military operations has recently increased, also increasing the demand for defense systems against UAV attacks. UAVs can also be used as countermeasures. Most available methods rely on UAV-to-UAV communication and global positioning. However, such resources may not be available in modern warfare scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a pipeline for ground-target protection against UAV attacks that employs autonomous swarms of UAVs. We assume a communication- and GPS-denied environment in which the UAVs use onboard sensors to track the target and coordinate as a swarm. We developed Kalman filters to estimate the states of unknown targets and the positions of UAVs in the swarm using only relative measurements. Also, our strategy is to encircle the target of interest to maximize coverage. To achieve that, we propose a decentralized swarm encirclement technique that adapts to the target's motion. Our approach was extensively validated using real robots, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting, encircling, and intercepting hostile UAVs.

</details>


### [338] [Self-Supervised Bio-Inspired Robotic Trajectory Planning with Obstacle Avoidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20743)
*Miroslav Krupa,Miroslav Cibula,Kristína Malinovská*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A neuro-inspired self-supervised trajectory-planning framework using forward and inverse models is feasible in obstacle-rich environments, but the planner tends to exploit the supervision signal; the work proposes and evaluates mitigation strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address inefficiency and limited generalisation in model-based trajectory planning by leveraging self-supervision to enable efficient planning with neural planners, reducing reliance on heavy sampling or expert demonstrations.

Method: Evaluate a neuro-inspired self-supervised learning framework where forward and inverse models provide internal supervision for trajectory planning in an environment with an obstacle; assess feasibility and the tendency to exploit the learning signal; propose and evaluate additional training regimes and mitigation strategies.

Result: Feasibility of the proposed framework is demonstrated; a tendency for the planner to exploit the learning signal is observed; multiple training regimes and mitigation strategies are proposed and evaluated.

Conclusion: The approach is promising for efficient trajectory planning but requires careful design of supervision and mitigation techniques to prevent exploitative learning and to enhance generalisation; future work should refine training regimes to robustly utilize forward/inverse supervision.

Abstract: Trajectory planning is a fundamental problem in robotics, requiring the generation of collision-free and efficient trajectories in a potentially complex environment. While sampling-based planners remain the dominant approach, they are often computationally expensive, particularly in high-dimensional spaces and obstacle-rich environments. Methods based on model learning offer a promising alternative, enabling efficient planning through a bounded number of forward passes through a neural trajectory planner, but commonly suffer from low sample efficiency or limited generalisation due to their reliance on exploration or expert demonstrations. This follow-up work tests our neuro-inspired self-supervised learning framework for trajectory planning that leverages forward and inverse models as the internal supervisory mechanism in an environment that contains an obstacle. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the approach while revealing a tendency of our planner to exploit the learning signal provided by the forward and inverse models. To address this issue, additional training regimes and mitigation strategies are proposed and evaluated.

</details>


### [339] [A real-time RGB-D perception pipeline for autonomous impact hammers in mining: self-filtering, rock segmentation and rock-breaking poses generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20748)
*Martín Gallegos,Francisco Leiva,Patricio Loncomilla,Michelle Cortés,Javier Ruiz-del-Solar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time RGB-D perception pipeline enables autonomous operation of hydraulic impact hammers in mining by jointly producing rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D workspace map at ~10 Hz (675 ms latency), validated in a scaled test environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underground mining often relies on teleoperated impact hammers, which limits efficiency and safety; automating perception-pose planning for these hammers can improve responsiveness and autonomy.

Method: An embedded real-time pipeline fuses image-based instance segmentation with geometric processing of point clouds to compute feasible rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D workspace representation; operates at ~10 Hz with ~675 ms end-to-end latency, suitable for closed-loop control.

Result: The pipeline runs on embedded hardware at ~10 Hz with latency ~675 ms and, in a representative scaled experiment, demonstrates real-time capability and suitability for autonomous operation of the hydraulic impact hammer.

Conclusion: The proposed perception framework constitutes a viable step toward real-time autonomous impact hammer operation in mining, enabling responsive closed-loop control and reducing reliance on teleoperation in underground settings.

Abstract: Impact hammers, also known as rock-breakers, are essential machines in mining operations, where they perform secondary reduction. In underground mining, these machines are typically teleoperated, limiting operational efficiency. This paper presents a real-time RGB-D perception pipeline as a step towards automating the operation of hydraulic impact hammers used in mining. The proposed system simultaneously generates operationally feasible rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D representation of the workspace. The proposed approach combines image-based instance segmentation with geometric point cloud processing, and operates on embedded hardware at approximately 10 Hz with a total latency of around 675 ms, enabling responsive closed-loop behavior when integrated with a control system. Experimental results in a representative scaled scenario demonstrate that the proposed system is suitable for real-time autonomous impact hammer operation.

</details>


### [340] [Emergent Compositional Skills in Mixture-of-Experts VLAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20771)
*Shlok Shah,Rhiaan Jhaveri,Tharun Kumar Tiruppali Kalidoss,Chirayu Nimonkar,Ishaan Javali*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A vision-language-action model with a simplified mixture-of-experts head learns emergent task decomposition into reusable, interpretable primitives, performing on par with a monolithic model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve modular, interpretable robot policies learned directly from data without pre-specified task decomposition or hierarchy, enabling reusable low-level primitives.

Method: Train a VLA with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head on expert demonstrations to see if routing through experts yields emergent decomposition into primitives; analyze expert reuse and behavior; compare to a monolithic baseline.

Result: Learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and map to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors. The router appears to perform high-level sequencing while experts serve as compositional primitives. The MoE matches the task performance of the monolithic baseline and shows meaningful expert specialization.

Conclusion: End-to-end learning can yield modular, interpretable robot policies emerging from data alone, with reusable primitives and implicit sequencing through MoE routing.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning compositional robot policies end-to-end from expert demonstrations, without any pre-specified notion of task decomposition or hierarchy. We ask whether a VLA trained with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head can emergently learn to decompose tasks into reusable, interpretable primitives. We find that learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and consistently correspond to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors, suggesting that the router implicitly learns to perform high-level sequencing while experts serve as compositional primitives. Our MoE matches the task performance of a monolithic baseline while demonstrating meaningful expert specialization, a step toward modular, interpretable robot policies that emerge from data alone.

</details>


### [341] [Socially Consistent Multi-Robot Navigation Using Decoupled Planning and Trajectory Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20772)
*Matthew M. Sato,Kincho H. Law*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A long-horizon, socially aware, partially decentralized framework for multi-robot navigation that decouples global path planning from trajectory coordination, embeds social norms in an A*-based planner, shares paths to build a social graph, and solves a mixed-integer convex program for conflict-free trajectories, yielding predictable and scalable robot behavior in human-centric environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for consistent, predictable, and socially compliant navigation in multi-robot systems operating around humans, by ensuring long-horizon planning constraints and reducing the burden on local planners.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) Modified A* that incorporates macroscopic social-norm costs; shared planned paths to form a social graph enforcing path consistency; (2) Leverage the emergent social graph to formulate multi-robot trajectory coordination as a mixed-integer convex program (MICP) for conflict-free trajectories, enabling scalable planning and dynamic task assignment.

Result: The approach yields socially consistent, predictable, and compliant paths; the social-graph-informed coordination simplifies the MICP problem and scales to large fleets while supporting dynamic task assignment.

Conclusion: Enforcing social consistency at the path-planning stage effectively improves long-horizon predictability and human-robot acceptance, while decoupling global planning from trajectory coordination reduces computational burden and enhances scalability.

Abstract: The successful integration of mobile robots in human-centric environments requires navigation that is not only safe and efficient, but also predictable and aligned with social conventions, key precursors for human comfort and acceptance. While significant research addresses short-term human-aware planning, these methods often lack mechanisms for ensuring consistent and predictable behaviors across long horizons. Without socially aware long-term planners, local planners are overburdened, resulting in inefficient and locally reactive movements that undermine predictability. This paper introduces a partially decentralized framework that generates predictable and socially consistent multi-robot motion by decoupling global path planning from trajectory coordination. First, we propose a modified A* planner that embeds macroscopic social norms into the planner cost function. Planned paths are shared across mobile robots to collaboratively build a social graph of established routes, which enforces path consistency and reduces future planning effort. Second, we leverage the emergent structure of the socially constrained paths to formulate the multi-robot trajectory coordination problem as a mixed-integer convex program. The convex program enables efficient computation of conflict- free trajectories, scaling effectively to large fleets and supporting dynamic task assignment. Our results demonstrate that enforcing social consistency at the path planning stage produces predictable, socially compliant mobile robot paths and simplifies the otherwise complex problem of multi-robot coordination.

</details>


### [342] [Robostral Navigate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20785)
*Arjun Majumdar,Avinash Sooriyarachchi,Benjamin Tibi,Chris Bamford,Elliot Chane-Sane,Guillaume Lample,Khyathi Raghavi Chandu,Ludovic Ho Fuh,Mathieu Poiree,Olivier Duchenne,Rosalie Millner,Srijan Mishra,Theo Cachet,Thomas Chabal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Monocular RGB-only navigation model (Robostral Navigate) achieves state-of-the-art results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE by predicting image-space waypoints with an 8B vision-language model, enabling cross-robot deployment with minimal sensors. Scales via synthetic data and efficient training; improves exploration with RL and a tree-based attention mask.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploy navigation systems at scale with minimal sensor assumptions and broad robot embodiment generalization. Depth sensors, multi-camera rigs, or pre-built maps increase hardware needs and deployment cost; a camera-agnostic policy that works across wheeled, legged, and aerial platforms is highly desirable.

Method: An 8B vision-language model that consumes only monocular RGB streams and predicts the next target location by pointing within the current camera view (image-space policy). Trains on 2.4 million trajectories across 350k simulated scenes; introduces a prefix-caching training recipe to compress episodes into single sequences (22x fewer tokens, training time reduced from months to days). Uses a tree-based attention mask to prevent conditioning on previous ground-truth actions, promoting visually grounded action prediction, and applies reinforcement learning to improve exploration and recovery.

Result: On Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE): 77.4% success rate, 10.5-point gain over best monocular method, 5.3-point gain over strongest depth- or multi-camera systems. On RxR-CE: 75.1% success rate, outperforming all monocular baselines.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that monocular, image-space navigation with scaling across robot types is feasible and efficient. The approach reduces data and computation requirements while achieving state-of-the-art navigation performance without calibration for intrinsics or scene scale, enabling deployment across diverse robotic platforms.

Abstract: Deploying navigation systems at scale requires a recipe that minimizes sensor assumptions, generalizes across robot embodiments, and trains efficiently. Yet, today's best systems depend on depth sensors, multi-camera rigs, or pre-built maps, limiting the hardware they support and increasing deployment cost. We introduce Robostral Navigate, an 8B vision-language model built around this scalability objective. The model consumes only a stream of monocular RGB images - the most ubiquitous sensor across robotic platforms and predicts waypoints by pointing to the next target location in the current camera view. Operating purely in image space, rather than robot-specific coordinates, makes the policy naturally robust to changes in camera intrinsics and scene scale, enabling deployment across wheeled, legged, and aerial robots without recalibration. We generate 2.4 million trajectories across 350k simulated scenes to reduce the reliance on real-world data collection and scale easily. We further introduce a prefix-caching training recipe that packs entire episodes into single training sequences, reducing training tokens by 22x and cutting training time from months to days. A tree-based attention mask prevents conditioning on previous ground-truth actions, encouraging visually grounded action prediction, and reinforcement learning is used to further improve exploration and recovery capabilities. On the Room-to-Room and Room-Across-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE and RxR-CE) benchmarks, Robostral Navigate sets a new state of the art. On R2R-CE, it achieves a 77.4% success rate, surpassing the best monocular method by 10.5 points and the strongest depth- or multi-camera system by 5.3 points despite using only a single RGB camera. On RxR-CE, it reaches 75.1% success rate, outperforming all monocular baselines.

</details>


### [343] [URF: A Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework for Stable Contact Aware Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20912)
*Jiyou Shin,Youngjin Seo,Jaeseog Won,Sungwon Seo,Hyunjun Kim,Seokmin Yoon,Tuan Luong,Hyungpil Moon*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: URF unifies learning-based manipulation with a single controller by predicting a virtual target, stiffness, and a controller-mode switch to blend admittance and impedance control, supervised by switch labels derived from contact forces; it improves success and reduces failure modes in rigid contact tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To fix instability and unsafe behavior arising from separating action prediction from low-level control in rigid contact, where poor compatibility with the controller can cause tracking errors, excessive loading, or tool damage.

Method: From multimodal observations, URF predicts: (i) a virtual target, (ii) a stiffness matrix, and (iii) an impedance-admittance switch ratio. Switch labels are derived from measured contact forces to supervise controller-mode prediction. The framework integrates with unified impedance-admittance control and is evaluated on box-flipping and line-pressing tasks.

Result: URF achieves higher task success rates and reduces failure modes common to admittance-only execution, such as rapid force buildup, large force oscillations, tool breakage, and safety stops.

Conclusion: Predicting controller behavior alongside compliant actions yields more robust, contact-aware manipulation policies and can generalize to different rigid-contact scenarios.

Abstract: Learning-based manipulation policies usually predict robot actions from sensory observations and leave their execution to a separate low-level controller. In rigid contact, this separation can be problematic: the same motion to a virtual target or compliant motion command can lead to unstable contact, tracking error, excessive loading, or tool damage, depending on the low-level controller. In this paper, we propose a \textit{Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework} (URF), which connects compliant action prediction with unified impedance-admittance control. Given multimodal observations, URF predicts a virtual target, a stiffness matrix, and an impedance-admittance switch ratio. The switch ratio determines when the controller should behave more like admittance control for accurate motion tracking and when it should move toward impedance control for safer rigid contact. Because demonstration data do not provide ground-truth environment stiffness, we construct switch-ratio labels from measured contact forces and use them to supervise controller-mode prediction. Across box-flipping and line-pressing tasks, URF achieves higher task success rates while reducing failure modes observed with admittance-only execution, including rapid force buildup, large force oscillations, tool breakage, and robot safety stops. These results suggest that contact-aware policies benefit from predicting not only compliant actions but also the controller behavior used to execute them. Project page: https://jiyou384.github.io/urf_project_page/

</details>


### [344] [Deep Reinforcement-Learning-Guided Model Predictive Control for Preventing Overtakes in Autonomous Racing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20973)
*Yufei Xi,Yijie Liao,Tulga Ersal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Hierarchical RL-guided MPC for defensive blocking in autonomous racing; a Soft Actor-Critic policy in Frenet space generates geometry-aware defensive references embedded as spatial regularization within a nonlinear MPC under friction constraints; demonstrated in simulation on Thunderhill West with real-time capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Defensive blocking to prevent faster opponents from overtaking near dynamic limits is not well served by lap-time minimization. The paper reframes defense as spatial occupancy regulation and leverages RL to produce strategic, geometry-aware references that constrain the ego vehicle while respecting tire friction limits, enabling safe, real-time anti-overtake maneuvers.

Method: A two-layer approach: a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) strategic layer operates in the Frenet domain to produce defensive references; these references are embedded into a nonlinear MPC (NMPC) as spatial regularization constraints, with friction constraints explicitly accounted for. The framework operates in real time to manage adversarial interactions on a racing circuit (Thunderhill West) in simulation.

Result: In simulation, average overtake time increases from 8.8 s to 14.6 s; opponent progress is significantly reduced; the ego vehicle utilizes 83.4% of available tire force; mean NMPC solve time is 33.3 ms with a standard deviation of 13.9 ms, indicating real-time feasibility.

Conclusion: The proposed SAC-guided MPC framework effectively enforces spatial occupancy to delay or prevent overtakes while maintaining high-speed operation within tire friction limits. It demonstrates real-time capability and improved defensive performance, with potential applicability to other circuits and adversarial driving scenarios. Limitations likely include transferability to real-world dynamics, sensitivity to friction model accuracy, and reliance on Frenet-domain representations.

Abstract: This paper addresses defensive blocking in autonomous racing, where a vehicle must prevent a faster opponent from overtaking while operating near its dynamic limits. Different from lap-time minimization, we formulate defense as a spatial occupancy regulation problem via a hierarchical reinforcement-learning guided model predictive control framework. A Soft Actor-Critic strategic layer operates in the Frenet domain to generate geometry-aware defensive references, which are embedded into the nonlinear model predictive control formulation as spatial regularization under friction constraints. Evaluated on the Thunderhill West circuit in simulation, the framework increases average overtake time from 8.8 s to 14.6 s while significantly reducing opponent progress. Meanwhile, it allows the vehicle to utilize 83.4% of available tire force. The framework achieves a 33.3 ms mean solve time (13.9 ms std), supporting real-time high-speed adversarial interaction.

</details>


### [345] [Distributed Model-Based Diffusion For Scalable Multi-Robot Trajectory Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20992)
*Haejoon Lee,Xinyi Wang,Taekyung Kim,Dimitra Panagou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces DMBD, a distributed diffusion-based planner for multi-robot trajectory optimization that decomposes the reverse diffusion into local conditional steps, enabling robots to denoise in their own subspaces while conditioning on others' trajectories broadcast by a server; exhibits strong scalability and sub-second coordination in diverse scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the shortcomings of centralized, high-dimensional inference in multi-robot diffusion-based optimization: poor sample efficiency due to curse of dimensionality and the need for global access to all robots’ dynamics, constraints, and objectives.

Method: A distributed server-robot framework that decomposes the reverse diffusion process into local conditional reverse diffusions. Each robot denoises within its own control subspace while conditioning on current trajectory estimates of other robots, which are aggregated and broadcast by a central server. The framework enables iterative, partially parallelized planning with communication of trajectory estimates.

Result: Extensive simulations in goal swapping, multi-floor coverage, parking, and rush-hour scenarios show DMBD scales well, solves many challenging coordination tasks in sub-seconds, and significantly outperforms existing baselines.

Conclusion: DMBD provides a scalable, distributed diffusion-based approach for multi-robot trajectory optimization. It reduces centralization and dimensionality bottlenecks by local denoising with conditioned guidance, at the cost of relying on server broadcasted trajectory estimates. Future work could explore theoretical convergence, robustness to communication delays, and extensions to dynamic environments.

Abstract: Trajectory optimization for multi-robot systems remains a critical challenge, particularly when navigating highly non-convex, non-linear, and non-differentiable environments. While Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) has recently emerged as a promising sampling-based optimization paradigm for single-robot trajectory generation, extending it to multi-robot systems results in a centralized, high-dimensional inference problem that (i) suffers from poor sample efficiency due to the curse of dimensionality and (ii) requires global access to all robots' dynamics, constraints, and objectives. To address this, we propose Distributed Model-Based Diffusion (DMBD), a distributed server-robot framework that decomposes the reverse diffusion process into local conditional reverse diffusion processes. This decomposition enables each robot to iteratively perform denoising independently within its own control subspace while conditioning on the current trajectory estimates of the other robots that are aggregated and broadcast by the server. Extensive simulations in goal swapping, multi-floor coverage, parking, and rush-hour scenarios demonstrate that DMBD achieves strong scalability, solving many challenging coordination tasks in sub-seconds and significantly outperforming existing baselines.

</details>


### [346] [TableVerse: A Large-scale Tabletop Dataset with Real-world Grounded Layouts for Generalizable Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21017)
*Boyuan Wang,Yue Zhang,Xutao Xue,Xueyu Song,Yu Sun*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TableVerse introduces a fully automated Real2Sim pipeline that converts unstructured in-the-wild images into high-fidelity, simulation-ready tabletop environments with accurate scales and stable physics, paired with automated task-conditioned trajectory generation to create the TableVerse-100K dataset of 100k environments and manipulation demonstrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalizable robotic manipulation requires large-scale, realistic data. Prior synthetic methods suffer from physical implausibility and fail to capture dense clutter found in real environments.

Method: A Real2Sim pipeline that deterministically reconstructs unstructured imagery into simulation-ready tabletop worlds with authentic metrics, topologies, and mechanical stability; integrates automated task-conditioned trajectory generation to produce high-quality, collision-free pick-and-place demonstrations; results in the TableVerse-100K dataset.

Result: Generation of 100,000 physically consistent tabletop environments with interactive manipulation trajectories; high-fidelity, realistic spatial distributions, and verified mechanical stability, enabling scalable data for learning-based manipulation.

Conclusion: TableVerse provides a scalable, high-fidelity data backbone to advance generalizable robotic manipulation by closing the realism gap between real environments and simulation, outperforming prior imagination-based layout methods.

Abstract: The development of generalizable robotic manipulation policies is inherently bounded by the availability of large-scale, high-fidelity scene data. While recent automated synthesis methods attempt to bridge this gap via text-to-layout hallucination or simplified procedural generation, they frequently suffer from physical implausibility and fail to capture the complex, dense clutter of actual human environments. In this paper, we introduce TableVerse, a fully automated Real2Sim pipeline that shifts the paradigm from imaginative layout generation to deterministic reconstruction from unstructured, in-the-wild image data. Our framework seamlessly processes unscripted internet media into high-fidelity, simulation-ready tabletop environments with accurate metric scales, authentic topologies, and verified mechanical stability. Furthermore, an automated task-conditioned trajectory generation framework is integrated to synthesize high-quality, collision-free pick-and-place demonstrations. Leveraging this complete pipeline, we construct the TableVerse-100K Dataset, a large-scale corpus comprising 100,000 unique, physically consistent environments paired with interactive manipulation trajectories. By capturing diverse asset compositions, realistic spatial distributions, and high-quality demonstrations, TableVerse-100K establishes a highly scalable and high-fidelity data foundation, providing significant value to facilitate future research in generalizable robotic manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [347] [ZONDA: Zero-shot Object Navigation with Dynamic Avoidance in Multi-floor Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21025)
*Shaomin Liang,Xuanhong Liao,Shiyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ZONDA enables zero-shot object navigation across multi-floor environments with dynamic pedestrian avoidance, using heuristic cross-floor planning, multi-view verification, and pedestrian prediction; demonstrates robust real-world and simulated performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current object-goal navigation methods assume static, single-floor environments and ignore pedestrians, hindering real-world deployment.

Method: Three components: (i) Heuristic multi-floor planning using height-difference traversable maps for stair traversal and cross-floor exploration without platform-specific learned controllers; (ii) Multi-view target verification using a vision-language model across multiple scales to reduce false positives; (iii) Dynamic pedestrian avoidance by tracking and predicting moving pedestrians to generate anticipatory behaviors.

Result: Evaluated on a real Direct Drive Tech TITA biped robot and simulations on HM3D and MP3D; ZONDA shows significantly improved results and robust navigation on the HM3D-DYNA dynamic benchmark relative to baselines.

Conclusion: ZONDA demonstrates feasibility and robustness of zero-shot cross-floor object navigation with dynamic avoidance, reducing reliance on platform-specific controllers and enhancing real-world deployment potential.

Abstract: In Object Goal Navigation task, existing methods are typically restricted to static and single-floor environments, ignoring cross-floor topologies and dynamic pedestrian, which limits their real-world deployment. To address these limitations, we propose ZONDA, a zero-shot object navigation with dynamic avoidance framework. In particular, ZONDA integrates three core components: (i) Heuristic multi-floor planning: from height-difference traversable maps, enables stair traversal and cross-floor exploration without a platform-specific learned controller; (ii) Multi-view target verification: cross-checks multi-scale observations with a vision-language model, significantly reducing false positives; and (iii) Dynamic pedestrian avoidance: explicitly tracks and predicts moving pedestrians to generate anticipatory behaviors. Evaluated on a real Direct Drive Tech TITA biped robot and extensive simulations on HM3D and MP3D, ZONDA achieves significantly improved results. Moreover, ZONDA can maintain robust navigation on the dynamic benchmark HM3D-DYNA compared to the existing baseline.

</details>


### [348] [A Real-Time Generalized Nash Equilibrium Framework for Interaction-Aware Autonomous Driving in Mixed Traffic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21043)
*Nouhed Naidja,Mohamed-Cherif Rahal,Steve Pechberti,Stéphane Font,Guillaume Sandou,Marc Revilloud*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GNEP-based decision framework for AV–human interaction solved in real-time with a PSO solver; validated on real vehicle; convergence under 50 ms; yields comfortable, human-like trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the core challenge of safe and efficient navigation in mixed-traffic environments, where AV decisions are interdependent with unpredictable human driver reactions, requiring shared safety and geometric constraints.

Method: Formulates driving interaction as a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem with coupled safety and geometry constraints. Develops a dedicated Particle Swarm Optimization–based solver to solve the non-convex problem in real time. Implements an end-to-end architecture and validates on a real test track with a Renault Zoé interacting with a human driver.

Result: The solver converges in under 50 ms and generates comfortable, human-like trajectories. Real-world experimental validation shows the framework can handle critical scenarios; benchmarks confirm real-time feasibility.

Conclusion: A GNEP-based decision-making framework with a PSO solver enables safe, efficient real-time navigation in mixed traffic, demonstrated through real-vehicle experiments and benchmarked feasibility.

Abstract: Safe and efficient navigation in mixed-traffic environments remains a critical challenge for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs), primarily due to the complex interdependence between the AV's decisions and the unpredictable reactions of human drivers. This paper introduces a comprehensive decision-making framework that formulates the driving interaction as a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem (GNEP). Unlike decoupled optimization approaches, this framework explicitly models shared safety and geometric constraints, ensuring that the feasibility of the AV's strategy is dynamically linked to the opponent's actions. To solve this non-convex problem in real-time, we propose a dedicated solver based on Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The complete architecture was validated on a test track using a real autonomous Renault Zoé interacting with a human driver. Experimental results demonstrate the system's ability to handle critical scenarios by generating comfortable, human-like trajectories. Benchmarks confirm the solver's operational feasibility, achieving convergence in under 50 ms.

</details>


### [349] [GuidedAttention: Interpretable and Correctable Visual Attention for OOD-Robust Robot Manipulation via Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21049)
*Masaki Murooka,Ryoichi Nakajo,Keisuke Shirai,Tomohiro Motoda,Hanbit Oh,Ryo Hanai,Yukiyasu Domae*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GuidedAttention introduces interpretable attention keypoints to condition a diffusion-based visuomotor policy; allows one-time human correction at rollout start; improves manipulation performance, especially under OOD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end visuomotor policies often act as a black box with limited interpretability and little room for human intervention to correct failures. There is a need for interpretable, correctable intermediate representations to diagnose and improve policy behavior, particularly under distribution shifts.

Method: Predict task-relevant attention keypoints from camera images and condition a diffusion-based action policy on these keypoints. At rollout initialization, users may inspect and optionally correct a subset of keypoints; a tracking module then propagates the corrected attention throughout execution.

Result: Experiments in simulation and on real robots show that GuidedAttention consistently improves manipulation performance, with pronounced gains under positional and appearance out-of-distribution conditions.

Conclusion: Introducing an interpretable, human-correctable attention representation within a visuomotor imitation framework can boost performance and robustness, suggesting a viable path toward more transparent and editable robots; potential applicability to broader visuomotor tasks and other attention mechanisms.

Abstract: End-to-end visuomotor policies provide little opportunity for humans to understand or correct the policy's visual attention. We propose GuidedAttention, a visuomotor imitation learning framework that introduces interpretable and correctable visual attention as an explicit intermediate representation. Task-relevant attention keypoints are predicted from camera images and condition a diffusion-based action policy. Users can inspect and optionally correct selected keypoints once at rollout initialization, after which the corrected attention is automatically propagated throughout execution by a tracking module. Experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that GuidedAttention consistently improves robot manipulation performance, particularly under positional and appearance out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions.

</details>


### [350] [Human-Inspired Framework for Robotic Craniotomy: Integrating Multimodal Fusion and Adaptive Trajectory Adjustment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21058)
*Renzhen Le,Xiao Zhang,Di Wu,Yuanyu Wei,Jiachen Zhu,Zhenzhi Ying,Pengfei Zhang,Liming Shu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A human-inspired closed-loop robotic craniotomy framework integrates preoperative planning with intraoperative sensing and adaptive trajectory execution to compensate for registration errors and tissue deformation. It uses an adaptive dual-contour fusion for planning and a CMA-TCN-Transformer with Bayesian filtering for multimodal perception, plus an in-situ projection-based trajectory adjustment. Validated on bovine ribs and ex vivo skull experiments, achieving high breakthrough accuracy and safe operation without dural injury, demonstrating autonomous closed-loop control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the limitations of open-loop robotic craniotomy that rely solely on preoperative images and are fragile to intraoperative registration errors and tissue deformation; to enable safe, autonomous, and robust craniotomies through real-time perception and adaptive control.

Method: 1) Adaptive dual-contour fusion algorithm to generate trajectories conforming to complex cranial geometries while preserving tool-bone relative pose. 2) Multimodal perception using a two-stage cross-modal attention block (CMA) with temporal convolutional network (TCN) and Transformer, combined with an adaptive Bayesian filter to fuse force and acoustic signals for breakthrough detection. 3) In-situ projection-based trajectory adjustment to compensate depth deviations and enable safe residual bone removal. 4) Validation on bovine rib models for breakthrough prediction (97%), latency (0.048 +/- 0.097 s), and overshoot (0.29 mm), plus four ex vivo cranial experiments without dural injury.

Result: Breakthrough prediction accuracy: 97%; detection latency: 0.048 +/- 0.097 s; maximum overshoot: 0.29 mm; four ex vivo cranial experiments completed without dural injury.

Conclusion: The proposed cybernetic framework enables safe and autonomous craniotomy with effective closed-loop control, demonstrating feasibility of real-time perception-guided robotic neurosurgical procedures.

Abstract: Manual craniotomy is a high-risk, skill-dependent procedure associated with surgeon fatigue and potential dural injury. While robotic approaches have improved safety, existing open-loop systems rely solely on preoperative images and cannot compensate for intraoperative registration errors or tissue deformation. To address this, we propose a human-inspired closed-loop robotic craniotomy framework that intelligently integrates preoperative planning with intraoperative execution. An adaptive dual-contour fusion algorithm is employed to generate trajectories that conform to complex cranial geometries while maintaining a consistent tool-bone relative pose. For intraoperative perception, a multimodal two-stage cross-modal attention block (CMA)-temporal convolutional network (TCN)-Transformer network combined with an adaptive Bayesian filter fuses force and acoustic signals to achieve robust breakthrough detection under varying bone conditions. Upon detection, an in-situ projection-based trajectory adjustment strategy dynamically compensates for depth deviations, enabling safe residual bone isolation. Experiments on bovine ribs show a breakthrough prediction accuracy of 97%, a detection latency of 0.048 +/- 0.097 s, and a maximum overshoot of 0.29 mm. All four ex vivo cranial experiments were successfully completed without dural injury. These results demonstrate that the proposed cybernetic framework enables safe and autonomous craniotomy with highly effective closed-loop control.

</details>


### [351] [RL-MACRO: A Cybernetic Closed-Loop Intelligence Framework for Multimodal Adaptive Robotic Craniotomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21113)
*Xiao Zhang,Jiaxuan Li,Renzhen Le,Di Wu,Chao Sun,Jiachen Zhu,Haoyuan Zhang,Xiang Li,Jian Liu,Zhenzhi Ying,Pengfei Zhang,Liming Shu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A cybernetic closed-loop RL framework (RL-MACRO) for autonomous bone cutting in craniotomy, integrating multimodal perception, offline reinforcement learning, and online trajectory control to handle partial observability and safety constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous robotic craniotomy faces partial observability due to unknown tissue properties and inability to measure cutting temperatures; continuous regulation of tool-tissue interactions is required to prevent mechanical/thermal damage while maintaining efficiency.

Method: A CNN-LSTM observer fuses force and sound to reconstruct hidden temperature (R^2=0.939, MAE=1.717 °C). The reconstructed temperature plus multi-sensor features feed an offline Implicit Q-Learning policy. A dual-head Actor tunes feed rate, spindle speed, and cutting depth; online trajectory re-planning and velocity servoing translate decisions into motions.

Result: Demonstrated robust perception and adaptive recovery from force/temperature excursions; smooth execution on irregular surfaces; validation on bovine ribs and ex vivo goat skulls, indicating safety and efficiency benefits in autonomous bone cutting.

Conclusion: The work establishes a data-driven cybernetic paradigm for safe and efficient autonomous bone cutting by tightly coupling perception, decision-making, and execution under uncertainty.

Abstract: Autonomous robotic craniotomy requires continuous regulation of tool-tissue interactions to mitigate mechanical overload and thermal damage while maintaining surgical efficiency. However, this process is inherently partially observable due to unknown, time-varying tissue properties and the inability to directly measure cutting temperatures under physical occlusion. To address these challenges, we propose RL-MACRO, a cybernetic closed-loop intelligence framework that couples multimodal perception, adaptive decision-making, and robotic execution. This framework empowers the surgical robot to autonomously perceive inaccessible states from partial sensory feedback and dynamically optimize its behaviors under uncertain environment. A CNN-LSTM observer first fuses force and sound feedback to reconstruct the hidden temperature state (R^2=0.939, MAE = 1.717 deg C). This reconstructed temperature, alongside multi-sensor features, forms the belief state for an offline Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) policy. A novel dual-head Actor dynamically coordinates the feed rate, spindle speed, and cutting depth to optimize efficiency within strict safety bounds. These decisions are seamlessly translated into spatial motions via online trajectory re-planning and velocity servoing. Experiments on bovine ribs and six ex vivo goat skulls validate the system's robust perception, adaptive recovery from force/temperature excursions, and smooth execution on irregular surfaces, establishing a data-driven cybernetic paradigm for safe and efficient autonomous bone cutting.

</details>


### [352] [FORGE-plus: Force-Budgeted Recovery for Contact-Rich Assembly with a Frozen LLM Supervisor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21227)
*Kyupaeck Jeff Rah,Midum Oh*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-layer framework uses a frozen, text-only LLM to assign per-object force ceilings and to select recovery maneuvers via a fixed action menu (textual force signatures); a low-level controller enforces the ceiling and the recovery policy cannot raise it; evaluated in simulation on fragile bottle placement and 0.4 mm gear insertion with two grippers; a single policy passes all episodes, achieving a mean peak force of 5.4 N, and force-signature based recovery fixes 40%–64% of grip-slip failures, outperforming a press-harder baseline; PPO and learned releases fail under strict force constraints; results are purely in rigid-body simulation with hidden break thresholds, no sim-to-real claim.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Force-constrained reinforcement learning enables tight-clearance assembly under a force ceiling, but practical deployment requires object-specific force limits and robust recovery that do not violate the limit. The paper seeks to decouple high-level force budgeting (via an LLM) from low-level control and to leverage compact force signatures for recoveries, addressing the gap between learned policies and safe physical operation.

Method: A two-layer system: (1) a frozen text-only LLM assigns a per-object force ceiling and, from a fixed action menu, selects recovery maneuvers described by compact textual force signatures; (2) a low-level controller enforces the force ceiling; the recovery policy cannot increase force, and a hidden breaking-threshold is known only to the evaluator. Experiments in rigid-body simulation involve fragile bottle placement and 0.4 mm diametral-clearance gear insertion using Robotiq 2F-140 and Franka Panda hands. Performance metrics include success across episodes (256/256), correct release timing, mean peak force (5.4 N), and recovery under in-grip slip (40% and 64% of failures fixed).

Result: A single policy achieves 256/256 success on both tasks for both grippers; mean peak force 5.4 N; force-signature recovery resolves 40% and 64% of failures for the two grippers under slip; baseline press-harder is ineffective or causes breakage; PPO fails under strict force constraints and learned release strategies are unsuccessful.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates that coupling a text-based high-level planner (LLM) with a force-enforcing low-level controller and a fixed recovery menu can achieve robust performance under force constraints in simulation, even for fragile objects. Limitations include reliance on simulated environments with hidden thresholds and the absence of real-world claims; future work could explore generalization, real-robot feasibility, and optimization of the force-signature vocabularies.

Abstract: Force-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) enables tight-clearance assembly under a commanded force ceiling, but practical deployment requires determining an appropriate force limit for each object and recovering from insertion failures without exceeding it. We present a two-layer framework in which a frozen, text-only large language model (LLM) assigns a per-object force ceiling before execution and selects recovery maneuvers from a fixed action menu using compact textual force signatures.
